`measureText` calls and not one layout between them. **4 ms over 120 fields; 4.5 ms over the
navigator's 1,175**, which is why it runs at the end of every `render()` and does not wait
for a frame. Waiting would cost more than it saves: a frame painted before the pass is a
frame of the untruncated string, on every keystroke.

### What measuring struck from the list

Three of the twelve came off, and each for its own reason.

**`.wl-title` is prose and `shorten()` would have destroyed it.** All 107 of Mensores'
findings contain a space and 80 contain a dot, so the middle-elide reads a title as a dotted
name: the head becomes ``self`` and the leaf becomes the whole predicate, and the *subject*
is elided out of the middle of a sentence. Prose is cut at its tail, where a sentence carries
least and a qualified name carries most.

But the field was in far worse shape than the list said. **94 of 94 rows clipped** — a 172px
box against a median title of 73 characters needing about 420. Every reader saw the first
thirty characters of every finding and none of them ever saw the predicate, on the surface
Tom clears. Tom's call: **two lines, then a mark, with the whole title on the hover**.
`-webkit-line-clamp` was struck from the constants card for being a *silent* filter and this
is the same mechanism without that fault — the clamp draws its own ellipsis and `prose` hangs
the full text on the hover, so the mark says something went and the hover says what.
92 of the 94 carry that hover; the two that fit in two lines carry none.

**`.srcpath-v` is a dead field.** `#srcPathV` is written by nothing in the whole tree — the
entirety of it is the 28-character literal in `index.html`, which fits with room to spare. Its
`overflow`, `text-overflow` and `max-width` were sizing a string that cannot arrive: the same
dead-CSS fault as the three rules struck beside it when the button went (rules 44 and 48).

**`.callhead code` was a contradiction, not a budget.** The expression is rendered through
`breakable()`, which marks every joint with a `<wbr>` so a name breaks on a dot instead of
mid-token — and `white-space: nowrap` here forbade breaking at all, so every one of those
marks was inert. `.callin code` and `.calldecl code` render the same strings through the same
function and wrap correctly: measured, **98 and 88 characters with no overflow**, against this
one clipping 1 row in 6 at 29 characters. One idea, two answers, and the wrong one was the odd
rule out (rule 13). It wraps now and needs no fitting at all.

### Four defects in the fitter itself, every one found on screen

*None of these was found by review, and three of them had a comment beside them asserting the
opposite.*

**It measured the pane mid-transition.** `.body` carries `transition: all`, so collapsing the
inspector animates the grid's columns. `render()` is synchronous: it writes the attribute and
the pass measures while the columns are still on their way, reading the width the pane is
*leaving*. Every field fitted itself perfectly to a layout that had already gone, and the tell
was three fields still overflowing after a pass that reported cutting nothing. A
`ResizeObserver` on the panes answers it for every cause at once — a pane toggled, a rail
dragged, a window resized, a reader changing their browser's font size, which reports no event
at all (rule 51).

**It measured a box its own last write had shrunk.** `.rank-name code` is a flex item with an
`auto` basis, so shortening its text shrinks the box to the shortened text and the next pass
measures what the last one left. It ratchets and can never grow back: driven across four
container widths from 300px to released, the box read **81px at every one of them** and the
string never changed. The first version of this pass carried a comment claiming the loop was
impossible; it was measured happening an hour later. Phase 1 now writes the whole string into
every field before phase 2 reads a single width — free, because all three phases are one
synchronous task and the layout flushes once however many fields there are.

**It measured the border box.** `getBoundingClientRect().width` includes padding and border and
text sits in neither, so every field was handed its own padding twice. `.trailstep` has `.3rem`
a side and was the one field of eight still spilling after a pass that reported fitting it:
**201px of text written into 192px of room**, by arithmetic that thought it had 201.
Subtracted from the rect rather than read off `clientWidth`, which is 0 on an inline element
and would collapse every such field to a single mark.

**It compared two floats for exact fit.** A fitted field is usually sized *to* its own content,
so the space available and the space needed are computed from the same text and come out
**exactly equal** — a strict `<=` is a coin flip on the last bit, and `mensores` lost it:
53.3px of text in 53.3px of room, declared too long, cut to `men…res`. Eight characters to
seven. `FIT_SLACK` is one constant used by the fitter **and** by `selfCheck`, so the two cannot
disagree about what fits (rule 13).

### And two layouts that were wearing a shortening rule's clothes

**The trail squeezed its steps instead of scrolling them.** `.trail` is `overflow-x: auto` and
`render()` scrolls the current step into view, so scrolling is what the bar was built to do —
but its items were left shrinkable, and a flex item that can shrink does, before its container
ever overflows. Three steps in a 404px bar were squeezed to fit and clipped. It looked like a
shortening rule for as long as the stylesheet was doing the cutting; `fitFields` is what named
it, by reporting `mensores` as `men…res`. A shortening that saves one character is not a
shortening, and the box was the thing that was wrong.

**A caller row cannot hold a name and a module on one line.** Splitting `.gotonode` into two
boxes fixed the *tail* — 7 of 11 rows had been overflowing 242px, with
`mensores.chaos.chaos_scriba_kill` and `mensores.chaos.chaos_broker_kill` both reading
`mensores.chaos.cha…`, two different modules drawn as one string — and could not fix the
*room*. On a 344px pane every side-by-side split measured as a trade: protect the name and
`mensores.disceptator._architect_dispatch` reduces to `dis…tch`; floor the module at 6rem and
the name goes to `resolve_a…_dispatch`. Neither field is worth having in those states.
**Tom's call, put to him with the three measured against each other: stack them**, which is
the shape the navigator has always used for this pair. Both whole, at 36px a row instead of 18.
All 11 rows now show their name and their module entire.

### A label is not the text on screen

A fitted field's text is a shortened one, so a trail step built from it records `stor…items`
as the place you were — rule 33 and rule 30 in the surface built to take a reader back. Every
label reader goes through `labelOf` now: `data-label`, then the unshortened `data-full`, then
the text, rebuilt from the children so a control *containing* a fitted field reads as it would
have read unfitted. Five call sites, one accessor (rule 51).

`.trailstep`'s title carried `note || label`, which was right while the label was always
wholly on screen. Once it can be elided, a step *with* a note had the whole of it nowhere —
its text cut and its hover talking about something else. It carries both.

### The band tables say what kind of string each column holds

`modules_explained` is why. Its meta column is a **path** where every other band's is a dotted
module, and its label is a **module** where every other band's is a leaf name — exactly
inverted. A kind guessed from the shape of the markup would drop a program root off a path,
find none, and look entirely deliberate. `labelFit` and `metaFit` are declared per band and
there is no default behind them: a band that forgets writes `data-fit=""` and the fitter
answers with a named error (design rule 16).

### Verified

**835 tests** (12 new), mypy clean, ruff clean, self-check green, console clean. Driven in
Chrome against the real pair at 1396px: **zero fitted fields overflow** on the cover, the
navigator, the change list, the worklist, the inspector and the flow panel; ten passes back to
back drift **not one character**; a field put through four container widths shortens and grows
back; 4 ms a pass.

**Twelve guards, each run against the defect it names, all twelve CAUGHT.** The mutation
harness proves its baseline green first (rule 59).

*One existing guard earned its keep.* Four of the explanations above were first written as
HTML comments **inside template literals**, where a backtick closes the literal and the page
comes up empty — the defect `test_no_backtick_hides_in_an_html_comment` was written for, on its
third occurrence. They were moved to JS comments above their functions, which they should have
been anyway: inside a `.map()` body each one shipped once per row.

### Not done, and why

`.navsub` keeps its constant. `max-width: 11rem` makes every row of it the same box at every
window and every root size, so 30 is honest there, and 1,175 fields through the fitter on every
keystroke is a real cost for no gain. The boundary is stated in `shorten()`'s docstring: a
**fixed rem width takes a constant, a flex-derived one is fitted**.

The fold's member rows keep the backstop deliberately. A member row carries an invocation line
— `_profile_name_or_none(self) → str | None` — which is not a jointed name, so the middle-elide
would cut it to `_profile…→ str` and throw away the parameters, which are the reason to have
opened the class. A signature's identity is at its head, like prose, so the tail cut is already
the right end. `selfCheck` does not watch it, because nothing there claims it fits.

**Still owed: a real window.** Everything above was measured at 1396px in a browser context
that reports `outerWidth: 0`, refuses to resize, and whose screenshots did not track the live
DOM — rule 38, the same debt the blank-graph fix carries. The numbers are measurements and the
guards are guards; what none of them is, is a look.


## No pane assumes what it was showing is still true — 2026-09-03

Reported at the keyboard, mid-rabbit: *"Found myself at `disceptator._extraction_state
<module>` ... When I change the center panel to Code, that panel shows
`mensores/_internal/_governed_gates.py` which is not what I expect to see. Is this accurate,
and I am seeing what I should, or is the center panel off?"*

**The panel was off.** `/api/node` gave `mensores/disceptator/_extraction_state.py` for that
node all along. What was on screen was `state.codeFile` — which is **persisted** — so it was
the file the constants session left open two days earlier, from a package the reader had never
opened, rendered with a title and a path and nothing to say it was stale. The store was right,
the selection was right, and the walk was right.

### One caller, and it was the wrong one

`followSelectionIntoCode()` opens with `if (!codeOnScreen()) return;` — correct, there is
nothing to walk when the pane is not up. It was invited from **exactly one place**, the end of
`loadSpecimen`. So selecting a routine while Code sat behind another mode returned at that
guard and left no trace, and the mode switch never asked again. The condition has two halves —
*the selection changed* and *the pane became visible* — and only the first was served.

### Tom's rule, which is larger than the defect

*"EVERY mode switch should re-verify where it should be ... Users can move around using nearly
any panel — left, center, or Inspector. Every possible venue that can change the point of view
should be considered, so no control should ever expect that it 'knows' what it was showing
before is still true."*

**This file already said so, in one branch.** The table's:

> *"Here rather than on the mode toggle because there are five ways into table mode — the
> toggle, `Enter` on a hovered navigator row, two crumb routes and the code browser's hand-off
> — and a call at each is exactly the list rule 51 says grows. Every one of them arrives here."*

The audit found three panes on each side of that lesson. Reconciling inside `render()`:
**table** (`ensureTableOverlay` + `revealSelectedRow`), **glossary/naming**
(`ensureVocabulary`), **curiosities** (`ensureCuriosities`). Relying on every call site to
remember: **code** (1 site, and the wrong one), **stack** (4 sites), **diagram** (7 sites).

So all three moved into `render()`, where every route arrives.

### And the four graph call sites were mis-ordered as well as incomplete

Every one of them sat **before** its own `render()`:

```js
if (state.graphLayout === "stack") ensureGraph();
render();
```

so each was mounting into the *previous* view's layout — the exact defect recorded on the mode
toggle as *"the graph should have been there"*, fixed there in 2026-08 and left standing at the
other three. A hidden container is 0x0 and `fitView` framed the stack for the whole window.
Arriving in `render()` they are ordered right by construction, for every route including the
ones nobody has written yet. The guard that watched the toggle now watches `render()`, which is
a stronger statement: it speaks for every route rather than for one handler.

### What it cost to make the reconcile safe

`render()` runs on every keystroke, so a reconcile must be **silent when there is nothing to
do**. Two of the three needed work for that.

**`ensureDiagram` claimed its lock before asking whether it had anything to do.** It ran to the
bottom on every call, found both content guards satisfied, and still finished with
`renderDiagram()` — which rewrites `#diagramMount`, the mount that exists precisely so
`render()` does not touch it, and takes the laid-out SVG and the reader's pan and zoom with it.
It compares the drawing it has against the drawing that is wanted first now. Verified: the
`<svg>` node is the same object after five renders, transform unchanged.

**The code walk had to stop fighting the reader.** An unconditional walk puts the pane back on
the next repaint, so a reader who opens a second file to compare it with the first could not
keep it for one paint — an automatic move fighting a deliberate one, which `revealSelectedRow`
and the trail scroller are both careful about. `codeFollowedFor` records *which subject* the
pane has been walked for, not *whether* it has been walked: a flag would be cleared by every
selection and set by every walk, and the deliberate open undone immediately. `openCodeFile`
marks the subject serviced, so the reader may go anywhere inside one selection and is still
followed the moment they pick something new.

`ensureGraph` needed nothing — *"cheap to call from anywhere that might land in graph mode; it
decides for itself"* was already true and already written down.

### Verified

839 tests (4 new), mypy clean, ruff clean, self-check green, console clean. Driven in Chrome on
the real pair, Tom's sequence exactly: land on `<module>` from graph mode with
`_governed_gates.py` persisted, switch the centre to Code — **`_extraction_state.py`**, the file
the node lives in. Then the two things a render-time reconcile could have broken: a file opened
by hand **held its ground across three repaints**, and picking a new routine **followed again**.
Seven centre-mode switches in a row, every one showing the selection's own file.

**Five guards, each run against the defect it names, all CAUGHT** — and one was blind first and
found by mutation: it asserted `codeFollowedFor` was *named* in the walk and passed with the
early return deleted, which is rule 37 again (naming a thing is not using it).

*`_fn_body` could not see an `async function`* and reported `ensureDiagram` as "no longer a
function declaration" — a message that reads as the code having moved rather than the helper
being blind, and whose obvious response is to weaken a guard that was pointing at the right
thing. Both ends of the slice take `async` now.

### Checked and not a regression

The stack's backing store is 300×150 against a 245×293 stage in the automation tab. Measured
against `HEAD` with the change stashed: **identical**, so it is the recorded rule-38 context and
not this. It is the same context that reports `canvas MISSING, frames 0`.

### It is rule 78

Tom's call, put to him because the numbers are permanent addresses in this project's
constitution and 768 citations point at them. **Rule 78: a pane brought up to date by the
control that moved it is only as correct as the last person to add a control.**

Its own address rather than a note under rule 51, and the distinction is the reason it earned
one: rule 51 is about a *rule* rotting across call sites, where this is about **state going
stale in silence**. Nothing throws, nothing logs, and the pane looks entirely deliberate —
which is why this arrived as a question about whether the tool was telling the truth rather
than as a bug report.

The body carries the three things that make it usable rather than agreeable: the reconcile
must be **silent when there is nothing to do**, because `render()` runs on every keystroke;
an **automatic move must not fight a deliberate one**, or the rule turns a pane into a cage;
and the guard's condition had **two halves with an event on only one**, which is the shape to
look for. Cited from four places in `shell.js` and from the guards.

Enumerated after adding it rather than counted: **1–78 with 21 absent, 77 rules, and the
index in `CLAUDE.md` and the bodies in `RULES.md` agree exactly** — no index without a body,
no body without an index. `BRIEFING.md`'s file-size table is left as taken and now says so:
its counts and byte sizes are of 2026-09-02, and rewriting one column without retaking the
other is a different measurement under the same label (rule 24).

### Left open

**`<module>` is answered in a routine-shaped inspector.** It draws *"Nothing in this map calls
it. That is either a way in, dead code, or a call DunneFlow cannot see"* — three plausible
sentences, none of them the true one, which the routine list already carries as its own `why`:
*"Module-level code: runs at import, before anything is called."* Same shape as the constants
defect: a pane answering a question this kind cannot be asked. `viewInspectorConstant` is the
precedent — route on kind. Not built; Tom found it on the way past this one.


## The code view, looked at — 2026-09-03

Four things in one screenshot, at Tom's own keyboard and his own window. **Three were real
and one was a question that answered itself.**

### The greenbar: a row was breaking twice

*"Every line has a blank between it, like old IBM greenbar printouts. Kind of takes me back
40 years, but that's not a good thing."*

`rows.join("\n")` — the reflex, the thing every other list builder in this file does, and the
thing that makes generated markup readable in devtools. Inside a `<pre>` it is not whitespace
between tags, it is **content**: `white-space: pre` renders it as a line break, and the row
span is `display: block` and has already broken the line. So every row was followed by an
empty one. **1,703 rows in 58,932px — 34.6px a row against a 17.28px line-height**, and
29,000px of scrolling carrying nothing. Now 29,520px.

**Three surfaces had it and only one was reported.** The centre's code table, the navigator's
code pane, and the glossary's citation viewer; the second and third were found by going to
look at the other `<pre>` builders once the first was understood. `srcPane` keeps its newline
and that is the rule rather than an exception to it — its rows are *not* wrapped in a block,
so there the newline is the only thing breaking the line. What has to hold is that **a row
breaks once**, never that a separator has one spelling, and the guard asserts both directions.

### The indent was not an indent

*"The indent is also large, so you have to scroll over to see the text. If that's real, ok,
but otherwise it needs to be removed."*

It is not real: it is the margin column, a fixed 12rem reserve where marks are drawn. Measured
on the file he was looking at, it fails **from both directions at once**:

| | |
|---|---|
| rows carrying no mark, paying the whole indent | **1,573 of 1,703 — 92.4%** |
| marks that exist and are clipped by that same 12rem | **49 of 130 — 37.7%** |
| mark widths | min 85px · median 185 · p90 341 · **max 1,263** |

A comment in `tokens.css` records that it was already narrowed once from 15rem to 12rem for
the first of those reasons. That treated the symptom: no single width serves both, because
the long tail means "wide enough for the marks" is 1,263px and "narrow enough for the code"
is zero.

Three ways out were measured against each other and put to Tom: fold it, move marks to the
end of the line, or size the reserve to the file's own widest mark. **His call: fold it.**
Code starts at 248px with the margin shown and **76px folded** — 172px back at a 16px root,
258px at his 24px.

**Folded, a marked line still says so.** A glyph from `MARK_GLYPH` — the same table the
navigator's pane reads — sits where the column was, carrying the whole mark on its title
(`markTitle`, the same function, so one answer serves two surfaces). Dropping it would make
the fold a silent filter over the one thing the margin exists to report (design rule 1, rule
45). Both forms are in the markup and a stylesheet chooses, so folding repaints nothing.

**And a file with nothing to mark renders no mark elements at all**, whichever way the fold
is set — the toggle is a preference between two jobs, this is a fact about the file. The first
attempt at that was a `.nomarks` CSS rule, and it **lost on specificity** to the fold's own
`:root[data-code-marks="off"] .codetable .cglyph` — (0,3,0) against (0,4,0) — so the column
stayed 20px wide on a file that could never fill it. Answered in the builder instead: not
rendering a thing cannot lose a cascade it is not in.

### The line numbers: asked and answered, nothing changed

*"There's a bit of space before the line numbers, I'm guessing that's to permit large numbers
— again, if that's the case, leave it."*

That is exactly what it is. `.cnum` is `3.5rem`, right-aligned, which holds four digits and
the file is 1,703 lines. Left alone.

### The grey area: provenance, and now a fold

It is the line that says these bytes came from the content-addressed sidecar **as measured**
at a recorded instant, not as the tree stands now — the same claim the inspector's source view
makes, and design rule 13's provenance. It is 46px of a pane whose whole job is the lines
above it, **22.6% of the body on a short window**, and it says the same sentence on every
file. So it folds, per Tom's standing rule that anything that can collapse should.

A fold rather than a hide: the bar stays and says what it is, so there is something on screen
to open (rule 45, design rule 23).

**That fold was itself a dead control in its first draft**, which is worth more than the fold
is. `render()`'s code branch repaints its chrome only when `codeDomKey()` moves — file,
availability, overlay — because rebuilding it re-attaches the table, measured at 1,358 ms on
`_server.py`. The footer is chrome. So flipping the state, persisting it and calling
`render()` set the field and **changed nothing on screen**: design rule 16 with every part
working, in a control added to satisfy a rule about controls. Putting `codeProv` in the key
would fix it and buy a full re-attach for a one-line toggle, so the handler writes the two
attributes itself — the narrow update this file already records for the file filter.

### Verified

842 tests (3 new), mypy clean, ruff clean, console clean. Driven in Chrome: row pitch 17.3px
against a 17.28px line-height on the centre and 16.8 against 16.8 in the navigator's pane;
the margin folds to 76px and back to 248 and survives a reload folded (rule 68); an unmarked
file renders **zero** mark spans, starts its code at 56px and draws no toggle; the glyph
carries `import: import — __future__.annotations` on its title.

**Eleven mutations across three guards, all CAUGHT**, including the counter-case that
`srcPane` must *keep* its newline — without it the rule reads as "never a newline" and the
next person deletes the one that is load-bearing.

*Two guards went blind rather than green on the way, which is the only reason they were
survivable.* One matched `<pre class="codetable"` including the closing quote and threw when
the class gained a conditional second token; the other was `_fn_body` failing on
`async function`. A guard that cannot find its subject must say so — one that quietly finds
nothing passes every mutation of itself (rule 37).

*And one self-inflicted defect worth recording*: the first pass added `const bare` at the top
of the builder while an older `const bare` still stood near the `return`, which is a
`SyntaxError` and took the whole page down. `test_the_javascript_parses` caught it on the next
run. Two declarations of one name in one scope is what a large, careful, multi-step edit does
when it is applied in pieces.

## Three broken buttons on the Code panel — fixed 2026-09-03

All three reported in one line each, all three real, and **no two of them the same bug**.

### "Clicking `margin 35` doesn't change anything"

The margin fold, built an hour earlier and tested at the keyboard by me before it shipped.
It worked then and it does nothing now, and both are true.

`wire()` runs at the end of **every** `render()` and calls `addEventListener` with a fresh
closure. For a control inside `#viewMount` or `#inspector` that is harmless — those are
rewritten each render, so the listener is discarded with the element it was on. **The code
chrome is the one surface that is not**: `render()` repaints it only when `codeDomKey()`
moves, precisely so a 1.37 MB subtree is not re-attached on every keystroke. So the button
survives every render and the listeners pile up on it.

Measured: five renders after a paint, **one click ran the handler six times**. Six toggles is
an even number and a control that visibly does nothing. One, three, five all work — which is
exactly why it passed its own test, passed the self-check, and passed the first look at it. I
clicked it immediately after a paint.

`CODE_ROUTES` is the answer and its own comment already said so: one delegated listener,
registered once at module load, keyed on the attribute. **A route cannot accumulate.** Both
new controls moved into it, and the guard is about the surface rather than the two buttons —
nothing written into the code chrome may be bound in `wire()`.

### "Clicking `files ›` doesn't seem to do anything"

It fired every time. `state.codeFile` went to `""`, and the navigator's Code group went back
to its list — so the route worked and the reader was looking at the wrong pane.
`loadCodeFile("")` returns at its **first line**, and `openCodeFile` never called `render()`,
so the centre went on showing the file with its title, its lines and its footer.

Rule 77's companion one route over: **a route correct for the caller it was written for is
wrong for the caller it has just acquired.** `openCodeFile` was the navigator's, where the
list is under the reader's eye and the centre is somebody else's business. The moment `Code`
became a fourth centre mode it acquired a second caller with a second pane and kept answering
for the first. Rule 78 names the remedy: the pane reconciles where every route arrives, and
this is a route that arrives.

### "Back then immediately Forward does not restore the screen I was viewing in Code"

`selectionSnapshot()` records `picks`, `selected`, `fold`, `flow`, `diagramId` and
`diagramBox` — **where the drawing is, and not where the code is.** Opening a file changes no
*selection*, so every step a file open filed was deduplicated against the one before it by
`sameSelection`, and Back stepped straight past the thing the reader had just done.

The comment beside `diagramId` says this about itself, in these words: *"None of them changes
the selection, so every step they filed was deduplicated against the one before it and Back
skipped straight past — rule 33 with the field simply missing."* The lesson was written down
one view over and never carried across, because `Code` became a centre mode after it.

`codeFile` is in all **three** places now, and a field in one or two of them is worse than
none: recorded but not compared still deduplicates away, compared but not restored survives
and takes nobody anywhere.

### Verified

843 tests (2 new, 5 mutations all CAUGHT), mypy clean, ruff clean. Driven in Chrome with
**seven renders between the paint and the click**, which is the condition the first test of
the margin button did not have: 76px → 248 → 76, both ways, every time. `files ›` clears the
centre to *"No file open"*. Back moves from `_governed_gates.py` to `_extraction_state.py` and
Forward returns, with the file on each step's subject.

**What the three have in common is worth more than any of them.** Every one was a control
whose *state* was right and whose *pane* was not, and none was visible to a check: the margin
button's listener was attached, the `files ›` route ran, the trail step was filed. The tell in
all three cases was a reader clicking and watching, which is the debt rule 38 names and the
thing three sessions running have now paid for.

## One file, two panes, and one button for both — fixed 2026-09-03

Reported as a question about whether the tool was telling the truth, which is the form the
useful ones take: *"Once again, I'm told there is no file open. Why does it say this? It
sounds wrong. The list of files is on the left side, and I had clicked on one of them, so it
must have been open, right? What was supposed to happen when I clicked on those buttons?"*

### What they did

| Button | Where | What it ran |
|---|---|---|
| `‹ files` | the rail | `data-codeback` → `openCodeFile("")` |
| `files ›` | the centre | `data-codeback` → `openCodeFile("")` — **the same control** |
| `open ▸` | the rail | switches the *centre* to Code mode; does not touch the file |

Two renderings of one button, with the arrows pointing opposite ways, and `state.codeFile`
is **one value serving two panes** — `codeList()` decided list-or-file purely by it. So a
control that reads *show me the list* closed the file everywhere. The reader was right and
the pane was wrong.

The centre's copy was the worse of the two: `viewCode()` has **no file list at all**. Its
entire effect was to remove what the reader was looking at and print *"Open the Code group in
the navigator and pick one"* — a button that empties a pane it cannot refill.

### It was mine to have surfaced

`openCodeFile` had never called `render()` until earlier the same day. Before that, `‹ files`
cleared the state and rebuilt the navigator while the centre kept its **already-painted**
chrome, so the rail's button looked pane-scoped by accident — until the next render blanked
it. The state was global the whole time; the fix made it honest, and honest is what exposed
this. Worth recording as the shape rather than the incident: **a fix that makes an
inconsistency visible will be reported as the fix's fault, and is not.**

### Two questions, two fields

`codeRailList` is where the **rail** is; `codeFile` is what is **open**. `codeback` sets the
first and touches nothing else, so the rail lists while the centre reads on. `openCodeFile`
clears it — every way a file gets opened arrives there, so a rail left listing after the
reader chose cannot happen (rule 51). The centre's duplicate button is gone.

Tom's own argument for putting code in the rail is quoted a few lines above `codeList`: *"it
should be able to run on the left menu as well. I want to be able to see code and graph at
the same time, and that's the only way."* A rail that must empty the centre to show its list
is that undone, and it had been since Code became a fourth centre mode.

### Verified

843 tests (1 new), mypy clean, ruff clean. Driven in Chrome: `‹ files` lists the rail and the
centre keeps `_anthropic.py`; picking it again returns the rail to the file; picking a
*different* one moves both; the search-back variant returns the rail to its 408 hits in 136
files with the centre untouched. The centre renders no back button at all.

**Four mutations CAUGHT and one control case correctly not caught** — a `data-codeback` added
inside the *rail* must not trip the guard, because the guard is scoped to `viewCode` and the
rail is where that button belongs. A guard that fired on both would be asserting the opposite
of the fix.

## Document mode, chunk 1: a body sidecar for documents — 2026-09-03

**Paused here.** Chunk 1 of six is built and committed; the plan for the rest is at
`~/.claude/plans/polymorphic-finding-swan.md` and was approved.

### Why the feature exists

Tom asked whether Document mode still had value now that Code mode works. Reading the record
gave a better answer than either of us started with: **Document mode was never "browse
documentation"**. The ratified `viewDoc()` (artifact `f993d319`) is a hand-written sample of
narrative prose about the current selection, noting it *"would read live from
`output/mensores/source.db`"*. Half of that arrived as Code mode; the other half — the
selection read as a document, scrolled to the routine you picked — has been buildable since
`documents.py` started putting a graph node id on every row, and simply had no view.

And the name promises a second thing that is real and entirely unmet. **Nothing in DunneFlow
could read a program's documentation.** `docs.db` stores what documents *say* — 29,980
headings, 235 definitions — and has no body column; `source.db` holds only the code the graph
was built from. Two rules were unmet: **design rule 13** (`senseOpens()` is
`provenance === "DECLARED_CODE"`, so all 235 documentation-derived definitions are a dead end)
and **design rule 11** (documentation and source are *equal inputs*; source had a sidecar and
a browser, documentation had neither).

Tom's direction: *"I don't want to abandon the old code, I want to resolve it."* Nothing is
being deleted for being unfinished — the narrative view's two claims each get a home, and the
eight generated documents get the reader they never had.

### What chunk 1 is

`sourcedb.py` was already a generic content-addressed blob store: blobs, paths per revision,
the revision spine, the inflate cache and every reader work the same on prose. The **only**
thing hard-coded to code was the `kind` stamp, so that is a class attribute now and
`DocSourceStore` is the same class with a different one. Its own file rather than a lane in
`source.db`, because design rule 14 turns on the two being separately handable — *"many will
send documentation and never source"*.

**`capture()` needed no change at all.** It takes a `dict[str, str]` and a root;
`DocStore.known_hashes()` returns exactly that. So there is no new capture path, no change to
`walk.py`, and no body carried back out of the extraction subprocesses — the bodies are
re-read from disk by the hashes the scan just recorded.

Measured on Mensores: **2,056 bodies for 2,064 paths, 38.7 MB of prose in 14.8 MB stored**,
against a prediction of 14.87. Prose compresses 2.6:1 where code manages 4:1. The 8 duplicate
documents cost nothing.

### Two defects found in the building

**`adopt_revision` exists because the first build had none.** `open_working` mints an id from
the clock, which is right for the store that *is* the authority — `source.db`, whose id the
graph and the document store are named after. A second sidecar is not that authority, and
without a way to say so the capture wrote 2,064 path rows under the right revision while
`revisions` stayed **empty**. Every row present, nothing saying the snapshot existed, and
every read resolves through that: the analyze line read *"2,056 bodies for 0 paths"*.

**And rule 16 had a hole, which is the one worth having.** `set_meta` does not commit and
`close()` does not either, so a sidecar created and closed with no write between landed with
all four tables and an **empty `meta`** — no kind, no schema version, no `paths=relative`
marker. `_refuse_wrong_kind` cannot tell *"no kind row"* from *"fresh database"*, so the wrong
class opened it and **restamped** it.

Production never reached it, because `analyze` always follows with a `capture()` that commits.
That is exactly the hazard: **the guard was intact everywhere it was exercised.** It became
visible only on building a second kind and asserting the two refuse each other — with one
kind there was nothing to be mistaken for. The stamp is committed in `__init__` now, because
a store's identity must outlive the process that made it.

### The library

`markdown-it 14.3.1` is vendored (125 KB, MIT) and recorded in `VERSIONS.json`, with the
extractor/renderer line written down beside it: `CLAUDE.md`'s *"no markdown library"* is about
**facts** — the extractor's output is a contract hashed into the cache key — and a renderer is
in no cache key and no fact depends on it. Nothing under `extractors/` may import it.

Both properties it was chosen for are **verified in the browser**, not assumed: every block
token carries `map: [startLine, endLine]`, and `html: false` renders `<script>alert(1)</script>`
as `&lt;script&gt;…`. `validateLink` also drops `javascript:` and `vbscript:` outright — I
briefly reported that as broken after matching the literal text rather than the `href`, and it
is not.

*Found while checking, and not yet handled:* `./rel.md` and `#anchor` render as **live hrefs**.
A relative link between documents would navigate the dashboard, so chunk 3 must route them to
open that document instead.

### Verified

850 tests (6 new), mypy clean, ruff clean. Five mutations, all CAUGHT — including the CLI
wiring, which was MISSED first: `tests/test_source.py` could not see `cli.py`, so removing
`adopt_revision` from the analyze path passed. Pinned on the caller, the way
`open_working`'s `tree=tree_leaf` already is.

### Where to pick up

Chunk 2 (serving: `/api/docs`, `/api/doc`, `/api/docsource`, and `_Base` gaining a `docs`
field), then chunk 4's lane 2 and the `where_` bug, then chunk 3's renderer, then chunk 5's
citations. Chunks 2, 4 and 5 need no library; the plan file has the detail.

**The server is stopped** — it was killed to re-analyse and not restarted.

## Document mode, chunk 2: the corpus served — 2026-09-03

Chunk 2 of the approved plan (`~/.claude/plans/polymorphic-finding-swan.md`). Chunk 1 gave
the 2,064 documents a body sidecar; this gives them a reader on the wire. No client yet —
that is chunk 4 — so everything here was verified with `curl` against a live server on
Mensores, which is how both of the session's defects were found.

**Three routes, one new module.** `web/corpus.py` is lane 1 — *the program's own documents*
— and `web/documents.py` is lane 2, *the map's eight*. Close names for different subjects,
so the module says which is which in its first paragraph. `/api/docs` is the whole list,
`/api/doc` one document with its headings and its text, `/api/docsource` a span for chunk
5's citations to open against. The SQL lives in `corpus.py` rather than `queries.py`,
because `queries.py` is the **graph's** query book down to its `DOC_*` entries — those
select from `routines` and `boundaries` — and a statement against `docs.db` filed beside
them would be two schemas under one heading.

Measured on Mensores, and every figure the plan predicted came back exactly: **2,064
documents** (2,019 Markdown, 45 text), 29,980 headings, 235 definitions, 8 duplicates, and
the class breakdown to the row — PLAN 1601 · OTHER 286 · DECISION 92 · RESEARCH 33 ·
TOOLING 12 · README 9 · REFERENCE 8 · ROADMAP 6 · SPEC 6 · NAMING_STANDARD 5 · GLOSSARY 3 ·
ISSUE 2 · CONTRIBUTING 1. All 2,064 openable. The list is 546 KB of JSON at **18 ms warm**,
1.7–2.3 s cold; the worst case — `.groma/ISSUES.md`, 1.33 MB and 18,299 lines — is **6–7 ms
warm** and 0.86 s cold. Both are whole and neither is paged: what makes that affordable is
that the bodies are not in `docs.db`, so the list is three grouped counts and 38.7 MB of
prose stays in the sidecar until somebody opens a document.

**The document store is now held on `_Base`, and the leak it was closed against has moved
rather than gone.** `_docs_for` used to open a `DocStore`, hand it to the glossary and close
it in a `finally`, because one held across a base switch leaked a 148 MB store every time
the reader moved between two versions. A document list cannot be served from a store that is
already shut, so the handle is a field of the base and the *swap* closes it — the lifetime
is a version's instead of a statement's. That makes it three closes where there was one: the
swap, `_Live.close()`, and the failure path of `open()`, because a build that raises after
opening it must not leave 148 MB behind for a switch the reader never got. The old guard
asserted a `finally` and now asserts all three, plus an exercised one that asks the outgoing
connection a question after the switch and expects sqlite to refuse it by name (rule 37).

**Two defects, and neither could have been found by a test.** Both came from starting the
server and typing `curl`.

*The first was a 000 and a stack trace on the very first request.* `DocStore` had no
`shared` parameter at all — `Store` and `SourceStore` both do — because it had only ever
been opened, read and closed on one thread. The base now **holds** it and
`ThreadingHTTPServer` hands each request to its own thread, where sqlite refuses a
connection made on another one: **by name, from inside the request, and only for the routes
that touch it**. `/api/cover` beside it was fine the whole time. Every unit test passed,
because a unit test calls `build_corpus` on the thread that opened the store. The guard for
it starts a real `threading.Thread`.

*The second is rule 70, one corpus over from where it was first paid for, and it is the
better of the two.* `_sidecar_revision` returns `None` for **this sidecar cannot serve the
version on screen**. Every store here reads `revision=None` as **the current one** and
resolves it to the newest snapshot. Two meanings, one spelling, and the newer one won:
serving Mensores' 2026-08-26 base — whose document bodies were never captured, because there
is one `docsource.db` and it holds the 08-29 snapshot — listed all **2,041** of its documents
as openable and served the **08-29** prose under them. Every heading's line number landing
wherever the text had since moved, and nothing anywhere looking wrong.

The source sidecar never showed this because it holds both snapshots, so the older base is
the first version anything in this tool has ever had no bodies for. `serving()` is the fix
and it is one function: `revision=None` is a refusal with a sentence from there down, never
a fallback. `_span` — which `/api/source` shares — had the identical hole and now refuses
above the store rather than passing it on.

Verified on the pair afterwards: the 08-26 base reports 2,041 documents, **0 openable**,
`sidecar: true`, and *"the document sidecar holds no bodies for the version on screen"*;
switching to 08-29 gives 2,064 and all of them openable. `sidecar` and `reason` are
deliberately two fields — whether the program *has* document bodies is a fact about the
directory and decides whether re-analysing would help; whether they can be read at this
version is a different question, and one flag answering both reported a program that has a
sidecar as one that does not (rule 32).

**Four absences, four sentences**, because they look identical on a blank pane and the thing
to do about each is different: never scanned (`--no-docs`), scanned but not captured
(`--no-doc-source`), captured but not for this version, and captured but not this path.
Design rule 21, and the guard asserts all four are distinct strings.

**Fifteen mutations, all CAUGHT** (baseline proved green first, rule 59): a document route
reading the *source* sidecar — which does not raise, because the two schemas are identical,
it just reports every document missing; the list bounded with a `LIMIT`; the swap forgetting
the outgoing store; a failed build leaking it; the sidecar opened as a `SourceStore`; both
routes reading the newest revision rather than this version's; the class counts filtering
rows the list keeps; an absent corpus shipping an empty list instead of a reason; the two
sidecars sharing one revision answer; the `None`-revision fall-through, at both readers; and
the `shared` flag removed again.

One fixture change worth noting: `test_base_switch`'s program had no `docs.db` at all, so
every new guard about the held handle would have passed on a `None`. It writes a document per
revision now — rule 37, a guard that cannot see the thing it is guarding.

868 tests (17 new in `test_corpus.py`, plus one rewritten and one added in `test_base_switch.py`), mypy clean, ruff clean.

**A candidate rule, not minted — it wants Tom's call, because a number here is a permanent
address.** *A lifetime change is an access-pattern change.* Nothing about `DocStore` changed;
what changed is who reads it. Opened, read and closed inside one function it never needed
`shared`, and the flag's absence had no symptom because there was nothing to have one. Held
on the base so a list could be served, it is read from a request thread — and sqlite refuses
by name, from inside the request, on the routes that touch it and nowhere else. The general
shape is that moving a resource's lifetime outward silently moves *who touches it* outward
too, and the guards that covered the old lifetime say nothing about the new one.

**Next: chunk 4's lane 2 and the `where_` bug**, then chunk 3's renderer, then chunk 5's
citations. Only chunk 3 needs the vendored library.

## Document mode, chunk 4 lane 2: the narrative view delivered — 2026-09-03

The half of the ratified design that was never built, and the `where_` bug found while
planning it. Lane 1 — the program's own 2,064 documents — still waits on chunk 3's renderer
and the pane says so.

**The `where_` bug, first, because it is the smaller and the older.** All eight `DOC_*`
statements aliased their location column `AS where_` — `where` is a SQL keyword and an
unquoted alias is a syntax error — while `documents.py` keyed the same column
`Column("where", …)`. `row.get("where")` returned `None`, so the **"Where" cell of every row
of all eight documents rendered blank**: a column that is there, headed, sized, and empty.
It had been that way for as long as the family existed and nothing noticed, because nothing
rendered these documents.

Fixed at the SQL end — `AS "where"`, quoted — because the key is the contract the client
reads and should not carry a SQL-syntax scar. What makes the direction safe is the guard:
every statement in the family is now **prepared against the real schema** and every `Column`
key asserted to be a column it returns, along with `node_col` and `group_col`. A prepared
statement reports its columns before it returns any rows, so the check runs on an empty
store and cannot be made to pass by a fixture that happens to hold the right data. Verified
on Mensores afterwards: **0 blank "Where" cells** across all seven documents that have one.

**Lane 2 is the ratified design's own sentence, delivered from rows.** *"The same selection,
as a document, scrolled to the routine you have selected."* `documents.py` has carried a
graph node id on every row since it was written, precisely so this could be built — matching
a name against the store afterwards would light up every `main` in a program that has a
great many (rule 5). So a row here is an **ordinary selection**: the stack lights, the
inspector fills, the navigator marks and reveals, the trail records the hop, undo reaches
it. All of that was driven and read back off the page rather than asserted.

Three smaller things came with it. A **strip** of all eight rather than a browse-then-open
pair, because eight fits and 626 files did not — so there is no second field to keep in step
with `docId`, which is the defect `codeRailList` exists to have fixed. The **"Where" column
opens the code browser**, which is what `Column`'s own docstring has said it is for since it
was written. And the **43-row table section**, whose rows are `NULL AS node` by design, now
selects the code that reads and writes each table — `queries.py` settled that a table is not
a node but selecting one means selecting its touchers, before anything rendered it. A
`Section` declares `table_col` for that; inferring it from a null id would be rule 30, since
*"this row names a table"* and *"this row's node could not be resolved"* look identical on
the wire.

### The first draft cost 9,568 ms per render, and two of my three fixes did nothing

`render()` runs on every selection, every keystroke and every message from the other window.
The first version rewrote the chrome around the document each time — which **detaches** the
built subtree, and re-attaching 4,786 rows pays the layout again. It is the code browser's
1,358 ms defect at six times the size, in a pane written by someone who had just read the
comment about it.

Measured on `routines`: building the markup **73 ms**, parsing it **329 ms**, laying it out
**2.0 s**. So the cost is layout, and the question is what to do about it.

**566 separate tables against one**, group headings as rows inside it: 2,049 ms against
2,103. **4,786 `<button>` cells against spans**: 2,103 against 2,003. Both were plausible,
both were measured, and **both were nothing** — rule 39, and the reason they are written
down rather than quietly dropped.

What worked was not repainting (the structural fix), plus two lines of CSS:
`content-visibility: auto` per group is **61 ms against 3,205**, and `table-layout: fixed` is
**1,769 against 2,389**. Fixed layout honours declared widths and nothing else, so a
`<colgroup>` is built from a weight per column *kind* — without it a one-word Direction takes
the same share as a signature.

Result: first paint **631 ms** on the largest document (from 5,169), 23–360 ms on the other
seven, and **19–94 ms** per repaint.

### Two defects the screenshot and the click found

**The group name covered every column header.** Both are sticky inside the same
`content-visibility` container and both defaulted to `top: 0`, so they stuck to exactly the
same pixel — and the name, one `z-index` higher, hid the headers completely the moment a
group reached the top of the pane. Nothing threw and nothing measured wrong. `--dochead-h`
is now one number in `rem` that the heading's height and the headers' offset both read, so
the scale control cannot move one without the other (design rule 3).

**And the trail note never landed — in three routes, one of them a year old.** `codelink`,
`docrow` and `doctable` all `await selectFromNav(...)` and then
`pushTrail(view, label, "why")`. `selectFromNav` records the step itself with no note, so the
note-carrying call arrived second on the same subject and `recordSelection`'s dedupe threw it
away whole. Every one of those routes read as though it explained the hop and none of them
did — design rule 16's defect three times over, invisible because the step it wanted was
already there and looked right. A deduplicated step now **adopts** a note the standing one
lacks, and only then. Found by clicking a row and reading `state.trail`.

**Twenty-one mutations, all CAUGHT** (baseline green first, rule 59): the unconditional
repaint; a skipped repaint that stops moving the highlight; the cache handed a built string
rather than a function; a key that forgets which document it holds; a control bound in
`wire()`; `docrow` declared before `docwhere`, which makes the location cell select the row
instead of opening the file; a row that stops selecting; a table row that stops selecting;
an unlinked row given a route anyway; the pane no longer following the selection; the note
dropped again; `content-visibility` removed; `auto` layout; the colgroup dropped; the headers
un-stacked; the shared height un-shared; the `table_col` declaration removed at three points;
and `where_` restored.

889 tests (11 in `test_documents.py`, 10 more in `test_web_controls.py`), mypy clean, ruff
clean. Self-check green, console clean.

**The rule-38 debt stands and this session added to it.** The automation window reports
1,267×539, refuses `resize_window`, and its screenshots crop at 784px — so every number above
was taken at a **537px centre pane and a 16px root font**, where each row is 70px tall
because the cells wrap. Tom's Chrome is 24px on a 4K screen. The pane width is load-bearing
for these figures, and the sticky-overlap defect was caught by a screenshot only because it
happened to be in the left 784px. **A real window is still owed a look.**

**Next: chunk 3's renderer**, then chunk 4's lane 1 on top of it, then chunk 5's citations,
then chunk 6's records.

## Document mode, chunk 3: the renderer — 2026-09-03

`prose.js`, and the vendored `markdown-it` it drives. The last piece before lane 1 has a
view. Nothing in Document mode calls it yet — that is chunk 4's lane 1 — so everything here
was verified by driving `Prose` directly against the live corpus, which is how three of the
four findings turned up.

**Its own file, and the boundary is `graph.js`'s.** It turns text into markup and knows
nothing about this page: which document is open, what a link means when clicked, what exists
in the corpus. What it has to say leaves as **data attributes** and the shell routes them. A
renderer that called `openDoc()` would be a second place deciding what a click means, and it
could not be tested without the whole application around it — which is why every check in
`test_prose.py` reads the module rather than the page.

**The line CLAUDE.md draws is now enforced rather than stated.** `VERSIONS.json` has claimed
*"a test asserts it"* since the library was vendored and **there was no such test** — rule
43's shape exactly, and the same shape as `shorten()`'s docstring promising a `selfCheck` for
a session without one. There is one now: nothing under `extractors/` may mention the library
or the vendor path, because the extractor's output is a contract hashed into the cache key
and must not depend on a third party's reading of a document. A renderer produces pixels,
sits in no cache key, and no fact depends on it.

**The property the library was chosen for, verified end to end rather than assumed.** Every
heading `docs.db` recorded must be findable in the rendered DOM at exactly its own line, or a
glossary citation opens a document *near* where it was read from. **825 of 825 headings
across 60 documents**, and 782 of 782 across a second sample of 41. `md.parse()` to tokens
and `md.renderer.render()`, never `md.render()`, which throws the maps away before anything
can be stamped on them.

**Every decision about links and images was taken from the corpus, not in general.** Measured
over 2,019 Markdown documents: **3,516 https · 6 http · 666 relative · 16 anchors · 6 other
schemes · 5 images**. So external links stay links and open in a new tab with
`rel="noreferrer noopener"`; relative links and anchors **lose their href entirely** and
carry where they wanted to go instead; `graph:`, `xs:` and `node:` render as text, because a
link nobody can follow is design rule 16's dead control.

**And an image is never fetched.** That is the one that is egress rather than navigation:
`![](https://tracker/x.png)` fires a request the moment it renders — no click, no consent —
out of a tool whose whole posture is deterministic and local (design rule 14). Five images in
this corpus and all of them relative, but the rule is about what a document *can* contain.
Each renders as a placeholder naming its source, so the reader knows something was there.

Verified on a sweep of **230 documents, 4.0 MB**: zero errors, **zero hrefs that could
navigate away**, zero `<img>`, zero `<script>/<iframe>/<object>/<embed>`. And directly: a
document containing `<script>`, `<img onerror>`, `javascript:` and `vbscript:` renders all
four as text with nothing executed.

### Frontmatter: half the corpus, and the obvious fix was the trap

markdown-it knows nothing about YAML frontmatter, so a document opening
`---\nkind: reference\ntitle: Glossary\n---` parses it as a **setext heading** — the metadata
becomes an `<h2>` above the document's own title, with an id of
`kind-referencetitle-glossary`. **989 of Mensores' 2,019 Markdown documents** begin with one.

The trap is the fix. **Cutting the lines out shifts every `token.map` below by the number
removed**, so every `data-line` is wrong by a constant, every heading in the nav scrolls to
the wrong block, and a citation opens near rather than at. The page renders perfectly and
every number on it is off by four. The lines are **blanked** instead: no arithmetic, so no
arithmetic to get wrong. Only a *closed* fence at the very top counts — a document opening
with a horizontal rule is not carrying frontmatter, and 30 of the 989 are blocks the
extractor could not parse as YAML and which are still not prose. The raw text is returned so
the caller can show it as what it is.

### Two process findings, both worth keeping

**A guard passed on the comment explaining it.** Dropping `noreferrer` from the code survived
a mutation, because this file's `_strip` blanked comment *lines* — the shell's treatment —
and these are long block comments whose continuation lines are plain indented prose. The
paragraph saying *why `noreferrer` is there* was still in the text being searched. That is
the exact defect `_code()`'s own docstring in `test_web_controls` records, reproduced in a
new file within an hour of reading it. `_strip` now tracks `/* … */` across lines, a guard
asserts the stripper is exact for this file, and the assertion targets the `attrSet` call
rather than the word.

**And a killed mutation harness leaves the tree mutated.** The run timed out at two minutes,
`finally` never ran, and `prose.js` was left with its anchor-collision handling removed —
which `git checkout` could not undo, because the file was new and untracked. Caught by the
next run reporting *"SKIPPED (no match)"* on a mutation that had passed minutes before. The
lesson is small and cheap: **commit before mutating**, so a killed harness is one `git
checkout` from clean.

**22 mutations, all CAUGHT** (baseline green first, rule 59): the extractor importing the
library; the library loaded at boot; `prose.js` not loaded at all; two callers both fetching;
`html: true`; `linkify: true`; `md.render()`; no `data-line`; the stamp landing on inline
tokens; a relative link keeping its href; an external link replacing the page; the referrer
leaking; an unknown scheme drawn as a link; a protocol-relative URL read as a corpus path;
images fetched; a path resolved against the document rather than its directory; two headings
sharing an anchor; plain text fed to the parser; frontmatter cut rather than blanked; an
unclosed fence eating the document; the renderer reaching into the shell; and the record
losing its reason.

Measured: the library is **29 ms** to fetch and configure, lazily. `.groma/ISSUES.md` — 1.32
MB — parses and renders in **40–72 ms**. 230 documents and 4.0 MB of prose, with their
fetches, in 927 ms.

904 tests (15 new in `test_prose.py`), mypy clean, ruff clean.

**Next: chunk 4's lane 1** — the document list grouped by class with its counts, a filter, a
reader with the document's own headings as a side nav, and the three link routes this
renderer emits. Then chunk 5's citations, then chunk 6's records.

## Document mode, chunk 4 lane 1: the program's own documents, read — 2026-09-03

The last piece of the feature. 2,064 documents that were mined for 29,980 headings and 235
definitions and readable nowhere in the tool now have a list, a filter, a reader and a side
nav. **Document mode is complete** but for chunk 5's citations.

**Two lanes sharing a pane, and they are two subjects rather than two views of one thing** —
prose this tool generates about the program, and prose somebody wrote. The switch says so in
those words. One mount, one subtree cache and one `render()` branch serve both, so the cache
key carries the lane: a subtree keyed on the other lane's page is handed back on a switch,
and that looks exactly like a switch that did not work.

**The list** is 2,064 rows in 13 class groups with the server's own counts — PLAN 1,601 ·
OTHER 286 · DECISION 92 and down — grouped because the classes are the first useful cut and a
reader looking for the charter is looking in one of four small groups. **The filter hides rows
rather than rebuilding**, for two reasons and the second is the one that reads as a broken
control: 2,064 rows per keystroke is the cost, and rebuilding also destroys the `<input>`
being typed into, taking the focus and the caret with it. So the query is deliberately *out*
of the cache key. Every group count is restated and an empty group is hidden (design rule 1) —
a heading still saying 1,601 over four rows is what a filter is most able to hide.

**The reader** is the document's own headings beside the prose, wrapping to one column when
the pane is narrow — **flex-wrap rather than a breakpoint**, because a `@media` query can only
ask how wide the *window* is and this depends on the *centre pane*, which the reader moves by
hundreds of pixels by collapsing a panel without touching the window. The bases are in `rem`,
so the wrap point moves with the scale control, which a breakpoint cannot do at all (rule 28).

**A document is rendered once when it is fetched, never at paint time.** Parsing is the one
cost a subtree cache cannot save — the cache holds a *node* and the parse happens before there
is one — so 1.32 MB is parsed on the fetch and every repaint after is 2 ms.

**All three link kinds are routed.** A relative link is **checked against the corpus before it
is followed**: 666 of them, and many point outside the scanned tree —
`.groma/milestones/1.1.0-ROADMAP.md` links to `ROADMAP-v1-archive.md`, which does not exist.
Following it opens a blank pane; saying so names what happened, and the sentence quotes both
what the author wrote and what it resolves to.

**And it goes in `docNote`, never `navNote`.** `navNote` is rendered in exactly one place —
the graph HUD — which is not on screen while somebody is reading a document. That mistake is
already recorded in this file: `revNote` exists because a notice put there *"was invisible for
its first hour"*. Reading the comment beside the field was what stopped it happening a third
time. The note also needs a narrow write of its own, because it lives in chrome that repaints
only when the cache key moves — set without one it would render nothing and throw nothing
(rule 44).

### The screenshot found what nothing else could: half the corpus was showing its own hidden notes

`.groma/adrs/0000-template.md` opened with a paragraph of editorial instructions —
*"Plan 14-01 Task 3 seeds this skeletal ADR template…"* — drawn as body prose.

**`html: false` does not hide an HTML comment. It un-hides one.** With raw HTML refused,
markdown-it disables the `html_block` rule *entirely*, so a comment is not a token that can be
caught: it arrives as an ordinary **paragraph** and is escaped into visible text. Verified
rather than assumed — parsing a document with three HTML constructs in it yields
`html_block: 0`, which is why the first fix, written against `html_block` tokens, counted zero
comments and changed nothing.

**7,317 comments across 505 of Mensores' 2,019 documents** — a quarter of the corpus showing
notes nobody wrote for the reader. They are lifted out before parsing, replaced by exactly as
many newlines as they held — the frontmatter rule, for the frontmatter reason — and **listed
with their line numbers** rather than dropped, because a silent filter is what design rule 1
exists to prevent and in a corpus of templates the comments are occasionally the most useful
thing in the file.

### And a heading that was not one, which found what chunk 5 will need

Sweeping the corpus after the comment strip, **one heading of 1,566 no longer matched**:
`docs/audit/discoveries-format.md:156`. It turned out to be `## Discoveries` **inside a fenced
code block** — an example of a heading, which the extractor recorded as a real one. Three or
four such cases in 29,980, so rule 12 is holding and this is not worth chasing; the renderer
is right and the map is the one that is slightly wrong.

What it exposed is not small. Blocks carried only their **start** line, and the lines anybody
opens at are mostly not the first line of anything — **a definition sits in the middle of a
paragraph, and that is exactly what chunk 5's citations open against.** With only starts
stamped, the nearest-at-or-after fallback lands the reader on the block *after* the one their
line is in: adjacent, plausible, and wrong. Every block now carries `data-line-end` and the
lookup takes the **innermost containing** block — `search.py`'s rule for the same question
asked of source. Verified: 1,565 headings match exactly, 1 resolves to the fence that contains
it, **zero unreachable**.

### Three guards survived their own mutations, all the same way

`if (!known)` → `if (false)`, the narrowing removed from the containing-block search, and
`lastDocRead = path` deleted from one of its two doors. Every one passed, because each guard
checked that a **name appeared** rather than that anything happened — `DOCS.documents.some`
was still computed, `innerSpan` was still declared, `let lastDocRead` was still there. That is
rule 37, three times, in guards written for a chunk whose own defects are rule 37's shape.
They now assert the branch, the comparison, and both doors.

**23 mutations, all CAUGHT** on the second pass (baseline green first, rule 59). The harness
takes a backup to disk *before* mutating and verifies every file restored at the end —
last session's timeout left an untracked file mutated with no way to `git checkout` it back.

Measured: the list is **56 ms** to first paint and **5 ms** to repaint; the filter over 2,064
rows is **2 ms**; the worst-case document (1.32 MB, 6,694 blocks, 327 headings) is **668 ms**
to open and **2 ms** to repaint.

912 tests, mypy clean, ruff clean. Self-check green, console clean.

**Next: chunk 5** — `senseOpens()` becomes a capability test rather than a provenance test, so
the 235 documentation-derived definitions open at their line. Everything it needs is now in
place: `/api/docsource`, the renderer, and `data-line-end`. Then chunk 6's records.

## Document mode, chunk 5: a citation into the corpus opens — 2026-09-04

The last chunk of the feature, and it is the one design rule 13 was waiting on: *every
reported meaning must carry its provenance, and the provenance must open*. Documentation
citations rendered a dead end for as long as `source.db` was the only sidecar. They open now.

**`senseOpens()` is a capability test rather than a provenance test, and that is the whole
change.** It read `s.provenance === "DECLARED_CODE"`, which was a true statement about the
tool until chunk 1 gave the document corpus a sidecar and stopped being true the moment it
landed. The question is no longer *which tier is this* but *does the corpus this tier quotes
have a sidecar this base can read* — and the page has no way to know that, so `/api/glossary`
carries it: a `sidecars` block, one entry per tier, `{opens, reason}`, computed from the live
stores and the base's two revisions. The two model tiers answer `false` by having no entry
rather than by being named, because a corpus that does not exist cannot be opened and listing
them would be a second place to keep the tiers in step (rule 51).

**Correcting the plan's number, which was wrong and had been carried into `BRIEFING.md`.**
The plan said *"all 235 documentation-derived definitions render a dead end"*. 235 is
`definitions_seen` — every definition the scan mined. Of those, **32 bind to a term the code
actually uses as an identifier and become citations**; the other 203 define words this program
never names, and they are the *mirror's* subject rather than the glossary's. So what was fixed
is 32 citations across 22 terms in 10 documents, measured on the served payload rather than
assumed. Counted before the change: 60 citation buttons on the glossary page. After: **92 —
60 code and 32 docs** — which is the number matching exactly, and the check that the tier
counts and the button counts are one answer (rule 13).

The 22 terms are the ones `CLAUDE.md`'s ground truth names: `groma`, `disceptator`,
`quaestor`, `scriba`, `signator`, `procurator`, `custos`, `dispensator`, `mensor`,
`mensores` — the pantheon, out of `NAMING.md` and `PROJECT.md`, plus `contract`, `decision`,
`worktree`, `drift`, `lifecycle`, `allowlist`, `citations` and four SCREAMING-case ones.

### The refusal, which is where the honest half is

Both sidecars can be absent independently, so `_sidecar_state` states which. Verified against
a real base rather than a fixture: `output/mensores` holds **source** bodies for both
revisions and **document** bodies for only the newer one, so serving the 2026-08-26 base is
the asymmetric case as it actually occurs.

| | `DECLARED_CODE` | `DECLARED_DOCS` |
|---|---|---|
| base 2026-08-31T22:53:57Z (08-29 tree) | opens | opens |
| base 2026-08-31T22:53:15Z (08-26 tree) | opens | *this sidecar holds nothing for the version on screen* |

On the older base the 32 documentation rows render as **plain text with no button** — no
control that resolves to nothing (design rule 16) — while the 60 code rows keep theirs. And
`/api/docsource` refuses rather than serving the newer prose under the older headings, which
is rule 70 holding at the place it was written for.

**The sentence was wrong when I first read it out loud, and only reading it caught it.** The
server's four reasons are not one part of speech: *"no document sidecar beside this map"* is a
noun phrase, *"this sidecar holds nothing for the version on screen"* is a clause. The first
draft embedded them in `because there is …` and produced **"It cannot be opened because there
is this sidecar holds nothing for the version on screen."** Every test passed. A dash takes
both, and the wording stays the server's own rather than being paraphrased into a third
spelling here (rule 51) — there is now a guard that the shell carries **none** of the three
sentences as a literal, and it tripped on the comment explaining the fix before it was taken
over `_code()`. That is the sixth time a guard in this file has failed on its own prose.

### Two readings of one citation, and both are wanted

The pane above the foot is the document **as measured** — Markdown syntax and all — which is
what proves the citation and is not how the sentence was meant to be read. So the foot offers
*Read it in the document →* for a documentation citation and for nothing else: it closes the
viewer, switches to Document mode lane 1, opens the document and scrolls to the block holding
the line.

**The line is held rather than scrolled to**, because `openDocumentAt` returns two awaits
before there is a block to scroll to — a 546 KB corpus list and then the document itself. It
is consumed by the paint that has it, after `attachDoc()` and after the scroll restore, and it
checks the *path* rather than a flag: consuming it against whatever document happens to be
mounted is how a reader who moved on lands somewhere arbitrary (rule 42).

Verified end to end on the live corpus: `mensores` → `.groma/PROJECT.md:474` → the viewer
shows lines 468–482 with 474 highlighted → the hop lands in the document, **scrolled 55,810px
into 459 blocks**, with the `<p>` spanning lines 474–475 flashed. That is the innermost
containing block, not the heading above it and not the paragraph after — which is exactly the
`data-line-end` lookup chunk 4 built and named as the thing chunk 5 would need.

**The refusal path switches mode anyway.** A base can move between the glossary being loaded
and the button being clicked, so the path is checked against the corpus first, `doclink`-style
— and the note goes in `docNote`, which renders in that pane and nowhere else. Setting it and
staying on the glossary would be a notice nobody sees, which this file has already paid for
twice (`revNote`, `navNote`).

### Measured

| | |
|---|---|
| `/api/docsource`, a 15-line span | **0.56–0.65 ms**, five reads |
| `/api/source`, the same shape | 0.60–0.61 ms |
| `/api/glossary` with the `sidecars` block | **1.53–1.57 ms** (cached payload plus a shallow copy) |
| a documentation citation opening, in the page | **999 ms** |
| a **code** citation opening, in the page | **999 ms** |

The last two are the point: a documentation citation costs exactly what a code one does. The
999 ms is the glossary page's own repaint of 1,214 terms on the render that follows the fetch
— pre-existing, identical for both tiers, and not this chunk's to fix. Taken at a 1,264×523
viewport and a 16px root font.

### 17 mutations, all CAUGHT

Baseline green first (rule 59), every file backed up to disk and verified restored against the
backup at the end. Ten against the shell — `senseOpens` reverted to a provenance test, the
fetch given a literal route, the unroutable refusal removed, the reason re-embedded as a noun
phrase, the hop offered under every citation, the pending line consumed against any document,
the scroll moved before `attachDoc()`, the corpus list never fetched, the mode switched only
on success, the binding renamed — and seven against the server, including the two sidecar
revisions crossed, which is the mutation that would silently report a documentation citation
as openable because the *code* sidecar has bodies for that version.

**928 tests** (912 + 16), mypy clean, ruff clean, console clean, self-check green.

### Still owed, and it grew rather than shrank

**A real window.** Every figure here was taken in the automation tab at 1,264×523 and a 16px
root font. Tom's Chrome is 24px on a 4K screen. Two things were measurable and are: the foot
lays the sentence and the button on one row down to 34rem of modal width and wraps the button
beneath at 26rem, and the button sits at the right edge, inside the foot, not overlapping.
Two things were not seeable at all: the button never appeared in a capture, because the modal
is 56rem wide and the capture frame is 784px; and the pointer path is unprovable here — clicks
did not land where `getBoundingClientRect` said the element was, so every interaction in this
session was driven by `.click()`, which proves the handler and not the path to it (rule 48).

## The naming standard says it was derived — 2026-09-04

Tom, on the Naming standard page: *"We're showing what is actually in the code, not what was
intended or required… we just need to talk more openly about the fact that we derived this
list of naming standards from what we discovered."*

He is right, and the dashboard was the place it was wrong. **`/api/naming` serves the Form
lane and only the Form lane** — 27 conventions counted off the graph, no stated rule at all —
and the page was headed *Naming standard*. Twenty-seven conventions, several holding 100% of
the time, under that heading reads as conformance to a rule somebody wrote. DunneFlow has no
evidence for that and, until a standards directory can be imported, no way to get any.

**What changed, and it is four surfaces rather than one label.** A reader arriving mid-page by
scroll wheel never sees a navigator label, so the label alone would have been the fix that
looks like a fix:

| Surface | Was | Is |
|---|---|---|
| navigator row | Naming standard | **Derived naming standard** |
| breadcrumb / trail | naming standard | derived naming standard |
| the page's leading note | *(none — it opened on "every figure here is counted")* | *"This standard was derived from the code, not required of it… none of it has been checked against a standard your team wrote — DunneFlow cannot yet import one. So a convention holding 100% of the time means the code is consistent, not that it is correct."* |
| the boot step | the naming standard | the derived naming standard |

### The one place "derived" would have been a lie

**The Markdown report carries both lanes**, and only one of them is derived: **Form** is
counted off the code, **Vocabulary** is *quoted* out of the project's own documents. Titling
that document "derived" would relabel a quotation as an inference — the single thing the four
provenance tiers exist to prevent, and rule 6's shape in prose.

So the report is titled **"Naming standard, as found"**, which is true of both lanes — found
in the code, found in the documents, required by neither — and its two section headings now
carry the claim each is making: **"Form — derived from the code"** and **"Vocabulary — quoted,
not derived"**. Its opening paragraph leads with *"Nothing here was required of this program."*
The per-line `STATED ·` / `MEASURED ·` badges were already honest and are untouched.

Both are guarded, and the guards check the page's own prose as well as the label, because a
label a scrolling reader cannot see is design rule 21's blank pane in another costume.

### What the survey behind it found, and it is filed rather than fixed

Tom's question was *can we import a standard and compare against it*. Surveying to answer it
turned up four things, all measured, all now in `BRIEFING.md`'s open list under **a known
standards directory**:

- Ingest exists — `doc_rules` already has `lane`, `scope`, `pattern`, `checkable` — but there
  is **no import gesture**, and it yields **5 rules from 1 of 29 rule-bearing documents**, all
  VOCABULARY, all `checkable = 0`. **Zero FORM rules corpus-wide**, so nothing checkable has
  ever existed to check.
- **Nothing compares.** `checkable` is read by exactly one sentence in the report; `scope` and
  `pattern` are read by nothing at all.
- **The best standard in this corpus is a table and the detector cannot see it.**
  `harness/rules/style.md:30` states seven conventions as `Type | Convention | Example` —
  Files kebab-case, Commands `paul:kebab-case`, Step names snake_case, and four more. Every
  row is a `scope` and a `pattern`, which is precisely what the FORM lane wants. The table is
  **fully captured** in `doc_tables`/`doc_table_rows`; `_maybe_rule` returns on
  `text.startswith("|")` (`markdown.py:468`) and never reads one. A table is how most
  enterprises write a naming standard, and this is the cheapest high-value fix on the list.
- **The scoping mechanism is already stored and unread.** `harness/rules/style.md` carries
  `paths: ['src/**/*.md']`, and **62 documents carry a `paths`, `area` or `applies_to` key**
  in `documents.frontmatter`. That is the *"only some parts are relevant"* half of the
  enterprise case, sitting in the store. `Society-Specs/01-naming-standards.md` is Society's
  own spec asking for the whole feature by name.

930 tests, mypy clean, ruff clean. The report was re-rendered against the real store to read
the new wording rather than trusting the template, and the page was read back out of the DOM.

## A naming standard written as a table is read at last — 2026-09-04

Chunk 1 of the known-standards work Tom asked for, and the reason it is first: **the
comparison machinery had never had an input.** `doc_rules` carries `lane`, `scope`, `pattern`
and `checkable`, and across 2,064 documents it held 5 rules, all VOCABULARY, none checkable.
**Zero FORM rules.** There was nothing for a comparison to compare.

**One shape accounts for all of it.** `_table()` consumes a table whole and the loop
`continue`s (`markdown.py:315-318`), so `_maybe_rule` is never offered a table's lines — the
