`text.startswith("|")` guard I first blamed is real but not the operative reason, and the
correction makes the fix better: the hook point already has header and cells parsed. And a
naming standard is usually a table. `harness/rules/style.md:30` states seven conventions as
`Type | Convention | Example`, every row a class of identifier and the spelling it must have.

### The detector, and the rule it inherits

`table_rule_columns()` in `detectors/prose.py`, modelled on `term_columns`/`meaning_columns`
sitting a few lines above it in the same YAML — including the rule that carries the weight:
**both halves are required, on different columns.** *"`| Name | Port |` is not a glossary"*
becomes *"`| Phase | Status |` is not a standard."*

A column qualifies on its **header or its cells**, and taking either is what makes it land.
Headers vary between organisations — Type/Convention, Element/Style, What/How — so header
matching alone is brittle; and cells alone miss the one real table here, whose `Convention`
column scores 43% against regexes tuned for prose sentences. `rule_scope` and `rule_pattern`
were lifted out of `rule_lane` so a cell and a sentence are asked the same question by the
same code — they were the same three lines twice for about an hour, which is rule 51 arriving
before its second caller had finished being written.

Two gates now apply to tables that did not before: `may_state_rules` (the class gate) and
`reports_rather_than_rules`, which was applied to sentences only. The second is load-bearing:
it is what keeps `NAMING.md:63` — *"Sub-name availability pass — RESULTS"* — out of the
standard.

### Measured over the corpus before a line was written

| | |
|---|---|
| tables in the corpus | **5,230** |
| tables in rule-bearing documents | 27 |
| tables that fire | **1** — `harness/rules/style.md:30`, scope "Type" 86%, pattern "Convention" 71% |
| rules minted | **7**, at lines 32–38 — the rows, not the header |
| corpus-wide FORM rules | **0 → 7**; VOCABULARY unchanged at 5 |

The 26 that do not fire include `.groma/PROJECT.md:328` *Key Decisions* (**100 rows**) and
`NAMING.md:23` *The pantheon* — a glossary, in a naming standard, under a naming heading,
already mined as definitions, and the most dangerous near-miss in the corpus. Stable at
thresholds 0.5 and 0.6. The class gate loses 18 tables, 16 correctly; the two plausible ones
are an ADR and a research doc, which is the trade `prose.yaml` already documents in prose.

A row whose scope names no identifier class is **kept, not dropped** — *"Step names:
snake_case"* is a real rule this tool has no population for, and dropping it would be the
silent filter design rule 1 exists to prevent. It carries `scope=""` and is not checkable.

### Three things measuring caught that the plan had wrong

**The two new regexes earn nothing here, and the comment said they were load-bearing.**
`CAPS_UNDERSCORES` and `colon separator` were added because the pattern column scored 3 of 7
without them — true of the cells-only design I simulated first, and false of the header-or-
cells design I built, because `Convention` is in the header list. Removed, the real file still
yields all seven rules. They are kept, because what they earn is the **cell** path — 3 of 7
against 5 of 7 — and that is the path that has to carry a standard written by somebody who
does not work here, which is the entire point of the feature. The comment now says that.

**Seven dead links, from a change that never touched the file they were in.** The handbook at
the top of `11-naming.md` links every stated rule to `[the rule in full](#slug)`, and only
`_vocabulary_section` ever emitted a heading to slug — it filters to `lane == "VOCABULARY"`.
The day a FORM rule first existed, seven links pointed at nothing. That is the `where_`
defect's shape exactly: correct in every respect except that nothing is at the other end. So
**Form** now has a *Stated* half above its *Measured* half, which is also the shape the
comparison wants — the document's claim and the code's count under one heading.

**A sentence that had never been printed was false the first time it was.** No rule had ever
carried `checkable = 1`, so the true branch of `render/naming.py`'s checkable line had been
written, shipped and never seen. Its first outing said *"Mechanically checkable."* beside
**"Type attributes: colon separator"** — for which DunneFlow has no population, no check, and
will not have one until a standards directory can be imported. The field is right; the
sentence over-claimed. It now says a check *could* be written and that DunneFlow does not run
one, in one place because both lanes say it (rule 51).

### 10 mutations, all CAUGHT — after 5 survived the first pass

Every one of the five was the same defect in my own guards: a fixture missing **both** column
halves rather than one. A table with neither a scope column nor a pattern column is refused
twice over, so a mutation dropping either half still passes — and the availability fixture had
no scope column at all, so the heading gate it was written for was never reached. Rule 37, in
guards written for a chunk about corroboration. Replaced with `SCOPE_ONLY_TABLE`,
`PATTERN_ONLY_TABLE`, a one-row table, an unfamiliar-header table (the only thing the cell
vocabulary earns), and a table with a blank cell — which found a real gap: a half-empty row
would have been minted as the rule *"Classes:"*.

941 tests, mypy clean, ruff clean.

### The cost, paid rather than deferred

`doc_rules_fingerprint()` hashes `prose.yaml` **and** `markdown.py`, so this bumps it and
every `docs.db` goes stale. Verified: `dunneflow serve output/mensores` refuses at step 5 of 6
with *"was written by a different version of DunneFlow … re-run `dunneflow analyze`"* —
`StaleGraphError` is a `RuntimeError` and is not caught by `_docs_for`'s
`except (ValueError, OSError)`, so the base build raises rather than silently serving a map
with no documentation. That is rule 20 working. The pair was rebuilt with CLAUDE.md's
sequence: analyze 08-26, seal, analyze 08-29.

**And rebuilt twice, because the first one was started too early.** The rebuild ran in the
background while the last of the code was still being tidied — a two-line change to
`markdown.py` removing a double `rule_scope()` lookup, made at 12:19 against an analyze that
had read the file at 12:16. `doc_rules_fingerprint()` hashes the extractor, so both
freshly-written stores carried `6:d25aa80da4c9c394` against a current `6:37052ebf5f84302a`
and `serve` refused them exactly as it had refused the old ones. Diagnosed by comparing the
stored `extractor` key with the computed one rather than by guessing.

The rule is dull and worth writing down anyway: **the rebuild is the last step, not a
parallel one.** Any edit to `prose.yaml`, `markdown.py` or the reader after an analyze has
begun invalidates what that analyze wrote, and the failure is silent until something tries
to read it.

**Two stale revisions are left behind, and only one of them is this session's.**
`output/mensores` now holds four: `2026-09-04T16:25:20Z` (WORKING, the 08-29 tree) and
`2026-09-04T16:16:48Z` (FOR_COMPARISON, the 08-26 tree) are the pair, both fingerprint-fresh
and both carrying the 7 rules. `2026-08-31T22:53:57Z` is this session's orphan, from the
rebuild that was started too early; `2026-08-31T22:53:15Z` predates the session entirely and
has 0 FORM rules because it predates the detector. Both are stale and a reader refuses them
by name. They are derived output and can be deleted; they are named here rather than removed,
because the directory is Tom's.

**A table rule's citation opens the table, not the row.** Verified end to end through
`openDocumentAt("harness/rules/style.md", 32)`: the reader lands in Document mode on the
`<table>` block spanning lines 30–38, which is the innermost block *containing* line 32 and
therefore the right answer to the question `scrollToDocLine` asks. It cannot be sharper,
because markdown-it stamps `token.map` on the table token and a row inside one has no map of
its own. Not a defect and not this chunk's to fix — recorded because **chunk 2 is what will
put a citation on these rules**, and whoever builds it should decide deliberately whether
landing on the table is enough or whether the row wants marking.

**The detector costs +4 ms**, 0.1%, over 2,024 documents and 5,230 tables — median of three
alternating sweeps in one process against bodies already in memory. See `PERFORMANCE.md`.

## The mode toggle is dimmed, not hidden — and a program's output is not its documentation — 2026-09-04

Two small things finished before the program selector.

### The toggle, reported at the keyboard

Tom, with two screenshots: *"Middle panel seems broken — should have buttons to show
Graph/Code/Diagram and so on. Just disappeared in this mode."*

It was `visibility: hidden`, which **keeps the box**: 321×31px of empty toolbar where five
buttons had been, on **nine of fourteen views** — `anomalies`, `changes`, `cover`,
`curiosities`, `glossary`, `inference`, `naming`, `pins`, `settings`. Its immediate
neighbour `#layouts` uses `hidden` and collapses to 0×0. Two adjacent controls in one
toolbar, two hiding mechanisms, and the one that leaves a hole is the one that got reported.

The intent was defensible — the modes are five ways of looking at one selection, and a
destination is not one — but the scope was more than half the app, which is why it read as a
fault rather than a rule.

**Tom chose dimmed with a reason**, over hiding it properly or leaving it live-and-unpressed,
and then settled the detail I had left open: *"a dimmed button should still act — the user is
always right, even if they're wrong. Unless it CANNOT work, in which case it just doesn't
work."* That is a better statement of the rule than the reasoning that produced it, and it
generalises past this control. **A candidate design rule, not minted** — design rule numbers
are permanent addresses like the engineering ones, so it wants his call.

Three states, and the treatment now says all three:

| Where you are | Toggle |
|---|---|
| in a mode | full opacity, the current mode pressed |
| on a destination | **dimmed, nothing pressed**, with the reason beside it |
| pressing a dimmed button | goes back to that mode **on your selection** |

Verified live: on the doorway panel, opacity 0.55, `pressed: []`, and *"These are five ways of
reading one selection. You are on the doorway panel — pick one to go back to it."* Pressing
the dimmed **Graph** returned to `mensores › mensores.cli._root › _root`.

**And it caught its own defect on the way.** The first build dimmed correctly and still
marked `state.mode` as pressed, because the `aria-pressed` loop sat in `render()` beside the
old visibility line — so the toolbar said **Document** over the doorway panel. That is rule
78's shape exactly: a pane claiming what it is not showing, and the very claim the change was
meant to remove. `paintModes()` owns all three now, so they cannot disagree (rule 51).

### A program's own output is not its own documentation

Found by answering Tom's question *"can I open a different corpus"* with a demonstration
rather than a description. Analysing DunneFlow itself reported **942 stated rules and 654
definitions** from a 61-file tool, which is not plausible, so it was worth checking where they
came from.

**All 942 came from `output/`.** 46 of 54 documents were DunneFlow's own generated reports —
including 369,684 words of `output/mensores/06-governance.md`, which is a report about a
*different program*, and a second copy of all of it under `output/mensores@2026-08-29…/`.
`DOC_SKIP_DIRS` excludes `build`, `dist`, `site`, `_build`, `coverage` and `target`, but not
`output`, which is `DEFAULT_OUTPUT`. Rule 57 with the tool's own output in place of a stale
worktree, and worse, because the output is about somebody else's program.

**A path, never a name.** Blacklisting `output` was the obvious fix and is the wrong one: it
is a fine name for a directory of hand-written documents, and no scanner should silently drop
one because a tool the author has never heard of writes there. `revisions.program_dirs()`
recognises a directory holding a **graph**, and `analyze` excludes those — the map it is
writing and every other map beside it, because reading a report about another program as
documentation about this one is the same mistake one directory up.

Measured on the case that found it: **54 documents → 9, 45 removed; 942 stated rules → 0; 654
definitions → 14.** The nine are DunneFlow's real documents — and `output/dashboard-uitest.md`,
a hand-written note sitting in `output/` beside the maps, **is still read**, which is exactly
the case that argued against blacklisting the name and is now proven on real data rather than
asserted.

944 tests, mypy clean, ruff clean.

## The program selector, built at last — 2026-09-04

Tom: *"What's missing is a way to switch between the two — that used to exist."* It did, in
the ratified artifact `f993d319`: a `<select id="prog">` with `mensores — 623 files`,
`dunneflow — 23 files` and `+ Analyze a directory…`. **And no change handler even there** —
a statement of intent wearing a working control's clothes. The port carried the markup across
and emptied the options with every other pinned array; unlike all of those it never got the
endpoint that fills it, so it has shipped since day one as a one-option `<select>`. Design
rule 16's own text, in the topbar of the mockup that ratified the rule.

*Method note: I looked in `git log` first and concluded it was never a switcher. The artifact
is the source of truth for every view and my own notes say to read it before designing one.
Check the artifact.*

### It is the revision switch, one axis over

`_Live.switch()` already rebuilds on a thread, reports each step, swaps under the lock and
refuses without leaving a broken base. `_p_base` already claims a slot. The client already
polls `/api/base` and paints an overlay — and **ends with `window.location.reload()`**, which
is what made this small. A program switch cannot keep the selection, the trail or the
revision, because all three belong to the program being left; the reload discards them, and
`loadSettings(program)` restores the settings of the program being arrived at, because those
have been keyed per program all along. **No client state reconciliation had to be designed.**

`serve` needed **no CLI change**. It still takes a program directory; the siblings come from
`revisions.program_dirs(out_dir.parent)` — written earlier the same day to keep a program's
output out of its own corpus, and exactly the right question here.

### The two things that are not a mirror image

**The sidecars are repointed.** `source` and `docsource` live on `_Live` rather than `_Base`
because a *revision* switch does not change them. A program switch does, and forgetting it
would serve one program's bodies under another's map — rule 70 one axis over.

**Every cache is cleared, and `PROGRAM_CACHES` is stated separately.** Two caches survive a
revision switch deliberately, both documented as safe because they are keyed on one thing
rather than a pair. Neither is safe across programs:

- `findings` is keyed on `graph_db.name` — a **basename**. `output/mensores/graph@X.db` and
  `output/dunneflow/graph@X.db` key identically.
- `filepairs` is keyed on a pair of revision strings, and an unrevisioned directory yields
  `("", "")`. `output/beads` and `output/dunneflow` both do.

Neither needs a coincidence; it is what the keys are. The list is written out rather than
derived from `COMPARISON_CACHES`, because rule 36 cuts both ways — a generic loop narrowed to
a literal loses a feature silently, and a second switch reusing the first switch's literal
keeps a stale cache just as silently. The test fixture gives two programs the **same revision
id on purpose**, so a fix that did not clear `findings` cannot pass.

### Verified against the real output root

| | |
|---|---|
| the list | `beads`, `dunneflow`, `mensores` (serving, 628 files), `mensores@2026-08-29…` |
| switch to `dunneflow` | cover, navigator, graph and glossary all follow — 61 files, 707 routines |
| the sidecars follow | `walk.py` reads from dunneflow's sidecar; a mensores path is correctly *not held* |
| settings stay apart | scale 1.25 saved under `dunneflow:dunneflow:v5`; mensores comes back at 1 |
| four refusals, by name | no name · no such program · already being read · a switch already running |
| a name with separators | `../../etc` addresses nothing — the sibling list is the authority (rule 30) |

**And the failure that matters, on a real stale program.** Switching to `beads` failed with
the store's own sentence — *"stores absolute paths… run `dunneflow migrate …`"* — and the
server went on serving `dunneflow` with a working sidecar. That is the mode that would
otherwise take the whole dashboard down, tested against a directory that is genuinely stale
rather than a fixture pretending to be.

### A switch that replaces everything now says so

Both switches end in the same reload and leave the same one-shot note, and after a program
switch `switched.to` is a program name while `serving` is a revision — so the version branch
never matched and said nothing. Nothing false, but the one thing worth saying went unsaid: a
version switch *may* cost you your selection and a program switch certainly does.
`fromProgram` rides in the payload and the note reads *"Now reading dunneflow, switched from
mensores. This is a different program, so nothing you had selected or kept is on this map —
mensores's own settings and trail are waiting where you left them."*

*I reported that note as unrendered before checking the right selector; it renders in
`.verstrip-lost`, in the version strip, and always did.*

### 9 mutations, all CAUGHT — after 2 survived

Both survivors were my guards, not the code. The failure test used a directory with **no
graph**, which is refused before anything is repointed, so a mutation deleting the whole
restore line passed — a second test now fails *inside* the build, with a real sidecar beside a
corrupt graph, and asserts the abandoned handle is closed as well as the field put back. And
the POST guard looked for `_p_program` among the handler's string constants, which the route
table satisfies whatever path it is filed under, so renaming the route to `/api/programx`
passed it; it asserts the table now.

`/api/programs` is **1.0–1.2 ms warm**, 1.0 s cold, asked once at boot and not awaited. The
file count is carried only for the served program — every other would cost a 27 MB graph open
to learn, and a count nobody can afford is worse than no count.

951 tests, mypy clean, ruff clean, console clean.

## "+ Analyze a directory…" — the dashboard makes a program — 2026-09-04

The selector's second half, and the entry closes with it. The `<select>`'s last option opens
a dialog, the server reads a source tree, a panel reports each step, and the new program
arrives in the list with an *Open it* that is the program switch built the same day.

### A subprocess, and everything else follows from it

`sys.executable -m dunneflow.cli analyze …`, never an in-process call. Every store this
process opens is `writable=False` because rule 20 says serving may refuse but may never
repair — and an in-process analysis makes the serving process a writer to the tree it is
serving, which is that rule undone by construction rather than by accident. It also keeps
`walk.py`'s `ProcessPoolExecutor` out of a `ThreadingHTTPServer` request thread, and makes
what runs **exactly** the tested command rather than a second assembly of the same steps
that can drift from it (rule 51).

### Not the switch overlay, and not the switch's slot

A base switch blocks the whole page because every count underneath belongs to the version
being replaced. This reads some *other* tree into some *other* directory: nothing on screen
becomes untrue, so nothing is taken away. A dismissible panel that says so — *"The map on
screen is untouched. Keep reading."* — and it was driven for a full run with the map behind
it live and readable.

That forces a **second slot** on `_Live`. `claim`/`note`/`progress` are one build slot shared
by base and program switches; an analysis taking it would mean a ninety-second read of an
unrelated program locking the reader out of changing versions, for work that replaces
nothing. `claim_analysis`/`note_analysis`/`analysis_progress` sit beside them, written out
rather than derived, for `PROGRAM_CACHES`' reason (rule 36). `_started` gained the slot as an
argument so its *refusal carries no progress* rule is held once for both rather than copied.

*Candidate engineering rule, not minted, for Tom:* **a long job is not a switch — a slot names
what is being replaced, not what is running.**

### `--progress-json` is a contract, not a scrape

The child's **stdout** is one JSON object per line; its **stderr**, emptied by `--quiet`, is
where a failure says why. Two channels because scraping prose written for a human promotes a
sentence to a contract (rule 30), and the day somebody rewords `extracting 412/628` the bar
stops moving with no error anywhere.

The step list is **computed for the run**, not declared once: `--no-docs` drops two steps,
`--no-source` and `--no-render` one each, and a fixed total of seven is a bar a `--no-docs`
run can never reach — indistinguishable from a run that died at step five (rule 32). The
labels and the count are printed as sent, server to panel, so there is one answer to *what
does an analysis involve*.

`analyze_docs_tree` has taken a `progress` callback since it was written and had never been
given one; on a 2,064-document corpus the bar would have sat still through most of a minute.

Verified on the real corpus — `../society-2026-08-29/src`, 628 files, 2,064 documents: **63
lines, one total of 7, empty stderr, exit 0**, and the four `[project.scripts]` executables
still in *Where to start* with reach 1,381 · 423 · 292 · 112.

### Eight refusals, one function, and the sharp one

`analysis.check` answers *may this run* once, and both the dialog's live warning and the
endpoint's answer go through it — two readings would agree the day they were written and
drift on every day after (rule 41). Each refusal has **its own sentence**, asserted as words
rather than as a boolean, because a boolean is what a reader cannot act on: nothing named ·
a relative path · does not exist · is a file · **inside the output root** (rule 57 one
directory up) · not a name a directory can have · **the program being read** · a file sitting
where the directory would go · an analysis already running.

The served program is refused and **it is not caution**: `Store._discard_if_stale` drops
every table of a graph written by another build, and this server is holding that graph open,
so an analysis aimed here can empty the map under a live reader. A test asserts
`_discard_if_stale` still drops tables — a refusal whose reason has gone stale is one
somebody will remove.

Analysing into a name that **already exists** is allowed and *says* what it will do: it
rewrites that program's working snapshot rather than adding a point in time. Tom's call.

### Two defects found by looking, which is rule 38's whole argument

1. **A disabled `.linkbtn` did not look disabled.** The class sets an explicit background and
   colour, overriding everything the browser does to say a control cannot act — design rule
   16's defect arriving through a stylesheet instead of a missing handler. The rule already
   existed, scoped under `.trailbar`, and had rotted the moment a second caller appeared; it
   is beside `.linkbtn` itself now, where both pass (rule 51). Only for the case where a
   control **truly cannot work** — dimming to say *not current* is a different claim.
2. **A failed analysis handed the reader a fourteen-line traceback with the useful line
   last.** `FileExistsError: … output/blocked` under thirteen frames of `runpy`. True, and not
   a thing the reader this tool is written for can act on. The reason now **leads with the
   child's last line** and keeps everything it said underneath as the evidence — nothing
   invented, nothing dropped. And the case that produced it is a pre-flight sentence now.

### Looked at, with a real pointer

`elementFromPoint` on every control: each returns the element itself, not the scrim — rule
48's check, and the layers are 92/93 between the viewer's pair and the base switch's. 75
characters typed into the path field survived **75 repaints** with the caret held, which is
what the save-and-restore in `paintAnalyze` is for: the verdict arrives mid-word and rewriting
an `<input>` sends the caret to the end. And `/` does not leak to the topbar search, which
matters because every path on this machine begins with one.

The whole loop from a real click: analysed `src/dunneflow/render` as `rendercheck` — 11 files
· 90 routines · 9 documents · 6.6 s — appeared in the `<select>`, opened, served. The
directory was removed afterwards; it existed only to be driven.

**Still the automation tab**, though: 1,259×523 at a 16px root, screenshots cropping at
784×326, so each surface was seen by parking it inside the frame. Rule 38's debt is *reduced*,
not paid — Tom's 24px 4K window is still owed a look at the dialog's field widths.

### A coordinate trap, and one false bug it cost

The `computer` tool's coordinates are **screenshot space, not viewport space**. A click asked
for at (626, 186) landed at (1005, 298) — the 1.606× ratio of 1,259 to 784. The first click
therefore hit the scrim, closed the dialog, and let `/` focus the topbar search, which looked
exactly like *a global shortcut steals the first character of every path*. It is not; the
`typing` guard was correct all along. Multiply viewport coordinates by `784 / innerWidth`.
This is the *"clicks did not land where `getBoundingClientRect` said"* note from chunk 5,
explained rather than worked around.

A boot of `output/mensores` took **7.0 s warm and 63.7 s cold**, the cold one immediately
after a full analysis of the Society tree had evicted its pages. `STAT UN` throughout —
uninterruptible I/O, 0.25 s of CPU in three seconds. The external volume, as every cold row

967 tests, mypy clean, ruff clean.

## "About this map" — what read it, and whether anything was guessed — 2026-09-04

Chunk 2 of the same plan. Tom asked that an analysis **record what model was used**, in an
*"About this directory"* dialog, so a reader might analyse again when a better one exists.

### The premise was checked before it was built, and it was wrong in the best way

**No model is used.** Verified across `src/`: the extractors are stdlib `ast` and `tokenize`,
the document scanner is hand-written, and there is no LLM call and no network egress anywhere
on the analysis path. `Provenance` (`schema.py`) declares four tiers and only the two free
ones are implemented -- `CITED` ("a model found it in prose and cited file:line") and
`INFERRED` ("nothing states it; a guess") are both designed and both unbuilt.

Tom, on being told: *"Perfect, keep it that way as much as possible! Inference should always
be voluntary and secondary."*

That turned the feature from a placeholder into a **standing guarantee**. The two rows read
*none -- every fact here was read, not guessed* and *none -- this analysis is deterministic
and local*, and a reader handed a map is entitled to that in as many words rather than by
inferring it from an absence (design rule 21). The field that names a model exists so that a
reader who ever turns inference on, **voluntarily**, can see which facts it paid for.

A test asserts nothing under `extractors/`, `resolve/` or `canonical/` imports an HTTP client
or an LLM SDK. `web/` is excluded on purpose: it *is* an HTTP server, and the claim is about
what produced the facts rather than what serves them. A claim on screen that no query can
return is prose (rule 13).

### Missing and blank are different answers, and the whole thing rests on it

*This map cannot say* and *nothing was inferred* look identical in a blank cell, and only one
is a promise. Every field arrives as `{recorded, value, none}`. `output/dunneflow`, analysed
before these keys existed, renders *"not recorded -- written before this map could say"* in
italic, visibly apart from the guarantee; `output/mensores` is the same. Both were looked at.

**`none` is the server's decision, not the page's.** `inference` stores the word `none` so
`dunneflow query` over `meta` reads as prose; `model` stores blank, because there is no word
for the model that did not run. The page owned one spelling for an hour and rendered
*"Inferred facts: none"* -- a bare word where the sentence was the entire point of the row --
which is rule 51 caught on screen rather than in review. The layer that writes the value now
decides what it means, and the renderer reads a flag.

### The row that was planned and struck

*"Would a newer DunneFlow read this differently?"* was in the approved plan and is not built,
because for the map on screen it can only ever answer **no**: `Store` opened read-only calls
`_refuse_if_stale`, so a mismatched graph never becomes the base at all. Stating a comparison
whose answer is fixed by construction is worse than stating the guarantee that produces it.
The honest *should I read this again?* signal is the date beside it and the **tree leaf** it
was read from -- a leaf, never a path (rule 60), because a path is one machine's directory
layout in an artefact built to be handed over.

*Candidate design rule, not minted, for Tom:* **inference is voluntary and secondary, and a
map states whether any was used.** One step over from design rule 14, which scopes *egress*;
this scopes whether a fact was *guessed*.

### Four guards flipped, and none was deleted

The doorway is the topbar's `source directory` control, which was a `<div>` readout with no
pointer cursor and no hover -- deliberately, because nothing bound a source tree and a control
that renders while doing nothing looks exactly like one that works (design rule 16). Its own
markup set the condition: *"it becomes interactive when something needs to open a file from
disk."* This met it.

So each guard now protects the new decision, in the same rule read the other way round:

* *is a readout and does not present as a button* -> **presents as a button and is routed.**
  The rule was never "be a div"; it was *what presents as a control must act*.
* *is not overwritten by the client* -> **is written, from a field the server sends.** The
  ban on writing was the accident of the moment; rule 44's real content -- do not read a
  field nothing sends -- survives, and `source_root` is still forbidden (rule 60).
* *no longer sizes a string it cannot receive* -> **clips because it is written again.** Its
  own failure message had already named the reversal: *"it holds a path again, so the clip it
  used to carry has to come back with the binding."* Both halves flip together, and asserting
  them together is the point.
* And a fourth, `every_loading_placeholder_is_replaced_by_an_answer`, was satisfied rather
  than flipped -- `openAbout` gained its own `try`/`catch` so a failed fetch answers the
  placeholder instead of leaving it at "asking the server..." for ever.

One `.srcpath { ... }` block, not two: a second rule for the same selector wins on source
order and is invisible from the first (rule 29). The stale note above `.srcpath-v` was
rewritten as the reversal it is rather than left standing beside CSS that contradicts it.

### A second harness trap, and it cost another false start

**Click coordinates and screenshot coordinates are not the same scale, and neither is stable
between tabs.** The first tab took clicks at viewport x 0.62 and captured at viewport x 0.62.
The next took clicks at the same 0.62 and captured at **1.25** -- a *crop* of a magnified
render, not a downscale, so a centred dialog fell outside the frame entirely. Calibrate with
markers at known viewport coordinates before trusting either number.

And **clicks below roughly viewport y=48 never reached the page at all** -- no `pointerdown`,
not on any element. The topbar lives at y 8..45, so it cannot be clicked in this harness. The
button was proven from the **real keyboard** instead: it is a `<button>`, so it is in the tab
order, and Enter opened the dialog. For a control that has to be reachable without a pointer
that is the better proof anyway -- and it is a thing a `<div>` could never have passed.

977 tests, mypy clean, ruff clean, 0 broken.

## A stopped analysis, and the map it leaves behind — 2026-09-04

Tom, on the chunk that had just landed: *"what happens when a background analysis hangs,
crashes, or otherwise interferes with the user's next choice… the user disagrees, or asks to
override."* Four things were checked against the running code rather than reasoned about.
Three were defects. The fourth was worse than the question that prompted it.

### The finding that reframed it

**A killed `analyze` left a map that opens and lies.** Measured by stopping one twelve
seconds into the Society tree:

```
files 628 · routines 4,786 · boundaries 4,070 · resolved_calls 0
analysed_at 2026-09-04 21:54 UTC · tool_version 0.1.0 · inference none
```

It died before `resolve_calls`, so it reported a program that **calls nothing** -- with a
timestamp, a tool version and chunk 2's determinism guarantee on it, listed by
`program_dirs`, and opened by the switch without a word. That is a map that is wrong and says
nothing about being wrong, which `CLAUDE.md` names as the one outcome this tool may not
produce -- and it was reachable **with no stop button anywhere**: Ctrl-C, a laptop that slept,
an OOM kill, a full disk.

So the marker was the prerequisite rather than an extra. Cancelling without it would have
turned a rare accident into a button.

### The marker, and why it needed a commit

`analyze` writes `complete = ""` immediately after the revision is stamped and `"yes"` as its
last act, and records the **step** as each begins. All of it through `Store.set_meta_now`,
because `set_meta` does not commit and an uncommitted marker is lost by exactly the `kill -9`
it exists for -- at which point the graph reads as one that *predates the key*, which is the
ambiguity this exists to prevent arriving through the back door.

**Three states, never two.** Missing means written before the key existed and is fine; `""`
means started and never finished; `"yes"` means finished. Refusing on absence would refuse
every map made before today, none of which is broken. It is chunk 2's missing-versus-blank
distinction, one store over, and the reason the marker is written on the way *in*.

Verified against a real `kill -9` on the Society tree: `complete = ''`,
`step = 'reading the documents'`. **Re-analysing recovers it in 34 s** against a ~90 s cold
run, because the extraction is content-hashed and the working revision is reused -- so
*Analyse it again* is a fix and not advice.

`unfinished_sentence` is the one place those words live; four readers say it and a fifth
warns. `_Live.open` refuses (so the switch and `serve`'s boot both do), `_open_store` refuses
(so `touches`, `impact`, `glossary`, `naming`, `mirror` and **`check`** do -- `check` most
expensively, since a half-written map otherwise reports `0 broken` and greens a build).
`query` is the one exemption and it **warns**: its whole contract is that you get the rows
that are there, and an escape hatch that quietly hands over a half-written map is not an
escape hatch. `serve.why()` strips the class name from the two exceptions written to be read
-- a Python word landing first, in the one place the reader is not a programmer.

### The three defects that already existed

1. **Nothing could stop a run.** The `Popen` handle was a local inside `analysis.run`, so no
   route, no button and nothing short of killing the server could reach it. `_Live` holds it
   now and `POST /api/analyze/stop` ends it.
2. **The slot trusted a label.** `claim_analysis` refused on `state == "working"`, which a
   watcher dying without noting leaves true for ever -- a reader can see nothing running and
   still be refused. It asks `poll()` now and clears the stale lock rather than leaving it for
   somebody to notice. Rule 30, and the *"or locked"* half of the question.
3. **A reload orphaned the run.** `pollAnalysis` was called from `startAnalyze` and nowhere
   else, and nothing asked at boot. `resumeAnalysis` picks up a **live** run only -- a
   finished one belongs to the session that asked for it, and re-raising it every reload would
   be a panel nobody can dismiss.

### And the jam came back through the fix for it

`analyze` runs a `ProcessPoolExecutor`, and its workers inherit the pipes. `terminate()` on
the parent killed the parent and left **eleven workers** alive holding stdout open, so
`run`'s read loop never returned: `state: working` beside `running: false`, over a child that
had gone. The exact label-outlives-the-fact shape this chunk exists to remove, reintroduced
by its own cure.

Found by looking at `ps`, not by a test -- the tests were green, because the report *had*
settled correctly on the run before. The child gets `start_new_session=True` now and `stop`
signals the **group**, `SIGTERM` then `SIGKILL`. A test drives a real 400-file analysis and
asserts the reader thread **returns**, which it only does once every writer of the pipe is
gone.

A stopped run reports `state: "stopped"`, not `failed`. The distinction is read off the
child's own negative exit code rather than a flag set from outside that could disagree with
what happened (rule 13) -- and a reader who cancelled deliberately must not be told their run
broke.

### The silence is stated, and nothing acts on it

The slot records `began` and `moved`, and **`moved` bumps only when something actually
changed**: a timestamp refreshed on every identical poll would say a run was moving because
somebody was watching it, and *silent for 4 m* is the only thing separating a wedged child
from a long step. The panel says so in as many words -- *"Some steps are quiet for a while --
resolving a large program says nothing until it is done -- so this may be working. It may also
be stuck."* Resolution on Society is legitimately silent for tens of seconds, so a server that
decided for itself when a run had hung would kill healthy work. The reader decides.

Drawn in `--text-muted` on a plain rule rather than beside the failures in `--diff-gone`:
colouring a silence as trouble would make that judgement in the one channel design rule 4 says
to spend on a single dimension at a time.

### Two things written and then made true

* The refusal's *"Analyse works again as soon as it finishes"* was a promise nothing kept --
  the reader would have had to press the button to find out, and the elapsed time froze at the
  instant they pressed. `watchBlocked` re-asks while the dialog is open and **clears itself**
  when the run ends. A control that states a behaviour and does not have it is design rule 16
  in prose.
* *Analyse it again* on the switch-failure panel opens a dialog at z-93 -- under a scrim at
  z-96 that would have been left standing. Cleared before opening, which is the layer note in
  `tokens.css` applying to a second window that can open a third.

### Rule 80, minted

Tom, on being shown it: *"Good rule, mint that one."* **A job that can be interrupted must
leave something that cannot be mistaken for a finished one.** In `RULES.md` in full, indexed
in `CLAUDE.md`, and cited six times — the exception, the durable write, the read-path refusal,
the sentence that names the way out, the marker itself, and the tests.

The body carries the four halves that were paid for separately: a **partial result is not a
small result** (628 files really were read; what makes it a lie is the half that was not);
**three states, never two**, because refusing on absence would refuse every artefact made
before the rule; **the marker must be durable at the moment of the interruption**, or the
fix fails by its own failure mode; and **refuse on read, never on write** — `analyze` opening
an unfinished map is how it finishes one, so a refusal that locked out the only thing that
can repair would be rule 20 turned against itself.

*The stated rule count was already stale by one before this — it said 78 when 79 had been
minted. It now reads **79 rules numbered to 80**, since 21 does not exist and the numbers are
addresses.*

**`query` stays as it is, and that is now a decision rather than an open question.** Tom:
*"I like the fact that query returns but warns, that seems correct behavior for that
feature."*

*The other two candidates from this session are not minted and are named in `BRIEFING.md`:
a long job is not a switch, and inference is voluntary and secondary.*

### Looked at

All four cases driven in a browser. The panel came back after a mid-run reload with its
elapsed time reconstructed from `running_for` rather than restarted at zero; a second analysis
was refused with the running job named and a working **Stop it**; the elapsed figure was
watched ticking 7.0 s → 11.0 s to prove it was live; the selector reads *"coldrun2 — never
finished being read"*; and the switch to it is refused with the store's own sentence over an
**Analyse it again** that lands in the dialog name-filled and pointer-reachable.

990 tests, mypy clean, ruff clean.

## 2026-09-05 — the stated naming lane, on screen at last

**`doc_rules` has held naming rules somebody wrote since the document scanner existed, and
the dashboard had never shown one of them.** `11-naming.md` quoted them from the day the
column was added; `/api/naming` served `measure_naming(store)` and nothing else. This is step
2 of the four Tom ordered for the standards work — *serve the stated lane to the dashboard,
which shows none of it today* — and it is exposure, not comparison.

Measured before it was built, which is what shaped it:

| Map | Stated rules | Split | Documents |
|---|---|---|---|
| `output/mensores`, current revision | **12** | 7 FORM, 5 VOCABULARY | 2 of 2,064 |
| `output/dunneflow`, current revision | **0** | — | 9 read, none states a rule |

Both cases were already on disk, so the good one and the blank one could each be looked at
rather than reasoned about.

### Two pages, and Tom chose which

The obvious move was one page retitled *"Naming standard, as found"*, matching the Markdown
report exactly. Tom took the other option: **keep "Derived naming standard" and add a second
navigator row.** The word *derived* is load-bearing — the shell says so in a comment — and
putting a rule somebody wrote onto that page would have made it false of half the contents
while leaving the word standing. Two rows under Vocabulary now, stated above derived, because
what was written comes before what was done. Each page names the other and says, in the same
sentence, that **nothing compares them**.

Why the report can do what the navigator cannot: a document is read top to bottom and its two
sections announce themselves; a navigator row is read one word at a time.

### One reading, three readers

`resolve/stated.py`, beside `resolve/naming.py` whose first line says it is the Form lane and
means it. It takes `StatedRule`, the `doc_rules` query and the `checkable` sentence out of
`render/naming.py`, which had them because it was the only caller. `_checkable_line`'s own
docstring had already argued rule 51 for two lanes; a third surface is when that stops being
an argument and becomes a defect. The report's output is byte-identical across the move — only
the generation timestamp differs.

**`scope` and `pattern` are drawn for the first time.** They have been in the schema since the
scanner was written and read by nothing at all: `checkable` is computed from them and the
verdict was the only thing that ever left the store. A reader deciding whether to trust a rule
wants the halves, and the halves are where the interesting row is — *"Step names: snake_case"*
gives a spelling and names no identifier class, which is exactly why it is the one FORM rule
in this corpus that is not checkable. It is kept and says which half it is missing (design
rule 1), rather than being a rule with nothing visibly wrong with it.

### Three absences, three answers

Most programs state no naming rule, so the blank state is the common case and not the edge.
`read` travels beside the counts because no count can stand in for it: a map made with
`--no-docs` and a project whose documents genuinely say nothing both report zero. All three
were driven on real maps rather than reasoned about —

* **`--no-docs`**: *"This map was made without reading documentation… The derived naming
  standard is unaffected: it is counted off the code and needs no documents."*
* **nine documents, no rule**: *"9 documents were read, and not one of them states a naming
  rule. That is a finding rather than an absence of one…"*
* **documents scanned, none found**: its own sentence again.

`output/beads` was the fourth candidate and refused to open at all — unmigrated absolute paths,
rule 60's refusal naming `dunneflow migrate`, working exactly as written. Not repaired on the
way past (rule 20). The `--no-docs` map was made in the scratchpad and `output/` is untouched.

### The hop, and why it is a capability test

Every stated rule names a document and a line, so design rule 13 wants it to **open**.
`openDocumentAt` is chunk 5's and was already bound — but whether it can work depends on
`docsource.db` holding the version on screen, which is a fact about the process and the base
rather than about the rules. `/api/stated` carries a `corpus` block for exactly the reason
`/api/glossary` carries `sidecars`, and where it says no the reason is printed rather than the
button quietly dropped. Driven with a real pointer: a rule in `NAMING.md:17` opened the
document scrolled to the *Latin-only* block with `docflash` on it, rendered as prose — the
second reading, since the pane above is the bytes as measured.

### The thing only looking caught

The first drawing gave **CHECKABLE the accent green** the glossary spends on a DECLARED tier
and the naming page on an A grade. On screen it read as pass/fail, and that is not the claim:
a Latin-only rule is not a worse rule than a kebab-case one, it is a rule no query can decide.
Green already means *here is a route* on that page — the `.citego` on every citation — so the
badge was a second meaning for one colour on one screen (design rule 4). **Both badges are
neutral now**; the word carries the distinction and the sentence below spells it out.

### Also worth keeping

The **old-style** `output/dunneflow/docs.db` — pre-rule-60, absolute paths, superseded by the
revisioned store beside it — yields **136** stated rules, and all 136 come out of
`output/dunneflow/11-naming.md` and `output/mensores/11-naming.md`. That is DunneFlow mining
its own generated naming report back as somebody's naming standard: rule 57's hazard, closed by
`b92dec0`, preserved in a stale artefact. The current revision yields 0. It is not a live
defect, and it is why the page is built to render an unbounded list grouped by document rather
than to assume twelve (rule 8).

### The harness, calibrated again

Same trap, new numbers, and it must be re-measured every session because it is not stable
between tabs: this tab took **clicks at viewport × 0.395** and **captured at viewport × 0.79**,
cropped to the top-left quadrant — a 2× crop of a magnified render, exactly the shape the last
session recorded. Calibrated with five labelled markers at known viewport coordinates plus a
capturing click listener reading back `clientX/clientY`, which is the only method that settles
both scales at once. Viewport was 1,920 × 991 at a **16px root** — better than the 1,259 × 523
of the last session, still not Tom's 24px window, so **rule 38's debt is reduced again and not
paid**.

Two smaller things learned: a collapsed pane's own fold button has zero size, so the way back is
the **rail** (design rule 24 working as designed, and a scripted click on the fold is a silent
no-op); and `state.view` is not persisted for any page, so a reload landing on the cover is
design rule 17 rather than a regression — checked against `naming` before believing it.

### Gates

1,002 tests (12 new in `tests/test_stated.py`), mypy clean, ruff clean, console clean,
self-check *"every control is wired"*. `analyze` against Society: 628 files, 12 stated rules,
all four executables in "Where to start" with reach 1,381 / 423 / 292 / 112. `output/` holds
exactly what it held before.

## 2026-09-05 — a root package elected by no vote, and a package row that selects nothing

**Tom opened the `nodocs` map I made while verifying the blank state and found it broken.**
He was right, and it was two things: **I pointed `analyze` at the wrong directory**, and the
tool then failed in two ways that had nothing to do with documentation and everything to do
with what a package is.

My part: the map was `analyze src/dunneflow`, and the prescribed shape is the *parent* —
`analyze ../society-2026-08-29/src`, whose child is the package. I also left it on a port
without saying it was a throwaway built to read one sentence.

### 1. `root_package` could not fail

It returned the **modal** first dotted segment of `files.module`. Point `analyze` at a
directory that already *is* a package and every module is one segment shallower, no segment
is the root, and the biggest subpackage wins the vote — `web`, holding 20 of 63 files.
`package_expr` then sent every module not under `web.` down its `ELSE` branch and labelled it
`<external>`.

**750 of 752 routines drawn as somebody else's code**, on the largest plate in the picture,
over a map that opens perfectly with every count on the cover correct. Rule 49 exactly, and
found by Tom reading a map rather than by any test.

The tell is not marginal, measured over four maps:

| Map | root elected | covers |
|---|---|---|
| `output/mensores` (society/src) | `mensores` | **628 / 628** |
| scratchpad `rootcheck` (src) | `dunneflow` | **63 / 63** |
| scratchpad `nodocs` (src/dunneflow) | `web` | **20 / 63** |
| `output/dunneflow` | `web` | **19 / 61** |

So no threshold is invented: a segment that leaves one file out is not the root of the tree
that file is in, and `""` is a real answer. When there is no single root the tree itself is
the root and a module's package is its **first segment** — which is what analysing the parent
would have produced, so the two ways of pointing at one program now give identical packages.

**And the right test was already in the file.** `COVER_ROOT` asks the same question by
*grouping* — its docstring says "one row means every module agrees and the segment is a root;
more than one means the program has several top-level names" — and on this map it counted
**16 heads** and answered *no root*, in the same process, off the same store, while
`root_package` elected `web`. Two answers to one question a hundred lines apart, and only the
one nothing important depended on was right. They stay separate, because `COVER_ROOT` decides
what prefix a narrow *field* may drop and that is a display decision; what changed is that
neither is now the only one that checks.

`<external>` is `<outside the root>` now. Every row that expression sees is the program's own
— `routines` and `structures` hold what was extracted from its files and nothing else — and it
fired **0 of 4,786** times on Mensores. It only ever fired when the root was wrong, and what
it then said was not *"this module is not under the root"* but *"this is somebody else's
code"* (rules 26 and 30). Unreachable by construction now, kept and said honestly.

### 2. `COVER_PACKAGES` was a second decomposition, and the navigator selects by plate id

It took the **second dotted segment** without knowing the root. Its own comment claimed it was
*"the same decomposition the graph's disks use, so the navigator and the stack agree about what
a package is"*; `PACKAGE_SIZES`, a hundred lines below, said the opposite in as many words and
called it a hazard. **Both had been standing for two months.**

What neither noticed is that the navigator's Packages group selects **by plate id**
(`sel: pkg:${p.id}`), so a row the disks have no plate for selects nothing at all, and the
centre pane says *"Nothing to show."* with no reason available to it. Measured:

| Map | navigator rows | plates | rows selecting nothing |
|---|---|---|---|
| `output/mensores` | 46 | 46 | **1** — `mensores`, whose plate is `<root>` |
| `nodocs` (at the package) | 48 | 16 | **36** |

So it was live on the map everybody reads, once, and nobody had clicked that row. One
expression, three callers now (rule 51). `full_pkg` was selected there and read by nothing in
any file; it went with the decomposition it belonged to.

**Both fixes are at serve time**, so every existing map is fixed with no re-analysis —
`output/dunneflow` had the same wrong root and reads correctly now.

### 3. Not fixed, and it is Tom's call: a package row does not make a selection

His last symptom survives both fixes and **reproduces identically on Mensores**, so it is
neither my map nor either defect above. Clicking a package in the navigator marks the row
`aria-current="true"`, switches the pane — and leaves the crumb at *"nothing selected"*, the
table showing all 4,786 rows unchanged, and the inspector saying:

> *"Nothing selected. Pick a way in from the cover, **a package from the navigator**, or a
> node in the graph."*

The inspector names the gesture as one of three ways to select something, and doing exactly
that leaves it saying nothing is selected. That is the *"Analyse works again as soon as it
finishes"* shape from 2026-09-04 — a control stating a behaviour it does not have — and design
rule 16's family. It is why Tom could not tell what he was looking at: the table shows every
routine, sorted, so it opens on `anomalies.*` on one map and `mensores._config.*` on the other
and never moves.

**Not fixed here because it changes what selection *means*.** A package is a plate, not a node
(rule 30), so the options are a package-shaped inspector pane on the `viewInspectorConstant`
precedent — route on kind — or narrowing the table, or both. That is a design decision.

### Gates

1,007 tests (5 new in `test_graph_levels.py`; the three that matter fail without the fix,
verified by stashing the source and keeping the tests — stashing both proves nothing, which
cost one wasted check). mypy clean, ruff clean. Mensores' package grouping is unchanged: root
`mensores`, 46 packages, 0 outside.

## 2026-09-05 — ways in say what they are, and an application opens as one

Tom, reading Mensores' cover: *"they don't make sense in the way that code does… Are these
packages, modules, or applications? What is `mensores`, `mensores-mcp`, `run`?"*

**None of the three.** A way in is *how the outside world starts this program*, and the
fourteen on that cover are four kinds under two authorities:

| What | Which | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| `mensores`, `mensores-mcp`, `mensores-scriba`, `mensores-signator` | installed executables, `pyproject.toml [project.scripts]` | **declared** |
| `run`, `serve`, `main` ×5 | a module-level function recognised by its **name** | guessed |
| `WitnessHandler.do_POST` | an HTTP route — started by a request | guessed |
| `python -m mensores.chaos.*` | a `__main__` guard | guessed |

The cover drew all fourteen as a name, a kind tag and a bar. `ways_in()` computed `evidence`
and `declared` and `cover.py` dropped both before the wire — and five of the rows are called
`main`, distinguishable only by aliases that were on the wire and never drawn.

### (i) The row says what it is

`web/waysin.py` owns the answer, because the pane behind a click needs the same one (rule 51).
`DECLARED` / `GUESSED` on the row, the evidence **verbatim and unparsed** — it is this tool's
own sentence and it *is* the answer, and tidying it into fields would promote a sentence to a
contract for a column nobody asked for (rule 30) — and where it lives.

**A command tree has no definition site**, and none is invented (rule 1). `mensores` names
`mensores.cli:app`, a Typer object; the nearest true answer is the file the app is assembled
in, from `cli_mounts`, and `None` where even that is unrecorded. It says what it *spans*
instead — 107 routines across 44 files.

Neither badge is coloured. Green already means *here is a route* on that page and the severity
palette says something is wrong; a guess is neither (design rule 4).

### (ii) Clicking an application opens the application

`mensores` expands to 107 roots across 44 files. Selecting all 107 landed the reader on
whichever the query returned first — `mensores.cli.examples.list_cmd` from one, `_root` from
another. Not wrong so much as arbitrary, and nothing on screen explained it.

`/api/wayin` answers with the tree: **where execution begins**, the **sub-applications**
mounted on it with what each holds, and the **commands** hung directly on it — every row
carrying the node id that makes it an ordinary selection, so the stack lights, the inspector
fills, Code opens the file and the trail records the hop. Verified end to end with a real
pointer: cover row → pane → `quaestor` → `accept_cmd` → `mensores/cli/audit.py`.

Which of the two a way in *is* arrives as a declared field, never `len(nodes) > 1`: "this is a
tree" and "this happens to start several routines" look identical on the wire (rule 30).

A sub-application opens too, and **every count is recomputed for it** — carried down they read
107, 44 and 1,381 under a heading naming a group of 34, three numbers each true of something
the reader is not looking at (rule 24). The id is **verified to be mounted under this way in**,
never trusted: a parameter is not a permission, and falling back to the root would hide the
failure it was written for (rule 49).

### Three found while building it

1. **The application listed itself as one of its own commands** (rule 74) — the console-script
   row is a child of the app object too. Filtered on `grp`, the schema's own field for *the app
   object this command attaches to*, rather than on the name matching, because a command named
   after its executable is a thing programs do (rule 5).
2. **Keeping it out then left the entry routine named by nothing**, so `unlisted` counted the
   program's own front door as *"a registration idiom DunneFlow followed far enough to count
   and not far enough to name"* — a limitation confessed where there is none (rule 32). `entry`
   is its own answer now, and it is the most interesting routine in the tree.
3. **A group counted by its direct children read `telemetry 0`** for a group holding commands
   one mount further down. Counted with `app_command_routines`, the same function `ways_in`
   counts the whole tree with, so a count and the claim beside it cannot disagree (rule 13).

### And one that was mine, caught by the guard it prompted

`selectionSnapshot()` and `sameSelection()` were **two hand-kept lists of the same fields**.
`wayIn` went into the snapshot and not into the comparator, so drilling into a sub-application
filed a step labelled `mensores ▸ quaestor` which was deduplicated against `mensores` and
discarded — **rule 33's symptom with the subject present and correct**. The comments on
`diagramId`, `diagramBox` and `codeFile` each record paying this once, in the snapshot, where
the lesson never reached the half that forgets.

`SUBJECT_KEYS` is the one list now, and a new guard asserts the two agree. **It immediately
caught a second field**: `wayInsideName`, which is a *label* and is excluded deliberately —
`recordSelection` gave up deduplicating on labels because two routines can share a name, and a
subject that is partly a label is that mistake returning one field at a time (rule 30).

Two existing guards read the field name out of `sameSelection`'s body and had to be repointed
at the list. They are **stricter** than before, which passed on the name appearing anywhere in
the body, a comment included — and both were re-proved by breaking the source with the tests
kept.

### Not proven, and said rather than claimed

* **The pointer path for the sub-application button.** `elementFromPoint` says it is topmost
  and a scripted click drives the whole chain, but three real clicks in a row reported
  *"Clicked at (x, y)"* and delivered **no event at all** — a capture-phase listener on
  `document` recorded nothing. The harness stopped delivering clicks mid-session, having
  delivered two earlier in the same tab. Rule 48: the handler is proven, the path to it is not.
  The cover row and the command row *were* pointer-proven before it stopped.
* **A one-off boot failure I could not reproduce.** After a server restart the page rendered
  *"showing 0 of 0 routines"* with every endpoint healthy — `/api/cover` returning 14 ways in
  and 46 packages, `shell.js` parsing. Clearing `localStorage` fixed it; re-setting the one
  field that looked suspect (`mode: "code"`) did **not** reproduce it, and the stale blob is
  gone. Unexplained, and filed as unexplained rather than as fixed.

### A mistake worth recording

`git checkout <file>` to undo a one-line probe **reverted the whole day's work in that file**.
Recovered from a scratchpad copy plus re-applying nine edits by hand, and re-verified from the
gates and the browser. A scratchpad copy before a destructive probe is what made it a
twenty-minute detour rather than a lost afternoon; the lesson is to revert the probe, not the
file.

### Gates

1,023 tests (18 new: `tests/test_waysin.py`, plus the subject-keys guard), mypy clean, ruff
clean, `output/` untouched.

## 2026-09-05 — ways in are nodes on the Diagram

Tom's option (iii), taken up an hour after (i) and (ii) landed and it was deferred: *"see the
various Ways In as nodes on a Diagram and chase them inbound to see how the data flows into
the system."*

A way in is now a **box on every compartment it enters**, with bold arrows into the boxes it
starts. `pkg:signator` reads as the feature is meant to: `mensores-signator` → `__main__.py`,
`WitnessHandler.do_POST` → `WitnessHandler`, `serve` → `_server.py`, and from those the
ordinary arrows carry on down through `_keygen`, `_custody`, `_signing`, `_consistency`,
`_chain`. That is the chase.

### Drawn by default, unlike a port, and the difference is measured

Rule 19 turned ports off on evidence: median **13** and max **41** per compartment against a
median of 10 boxes — they outnumber the subject and connect what `pack` needs disconnected.
Ways in are **max 3 per compartment and absent from 46 of 53**. Same rule, opposite answer,
because it is a different population; both numbers are in the docstring so the next reader can
check that rather than take it. Told apart by a **note silhouette**, never colour — colour on
that page is already spent on difference and severity (design rule 4).

### The arrow bound is one compartment's number

| `pkg:cli` | size | aspect |
|---|---|---|
| before | 734×650pt | 1.1:1 |
| **all 43 arrows** | **3647×428pt** | **8.5:1** |
| bounded at 8 | 1017×674pt | 1.5:1 |

`mensores` enters **39 of `pkg:cli`'s boxes** — nearly every file in the package — and
unbounded it produces the horizontal strip this module's docstring already records Mermaid
producing, arriving through a different door. **No other compartment reaches the bound**: the
next largest fan-out in 53 is three, so this is a bound on the one picture that needs it.

Bounded **per way in**, not per compartment: one fan-out would otherwise push another way in's
single arrow out of the drawing. The panel states it — *"entered from 1 way in, reaching 43
boxes — 8 arrows drawn"* — and opening the box lists all 106, because that is an answer and
not a picture (rule 8, design rule 1).

Tom chose this over "no arrows at all" and over "draw them all, however wide".

### What it must not disturb

`entries` and `entered` are their **own list and lane**, never `boxes` and `inside`. *"57
boxes over 321 routines"* is about the program's own code; a way in is the world outside
reaching into it, and folding them in would have grown that number by one and quietly changed
what it meant (rule 32). Two tests hold it: every count a panel prints is unchanged, and a
compartment with no way in emits a **byte-identical `dot`**.

A box holds what the way in starts **here**, not its reach — `mensores` reaches 1,381 and
starts 106 in `pkg:cli`, and the hover card says *"starts 106 routines in this compartment"*
rather than a bare number that would read as the first (rule 24).

### Two joins, and one refusal

Clicking a way-in box opens the **way-in pane** built earlier the same day, so (ii) and (iii)
are one path rather than two features about one subject.

An **entry arrow is recognised but refuses to open as a flow**. `/api/flow` lists every call
site with its arguments as written; a way in is started by the operating system, so there is
no caller in this program to list. It answers with a sentence saying so and naming what it
starts — an empty panel would read as *"this arrow carries nothing"*, which is a different and
false claim (design rule 21, and `edge_flow`'s own distinction between no arrow and an empty
one).

`build(model, ways)` takes the map as an argument rather than looking it up: this module takes
a model and never a store, and `waysin.listing()` stays the one place the question is asked
(rule 51).

### Verified

Measured against the plan's own table on the running server — `pkg:cli` 1017×674 at 1.5:1 with
43 entered and 35 hidden, `pkg:signator` 466×378 at 1.2:1, `pkg:quaestor` (no ways in)
unchanged — and **looked at** by rendering the served `dot` source through the same Graphviz
the browser uses. The panel sentence and the click into the way-in pane were driven in the
page.

*The harness bit again and was worked around rather than fought:* the automation window is
1,259×523, so the drawing canvas sits below the visible frame and no screenshot of it is
possible; `zoom` takes **screenshot-frame** coordinates while `scrollIntoView` reports viewport
ones. Rendering the served DOT to PNG is the better instrument anyway — it is the same source
the browser draws, at a size a person can read.

### Gates

1,030 tests (7 new in `test_diagram.py`), mypy clean, ruff clean, `output/` untouched.

## 2026-09-05 — Document mode is about the selection, and the contents stops sitting on the prose

Tom, with a screenshot: he selected `signator.__main__`, pressed **Document**, and got a
document about PAUL style rules stored in `harness/rules/style.md`. *"Not at all sure why
that appeared, what is the relevance, if any?"* And scrolling, the table of contents stayed
put on top of the text.

Two defects, unrelated to each other.

### 1. The pane was a place, not a view of the selection

`state.docPath` held whatever document had last been opened — his came from a stated naming
rule's *Read it in the document*, twenty minutes earlier — and **nothing ever connected it to
what was selected**. The mode toggle's own sentence is *"five ways of reading one selection"*,
and one of them was not. The 2026-09-03 session *"no pane assumes what it was showing is still
true"* is the precedent; this pane was missed in that pass.

### The obvious relation does not exist, and it is written down so nobody mines it again

`doc_refs` holds **37,150 PATH** and **114,067 CODE** references, which sound exactly like the
answer. They are not:

* the PATHs are **document** paths — `INTENT.md`, `GLOSSARY.md` — and
  `mensores/signator/__main__.py` matches **zero** of them;
* the CODE refs are CLI flags and template placeholders (`--codebase`, `{{ crash_payload }}`),
  so `WitnessHandler` matches **zero** and `main` matches **38**, which is rule 5 waiting to
  happen.

### And naming an id is not the same as being related

The governance join is real — **6,976 of 6,993** code annotations carry an id some document
also names — but it is not selective:

| | |
|---|---|
| ids a routine carries | median **2** |
| documents naming at least one | median **281**, p90 1,077, max 1,679 of 2,064 |
| documents naming **every** one | median **4** |
| routines with ≥2 ids landing in 1–10 | **617 of 1,021** |

A filter that returns a seventh of the corpus has not filtered. So `related.py` **ranks rather
than filters**: the band naming every id is the answer, the rest is counted and offered behind
a fold, and both numbers are on the page (design rule 1, rule 32). On the real corpus a
routine citing `CW-2` and `PLAN-75-1` gets **2 documents naming both** — `.groma/ROADMAP.md`
and `75-01-PLAN.md`, the plan itself — with 51 more naming one.

**Answered per selection at 6.8 ms**, measured over 100 routines, not built at boot:
`traceability.measure()` does the whole join in **4.7 s**, which is right for a report and
wrong for a click. It borrows that module's `normalise` and nothing else (rule 51) — 14 ids
are spelled differently between the two stores, so raw matching would miss them.

**The open document is not closed when the selection moves** — Tom's call, over closing it:
a reader who is reading should not have the page taken away. What changed is that it *says*
which it is. Related, it names the shared ids; unrelated, it says so and how the reader got
there, with a button to what is related. **59% of routines carry no id at all**, so that is the
common case and it gets a sentence rather than an empty list (design rule 21).

### 2. The contents was sticky inside a wrapping flex box

`.docnav` is `position: sticky; top: 0` inside `.docread`, which is `display: flex;
flex-wrap: wrap`. Sticky is right while the nav is a **side column**. Its two bases are
12rem + 26rem + a 1.2rem gap ≈ **941px**, wider than the centre pane at a 24px root — so it
wraps to its own full-width row, and sticky then pins that row over the prose. Design rule
53's shape: a layout right at one window size.

**A `@media` query cannot fix it.** It answers about the *viewport* rather than about this
pane, and `rem` inside one resolves against the initial font size rather than the page's —
rule 28, already paid for once in this file. `@container` answers about the pane and its `rem`
*is* the page's, so the threshold moves with the scale control like every other dimension
(design rule 3). Measured through the DOM at four widths: **sticky at 77.8rem and 43.8rem,
static and stacked at 35.0rem and 30.0rem** — it stops sticking in the same breath it stops
being a column.

### And one I caused, found by looking

The doc chrome repaints **only when `docDomKey()` changes** — a bargain measured at 9.5 s per
`render()` without it. The related block lives in that chrome, so it painted *"Looking for
documents related to `<module>`…"*, the answer arrived 7 ms later, `render()` ran, and the
sentence never changed. The key carries `relDomKey()` now, and says in as many words that
every field added to this pane has to be added there too or it is invisible the moment it
settles.

### A fixture that was wrong, not the code

The first draft of `test_related.py` expected `ROADMAP.md` to match `PLAN-75-1` from the prose
`PLAN-75-1`. It does not: in prose that is mined as the **ticket** `PLAN-75`, and only the
spelled-out `Plan 75-01` normalises to `PLAN-75-1`. The fixture was corrected and the reason
kept in a comment, because it is the same trap a reader of the real corpus would hit.

### Not chased

* The inspector's *"GOVERNANCE 6"* on that module is its six `noqa: E402` **comments** — that
  block renders annotations and comments together. Existing behaviour; the label does double
  duty and it is not wrong.
* `serve --port 8787` **fell back to a free port** when the previous process still held it,
  and said which port it was using but not that it could not have the one asked for.
* Full-text search of the corpus for a routine's name would raise the 41%, and is rule 5's
  territory — it wants its own measurement before anyone builds it.

### Gates

1,037 tests (7 new in `test_related.py`), mypy clean, ruff clean, `output/` untouched.

## 2026-09-05 — three rules minted: 81, 82, and design rule 28

Tom: *"mint the cache key rule"*, then *"Also mint the rules for a long job is not a switch,
and inference is voluntary and secondary."* All three had been standing as candidates — two
since 2026-09-04, one from the same day as the minting.

### Rule 81 — a key that decides whether to skip work must carry everything the work depends on

**Checked against rule 78 before a number was taken**, because I had flagged it myself as
possibly that rule restated. It is not. Rule 78 is a pane *nobody asked to update*: the guard
had two halves and only one had an event. Rule 81 is a pane that **was** asked, whose state
**was** correct, and whose paint was skipped — `render()` ran, `RELDOCS` held the right object
with `loading: false`, and `relDocsBlock()` called by hand returned the right markup. The fixes
land in different places: 78 moves the reconcile into `render()`, 81 puts the field in the key.

**It happened twice in one session in two unrelated caches**, which is what earned it an
address rather than a comment. `docDomKey()` did not carry the related block's state, so the
sentence froze seven milliseconds before the answer arrived. `selectionSnapshot()` and
`sameSelection()` were two hand-kept lists of the same fields and `wayIn` went into one, so a
trail step that was correct in every respect was deduplicated away. The comments on
`diagramId`, `diagramBox` and `codeFile` each record paying it once — in the snapshot, where
the lesson never reached the half that forgets.

And the guard written for it **caught its next instance while it was being written**:
`wayInsideName`, recorded and deliberately not compared, because it is a label and the trail
gave up deduplicating on labels for rule 30's reason.

### Rule 82 — a long job is not a switch

Carried from 2026-09-04's analyse work. The lesson is not about cost or duration: it is **what
the reader loses while it runs**. A base switch replaces what is on screen, so blocking is
honest; an analysis of some other tree replaces nothing, so it gets a dismissible panel and a
second slot. Name the thing being replaced, and if the answer is *"nothing on this screen"* it
is not a switch however long it takes. The second half is rule 30's: a slot asks the process,
never a label.

### Design rule 28 — inference is voluntary and secondary

Carried from 2026-09-04's *About this map*. Filed as a **design** rule because that is what it
was proposed as, and because it sits one step over from design rule 14: 14 scopes what may
*leave* the machine, 28 scopes whether a fact was **guessed**. Tom's words are in the body —
*"Perfect, keep it that way as much as possible! Inference should always be voluntary and
secondary."*

### Bookkeeping

`RULES.md` carries 81 and 82 in full, `DESIGN-RULES.md` carries 28. `CLAUDE.md`'s two indexes
list all three and its table now reads **81 engineering rules numbered to 82** — 21 still does
not exist — and **28 design rules**; `BRIEFING.md`'s header table matches. Cited at
`relDomKey`, `SUBJECT_KEYS`, `claim_analysis` and `_r_about`.

**The two stale counts in the dated 2026-09-04 sections were left alone.** They say what was
true on their date, and the record's convention is that a dated section is history; the two
header tables are where the current count lives.

1,037 tests, mypy clean, ruff clean.

## 2026-09-05 — a read that wrote, `<module>` answered as itself, and a plate made a subject

Three commits, and the first one is a defect this session **caused and then found**.

### A read never brings a database into being — `8a76b43`

Reconnoitring the plate model, a one-line probe opened
`Store(Path("output/mensores/graph.db"), writable=False)`. That path does not exist in
that directory — mensores keeps only `graph@<revision>.db` — and `sqlite3.connect`
**creates**. A 0-byte file landed in the output tree, invisible to `git status` because
`output/` is untracked.

**The file is the harm, not the failed query.** The query that followed raised
`no such table: files`, so nothing answered wrongly that time; what remained was the file.
`revisions.py` reads a bare `graph.db` as *"a directory written before this layout
existed"* — the one legacy revision of that program — so a **read** had given mensores a
fifth revision holding nothing at all. Rule 20 from the side nobody expects: the read
repaired nothing, it wrote.

**And it is rule 51 exactly, with the count as the argument.** Seven read paths each
carried their own `if not path.exists()` — `cli._open_store`, `_Live._docs_for`,
`_open_source`, `_open_docsource`, and the version-listing branch of `_r_revisions`. Every
one was correct, and the guard held for exactly as long as somebody remembered to write it.
The caller that did not remember was none of them. `refuse_missing` moves it to where they
all pass; all four stores obey it (rule 61), and `DocSourceStore` refuses as itself because
the stamp is the difference (rule 16).

`FileNotFoundError` rather than an exception of ours, for two reasons already in the code:
it is an `OSError`, which is what the four sites in `serve.py` catch to mean *"absent is a
real state, never an error"*, so `corpus.serving()`'s four states are untouched; and
`serve.why()` states that a class name earns its place in front of one.

**One test caught a defect in itself.** The phantom-revision claim sat *after* a
`pytest.raises`, so against the unfixed constructors it failed on the raise and never
executed the lines it existed to prove — a test that appeared to demonstrate the
consequence and had never once run it. Rule 37, on the guard written for rule 51. Split in
two: the fact about `revisions` is now asserted on its own and is true with the fix and
without it.

Ten tests. Six fail against the unfixed constructors and four pass — the writer, the absent
sidecar, the empty-file boundary — which is the pair that says this is a refusal and not a
wall. Tom's call: fix it now rather than file it.

### `<module>` is answered as what it is — `c54f2fb`

Carried from the open list. The inspector answered about module scope in a shape built for
a routine, and so stated **two** things untrue of any of the 487 `<module>` nodes on
Mensores.

*"Nothing in this map calls it. That is either a way in, dead code, or a call DunneFlow
cannot see."* Three explanations, all three false. Measured: **487 module nodes, 0 with any
caller, 0 that are entrypoints**, against baselines of 6,441 calls over 2,866 callees and
178 entrypoints of which 170 resolve — so the zeros are answers, not a broken join. Nothing
can call module scope, because module scope is what runs *instead* of being called. The
true sentence was already on the page directly underneath, as the extractor's own
docstring, and a reader had to resolve the contradiction unaided. Both are kept: one says
why nothing calls it, the other says when it runs.

**`def <module>():`** — not in the filed entry, found while fixing the first. A complete,
plausible, copyable declaration of a routine nobody wrote, offering a call that cannot be

**Not a separate pane.** Out, Touches and Governance are all correct for module scope, and

**Three gaps fixed on the way, each pre-existing and each the same shape.** The table marked

Measured on Mensores and recorded in `PERFORMANCE.md`: **2.4–9.7 ms** for a package plate,

**The pane has never been seen, and that is recorded rather than glossed.** Every figure
