## 2026-09-08 — the maps that could not be opened, and the command they were sent to

The second item of the scheduled pass read: *"Two maps in `output/` cannot be opened, both
refusing exactly as designed and both one command away."* Two of those three claims were
wrong.

**There were three, not two.** `revisions.program_dirs(output/)` lists four — `beads`,
`dunneflow`, `mensores` and `mensores@2026-08-29T19-43-39Z` — and only `mensores` opened.
The fourth had never been counted because nothing had opened it since the layout that named
it went away.

**And the command each was sent to would have refused it.** `Store._refuse_if_stale` is
written to name *which* of two fixes applies, and its docstring is careful about why:
`migrate` rewrites in place and keeps a sealed snapshot whose source tree may be long gone,
so telling that reader to re-analyse asks them to rebuild from a tree they do not have. But
the test it used was `paths_are_relative` alone — *when* the store was written — while the
thing that decides is `_require_previous`, which admits exactly one fingerprint, on the claim
that making paths relative is the only thing that changed. Two facts, one test, and the
sentence was reading the wrong one.

Every store older than that single gated version was therefore told to run
`dunneflow migrate`, and the migration refused it in turn. Rule 49's shape in prose: a
plausible remedy standing where the real one should be, and it costs nothing at all until
somebody keeps an old map.

Run, all three said so:

```
refused: graph.db was written by extractor (unrecorded), and this migration can only
speak for 5:ec365db458b9d64e …
refused: source.db holds bodies for 2026-08-29T19:43:39Z and there is no graph beside it
recording which tree they were read from …
```

`beads` carries no `extractor` key at all and `schema_version 1`; `dunneflow` and
`mensores@2026-08-29T19-43-39Z` carry `5:20ecd553bee5e82b` and `5:c9bf8451cc07caa7`, neither
of them the gated value. Nothing was damaged by trying: `_migrate_one` refuses before
`BEGIN`, and `migrate_program` reads the sidecar first, so the second directory's graph meta
was byte-identical afterwards.

**The fix is one predicate, in the module that owns the gate.** `migration_speaks_for` lives
in `migrate.py` beside `_require_previous`, and both refusals ask it — `store.py` on
`PREVIOUS_CODE_EXTRACTOR`, `docstore.py` on `PREVIOUS_DOC_EXTRACTOR`, the compared value
being the only thing that differs (rule 51; the two sentences were already copies of each
other, and a copy is where this kind of thing goes unnoticed twice).

It tests the fingerprint and **deliberately not the recorded root**. `_migrate_one` has a
second refusal — a store recording no tree has nothing to be made relative *to* — and
answering that here would mean rebuilding `recorded_roots`' per-revision bookkeeping inside a
read path in order to word a sentence. It is also reachable only *past* this gate, so a store
this admits and the migration then refuses is told the truth twice, one refusal after the
other, which is the honest failure rather than the plausible one.

**The guard that was missing is the one for the case nobody had.**
`test_a_reader_refuses_an_unmigrated_store_names_the_fix_and_repairs_nothing` builds its
legacy store *with* the gated fingerprint, so it passed before and passes now. The new one
stamps an older fingerprint, asserts the refusal names `analyze` and not `migrate`, and then
asserts `migrate_program` would indeed have refused it — so the sentence is readable off the
thing that decides it (rule 13). A second guard asserts both modules ask the predicate and
neither still branches on `paths_are_relative`.

**Then the maps themselves.** `dunneflow` re-analysed into its own working revision (71
files, 849 routines, 9 documents — `program_dirs` keeping `output/` out of its own corpus,
which is what that function was written for). `beads` re-analysed too: it is a **Go** program
with 30 Python files, of which 14 are in the map, so it was always a probe rather than a
subject — but a probe that lists in the selector and refuses is worth one command. Three of
the four now open.

**The fourth is a decision rather than a defect.** `output/mensores@2026-08-29T19-43-39Z` is
an old-style directory whose name is a revision stamp from before the revision layout existed,
and its `source_root` is `mensores-overhaul` — the third tree `CLAUDE.md` warns is neither end
of the pair, and which cost a wasted analysis once already. Re-analysing it would re-read
exactly that tree into a directory whose name is a leftover. Left for Tom: drop it, or leave
it listed and refusing.

*Two dead files sit beside each of the rebuilt maps* — a bare `graph.db` and `docs.db` from
before the revision layout, superseded by the `graph@…` pair and never chosen by
`revisions.newest`. Inert, and not swept: `sourcedb.py` owns no `DROP` by design, and this is
the same manual pass a superseded sealed snapshot gets.

## 2026-09-08 — the looking pass: two answers, one dead sentence, and 335 rows

Item 1 of the scheduled pass was three things that had never been *looked* at. Two are now
answered and the third is still Tom's eye — but the looking found something nobody had
scheduled.

### The instrument, first, because it decided what could be verified

Rule 83 measured rather than assumed: **pointer space and capture space are both 784 px wide
and differ by exactly 2×.** The pointer spans the whole 1222×553 viewport (a hover at
(400,200) arrives at `clientX/Y` (623,312), a factor of 1.5581); the capture spans only the
top-left 611×277 CSS px of it. So `pointer = viewport / 1.5581` and
`viewport = screenshot × 0.779`, and `transform: translate(-336px,-219px)` on the body pans
one over the other. The window would not resize — `resize_window` reported success and
`innerWidth` never moved — so this is the frame the whole session ran in.

**And the pan breaks what it lets you see.** Hovers dispatched while the body carried a
transform reached nothing at all; the same coordinates un-panned reached the canvas. Pan to
find a target, un-pan to touch it.

### A kept fold and a kept flow both open

Verified at the pointer, in `pkg:standards` (20 boxes, 9 arrows). Keeping the `EarsValidator`
box and the `FrameworkRegistry → _framework_plugin.py` arrow wrote two subjects to
`dunneflow:mensores:v6` carrying `kind: "fold"` and `kind: "flow"`, and the shelf said
*"◆ 2 kept"*.

Opening the **fold** from the shelf returned to Diagram mode and the `standards` compartment,
outlined the box, lit its two routines in the navigator and filed a trail step. Opening the
**flow** filled the inspector with the arrow itself — `class → file`, `FLOW CALL`, *1 along
it*, `◆ Kept`, the one call site with its argument bound (`criteria_raw → criteria: object`)
and *Touches 0* with its own sentence — and lit both ends (`node dgm-on`). No console error
on either.

**The stated cross-compartment limitation is honest.** `PIN_ROUTES.flow` says a flow kept in
one compartment and opened from another "is routed anyway and says nothing false". Switched
to `pkg:adr` and opened it: the compartment stayed `adr`, nothing lit, and the inspector
opened on the arrow itself with every field intact. Exactly as written.

*Two pluralisations noticed in passing and not fixed:* "**1 boxes**" in the compartment
selector and "**1 call sites**" on the keep button's note.

### The hover card's shadow sentence is dead code, and rules 23 and 31 killed it

`e60c050` named this as the one thing it could not verify. It cannot be verified because it
cannot happen.

`hoverSkeleton` draws *"A stand-in. This routine lives on X — the copy you are pointing at is
a placement device and is never an endpoint"* when `h.shadow` is true. `h.shadow` is
`raw2.shadow[i] === 1` at the **picked** index, and there are exactly two ways that index is
set:

* **The node layer.** A shadow is given `radii[i] = 0` and `colors[i*4+3] = 0` — never drawn,
  so never picked. Measured: a sweep of the whole drawn stack returned **1,989 picks over 562
  distinct nodes and not one shadow**, against 5,855 shadows in the payload.
* **The rim-arrow layer.** `pointerData` builds each mark as
  `{ index: realIndex(d, p.index) }` — with the comment *"a shadow is never an endpoint (rules
  23, 31)"* — so `info.object.index` is always real too.

There is no third path: the reticule layer over the top is `pickable: false`.

So the branch renders for nobody, and it renders for nobody *because the rule it describes was
applied correctly everywhere else*. The engine's own comment above `emit('hover', …)` still
says "`shadow` still travels, because the reader is entitled to know they are pointing at a
stand-in" — written when a shadow could still be pointed at. **Design rule 16 from the far
side:** a control wired to a condition that can no longer arise looks exactly like one that
works, and no test that did not already know the branch existed could say otherwise.

*Left for Tom rather than deleted:* the honest fix is to withdraw the branch, the `shadow`
field and that paragraph together, recording that rules 23 and 31 closed it. That is a
deletion of reasoning somebody wrote on purpose, so it is his call.

*Also worth knowing:* deck.gl's own `pickObject` answers correctly at every one of those
points, so the picture is not at fault — what fails is the **extension's** synthetic
`mousemove`, which never becomes the `pointermove` mjolnir listens for. Rule 72 exactly: an
instrument that cannot reproduce a gesture reports its absence just as confidently. The
hover card cannot be verified at the pointer with this instrument at all, which is what
`e60c050` was really recording.

### And the thing nobody scheduled: 335 navigator rows print their name over their counts

Found by looking at a screenshot of an ordinary routine list.
`standards._framework_registry._schema_validator` runs straight through its own `1← 1→`, and
`_maybe_apply_source_o…` through `1← 5→`. Measured across the whole navigator at scale 1:
**335 of 1,395 rows overlap, 24%**, worst case **101 px** of overprint where a 62 px box holds
170 px of text.

**Rule 53, exactly.** The remedy already in the stylesheet is two shrink classes chosen in
`dressNavItems` from the **character count alone** — `>25` is `xlong`, `>17` is `long` — and
the budget is not a property of the name. `.navsub` takes up to 11rem of the row, so the room
left for the label swings from about 200 px down to 68 px depending on how long the *module
path* is. The classes are being applied and are not enough: **65 of 84 `xlong` rows still
overlap, and 103 rows carrying no class at all overlap too** — one of them ten characters
long.

`selfCheck` cannot see it: it inspects `[data-fit]` elements, and a nav item's `.navlabel`
carries no `data-fit`, which is why it reports every control wired while a quarter of the
primary way in is unreadable.

The stylesheet holds **two comments arguing for two different mechanisms** over the same
declaration — *"A long name wraps rather than being cut… the count stays put"* and *"A long
name shrinks to fit rather than breaking mid-token"* — and neither is what happens. What
happens is that `overflow-wrap: normal` forbids a break inside a single token, so the flex
item cannot shrink below its min-content width and simply paints outside its box.

**The fix is a design call and is Tom's**, because every obvious mechanism is one the existing
comments reject: truncation hides a name with nothing beside it, `overflow-wrap: anywhere`
gives `do_PO / ST`, and shrinking further is more small type. The fourth option is rule 84's
shape — let the row grow and put the counts on their own line when the name will not fit
beside them. `navWidth: 21` was widened from 14.5 with the note *"a qualified name is the
thing it has to be able to show"*, and 335 rows say it still cannot.

## 2026-09-08 — Tom's three calls, and two measurements I had to take twice

### The dead shadow branch, withdrawn

Tom's call. The `hc-shadow` "A stand-in…" row is gone from `hoverSkeleton`, the `shadow`
field is gone from the hover payload, and the paragraph in `graph.js` that explained why it
travelled is rewritten to say why it no longer does. The **resolution** stays — `raw2.shadow[i]
? raw2.real[i] : i` is what makes rules 23 and 31 true from that handler — only the flag went,
because a field that is always `false` is a claim the card cannot use.

`.hc-shadow` the CSS class survives: the *lean* sentence beside it still uses it. The comment
that said the lean row was written "on `hc-shadow`'s pattern" now says the class was named for
a row that is gone, so nobody reads it as being about shadows.

`test_no_hover_can_carry_a_shadow_and_no_card_claims_one` asserts the two facts the argument
rests on (`d.radii[i] = 0` for a shadow, `pointerData` carrying a resolved index, the reticule
`pickable: false`) *before* asserting that nothing emits or reads the flag — so if a level ever
draws a shadow, the guard fails at the fact rather than at the consequence.

**The guard caught my own comment first**, which is the lesson worth keeping: the note left
where the row used to be names `h.shadow`, and an assertion on the bare name cannot tell a
mention from a use (rule 37). It matches `${h.shadow` — the interpolation, which is code.

### The navigator rows: it helps by a fifth and does not close it

Tom chose *let the module path yield first*. `.navsub` was `flex: none` at up to 11rem, so it
was a fixed cost the name had to fit around; it is now `flex: 0 1 auto` with a `min-width: 4rem`
floor, and it keeps the `overflow: hidden` + ellipsis it already had. Nothing that was not
already designed to be shortened gets shortened.

**Measured as a controlled pair** — one page, one set of rows, this one declaration toggled:

| navigator width | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 21rem (336px, declared) | 335 rows / 101px | **266 / 49px** |
| 16rem (260px) | 1,037 / 163px | 951 / 108px |
| 12rem (192px) | 1,293 / 188px | 1,289 / 176px |

`_schema_validator`, the row that started this, goes from a full overprint to 9.4px as its
module column yields 154px → 132px. Short names leave the column at full length and sit clear
by 20–33px.

**It is an improvement, not a fix, and the remainder needs a decision about the name** — wrap
it, truncate it, or let the row grow (rule 84) — each of which one of the two comments over
`.navlabel` rejects. Filed rather than guessed at.

### Two measurements I got wrong first, and both are the same mistake

**I reported "0 of 1,395 overlapping" and it meant nothing.** The ROUTINES group was collapsed,
and a hidden row has a zero-size rect, so every overlap test passed by measuring nothing. Rule
45 from the measuring side: hidden is not absent, and a check that cannot see cannot report
(rule 38).

**Then I compared 335 against 1,289 across two different window widths.** The first number was
taken at a 1222px viewport and the second at 864px — and `@media (max-width: 1088px)` drops the
navigator from 21rem to **12rem** below that breakpoint, which is most of the difference. The
comparison said my change made things four times worse; the controlled pair above says it makes
them a fifth better. Rule 24: a measurement must measure the thing it names, and a before and
an after taken under different conditions are two measurements with one label.

*Worth knowing for the next session:* this browser would not resize — `resize_window` reports
success and `innerWidth` never moves — so the window it happens to open at decides which
responsive band everything is measured in. **Check `innerWidth` against 1088 before trusting
any navigator figure.** Setting `body.style.gridTemplateColumns` directly is how the three rows
of that table were taken without a window that would cooperate.

## 2026-09-08 — the plates, ordered by what they link to

Tom's feature request: the force layout has cycles that improve verticality using the shadow
nodes — could the same mechanism minimise vertical *distance* and so choose the plate order?

**Measured answer: not that mechanism, but yes the idea, and by a lot.**

### What was tried first, because it is what was asked

Plates as particles on a line, springs weighted by how many links two plates share, relaxed
and then ranked — `forcelayout.js` one dimension over, built and measured before anything
else. **-11.3%.**

A spring relaxation minimises `sum(w·dz²)`; the question is `sum(w·|dz|)`. Worse, the
continuous optimum is a poor guide to the *permutation*: a plate linked in both directions
settles near its own middle whatever its neighbours do, so the ranking comes back nearly the
order it started from. Searching the permutation directly — weighted **minimum linear
arrangement**, NP-hard in general and trivial at 53 plates — gives **-82.8%**.

Same evidence either way: the cross-plate edge list, which is the shadow list rule 23 already
maintains and the force solver already reads. Different solver, and `plateorder.py`'s
docstring says so rather than letting the next reader assume one mechanism does both.

### What it buys

Mensores at 2026-09-08T13:39:50Z, 53 plates, 5,101 crossings, 403 connected pairs:

| how far a crossing travels | by size | by what they link to |
|---|---|---|
| the plate next door | 190 (3.7%) | **1,724 (33.8%)** |
| 2-3 plates | 388 (7.6%) | 940 (18.4%) |
| 4-8 | 326 (6.4%) | 1,341 (26.3%) |
| 9-20 | 459 (9.0%) | 975 (19.1%) |
| **21 or more** | **3,738 (73.3%)** | **121 (2.4%)** |

Total 157,028 → 27,067 slot-links, mean **30.78 → 5.31** plates. Module level: 30,859 →
8,004, **-74.1%**, mean 20.56 → 5.33.

**And the picture says it without the numbers.** The stack stops being a funnel — big plates
at the top tapering to nothing — and becomes a **spindle**: the densely-connected hubs move
to the middle where everything can reach them, and the leaves go to both ends. That shape
*is* the result, and it is the first thing a reader sees.

### The two variants, and Tom's call on both

The best order **interleaves boundary plates among the packages** — `ext:DATABASE` just above
`storage`, `ext:STDIO` between `scriba` and `cli`. That reads well, and it overturns what the
current default means: your code on top, the world below. Holding that grouping keeps 31.5%
of the saving at routine level and 34.7% at module.

Tom's calls: **build both** (design rule 2 — they are interchangeable on what the reader
wants, not on the numbers), and **keep `by size` the default**, so this is opt-in exactly as
the force layout is.

**They are called "by what they link to" and never "by connection."** The plate-layout button
already says *by connection* and means the arrangement of nodes *within* a plate. One phrase
for two controls is rule 71 in the reader's language rather than in the code's, and the way it
shows up is somebody choosing the wrong control and concluding the tool is wrong. A guard
asserts no plate-order label is exactly that phrase.

### The defect underneath it, which had to be fixed first

**The plate-order control did not order plates.** `state.sortMode` was read in exactly one
place — `sortedDisks()`, called only from `renderLegend()` — and the `gsort` handler ran
`renderLegend(); persist()` and never `Graph.setOptions({ diskOrder })`. So *by name* and *by
kind* renumbered a legend and left every plate exactly where it was.

Design rule 16 with the control genuinely wired: the handler fired, the state changed, the
list redrew, and the one thing the control is named for did not happen. It hid because the
default very nearly agrees — `defaultOrder` in `graph.js` is *by size* with one clause added
— so the only mode anybody checked looked right. The two disagreed even at boot, the legend
opening on `ext:STDIO` (991 nodes, biggest of all) over a stack opening on `pkg:disceptator`
(961, biggest *package*).

`applyOrder()` is the missing half, and it is called from the one handler rather than from
each branch (rule 78): a seventh order added later cannot forget to move the plates, because
moving them is not the branch's job. Fixing it repaired *by name* and *by kind* as a side
effect — verified afterwards, all six modes moving the stack and the legend matching it.

### Three instrument failures, and the third nearly went into a commit message

This is the part worth carrying forward.

1. **The first "confirmation" of the defect dispatched the wrong event.** The `gsort` branch
   lives inside `mount.addEventListener("input", …)` and I dispatched `change`. The stack did
   not move, which is what I expected to see, and it proved nothing — the handler had not run
   at all. The claim was sound on the exhaustive grep, but the observation I called
   confirmation was worthless, and I nearly wrote it into a commit message as evidence.
2. **The second sweep held a stale element reference.** `renderLegend()` rebuilds the
   `<select>`, so a cached `sel` is detached after the first change and every later dispatch
   fires on a node outside the document. All four modes reported identical output — which
   read exactly like the fix not working.
3. **And rule 83 again, differently.** This window's pointer factor was **1.0** where the
   previous session's was 1.5581. It is a property of the window, not of the instrument, so
   it must be re-measured every session. Measure it before trusting a coordinate.

The habit that caught all three: when a result looks like the code is broken, check the
instrument first. Twice out of three it was.

   **eight** of them — see the section below.*
4. **The legend rail does not restore the pane.** Clicking `#legendRail` left
   `data-legend="off"` twice, and the panel had to be reopened by writing `panels.legend`
   into settings. Found while doing something else and not chased — design rule 24 says a
   pane collapses to a rail and the rail says which pane it is, which implies the rail brings
   it back. *Moved into `BRIEFING.md` the same day: this list should never have held an item
   that one did not.*
5. Then the standing backlog, none of it scheduled.

### The habit this session paid for twice

**When a result looks like the code is broken, check the instrument first.** Three failures,
two of which looked exactly like a real defect:

* a `change` event dispatched at a handler listening on `input` — the handler never ran, and
  the nothing that happened was read as confirmation of a defect;
* a cached `<select>` reference that `renderLegend()` had already replaced, so five of six
  modes reported identical output that read as the fix not working;
* rule 83's pointer factor, **1.0 in this window against 1.5581 in the previous one** — it is
  a property of the window and must be re-measured every session, not carried.

And the same failure in the measuring rather than the driving: *"0 of 1,395 rows overlapping"*
taken with the group collapsed, where a hidden row has a zero-size rect and every test passes
by measuring nothing.

## 2026-09-08 — the counts that can be one, and there were eight

The scheduled item read *"two pluralisations, `1 boxes` and `1 call sites`, need nobody and
are not done."* Both halves were true and the number was not: there are **eight** counts that
can be one, seven of them in a single sentence, and the entry named the two that had been
*seen* rather than the ones that are *there*. Measuring first was most of the work (rule 24).

### What is one, and how often

Taken against `output/mensores` at `2026-09-08T13:39:50Z`, over `/api/diagram`,
`/api/inside` and `/api/flow`:

| the count | how often it is exactly one |
|---|---|
| `N boxes` — every option of the compartment picker | **8 of 53** compartments |
| `N routines` — the second level, inside an opened box | **97 of 250** boxes opened |
| `N other boxes` — what an opened box crosses to | **43 of 250** |
| `N flows within` | **24 of 250** boxes, and 3 of 53 compartments |
| `N other compartments` | 2 of 53 |
| `reaching N boxes` · `N arrows drawn` | 2 of 53 compartments enter one box |
| `N call sites` — a kept arrow's note | **116 of 476** arrows |
| `N touches` — the same note | 17 of 476 |

The second level is where it matters most: **97 of 250** opened boxes hold one routine, so
*"1 routines"* is not an edge case there — it is close to what the surface mostly says.

### The one judgement, and it is a refusal

**`crossing` is left alone.** `<b>5</b> crossing to <b>2</b> other boxes` is a reduced
relative — *five [flows] crossing to two other boxes* — and reads correctly at one. So does
`${id.weight} along it` beside the kept-arrow note, which carries no noun at all. Both are
named in `_UNCOUNTED_NOUNS` in the guard rather than left as an absence for the next reader
to read as an oversight; the next noun added to that sentence must fail the guard.

### Two guards, and the first version of one was wrong in the way it was written to catch

Built on `test_a_file_band_states_a_count_of_one_in_english`, which had already earned this
lesson one surface over — *"1 modules explained differently"*.

* `test_the_diagram_head_states_a_count_of_one_in_english` is over the **shape**, not over a
  list of nouns: every `<b class="num">…</b> word` in `renderDiagram` must be followed by its
  own `=== 1 ?` choice. **The noun is the last word of the phrase, not the first** — the first
  version captured `([a-z]+)` and so read `other` as the noun of `other box${…}`, which passes
  a sentence saying *"1 other boxes"*. It failed on its own first run, on the real source.
* `test_a_kept_arrow_states_a_count_of_one_in_english` reads the `pinBtn` call in
  `viewInspectorFlow` and requires each of `call site` and `touch` to choose against the count
  that produced it — the count is named, so a choice made against the wrong variable does not
  pass.

Both were mutation-tested: reverting each fix in the source fails its own guard and nothing
else. And one existing guard broke, correctly —
`test_the_diagram_head_says_which_altitude_it_is_at` asserted the literal `"routines ·"`,
which an interpolated plural dissolves. Its marker is now `</b> routine`, the noun beside its
own count, which is what that assertion always meant.

### Seen, not only tested

Server on 8787, Chrome, real pointer:

* the picker lists `CRYPTO — 1 box` … `_config — 1 box`, eight of them;
* `_config` reads **"1 box over 3 routines · 0 flows within · 1 crossing to 1 other
  compartment"**;
* `conventions ▸ _schemas.py`, opened by a real **double-click** on the box, reads
  **"1 routine · 1 flow within · 1 crossing to 1 other box"** — three singulars and the
  reduced relative, in one line;
* the arrow `frontmatter.py → _schemas.py` was kept with the pointer and stands on the shelf
  as **"1 call site, 0 touches"**, then dropped — `dunneflow:mensores:v6` back to zero pins.

**Rule 83, re-measured this session as the last one insists it must be:** a click at tool
coordinate (400, 300) lands at CSS (624, 468), so `pointer = css × 0.641` and
`css = pointer × 1.560`. Close to the 1.5581 of two sessions ago and nothing like the 1.0 of
the session between. It is a property of the window.

### Found while looking, and not acted on

At `innerWidth 1224` the document's `scrollWidth` is **1336**: the inspector's own controls —
the keep button among them — sit off the right edge and the whole page scrolls sideways. That
is below Tom's window and above the `@media (max-width: 1088px)` band, so it is a third
window band nobody has looked at. Filed in `BRIEFING.md`; it is a layout call rather than a
defect with an obvious remedy (rule 53).

### And a second copy of the open list, closed

The previous entry's *"what the next session should pick up"* carried a fourth item —
**the legend rail does not restore the pane** — that `BRIEFING.md` did not have, and

## 2026-09-08 — three settings for what the window cannot fit

Tom: *"Create a Setting that permits navigator name wrap or truncate. Another Setting to keep
the top Toolbar items always visible, but smaller… Same for the row below the Toolbar that
starts with BASE… (current behavior will be default for all of these)."* His two calls on the
mechanism, taken before any code: the toolbar goes **narrower first and smaller only for what
is left**, and the BASE row's alternative is **one line, clipped, scrolling**.

Three surfaces, one subject: a row narrower than the thing in it. `navName`, `topFit`,
`verStrip`, each shipping today's behaviour as its default — because each alternative is a
preference rather than a repair, and design rule 2 says the usage counter retires the loser.

### What the default reaching no rule at all buys, and why it is asserted

Every one of these stamps **nothing** on `:root` in its default state, matching
`data-coverbars` and `data-theme`. A reader who never opens Settings carries an
attribute-free root and reaches not one of the new rules, which makes *"today's behaviour is
the default"* a fact about the stylesheet rather than a promise in a comment. A guard asserts
there is no `[data-navname="over"]` rule anywhere.

### The navigator, measured

1,404 rows with their counts drawn, at the declared 21 rem:

| `navName` | paints outside its box | of those, onto the count | worst | on two lines |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `over` **(default)** | **374 — 26.6%** | **268** | **56 px** | 0 |
| `clip` | 0 | 0 | — | 0 |
| `wrap` | 0 | 0 | — | 414 |

**The condition is load-bearing and is stated beside the figure** (rule 24). `routineFan`
returns `""` until the graph is mounted *and* the navigator is rebuilt, and with the counts
undrawn the same measurement gives **11.4%** — the names still leave their boxes, they simply
have no digits to land on. The record's 24% was a different window; this is this one's.

**The instrument was wrong first and was checked before it was believed.**
`getBoundingClientRect()` on a flex item returns its *box*, so the first pass reported 0
overprint in all three states — identical numbers, which is what gave it away. The honest
measure is `scrollWidth − clientWidth` for *whether the name fits*, and
`getComputedStyle(lab).overflow` for *whether the residue is painted*: the first is the same
in all three states, because it names the population rather than the outcome.

**Both objections in the stylesheet turned out to be answerable**, which is why these are
worth building rather than imposing:

* *"Truncating would hide a name with nothing beside it."* A routine row is `data-card`, so
  `navHoverSkeleton` already shows the leaf **and** the qualified name, and clicking has
  always shown it whole.
* *"`do_PO / ST` is worse than small type."* True of a break chosen by where the box ends —
  which is the argument written above `breakable()` one surface over, from
  `resolve_session_ / id`. `jointed()` marks the seams (`.`, `_`, a camel hump) with `<wbr>`,
  a **sibling** to `breakable` rather than a change to it, because folding the two would put
  underscore breaks into every qualified name on every surface and that is a different call.
  On screen: `open_graph_composition_` / `read_backend`, with its `1←` still on line one.

The two comments arguing for two different mechanisms over that one declaration are rewritten
as the reversal they are, rather than left standing beside code that contradicts them.

### The toolbar, and the half that is not about the toolbar

`.app` is a grid with one implicit `auto` column and **no `min-width: 0` on its children** —
unlike `.body > *`, which has it. The widest of the three rows therefore sets the width of all
three, which is why `#settingsBtn` at x≈1336 and the inspector's right edge at x≈1336 are one
symptom and not two. **A toolbar that only shrank itself would change nothing a reader could
see**: design rule 16 arriving from the layout rather than from the wiring, which is the kind
that ships. So `topFit` releases that column too, and only while it is on.

At `innerWidth 1280`:

| | off (default) | on |
|---|---|---|
| document width | **1336** | **1280** |
| toolbar `scrollWidth` | **1337** | 1280 |
| ⚙ Settings' right edge | 1323 — **43 px past the window** | 1266 — **14 px inside** |
| `--topbar-fit` | — | **1 — nothing shrank** |

**Yielding alone carries an 820 px toolbar** with no type change at all; that was not the
expected result and it is the reason Tom's *narrower first* was the right call rather than a
compromise. The multiplier is a backstop: 87% at 700 px, and the 85% clamp from 600 down,
where ⚙ Settings is still 6 px inside the window and only leaves it at 520.

**One ratio does not converge, and the sentence it produced was false.** Shrinking the type
shrinks the contents, so `scrollWidth` moves with the multiplier — but not proportionally,
because `.tb-search`'s padding and `.tb-select`'s `max-width` have floors of their own. A
single pass landed on 0.947 with 32 px still over, and the note said *"as small as this may
go"* — a claim about a clamp that had not fired (rule 13). Now it is three passes, bounded and
stated (rule 55), and `floored` travels separately from `short` so the two outcomes read
differently: *"85% — as small as this may go… widen the window"* against *"Fitted at 87% and
20 px still will not fit — something in this row has a width it will not give up."* They send
the reader different ways.

### The BASE row

`.verstrip` was already `flex-wrap: wrap` and its comment says why — it is prose, and the
alternative to wrapping is truncating the thing it exists to say. That argument stands and is
still the default. What it never weighed is the **cost**: `.app`'s middle row is `auto`, so a
second line comes off `.body`.

| body width | wraps (default) | clips (on) | returned to `.body` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1280 | 34 px, one line | 34 px | — |
| 900 | **55 px, two lines** | 39 px, 345 px scrolled | **+24 px** |
| 700 | **77 px, three lines** | 39 px, 545 px scrolled | **+46 px** |

`flex: none` on the children as well as `nowrap` on the box, and the guard says why: a flex
item's default is `1 1 auto`, so a strip merely told not to wrap **squeezes its contents onto
one line** — nothing clips, nothing scrolls, and the setting looks exactly as though it had
worked while doing something else.

**Design rule 29's distinction was checked rather than asserted.** Under `clip` the assumption
button sits at x=831 in a 700 px strip. Focusing it scrolls the strip **545 px**, brings it to
x=286, and `elementFromPoint` returns the button itself; `display`, `visibility` and
`pointer-events` are untouched. That is the difference between scrolled away and hidden, and a
guard now refuses `display: none` and `visibility: hidden` inside any of the four new stamps.

### The defect the looking found, and it is the one rule 47 exists for

**`data-navname` was both the stamp on `:root` and the route on the control.**
`$$("[data-navname]")` walks the whole document, so the moment a value other than the default
was chosen the setting's handler was bound to `<html>` and **every click in the application
ran it**. Redundant while a value was stamped — and the moment the reader chose the default
again the attribute was *removed*, `dataset.navname` became `undefined`, and the next click
anywhere stamped `data-navname="undefined"` on the root. A value no rule matches and no
control shows, from a setting that had just been set correctly.

`data-palette` / `data-palette-set` is the shape, and its comment says exactly this. The route
is `data-navname-set` now. **The existing guard could not see it**:
`test_a_pane_track_attribute_is_never_also_a_route_attribute` covers `PANELS`' fold attributes
against `NAV_SELECTOR`, and a settings stamp is a different family. The new guard asserts the
rule over both families at once — no attribute written to `documentElement` may also be a
selector this shell binds a listener to — and it is derived from the source rather than from a
list, so the next stamp is covered without anybody remembering.

*Found by reading the DOM, not by a test, and its wreckage is worth recording:* the usage
counter held `navname:undefined: 120` and `navname:clip: 239` against 11 real choices. Those
counts were cleared from `dunneflow:mensores:v6` before the session ended, because design rule
2 retires a setting on exactly that evidence and poisoned evidence is worse than none.

### Two more, both rule 78

* **`dressNavItems()` runs from `buildNav()` and at boot**, and nothing rebuilds the navigator
  when a centre-pane setting changes — so choosing `wrap` stamped the stylesheet and left
  every row already on screen unmarked, breaking wherever its box ended. The picture the
  setting exists to avoid, produced by the setting itself. It re-dresses an existing label now
  instead of skipping it, and the control calls it.
* **The fit is a ratio against the window**, so it was stale the instant the window moved.
  `fitTopbar()` joined the resize handler beside `scheduleFit()` — rule 78 again, with the
  window as the control nobody had added.

### Nine guards, every one mutation-tested

Three per-setting on the *"four halves, each of which passes alone while the setting is dead"*
pattern, and six from a way each could ship looking correct: the cut without its ellipsis; the
wrap without its seams, or with the seams and no CSS; `topFit` without `.app`'s column; the
clamp unstated or misstated; the strip's children left shrinkable; a stamp that is also a
route; and `display: none` used to make room. Reverting each fix fails its own guard and
nothing else.

### What could not be done, and it is the instrument

**The pointer.** `resize_window` reports success and, after it, **no synthetic click reaches
the page at all** — not in that tab, and not in a tab created afterwards. The window itself
did resize; the pointer frame stopped mapping onto it. Rule 72, and the same tool the record
already warns about. Three recoveries were tried and none worked, so it was stopped rather
than looped on.

Everything here was driven through the page's own handlers and every number is a measurement
off the live page, and the screenshots are real — but **a scripted click proves the handler
and only a pointer proves the path to it** (rule 48). The pluralisation work earlier in this
same session *was* verified at the pointer, before any resize, so the tell is clean. The three
toggles are `id`-bound like their six siblings, which `selfCheck` provably cannot see either;
each therefore has a guard naming its id.

**Still to do at the pointer, next session:** press each of the five controls with a real
pointer at a window that has not been resized by the tool.

## 2026-09-08 — the toolbar fit, reported from a real window an hour after it shipped

Tom, with a screenshot: *"Toolbar icon text overlaps the icon on the right when total window
width is too small for them all. In this shot, the SOURCE DIRECTORY and the Font Size are the
worst two."* And a second screenshot of *"the server could not be asked: Failed to fetch"* on
clicking SOURCE DIRECTORY.

**The second one was mine and was not a defect at all: I stopped the 8787 server as session
cleanup while he was reading it.** Restarted before anything else. Worth recording because the
dialog is indistinguishable from a real fault and the next reader should not go looking for
one — and because "clean up the server you started" is wrong when somebody else is on it.

### The first one is a defect, and it is `.navlabel`'s defect wearing a toolbar

`min-width: 0` is not *"be narrower"* — it is **a licence to overflow**. It permits a flex item
to shrink below its own min-content, and whatever will not fit is painted outside the box, on
top of the neighbour. `topFit` handed that licence to `.tb-right` and `.scale-group`, neither
of which can absorb anything: the slider is a fixed width and the group is three buttons held
to the right. So the slider and `100%` were drawn straight through *System* and *Settings*.

That is precisely the mechanism the navigator setting in the **same commit** exists to give a
reader a way out of, reproduced in the toolbar by the fix for the toolbar, a dozen lines from
the comment explaining it. The rule the two cases share, now written where the licence is
granted: **yielding is for things that have somewhere to put what they give up.**

* `.tb-right` and `.scale-group` are `flex: none`. The **slider** — the one part of that group
  with a spare dimension — yields instead, `flex: 0 1 auto` down to a `2.5em` floor. Design
  rule 30 is why there is a floor and not a dropped control: a 2.5em thumb is still a thumb
  you can drag. *Tom's suggestion — drop the slider and keep the two `A`s as steppers below
  some width — is a better answer if 2.5em turns out to be too small to aim at, and is filed
  rather than taken, because it is a new control and this was a regression.*
* **`SOURCE DIRECTORY` is a caption, not prose.** Two words in a narrow box wrap; a wrapped
  caption makes the button taller than everything else in the row, so the row grows and the
  value hangs out of the bottom of its own rounded rect — which is exactly what the screenshot
  shows. One line now, eliding, and the whole thing has always opened on click, which is what
  Tom proposed and what the button already did.

### Three more found by measuring the fix rather than by looking at it

* **A clip cannot shrink a box that is sized to its content.** `.srcpath` is a *column* flex
  with `align-items: flex-start`, so its caption and value size to themselves and do not
  shrink with the parent. `overflow: hidden` then clipped each child's text to a box that was
  itself 95px too wide — a clip that clips nothing. `max-width: 100%` is the half that was
  missing.
* **A cap a later rule of equal specificity discards is not a cap.** `.srcpath-v` carried
  `max-width: 100%` from the yielding rules and `max-width: 11em` from the sizing rules
  further down the file; equal specificity is settled by source order, so the one holding the
  value inside its shrinking button lost and the text ran 121px out at a 560px toolbar.
  **Rule 29's own mechanism, one stylesheet over from where it was minted.** Written as
  `min(11em, 100%)` rather than by moving the rule, because *whichever is smaller* is the
  thing meant and a line's position in a file is not an argument.
* **An out-of-flow child does not shrink with its parent, it escapes it.** The three search
  flags are `position: absolute` inside the field, so they contribute nothing to any
  min-content width — and once the wrapper was narrower than they are, they hung out of its
  **left** edge and were drawn over the revision menu: 4px at a 900px toolbar, **50px at
  700**. Nothing in the flex layout can see that. The wrapper now carries the floor its own
  overlay implies, in `em` so it falls with the multiplier as the flags do.

### Measured after, over the whole range

Every pair that can touch, at 1220 · 1000 · 900 · 800 · 700 · 620 px:

| | worst gap |
|---|---|
| scale group → theme | **−5 px** (a gap, at every width) |
| theme → settings | **−5 px** |
| search flags → revision menu | **−23 px** |
| caption / value out of their button | **−1 px** |
| button height vs toolbar height | 37 of 54 — one line, always |

Yielding alone still carries it to a **700px toolbar** at 99%, and the 85% clamp is reached at
620 where ⚙ Settings is 22px out and the note says so. The whole range is overlap-free, which
it was not at any width before.

*Five mutations, five catches.* The guard parses the rules rather than scanning the branch —
because the declaration that matters is on a different line from the selector that names it,
and a scan of the block passes on `white-space: nowrap` belonging to `.brand > *` while the
caption is still free to wrap (rule 37). It strips comments first, or the prose explaining
these selectors is parsed as a selector list and the explanation is reported as the defect.

*And two existing guards had to be anchored.* `test_the_source_directory_presents_as_a_button`
and `test_the_source_path_readout_clips` split the stylesheet on the bare `.srcpath` /
`.srcpath-v` selector, which now finds the **stamped branch** first — so both silently moved
to a rule that was never the one they meant. Anchored at column 0, on the declaration every
reader gets.

## 2026-09-08 — the rail that could not be reached, and the fourth fit setting

Item 6 of the scheduled pass, filed as *"the legend rail does not restore the pane"*. It
does. The diagnosis was wrong and the symptom was real, which is **rule 39** exactly.

### What the rail actually does

Pressed with a real pointer at viewport (970, 471), `#graphMount`'s `data-legend` goes
`off` → `on` and the rail re-hides. A scripted `.click()` agrees and is idempotent on a
second press; the navigator rail restores the same way. The handler in the `[data-fold],
[data-pane]` listener was never at fault — `opening = Boolean(btn.dataset.pane)` is right,
and `applyPanels()` does both halves.

### What could not be done was reach it

`.app` is a grid with **one implicit column**, and an implicit column is `auto`: sized to
the widest of its three rows. The toolbar does not wrap, so its max-content width is the
column's width and therefore `.body`'s — and every rail on the right-hand edge is carried
out of the window with it. Measured at `innerWidth 1220`, both panes folded:

| | legend rail | inspector rail |
|---|---|---|
| as it ships | **1281–1309** | **1309–1337** |
| with the new setting on | 1164–1192 | 1192–1220 |

Both are *wholly* outside the window at the default, and `document.elementFromPoint`
returns `null` over either. They are still reachable by scrolling the whole page sideways,
which is what keeps this a preference and not a repair.

**A rail is the only way back to a folded pane** (design rule 24), which is what makes it
different in kind from the overhang `topFit` is about: the toolbar running off is a
nuisance, a pane you cannot get back is a trap.

### Tom's call, and it is design rule 2

Put to him with the measurement and three alternatives. His answer: *build both and make it
a Setting*, with today's behaviour as the default — the same shape as the three that landed
earlier the same day. So `paneFit` joins them, off by default, and the family header, the
shared design-rule-29 guard and the Settings copy all now say **four**.

### The mechanism, and the half that would have failed silently

Three declarations, each load-bearing:

* `grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr)` makes the column explicit and bounded, so it is
  the container's width rather than the widest row's. On its own that is the whole fix for
  `.body` — 1336 → **1220**, and both rails inside.
* `overflow-x: auto` on `.topbar` gives the toolbar back the behaviour the column used to
  give it. **Pinned and left alone the row does not run off, it gets taller** — measured
  63 px → 67 px as its items squeeze and wrap inside themselves, a third behaviour neither
  this setting nor `topFit` offers.
* `flex-shrink: 0` on the children, because `nowrap` alone squeezes rather than overflows.
  That is `test_the_version_strip_clips_its_children_as_well_as_its_box` one row up, and
  this is the same mechanism deliberately. **`flex-shrink` and not `flex: none`**:
  `.tb-searchwrap` is `flex: 1 1 auto` and still has to *grow* into a wide window, and
  `flex: none` would take that away with the shrink.

**The two settings compose rather than compete, and the specificity is why.** Every
`[data-topfit="on"]` rule that hands a child permission to yield is a class selector and
outranks `.topbar > *` here, so with both on the toolbar shrinks to fit exactly as it does
today and only what the 0.85 floor could not absorb ever scrolls.

### Verified at the pointer, and one thing that could not be

Pressed the real control at viewport (1056, 455): `aria-pressed` true, `data-panefit="on"`
stamped, document 1336 → 1220, `.body` 1337 → 1220, the toolbar's box 1220 with a
`scrollWidth` of **1377** — running off inside its own row. Written to storage, and the
stamp survives a reload, which is rule 68's half.

**The claim in the Settings copy was measured rather than asserted**: scrolling the
toolbar's own row to `scrollLeft 157` brings ⚙ Settings from 1285–1363 to **1127–1206**,
inside the window, while `scrollX` stays 0, the document stays 1220, and the inspector rail
does not move. The toolbar still runs off; it does it in its own row now.

*~~What could not be done is press the four settings controls' **Settings button** with a
pointer, and that is the instrument.~~ **This paragraph was wrong and is kept because it was
acted on.** It read: the pointer stopped arriving above a floor that drifted during the
session — y=45 landed, y=40 did not, and after a reload y=88 stopped landing on a page where
y=109 and y=144 had worked twenty minutes earlier; the toolbar occupies viewport y 8–54,
below the best floor measured, so ⚙ Settings cannot be pressed at the pointer at all.*

*There is no floor.* The automation's window had gone behind another, and
`document.visibilityState` said `hidden` the moment anybody asked. A screenshot is captured
from the tab and a click is delivered to the screen, so JavaScript, screenshots and tab ids
all went on addressing the right page while the pointer did not — and the tool reported
`Clicked at (…)` either way (rule 76). With the window in front, ⚙ Settings was pressed at
the pointer at the first attempt. **Rule 90** is minted from it, and item 0 was paid the same
day — see the entry below. Settings was opened for the `paneFit` press by focusing the button
and pressing Return, which was a real key event through the real handler and was recorded as
not-the-pointer; that part stands.

*The pointer/viewport mapping this session was `viewport = pointer × 1.7111`, measured from
a `pointerdown` probe rather than assumed: pointer (400, 300) arrives at (684, 514). It is
not the ratio the last session recorded, so it is worth measuring every time rather than
carrying.*

## 2026-09-08 — item 0 paid: the five controls, pressed

Tom, having read that the pointer could not reach them: *"it's in front now, go."* It was
in front, and every one of them was reachable. The obstacle recorded three hours earlier
was **rule 90** and not a product fact.

Tom's own arrangement was in force and is what they were pressed against — `navName: wrap`,
`topFit: on`, `verStrip: on`, **`paneFit: on`** (he had turned the new one on himself), at a
1227×522 window he sized, which the automation never touched (rule 72). The mapping was
measured from a `pointerdown` probe rather than carried: `viewport = pointer × 1.5667`,
against 1.7111 the session before. Every press was preceded by an `elementFromPoint`
pre-check that the control was actually the thing under the target pixel — which is the
hit-test the pointer exists to prove — and followed by its **consequence**, never by
`aria-pressed` alone.

| # | Control | What the press was shown to have done |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **As it is** | `:root` carries no `data-navname` — the default stamps nothing — and **2,309 → 0** `<wbr>` across the same 1,454 labels |
| 2 | **Cut it** | `data-navname="clip"`; **1,039 of 1,604** visible labels overflowing, worst `_assert_no_forbidden_phrase_in_probes` at **196px in a 104px box**, computed `text-overflow: ellipsis`, one line |
| 3 | **Wrap it** | `data-navname="wrap"`; **0 → 2,674** `<wbr>` inserted into rows *already on screen*; overflowing **1,039 → 0**; the witness reads `_<wbr>assert_<wbr>no_<wbr>forbidden_<wbr>phrase_<wbr>in_<wbr>probes`, 15px → 45px |
| 4 | **Fit the toolbar** | off: stamp gone, `--topbar-fit` **cleared**, note emptied, toolbar 1377 vs 1228 (149px over), ⚙ Settings' right edge 1363. on: stamp back, note *"Fitted at 95%"* against a multiplier of **0.9538** — they agree (rule 13) — 1px over, ⚙ Settings at 1216 inside a 1227 window |
| 5 | **Version strip on one line** | off: stamp gone, 39px → **55px**, `flex-wrap: wrap`, children back to `shrink: 1`, nothing clipped — and `.body` **426px → 409px**, so the second line's cost comes off the pane being read, exactly as the copy says. on: stamp back, one line, `scrollWidth` 1245 vs `clientWidth` 1228 |

Number 3 is the one that mattered. The `<wbr>` seams are inserted by `dressNavItems()` into
rows the navigator had already drawn — nothing rebuilt the navigator — which is **rule 78**
observed rather than argued, and it is the half a scripted call to the handler would also
have shown while proving nothing about whether the button could be hit.

Tom's four settings were left exactly as found; the last two presses restored them.

### And the screenshot found something no measurement had

Looking at it rather than only measuring it, in the navigator: **`disabled` is drawn as
`disable / d`.** Under `[data-navname="wrap"]` the label computes `overflow-wrap: break-word`,
so a name `jointed()` can find **no seam in** is broken at an arbitrary character. **160 of
1,604** visible rows are in that state — `disabled`, `review` (six letters, in a 36px box),
and every `<module>`.

That is the exact picture the setting exists to avoid, and both its comment and its Settings
copy promise the opposite: *"broken on the name's own seams (`do_ / POST`, not `do_PO / ST`)"*.
For a name with seams that promise is kept — number 3 above proves it. For a name without
any, `break-word` takes over and the promise is false.

*Not fixed, because it is a trade and the trade is Tom's.* A seamless name that will not fit
can be broken anywhere (today), left to overflow its box (which is `over`'s behaviour arriving
inside `wrap`), or cut with an ellipsis (which is `clip`'s, inside `wrap`). Filed in
`BRIEFING.md`, which owns the open list. *The first count taken was **375** and it was wrong —
it thresholded a one-line row at 18px when one line is 17–19px here. 375 is how many labels
have no seam at all; 160 of them are actually broken across lines.*

## 2026-09-08 — a name with no seam, divided rather than cut anywhere

Item 7, filed and closed the same day. Tom: *"proceed with a reasonable fix that breaks
words at smart intervals, not just arbitrary characters. Re-use what's been written where
possible."* A fourth option, and none of the three I had put to him.

### The interval is measured

`jointed()` marks three seams — after a dot, after an underscore, before a camel hump — and
across Mensores' 4,823 routine names those cut **13,175 runs whose median length is 5**, the
longest 15. So `SEAMLESS_TARGET = 5`: an invented break aims at the length the language's own
seams already produce, and a divided name looks like a name an underscore broke rather than
one the edge of a box did. `SEAMLESS_MIN = 3` is the floor no piece may go under, because
orphaning one letter is the whole defect.

| | |
|---|---|
| seamless names divided | **789 of 1,013** (524 of them `<module>`) |
| left to the `break-word` floor | **224** — every one a short word: `run`, `name`, `get`, `id`, `up`, `ok` |
| shortest piece anywhere | **3** |
| names with seams, untouched | **3,810 of 4,823** |

`disabled → disa / bled` · `review → rev / iew` · `adjudicate → adjud / icate` ·
`canonicalize → canoni / calize` · `<module> → <mod / ule>`.

### Two decisions that are the whole of it

**Only a name with no seam at all is touched, and that is rule 1.** All `<wbr>` are equal to
a browser: it takes the last opportunity that fits, with no notion that an underscore is a
better place than the middle of a word. Marking the long *runs* inside an already-seamed name
would hand it a mid-run opportunity it would prefer, turning today's `_assert_no_ /
forbidden_phrase` into `_assert_no_forbi / dden`. Improving the bad case would have spoiled
the good one, and the population actually drawn wrong was the seamless names.

**`break-word` stays, as the floor rather than the mechanism**, and the stylesheet now says
which it is. A name shorter than six cannot be divided without orphaning a letter; for those
the choice is breaking badly or painting over the count, and the second is what the whole
setting exists to end. Reached by 224 of 1,013 now, rather than by all of them.

`seamlessParts` slices the **raw** name and leaves escaping to its caller. Not tidiness:
slicing an already-escaped string cuts `&lt;` in half, and 524 of this corpus' seamless names
are `<module>`. Confirmed in the live DOM as `&lt;mod<wbr>ule&gt;`.

Both promises were rewritten rather than left standing — `settings.js`'s comment and the
Settings copy the reader sees both said *"broken on the name's own seams"* and were false for
a name that has none. The copy now states the five and the three, because a break at five is
a claim (design rule 1).

### What was verified, and what was not

In the page: `disa<wbr>bled`, `rev<wbr>iew`, `adjud<wbr>icate`, `rele<wbr>ase`,
`&lt;mod<wbr>ule&gt;`; marks 2,674 → **3,018**; 72 of 1,654 labels left with none, every one
of them short. Over the corpus: the four figures above, taken from `graph@2026-09-08` rather
than from the page.

**The rendering itself was not seen.** The automation's tab was hidden, and this is the
extension to rule 90 that cost nothing only because I checked first: a hidden tab has no
layout at all — every `getBoundingClientRect` is zero — so the *geometry* half is exactly as
blind as the pointer half, while the DOM goes on answering perfectly. What stands is the
markup and the corpus; the picture is unconfirmed, and one look with the window in front
settles it.

Nine mutations, nine catches. `jointed()` is called from `dressNavItems` and nowhere else, so
the change is contained to the navigator under `wrap`.

## 2026-09-08 — a narrow window deleted a pane instead of collapsing it

Tom, with a picture: *"With a narrow window, the left Navigator pane collapses and cannot be
brought back without making the window wide again. It would be better to collapse it and
permit horizontal scrolling, with a visible bar at the bottom of the screen. The BASE works
like this, and that is fine."*

**It was not collapsed. It was deleted**, and the difference is the whole report.

### What was there

```css
@media (max-width: 1088px) { .body { grid-template-columns: 12rem 1fr; }
                             .body > .inspector { display: none; } }
@media (max-width: 768px)  { .body { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
                             .body > .navigator { display: none; } }
```

Collapsing is `data-navtrack="off"`: the track becomes a rail, the rail is drawn, and
pressing it brings the pane back (design rule 24). These did something else — `display:
none` on the pane while `state.panels.navigator` stayed **true**. So `applyPanels` hid the
rail, because a rail is only drawn for a pane that is *closed*, and this one was open. Open,
undrawn, and nothing to press.

Reproduced at `innerWidth 380`: `data-navtrack="on"`, the column really **192px**, and
`.navigator` at `display: none` inside it. **That is exactly the hole the comment four rules
above it warns about** — *"a pane hidden with `display:none` while its column stayed 22rem
would leave a 22rem hole"* — arriving in the same file, under a comment of its own.

**The inspector had it too**, at 1088 rather than 768, and it was not in the report because
Tom's inspector was already folded. Opened at `innerWidth 950`: `data-insp="on"`,
`.inspector` `display: none`, `#inspectorRail` `hidden`. Same defect, same cause, found by
opening it and looking.

**And neither `grid-template-columns` ever applied when it mattered** — rule 29, inside the
block whose own comment cites rule 29 for its sibling. A media query contributes no
specificity, so the bare `.body` in it was outranked by `.body[data-insp="off"]` above: at
380 the columns were still `192px 152.5px 28px`, three tracks for two visible panes, with
the survivors auto-placed one track to the left (that is why `#inspectorRail` measured 153px
wide, in the centre's track). Only the `display: none` won, because it alone was written
`.body >`.

### What replaced them, and it is Tom's mechanism

The centre gets a floor and the row scrolls — the version strip's mechanism a third time,
which is what *"the BASE works like this"* points at.

* `--centre-floor: 16rem`, a token because `CENTRE_FLOOR_REM = 16` in JS sizes the navigator
  against the same number; a test keeps them equal, since a floor that disagrees with itself
  is a pane that vanishes at one width and not the other.
* All **four** `.body` track declarations take `minmax(var(--centre-floor), 1fr)`. Four
  copies of a track list is four places to forget one, so the guard checks all four rather
  than the base.
* `.body` gets `overflow-x: auto; overflow-y: hidden; scrollbar-width: thin` — the strip's
  own declarations. `overflow-y: hidden` is not tidiness: `overflow-x: auto` computes the
  other axis to `auto` by spec, and the horizontal bar's ~15px would then raise a vertical
  bar over panes that already scroll their own contents.

### Measured after

| `innerWidth` | columns | panes | `.body` | page |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 380 | `192px 256px 352px` | all three drawn | 380 of **800**, scrolls, 5px bar | does not scroll (`docSW` 380) |
| 950 | `288px 310px 352px` | all three drawn | fits, no bar | does not scroll |

And the cycle that was impossible, at 380: fold → `28px 256px 352px`, `.navigator` gone,
**rail drawn at 28@0**; press the rail → back to `192px 256px 352px`. Design rule 24 honoured
at a width where it could not be before.

*What was deliberately not built is an **automatic** collapse.* With the row scrolling there
is no longer a need for one, and a window that changes the reader's arrangement by itself is
a different call — the existing `inspectorAuto` shows the shape it would have to take,
including the trap its own comment records: *"the rail would be unclickable: it would reopen
and immediately re-collapse, which reads as broken."* Offered rather than assumed.

`.navgrip`'s own `@media (max-width: 768px)` went with them: it hid the grip because below
that width there was no navigator to resize, and now there is.

Seven mutations, seven catches — run before the sentence was written this time. The guard
strips comments before scanning, and learned that the way
`test_every_dimension_is_in_rem` did: the block explaining why these breakpoints were
deleted **quotes them**, so a raw scan finds `.navigator { display: none }` inside the prose
recording its removal and reports the explanation as the defect.

## 2026-09-08 — a pane that folds itself, and the trap it was deferred on

Tom, asked for the call filed as item 8 the day before: *"Item 8 should auto-collapse."*

### What it replaces, and why the floor was not the answer

The narrow-window fix earlier the same day deleted two breakpoints that set `display: none`
on a pane whose grid track and whose `state.panels` entry both stayed — open, undrawn, and
with no rail to press, which is design rule 24 broken in the one place it matters most. What
replaced them is a centre floor and a horizontal scrollbar on `.body`, so nothing vanishes at
any width.

**That is a floor rather than an answer**, and the entry that offered this said so: at 380px
the reader reaches the centre by dragging a bar. A pane that folds *properly* — the fold that
leaves a rail — is the answer, and it needed Tom's call because a window that rearranges the
reader's panes by itself is a different thing from one that stops deleting them.

### The rule

**One question, asked in one place.** `panelIsOpen` already decided whether a pane is open,
and it now weighs three rules in order: the window, then the inspector's own *nothing to say*
rule, then the reader's fold. The window is first because it outranks both — an inspector
with a subject is still a pane that does not fit — and a test asserts that order, because
weighing it last reports a pane open while the grid has given its track away.

**Asked at the panes' narrowest, never at the width the reader dragged.** `applyNavWidth`
already clamps the navigator down to `NAV_MIN_REM` to make room, so the fold is decided
against `NAV_MIN_REM + CENTRE_FLOOR_REM +` the inspector's track — narrower first, and folded
only for what is left, which is `topFit`'s mechanism one surface over. It is also what keeps
this out of a loop: `navMaxRem()` asks `panelIsOpen("inspector")`, so a rule that asked back
for the clamped width would be asking itself. A test asserts `navWidth(` never appears in
`narrowFolds`, and counts **both** comparisons rather than containing one — the first
mutation ran passed against a broken first branch because the second branch still held both
names (rule 37).

**Never a media query**, which is the other half of why the breakpoints were wrong. A `rem`
inside `@media` resolves against the browser's font size and ignores `:root` (rule 28), so
the CSS version of this rule folds at 800px for one reader and at 1,200px for one whose
Chrome default is 24px. Measured off `innerWidth` and the root font size, as the drag is.

**The inspector's track is a token now.** `--insp-w: 22rem`, read by the two `.body` track
lists that carried the literal and by `paneCostRem()`. `--centre-floor` earned its own test
for exactly this; a number in two languages is a pane that vanishes a little before or after
the point where it would not have fit, with nothing on screen to explain either. `--rail` was
already a token and is read the same way. A token that cannot be read is **announced** and
not quietly replaced — rule 49 is the whole reason `remToken` says anything at all.

### The trap, which is what the feature sat behind

Recorded beside `inspectorAuto` a day before this existed: an automatic collapse makes the
rail unclickable, because pressing it opens the pane and the rule folds it again in the same
frame — *"which reads as broken"*.

`paneHeld` is the answer, and it is only an answer if all three halves are there: the fold
handler writes it, `autoFoldsHere` reads it, and a resize gives it back. Two of those three
are rule 35's shape exactly — a flag nothing assigns, or that nothing reads, is a feature
with no symptom — so the guard checks all three.

**Not in `state`, and not persisted, which is the difference from `inspectorAuto`.** It is an
answer about *this* window: a reader who held the inspector open on a narrow screen must not
find it held open tomorrow on a wide one, where the rule that made holding it mean anything
is not running. The same *re-clamped rather than remembered narrower* decision the
navigator's width makes two functions down.

### Rule 78, arriving through the divisor

**Two controls move this fold and only one of them is the window.** The rule is `innerWidth /
rootPx`, and `--scale` is that divisor — design rule 3 puts every dimension in `rem` precisely
so one multiplier drives them together, which means the scale slider narrows the page in
exactly the units this rule counts. A reader at 1,215px who takes the scale to 160% has a
**47.5rem** window and no room for three panes, and nothing would have told the panes so
until the next time they moved the window.

So `refitPanes()` is invited from `applyScale`, which all four scale routes already pass
through, rather than from the slider that happened to be the second one found. *Found while
verifying, not while writing.*

*Noted and not fixed:* the same argument reaches `fitTopbar`, whose fit is a ratio of the
row's contents to the window and is therefore also wrong the instant the scale moves. It is
pre-existing, the live drag deliberately avoids `render()`, and refitting the toolbar on every
frame of a drag is a measurement nobody asked for. Filed rather than done.

### Measured, in the page, at `innerWidth 1215`

Driven through the product's own scale rather than by resizing the window — `resize_window`
reports success and changes nothing (recorded 2026-09-06), and the scale is the same divisor
the rule reads, so raising it *is* narrowing the window in the units this counts.

| # | | window | rule wants | held | drawn | inspector rail |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | narrow | 27.1rem | inspector + navigator | — | `nav=off insp=off` | drawn |
| 2 | press the rail | 27.1rem | inspector + navigator | inspector | `nav=off insp=on` | hidden |
| 3 | refit, same width | 27.1rem | inspector + navigator | inspector | `nav=off insp=on` | hidden |
| 4 | ease to 31.6rem | 31.6rem | inspector | inspector | `nav=on insp=on` | hidden |
| 5 | widen | 75.9rem | — | — | `nav=on insp=on` | hidden |
| 6 | narrow again | 27.1rem | inspector + navigator | — | `nav=off insp=off` | drawn |

Row 3 is the trap, closed: the pane the reader asked for survives the rule being asked again
at the same width. Row 5 is the release, and row 6 is the proof it was a release rather than
a forget. **`state.panels` reads `nav=true insp=true` in every one of the six** — the fold is
laid over the reader's arrangement and never written into it, which is what makes widening
give them back what they had rather than what the rule left.

*What was not verified is the pointer.* `document.visibilityState` said `hidden` throughout,
so a click would have landed on whatever window was in front (rule 90), and the capture
window would not line up with the rail at the right-hand edge (rule 83). The rail-press path
itself was pressed with a real pointer on 2026-09-08 for the legend and navigator rails; what
is new here is `paneHeld`, and it is scripted evidence. **Worth one pointer press with the
window in front**, which is a minute of Tom's screen.

*And one thing put back:* pressing a rail calls `persist()`, so the scale I had driven to
2.8 went into `localStorage` under the reader's settings. Restored to 1 and confirmed
saved — a measurement that leaves the instrument changed is not free.

### Where it ships

A fifth setting beside the four from earlier the same day, and **the only one of the five
that ships on** — Tom's call. Off is what the dashboard did before, which is design rule 2's
other half.

Nine mutations, nine catches, two of which the harness found and review had not: a guard
whose span reached the wrong `resize` listener entirely — there are two, and the first is a
three-line one that hides a hover card — and the counted-versus-contained one above.

**Gates:** 1,247 tests, mypy clean over 121 source files, ruff clean.

## 2026-09-08 — a map belongs to a revision

Pulled from the standing backlog, where it had sat since 2026-08-31 as one line: *"the
rendered markdown is not revision-named, so a second analysis overwrites the first's map."*

### Why this one, of the six on that list

Everything else on it is a convenience. This is the only entry where a **sealed snapshot
loses something it was sealed to keep.** `CLAUDE.md` says a sealed snapshot exists *"so it
can be read after its source tree is gone"*, and rules 25 and 62 forbid re-analysing one in
place. Its graph and its document store are revision-named and survive; the fifteen
documents of its **written map** went flat into the program directory and were overwritten
by the next analysis. So the half a reader who does not write code actually reads was the
half that did not survive — and `output/mensores` is in that state now: the sealed
`2026-09-07T15:32:31Z` has a graph and no map of its own.

The entry's own note said *"the dashboard reads the databases, so nothing is broken"*, which
is true and is exactly why it stood for eight days: nothing on screen ever showed it.

### The layout

`map@<revision>/`, the same `@` idiom as `graph@…db` and `docs@…db` beside it, through the
same order-preserving `as_filename`.

**A directory rather than `01-entrypoints@<revision>.md`, and the links decided it.** The
map's own README points at its fourteen siblings by bare name, and every one of those would
have to be rewritten per revision to go on saying the same thing. Inside a directory they
are already right, and the program directory stays something a person can look at.

**Decided at the call site, not inside `render_all`.** That function writes the map into the
directory it is handed and goes on knowing nothing about revisions; *which* directory is a
question about time, and `cmd_analyze` is the caller that knows the answer. It also left
`test_completeness.py` — the only other caller — untouched.

### The index, and the three absences it states

`README.md` in the program directory is now a listing: every revision, its state, its
capture instant, its file count, its label, and a link into its map. A handed-over directory
opens on a sentence instead of on a heap of `map@…` names.

Built from **what is on disk**, never from what the run just wrote, so three things that are
not the happy case each get their own answer rather than an empty cell (design rule 21):

* a revision with a graph and no map — `--no-render`, or an analysis older than this layout;
* a map with no graph — a snapshot whose stores were dropped by hand, which the rebuild
  recipe in `CLAUDE.md` tells the reader to do;
* the older flat map, if one is lying there. **Named in full and left alone.** Which revision
  those fifteen files describe is recorded nowhere — not in the text, not in the names, so
  not even rule 30's *"a name is not an identity"* applies, because there is no name. Filing
  them under a guess would be worse than saying so, and deleting a reader's documents to
  tidy up a listing is not this tool's decision.

The rows come from `SourceStore.revisions()`, **taken from the handle `analyze` already has
open** rather than from a second read-only one: rule 58 puts that at 36x, and a second open
would also have to happen after the close to be correct. One ask, one answer.

`analyze` now prints two lines where it printed one — `map:` naming the map it just wrote and
`index:` naming the listing. Both files are called `README.md` and they answer different
questions, so the line that says *start reading here* has to name the one inside the map.

### The sharp edge, and it is not the layout

**A map is fifteen Markdown documents written inside the output tree**, which is where rule
57 was minted: pointing DunneFlow at itself once read 46 of 54 documents out of `output/` —
its own reports, about a different program — and every one of the 942 naming rules it then
claimed came from them.

`discover_docs` prunes an excluded directory out of `dirnames`, so excluding the program
directory excludes everything beneath it and a map is safe without the exclusion list
learning a new name. **That is the reading the call site does not make obvious**, and the
opposite reading — that `exclude` matches the directory itself — is equally plausible and
would let every map be read back in as prose. So it is asserted twice: once directly on
`discover_docs`, and once end to end through a second analysis, which is the only run where
a map is already on disk while the corpus is being scanned.

Measured at scale, analysing DunneFlow itself twice: **9 documents, then 9 documents** — 15
map files and an index on disk for the second run, and not one of them read.

### Verified against real code

Into **fresh** program directories, never `output/mensores`: 8787 is serving it, and
`Store._discard_if_stale` drops every table of a graph written by another build, so an
analysis aimed at a served directory can empty the map under a live reader. The dashboard
refuses that for its own analyses; the CLI does not, and this is the case it exists for.

| | |
|---|---|
| Society at 08-29 into `output/mapcheck` | 628 files, 4,823 routines, 30,544 calls, 36 s |
| the map | `map@2026-09-08T23-43-37Z/`, 15 documents, index beside it |
| ground truth: the four executables | `mensores` 1,381 · `mensores-mcp` 423 · `mensores-scriba` 292 · `mensores-signator` 112 |
| DunneFlow itself, twice | 9 documents both times |

Both scratch directories were removed afterwards. **`output/mensores` was not touched** —
its next analysis is what will give it this layout, and the recipe in `CLAUDE.md` requires
`--standards` on that run (rule 88).

*Not built, and filed rather than assumed:* **a way to render a named revision's map from
the graph it already has.** It would give the sealed `2026-09-07T15:32:31Z` the map it lost,
and it is not analysis — it opens a sealed graph read-only and writes documents into a new
directory, so rules 25 and 62 are untouched. Going forward the promise now holds without it,
which is why it is an item and not part of this one.

**Gates:** 1,253 tests, mypy clean over 123 source files, ruff clean.


## 2026-09-09 — a new checkpoint, and the map a sealed snapshot lost

Two jobs, in Tom's order: *"pull a new version of society, name it whatever you like and use
that as a new checkpoint… After that, start work on the build of the filed item."*

### The checkpoint, and "a lot of changes" measured rather than believed

Tom: *"There have been a lot of changes lately."* The remote does not agree, and the reason
is a trap worth keeping.

**`main` is not where Society lives.** It sits at `09b9ef11`, dated **2026-06-10**, with 384
Python files under `src/` — three months behind the tree already analysed. A plain
`git clone` gets it, it analyses perfectly, and nothing anywhere says it is stale. The work
is on `feat/spec-lifecycle-and-evidence`, whose head `7baa17bf` is dated **2026-08-30**. That
is now named in `CLAUDE.md` beside the trees.

Against `03ebbd93` — the 2026-08-29 clone — it is **6 commits, 43 files, 6,044 insertions,
112 deletions**, and **3 source `.py` files** among them: `governance/_tracker_census.py`,
`governance/_write_roles.py`, `mcp/_server.py`. The rest is tests and ADRs. So *a lot of
changes* is true of the repository and not of the code this tool reads — which is exactly
the distinction a map exists to make, and it is a sharp little pair for the change worklist
rather than a disappointment.

**The analysis confirmed the git diff through a different instrument**, which is the part
worth recording: the source sidecar reported **3 read, 625 already held**. Two independent
measurements of the same delta, and they agree.

Named `../society-2026-08-30` for its commit date, following `society-2026-08-26` and
`society-2026-08-29`, and checked out detached at `7baa17bf` as those are. Read-only, like
the other three.

Sequence, and the order is the recipe in `CLAUDE.md`:

```bash
uv run dunneflow revisions output/mensores --seal --label "Society at 03ebbd93 - 2026-08-29"
uv run dunneflow analyze ../society-2026-08-30/src --name mensores \
    --standards ../dunnecorp-standards
```

**Sealing first is what made it safe to analyse into the directory 8787 is serving.**
`open_working` reuses the open working revision, so analysing without sealing would have
rewritten `graph@2026-09-08T13-39-50Z.db` — the very file the live server holds. Sealed, the
analysis opens a fresh revision and writes new files beside it; 8787 answered `200` on
