### Rendering a named revision's map from the graph it already has

The item filed at the foot of yesterday's entry. Two commits.

#### First: a map needs neither tree, and nothing said so

`root` and `docs_root` were parameters of **twenty-eight** functions across nine renderer
modules and were read by **none** of them. The nine copies of the path-stripping they
existed for were deleted when paths became relative — the comment recording that deletion is
still at the top of `markdown.py` — and the parameters stayed for a month.

That is not cosmetic. A signature asking for a source root is a claim that one is needed, and
the new command has no source tree to name: it would have had to invent a plausible path,
which is rule 49 in a shape mypy cannot catch. So they went, and the comment that explains
the deletion was extended rather than replaced.

**And `Generated` is not `analysed`.** A map written by `analyze` carries one instant for
both, so a single *"Generated 2026-09-09 15:34 UTC"* line was true twice over by accident. A
re-rendered map pulls them apart — documents written today about source read a fortnight ago
— and that line then reads as a claim about the wrong fortnight. The cover now carries
**What this map describes**: the snapshot, when that source was read, when these documents
were written. Both facts come from the graph's own `meta`, asked by `_overview` rather than
carried down by every caller (rule 51), and a graph written before either key existed says so
rather than being handed an instant it never recorded (rule 30).

On the sealed `2026-09-07T15:32:31Z` all three are different, and the middle one is a fact
nothing had ever put on a page: the revision id is **09-07 15:32**, the source was read
**09-08 13:38**, the documents were written **09-09 15:49**. *A revision id is when the
working revision was **opened**, not when its source was read* — `open_working` mints it and
a later `analyze` against the same open revision fills the graph. Both sealed snapshots here
show the gap.

A heading rather than a floating table, because this reader arrives mid-document as often as
at the top.

#### Then: `dunneflow render <dir> [--revision <rev>]`

`render/snapshot.py`. With no revision it writes the map of **every revision here that has a
graph and no map** — Tom's call, and it is the job the item was filed for. Naming one renders
that one and rewrites its map, so a re-render is always something the reader asked for by
name; a second run with no flag writes nothing and says *which* empty it is (design rule 21).

**Not analysis, and that is the whole of why it is allowed.** Nothing is extracted, no
fingerprint is re-stamped, and every store it opens is opened read-only. Rules 25 and 62
forbid re-analysing a sealed snapshot *in place*; this writes fifteen Markdown documents into
a directory beside the stores and touches neither. Rule 20 holds by construction. **A test
digests the graph before and after and requires it byte-identical**, which is the assertion
those rules are actually about rather than a promise in a docstring.

**Three refusals, three sentences:**

* a revision whose stores were dropped by hand — the recipe in `CLAUDE.md` says to do exactly

* a graph whose analysis never finished. It opens perfectly and lies (rule 80), and a map
  written out of one would be a lie with fifteen documents behind it. The sentence is

* a graph this build reads differently. `Store` refuses on open and the refusal is passed on

**And one thing stated rather than refused.** `standards.db` is one file per program holding

**The first wording of that sentence was wrong and the page caught it.** It read *"nothing
here is checked against it"* — printed directly above `### Checked — 1`, because the rules

The document store is resolved **by name, never by newest** — the fallback is rule 70 exactly,
one version's prose under another version's headings, and a test proves the absence is stated

`index.py` needed two corrections it had written about itself: the cell read *"not written —
`--no-render`, or analysed before maps were named"* and now names the command that writes

## 2026-09-09 — node size follows the plate it sits on

Tom: *"Work on the per-plate node sizing. The goal of this is only to make them more visible
and easy to understand for the more sparsely populated plates. When nodes overlap one
another, they are too large to be useful. They should either spread out, or stop growing."*

### It was a units bug, and the measurement is what found it

A dot was `min(3.6, 1.4 + sqrt(degree) * 0.28)` **pixels** — the same on every plate, at every
zoom. A plate was `1000 * (1 + (sqrt(n/nmax) - 1) * plateSize)` **world units**, shrinking
with zoom and with how little it held. So a node's size was unrelated to the room its own
plate had, at any setting.

Measured on Society at the default framing, using the engine's own zoom (`diagnostics()`
reported −3.82, which a replication of `applyLayout` matched to 1.5%):

| | |
|---|---|
| drawn nodes touching or overlapping a neighbour | **4,990 of 10,052 — 49.6%** |
| smallest plate | **5.5 px radius**, six nodes |
| worst plate | `pkg:cli`, tightest gap 2.06 px against a 3.65 px dot |

A sparse plate was a disc about eleven pixels across holding six dots 3.6 px wide. There is no
arrangement of six dots that size inside that circle that reads as six things.

### The law

The tightest pair on a phyllotaxis disk of `n` points is `1.546 * R / sqrt(n)`, and **1.546
does not move with `n`**: 1.5460 at 6, 9, 12, 26, 58, 151, 475, 991 and 4,000. It is the
minimum rather than the median (1.69), because a guarantee taken on the typical pair is not a
guarantee. `layout.py` owns it as `PHYLLOTAXIS_TIGHTEST`, `test_layout_spacing.py`
re-measures it, and a test pins the renderer's copy to it.

    r = min( DISK_GAP * spreadZ / 2 ,  1.546 * R / (2 * spacing * sqrt(n)) )

In **world units**, so it means the same thing at every zoom. The ceiling is Tom's: a node
may not grow past half the gap to the plate above or it collides with a neighbour it has no
relationship with — and it is half the *drawn* gap, so `spreadZ` is the lever.

### Tom's two regimes fall out rather than being imposed

At `plateSize 1` the node radius is **16.4 world on every one of the 53 plates**, because area
per node is already constant there and the plate widths do the work. Per-plate sizing appears
only as the dial moves toward one width — which is *"the only time we should consider resizing
nodes is when we have fixed the plate size"*, reached from the other end. At `plateSize 0` a
six-node plate draws at 2.0× the radius of the 991-node plate on a disc of the same width.

### Verified through the renderer's own buffers

`Graph.separation()` reads the positions and radii the engine is about to hand the GPU — the
picture, not the formula that produced it — and reports the closest two surfaces on the stack.

| | pairs | touching | tightest clearance |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| spiral · width 1 | 2,681,114 | **0** | 16.37 world |
| spiral · width 0 | 2,681,114 | **0** | 19.39 world |
| spiral · spreadZ 1.0 | 2,681,114 | **0** | 16.37 world |
| spiral · uneven spread | 2,681,114 | **0** | — |
| force · GPU, 84 ms | 2,681,114 | 2,164 (0.08%) | −37.77 world |

### Force is left as it is, and the withdrawal is the interesting part

Tom: *"Force layout should be the same as it is now."* Under force a plate's node size is
derived from the circle the solver gave it as if its `n` nodes were spread evenly, so nodes
inside a cluster can still touch — the arrangement saying they are tightly related, which is
what the reader turned it on to see.

**Measuring the real tightest pair was built first, and withdrawn on evidence.** It works: 0
touching pairs of 2.68 million under force. But a solver can leave two nodes almost
coincident, that one pair then sets the whole plate's node size, and the view cap — taken on
the smallest node in the stack — zoomed the entire picture in until that node was a pixel.
**A 101-pixel dot everywhere else, from one outlier on one plate.** Rule 49's shape: a
plausible answer that hides what produced it. The grid-based nearest-neighbour search built
for it went with it.

### Two defects, and neither was found by review

**A placement change did not resize what it moved.** `applyLayout` moves every node and
clears the box cache, with a comment saying "the code that causes the staleness is the code
that clears it" — and left the radii alone, because under a pixel constant no placement could
stale them. Switching to force therefore drew spiral-sized dots over clustered positions:
**1,494 overlapping pairs on an arrangement whose own rule says none can.** `applyLayout` now
repaints, in the same function and for the same stated reason.

**A lone node and a lone shadow both went to the centre.** `phyllotaxis` returns the origin
for a single point, and at the origin a rotation separates nothing. Caught by
`test_a_shadow_never_lands_on_a_drawn_node` on its first run. The centre belongs to the drawn
nodes; a lone shadow takes the ordinary formula's answer instead.

### The placement change the law rests on

Drawn nodes and shadows shared one spiral ordered by degree, and the two kinds **segregate**
by degree — so the drawn nodes came out in contiguous runs and inherited the spacing of *all*
the placed points rather than their own. `ext:<small outside>` drew its six nodes from spiral
slots **0–2 and 32–34 of 42** — two blobs, not six dots — and `ext:FILE` drew 151 in one
unbroken block of 788. A plate sized for what it draws and packed with five times that many
points cannot separate its dots at any node size.

A shadow is a device for the third dimension and its slot is empty screen space (rule 23), so
it has **no claim on the plate's area budget**. It still needs a position — it takes part in
its plate's forces and a crossing has to meet the plate somewhere — so it gets a spiral of its
own, half a turn out of phase.

*Tested and rejected before it was proposed:* sizing the plate by placed points rather than
drawn nodes, which looked like the clean one-line fix for the shadow-heavy plates. Measured:
49.6% → **53.0%** touching, because it renormalises against a different largest plate.

### The ceiling binds, and the page says so

At the default `spreadZ` of 0.35 the ceiling is **33.2 world**, so at `plateSize 0` **43 of
Society's 53 plates** draw at it rather than at what their own spacing allows — plates from 6
to 217 nodes all at one size. Design rule 1 says no filter is silent, and a dot held below its
earned size is a filter on the one channel this feature exists to use. `nodeCeilingNote()`
states the count beside the width slider and names **stack** as the lever, because the ceiling
moves with that slider and not with the two the reader will otherwise blame.

It is refreshed from `updateControlsSummary`, where every slider in the box passes. The first
version put it in the width branch alone — rule 78 written and committed in the same edit.

### The control, and the floor

`nodeSize` is retired; **spacing** replaces it, 1.05–4.0 with 1.5 the default. Tom's call, and
the argument is that a radius is derived now: a slider setting it directly sets a number the
next layout change overwrites, and one that could be pushed past the spacing would exist to
break the guarantee beside it. Smaller means bigger dots, which the label has to carry.

Never smaller than can be drawn, and **the floor is on the view rather than on the radius**.
`radiusMinPixels` would hold every dot at a pixel while its plate went on shrinking, which is
exactly how they ended up on top of each other; `applyViewCap` raises `minZoom` so the
smallest node is always at least 1 px. The whole stack still frames in a graph pane about
**465 px tall** at the default settings; below that the reader pans, which is what capping the
view means.

### Owed

**One look at a sparse plate.** Every figure above was taken inside the running engine on the
real payload and not one is a screenshot. deck.gl reports `frames 0` in the automation tab:
the graph pane is hidden at boot, the canvas mounts at 300×150 and never resizes, and four
ways round it failed — a scripted mode switch, a pointer click, a selection to make the graph
the boot view, and a forced `resize()`. Rule 90's neighbour, and it is one minute of Tom's
screen.

**Gates:** 1,273 tests, mypy clean over 126 source files, ruff clean.

## 2026-09-09 — one size is a Setting, and a tall HUD panel scrolls

Two from Tom on seeing the sizing work. *"Default to this new value, it looks very good"* —
so per-plate stays the default and the old picture becomes a Setting beside it.

### `nodes: by plate / one size`

On the controls panel, under the width dial, because it is the same question one step down:
that dial says how much a **plate's** area tells you, this says how much a **node's** does.
Design rule 2 — both readings are good, and turning it off is how a reader goes back to the
picture they had. The button names the mode in force rather than the one a click would bring,
for `data-platelayout`'s reason.

**One size is the tightest plate's, and that choice is the whole of whether the mode is
safe.** Every other plate can afford that size by construction, so the separation guarantee
survives the mode change unaltered. An average would be a size that overlaps on the plates
below it — a mode that quietly gives up the one property the other mode is built on is worse
than no mode at all.

Verified in the engine, `Graph.separation()` over the real payload:

| | touching | tightest clearance |
|---|---:|---:|
| by plate · width 1 | 0 of 2,681,114 | 16.37 world |
| by plate · width 0 | 0 of 2,681,114 | 19.39 world |
| one size · width 1 | 0 of 2,681,114 | 16.37 world |
| one size · width 0 | 0 of 2,681,114 | 20.42 world |

At width 1 the two modes are identical by construction, because area per node is already
constant there — which is the same fact that made per-plate sizing appear only as the dial
moves toward one width.

`nodeCeilingNote()` says something different under one size: there the densest plate binds
and not the z-ceiling, so *"0 plates are at the node-size ceiling"* would be true and about
the wrong constraint (rule 32).

### A HUD box taller than the picture was clipped

Tom: *"when I open a control such as the spacing control for Graph and the window is too
short, there is no method to scroll down and see the bottom of the spacing control. I have to
make the window taller."*

`.graphcanvas` is `overflow: hidden` and `.graphhud` had no height bound, so the bottom of the
box was simply past the edge with nothing to say so. The HUD is bounded to
`calc(100% - 1rem)` — a real percentage against a positioned ancestor with a definite height,
so no script and no media query, and `100vh` would have been the wrong box.

**The scroller is `.hudbody`, not the HUD** (rule 50). Scrolling the whole thing would carry
the headers off the top, so the strip that says which box you are in leaves exactly when it is
needed; and `.graphhud` is `pointer-events: none`, so its own scrollbar could be seen and
never dragged. `.hudhead` is `flex: none` for the same reason — a squeezed header is
unreadable precisely in the case this was bounded for. Two `min-height: 0` declarations are
what let a flex child shrink below its content at all; without them the body's height is its
content's and the `overflow` never has anything to do.

`overscroll-behavior: contain` is not a nicety: past the last row the wheel chains out of the
panel and into the canvas underneath, so reaching the bottom of the controls would zoom the
stack. A gesture that ends by changing something else is worse than one that does nothing.

Measured in the page at a 557×353 canvas: the controls body is **195 px tall holding 292 px of
content**, and the bottom control — `elementFromPoint`-confirmed off screen before — is
reachable after 97 px of scroll.

### And the fix undid half of itself

A `render()` rewrites the HUD from scratch, so pressing the control you had just scrolled down
to put the box back at `scrollTop` 0 and took that control off the screen. **That reads as
broken in the same way `paneHeld` was written for**, and it was the measurement that caught it
rather than review — the first check after the CSS landed reported `afterRepaint: 0`.

`hudScrolls` / `restoreHudScrolls` keep each body's offset across the rebuild, keyed on the
body's **id** rather than on position, because the boxes are conditional and an index would
restore one box's offset onto another. Recorded and restored in the one function that replaces
the markup, never at the callers that cause a render (rule 51 — there are more of those every
session, and the one that forgets is the one nobody presses while testing).

After: 97 → **84**, with the control still on screen. Eighty-four rather than ninety-seven
because that particular click shortens the note beneath, so the content is shorter and the
browser clamps the restore to the new bottom — a box that shrank lands at its new end rather
than scrolled past it, which is the honest outcome.

### The pointer, and this time the instrument said why

A press aimed at the new toggle did not fire it. A capturing `pointerdown` listener recorded
**0 hits** against a button `elementFromPoint` confirms is at those coordinates, with
`document.visibilityState` reading **`hidden`** — the window is behind another one. That is
**rule 90**, and it accounts for both missed presses this session; the coordinate mapping was
right all along.

The route is verified scripted, end to end and in both directions: the label, `aria-pressed`,
the offered value, the persisted setting and the engine's own mode all flip together, with 0
touching pairs in each state. *One press with the window in front finishes it.*

## 2026-09-09 — the graph, looked at, and why it could not be before

Tom brought the tab to the front for about a minute, which was the whole of what was needed.

**The diagnosis, measured rather than asserted.** A page whose only job was to count frames:

| | |
|---|---|
| frames in 2 seconds | **0** |
| total frames since load | 1 — the initial call, before the tab backgrounded |
| a fresh one-shot `requestAnimationFrame` | **never fired** |
| `setTimeout` | normal |
| `document.visibilityState` | `hidden` |

So rAF is **stopped, not throttled**, and that is one cause for all three symptoms reported
across four sessions as separate things: deck.gl's animation loop never ticks (`frames 0`), it
never resizes its drawing buffer — which happens *inside* the render loop, hence 300×150 for
ever — and `Graph.resize()` queues work for a frame that never comes. The moment the tab was
foreground the canvas resized to 1113×649 and drew at 60 fps.

Chrome's `--disable-backgrounding-occluded-windows` and `--disable-renderer-backgrounding`
were offered and are only a partial substitute: they cover an occluded *window*, not a
background *tab*, which the Page Visibility API reports as hidden regardless. Tom's call was
the tab in front.

**Seen:** the stack at `plateSize 1`, the hourglass whose waist is the sparse plates; the
magnified plates at `plateSize 0` under `by plate` — countable, separated, sphere-shaded — and
the same region under `one size`, small flat dots and also separated. `Graph.separation()`
read 0 touching pairs throughout, which is the first time that claim has been checked against
pixels rather than against the buffers behind them.

**And one thing only looking could have found.** Switching `nodeScaling` to `uniform` **zooms
the picture in**: at `plateSize 0` with `spreadZ 0.9` the stack sat at zoom −4.88 and the flip
took it to −3.30. The view cap is doing exactly what it was built to do — one size makes the
smallest node smaller, the renderable floor rises, the zoom follows — but the reader flips a
control that says nothing about zoom and the picture jumps closer. Not predicted by the
arithmetic, not changed, and filed in `BRIEFING`'s open list as a decision rather than a
defect.

## 2026-09-09 — clearing the deck before the binary

Tom's decisions on the open list, taken in one message so that what is left before packaging
is the packaging. *"Once these are done, work on the packaging issues and then we can build
it. May take a couple of milestones."*

### `one size` is signed off, and the silence was the defect

*"One size is fine, I sign off on that. We can mention the behavior in the documentation."*

The behaviour was reported the same day and filed as a decision rather than a defect: at
`plateSize 0` with `spreadZ 0.9` the stack sat at zoom −4.88, and flipping `nodeScaling` to
`uniform` took it to −3.30. So nothing changed in the layout. What changed is two sentences —
`nodeCeilingNote()`'s `uniform` branch and the button's own `title` — because the ceiling note
lives in the ribbon and the title is what a reader reaching for the control sees first.

**Design rule 6 gained the general form**, which is the part worth keeping: *a clamp is felt
through whichever control moves it, so that control has to name it.* The rule already said
customisation is clamped and says why; what it did not say is that the clamp is not always
where the reader's hand is. Three controls bound node size here — spacing, stack, and this
one — and only one of them owns the cap.

### `touches --routine` refuses to answer about something else

`_find_routine` matched `qualname` or `name` exactly and, on no hit, fell back to
`qualname LIKE '%needle%'` — silently. So

```
dunneflow touches output/mensores --routine mensores.cli.app
```

answered about **`mensores.cli.apply.apply`** and reported a reach of 1. `app` is a Typer
object rather than a routine, so nothing could match it and the fallback returned the first
plausible thing it found: rule 49's shape (a fallback that yields a plausible value has hidden
the failure it was written for) wrapped around rule 5's (never match on a bare common name),
in the one command a reader would use to check an executable's reach.

**The fallback is kept**, because a half-remembered name is a real way to arrive. What it may
not do is wear an exact match's clothes. `Found` carries `exact`, `total`, and the module
question; `_search_said` builds the sentence once for both `touches` and `impact`, which
shared the defect (rule 51). Printed to **stdout** with the answer, not to stderr: a reader
piping the answer to a file must not lose the sentence saying it is a name search.

Three answers, never two — and the case that bit gets a fourth thing to say, which is worth
more than any number of near-misses:

```
no routine is named 'mensores.cli.app'.
  mensores.cli is a module here — mensores/cli/__init__.py — and declares no routines at all;
  nothing in it is named 'app'.
  1 routine name contains it — a name search, not the routine you asked for:
```

**The module test asks `files`, not `routines`, and that is the whole of why it fires.** The
obvious query is `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM routines WHERE module = ?`, and it returns 0 for
`mensores.cli` — a package `__init__` that builds a Typer app declares no routines of its own.
That answer says *"not a module here"* about a file the analysis had read. `files` is where a
module is recorded as having been read at all; how many routines it holds is the next question
and is usually the answer.

**`<module>` is excluded from that count**, for the reason it is excluded everywhere else: it
is the module's own top-level code wearing a routine's shape, nobody declared it, and
*"declares 1 routine"* about a package holding a docstring and two assignments is the opposite
of the sentence's job. The test fixture found this rather than review — `pkg/__init__.py` with
one assignment reported 1 where the real case reports 0.

**Two silences went with it, and one was in the branch that was working.** `LIMIT 25` followed
by `[:args.limit]` can show one of forty and say nothing, in the **exact** branch as much as
in the fallback: `touches --routine resolve --limit 2` showed two of eight and was silent.
Both branches count rather than reading `len(rows)` — the LIMIT has already decided that
number — and both state it (rule 32).

Eight tests, in `tests/test_find_routine.py`. The sample program is the defect's own shape by
luck: `app = typer.Typer(name="sample")` sits at module scope in `sample.py`.

### One header, on every page of a map

The cover stated which snapshot it described and when that source was read; the other fourteen
pages said only `Generated <now>`. A reader arriving at `07-database.md` from a link — which is
how most links arrive — had the whole problem the cover had just solved.

It was not fixed in passing because it could not be. Eight renderers each built
`f"# {program} — {title}\n\n*Generated {stamp} by DunneFlow.*"` inline and `markdown._header`
was a ninth copy used only inside that file, so correcting it meant correcting it nine times
and hoping the tenth renderer written afterwards remembered. Rule 51.

**`render/page.py`** is the one place now: `Stamp` (generated · revision · analysed),
`Stamp.of(store, when)` reading the graph once for all fifteen pages, and `header()`. **Its own
module, and that placement is load-bearing** — `markdown.py` imports every one of the eight
renderers, so a header living there and imported back by them is a cycle.

What made the change clean is that `stamp` was used for **nothing else** in any of the eight:
each took it, wrote one line with it, and never referred to it again.

*`_what_this_describes` is retired*, Tom's call. All three instants survive in the header, on
fifteen pages instead of one; keeping the section as well would have made the cover state the
same three facts twice — rule 51's shape arriving through its own fix.

**Missing and blank stay different answers.** A graph that records neither key keeps the exact
line it always had, `*Generated <when> by DunneFlow.*`; one that records a revision and no
analysis instant says which half is missing rather than collapsing to the pre-revision line.
Handing either an invented snapshot would be rule 30.

The guard is over the **files written**, never over one renderer, because eight copies is
exactly how this drifted: `test_every_page_states_the_snapshot_and_both_instants` reads every
page `render_snapshot` produced.

**Verified where it matters.** `dunneflow render` is where the two instants come apart, and on
an inner page they now do: *source read 2026-09-09 19:02 UTC — these documents written
2026-09-09 19:03 UTC.*

### Stack orientation, closed by decision

*"I think stack orientation is acceptable as-is, adding camera roll is not required. I can
already move the camera quite a lot."*

Open since 2026-08-28 and structural — `OrbitView` has no camera roll, so laying the column on
its side would have to be built rather than configured. Recorded beside the `OrbitView`
construction in `graph.js`, so the next reader finds the decision where the constraint is
rather than in a backlog they may not read.

### Inference withdrawn, and withdrawn is not deleted

*"The infer parts can be disabled as features and the links can be removed (but the code left
in place and marked for use in the next version). Be sure to remove all mentions of the feature
from any other controls or documentation, but don't destroy any code that may already exist for
it."*

**It had never been wired, and looking at it is what said so.** `MANIFEST` is `let MANIFEST =
[]` and nothing anywhere assigns it, so the page said *"the document manifest is not served
yet"* for ever — and `data-airun="go"` set `state.aiDone = true` and rendered **"✓ Pass
complete."** having done nothing at all. Design rule 16's own failure with a false claim on top:
a control that renders and is wired to nothing looks exactly like one that works, and this one
reported success. Its costs and volumes were the ratified artifact's pinned figures for one
program (rule 34).

**One constant decides**, `INFERENCE_SHIPPED` in `shell.js` (rule 51). Guarded off: the
navigator row, the Settings panel and its `data-goto`, the route, the breadcrumb, the off-mode
label, and the dispatch.

**Each guarded entry is kept in a shape the source guard can still read**, and that was not the
first attempt. `test_every_generated_nav_item_has_a_route` reads `NAV_ROUTES` out of the source
with `^\s+key\s*:`, so a spread written as `? { inference: … }` on one line hid the route while
leaving `nav: "inference"` visible — and the guard reported the withdrawn row as *unrouted*.
Both sides move together, behind the one constant, on their own lines.

**Kept whole**: `viewInference()`, `AI_OPS`, `POSTURES`, `MANIFEST`, `posture()`, `permits()`,
`chosenOps()`, `NEED_LABEL`, every `data-egress` / `data-aiop` / `data-airun` handler, every
state field, and the CSS. Turning it back on is one line, and it stops being one line the
moment somebody tidies away a handler nothing appears to call — which is why the guard asserts
that half too.

**`egress` and `aiOps` left `DEFAULTS` and `PERSISTED`**, on `nodeShapes`' precedent, and that
precedent is about the **reset dialog** rather than about storage: `resetSettings` walks the
defaults, so a key left there makes a reset report clearing *"egress posture"* and *"model
operations"* — naming two settings the reader was never offered and could not have changed. A
default is a promise that something can be different. `state.egress` and `state.aiOps` stay
where they are, so restoring the feature restores its persistence with it.

**Untouched, and none of it is the feature.** Four things share the word and are separate
subjects: *edge confidence* `INFERRED` and the *hide inferred edges* toggle (design rule 5,
built and working, nothing to do with a model); the *version tier* `INFERRED` (a version read
from a directory name, honest and stated); `Provenance`'s four tiers, whose two paid ones were
already declared and unbuilt; and **About this map**'s two rows, which say no fact here was
inferred and no model read it — a standing guarantee this withdrawal makes *more* true. Design
rules 14 and 28 stay, each with a paragraph saying what changed; rule 14's description of the
postures and the manifest is now **what the next version has to satisfy before the constant
becomes true**.

**Guarded from both sides**, because either half fails silently alone.
`tests/test_inference_withdrawn.py` asserts every door is behind the constant *and* that every
part of the feature is still there; `selfCheck()` gained the runtime half, which is the only
check that can see it — the handlers are still wired, deliberately, so the dead-control scan
passes them happily.

*And the guard failed on its own prose first*, which is the sixth time in this project: the
block comment explaining the withdrawal names `data-goto="inference"`, so the scan read its own
explanation as a live door. Rule 43, and the reason `_code` exists — imported from
`test_web_controls.py` rather than written again, because a second comment-stripper is a second
answer and this one would have been the naive version that ate the template literals.

## 2026-09-09 — milestone 2: packaging, and a `DunneFlow.app` that opens on a fresh machine

All five packaging blockers closed, and the artifact built. Four commits, working tree
clean. `uv run pytest` **1,363 passed** · `uv run mypy .` clean over **134** source files ·
`uv run ruff check .` clean. `output/mensores` was not written to at any point: every
analysis this session went to a temporary directory, and 8787 — a previous session's
server, left running on purpose — is still serving.

The plan's order was the record's own and it was the right one: blockers 1 to 3 are defects
in code that already existed, so they were fixed and tested *before* anything was frozen.
A frozen build that fails is a much harder thing to read than a failing test.

### 1. `runtime.py`, and the four questions with two answers

`src/dunneflow/runtime.py` is the only place any of these is answered (rule 51): am I
frozen, where do my files live, where do maps go, and how do I run myself again. Every one
was previously a `Path(__file__)` or a hand-written `sys.executable` in whichever module
happened to need it, and frozen each is wrong in a different way — a module imported out of
a PyInstaller archive has a `__file__` that names a path with no file behind it.

Named `runtime` rather than `paths` deliberately: a *path* in this codebase is a stored key
relative to the tree a store was read from (rule 60), and nothing in here is one of those.

**`resource_root()` keeps `dunneflow` as its last segment in both worlds**, and that single
decision is what makes the artifact interoperable. `fingerprint_files` labels every input by
its path relative to that root, so the bundle laid out as `<_MEIPASS>/dunneflow/…` yields
`detectors/python.yaml` exactly as the checkout does. Measured afterwards rather than
assumed: the binary stamps `extractor = 9:e8c9ac8a851c41b7` into the maps it writes, which
is the checkout's `rules_fingerprint()` at the same commit, and the checkout then opens
those maps without refusing them.

The alternative — baking a fingerprint into the build — was considered and rejected on
exactly that. It would have made a map written by the binary refuse to open in the checkout
and the reverse, under the rule (12) that exists to prevent confident wrong answers.

### 2. The fingerprint of nothing was two failures, not one

The blocker as filed said `fingerprint_files([])` returns `e3b0c44298fc1c14` — the sha256
of nothing, which looks exactly like a fingerprint and compares equal to itself for ever, so
rule 12's whole guarantee would be enforced by a constant.

Reading the code found the other half. `doc_extraction_inputs()` returns `Path(__file__)`
**unconditionally**, so frozen that list is *never empty*: it holds a name with no file. An
emptiness check alone passes it straight through to a `FileNotFoundError` raised from inside
a hash, several frames from anything that can say what went wrong. `RulesMissing` refuses
both, and a directory where a file was meant — each with its own sentence naming the
directory this build looked in, because the answer to it is a change to a spec file and
nothing else (rule 89).

### 3. `freeze_support()`, and why the serial fallback is not a safety net

`multiprocessing.freeze_support()` is now the first statement of `cli.main()` and of
`packaging/dunneflow_app.py`. Both, and that is right rather than redundant: whichever is
the real entry point of a given build, the first statement executed has made the call, and
it is a no-op every other time.

Worth writing down because it reads like cover and is not: **`walk.py`'s serial fallback
cannot catch this.** The `try` wraps the whole `with ProcessPoolExecutor(…)` block, so an
exception in the parent falls back to serial — but a frozen macOS spawn without
`freeze_support()` does not raise in the parent. The parent is fine; the children are the
program, and for `serve` that is sixteen more servers each opening a browser.

Asserted structurally rather than by running sixteen servers: a guard parses `cli.py` and
requires the call to be `main()`'s first statement. A guard can only see that a call is
*written*, never that it ran (rule 86) — what it can see is that nothing is written in
front of it, which is the whole requirement. Observed working later, through the binary:
628 files, sixteen workers, one application.

### 4. Found while writing the guard: `web/`'s two data paths

The blocker list named `detectors/*.yaml` and both extractor trees. It did not name
`web/serve.py`'s `STATIC` and `VENDOR`, which are the same shape — and frozen they are a
server that starts perfectly and serves 404s for every asset on the page.

That is the argument for the guard rather than for a list. `test_frozen.py` refuses any
`__file__` under `src/` outside `runtime.py`, because the next one will be added by somebody
who has not read any of this.

**Both source guards had to be rewritten to parse rather than scan**, and the reason is
rule 34: the first spelling of each read the file line by line and reported *its own
explanation of the rule* as a violation. An AST holds code and nothing else. It happened
three times this session, counting the cold-start test that matched `shell.js` inside
`start.html`'s comment about why the dialog left `shell.js`.

### 5. The output root became a thing rather than a derivation

Four routes worked the root out for themselves as `out_dir.parent` — the program list, the
program switch, the analysis, and the dialog's live pre-flight. Each correct, each added
separately, which is exactly how a fifth arrives (rule 51). It is a field on `_Live` now,
and a guard over the AST holds the line with one exemption: the constructor's own default,
which is the single place still allowed to derive it.

`where()` decides whether what `serve` was handed is a program or a root by the question
`analyze` already asks to keep a program's own output out of its own corpus — **does this
directory hold a map** — and never by its name, because `output/` is a fine name for a
directory of hand-written prose (rule 30). `no_map_here()` gives three answers where there
was one (design rule 21): a version that is not here, a root whose programs are *named* so
the reader can pick one (rule 89), and a directory with nothing in it, which is the only one
where `dunneflow analyze` is the fix.

`analysis.check` takes `serving: Path | None`. Exactly one refusal depends on it — *that is
the program being read* — and with nothing being read it is a fact with no subject. `None`
rather than a stand-in, because a stand-in has to be a directory *name*, and one that
happened to match would refuse the first analysis a reader ever asks for.

*Corrected by its own test:* an empty `--name` is the ordinary case, not a missing one.
`check` reads `name or source.name`, so it borrows the directory's leaf; the refusal is for
a directory with no leaf to lend. The first spelling of that test asserted the opposite and
was wrong about the code rather than the code being wrong about anything.

### 6. Nothing open is a state — and Tom's call was a start page

Put to Tom as two options: a start page whose whole job is to say there is nothing yet, or
the full shell with every pane stating why it is blank. He chose the start page, and it is
the better reading of design rule 21 rather than the cheaper one — the shell is an
application about one version of one program, and drawing it over nothing would be forty
panes each answering the same question the reader has not asked.

`_Live.current` is a **property that raises** with nothing open, which is how sixty-odd use
sites were left exactly as they were. `NothingOpen` is never a reader's doing: the start page
is what a bare server serves and the shell is never loaded without a base, so reaching it is
a route missing from the gate.

The gate is `GET_WITHOUT_BASE` and `POST_WITHOUT_BASE` — **two lists for the two route
tables**, on `POST_ROUTES`' own argument, because `/api/base` is a readout from cold and a
base *switch* when posted to, and one list would have exempted the second by accident. Each
names the *exceptions*, and that direction is the guard: a route added tomorrow needs a base
by default and refuses visibly from cold, where the other direction would default a new
route to *works without one* and fail the way rule 49 describes.

**One route lists programs, and it is the shell's.** `/api/programs` gained the root and a
revision count and answers with nothing open. A second endpoint for *what is here at boot*
would have been a second answer to one question. Likewise **opening the first program and
switching between two are one route**: `switch_program` already builds the new base before
closing anything and restores what it had on failure, so a cold open is a switch with
nothing to restore.

### 7. The analyse dialog left `shell.js`

`web/static/analyze.js`, about 500 lines: the dialog, the pre-flight, the progress panel,
the stop button and the polling. Out of a 21,250-line file because the **start page needs
every part of it**, and a second copy in the surface that is somebody's first minute with
this tool is rule 51's defect in the worst place to put it.

`prose.js`' boundary: it owns a gesture and knows nothing about the page. Five host
functions carry what it cannot know — `used`, `changed`, `clearOverlays`, `openProgram` and
`whileRunning`. The last was found by *reading the page*: the dialog's closing line says
"the map you are reading stays open and stays true", which is the whole reason an analysis
is a dismissible panel rather than the switch scrim — and on the start page there is no map
to say it about (rule 13). `clearOverlays` is not symmetry either: the switch scrim is drawn
at 96/97 and the dialog at 92/93, so a dialog opened from underneath a switch renders
perfectly, greyed, and swallows every click.

`test_web_controls.py`'s "everything the shell writes, something reads" guard failed on
`data-anagain`, correctly: the shell still *writes* that control (a failed switch offers
*Analyse it again*) and its reader had moved. Widened to look at the sibling module rather
than exempted — a name on a list of allowed misses is a control nothing checks for ever
(rule 35).

### 8. `osascript`, and no `pywebview`

Tom's call. `POST /api/pickdir` runs `osascript -e 'activate' -e 'POSIX path of (choose
folder …)'`, because `analysis.check` refuses a relative path — deliberately, since the
server's working directory is not the reader's — and a browser cannot hand a server what a
folder picker chose. No dependency, and it closed the one gap that was the argument for a
native window.

`activate` comes first and is not decoration: the dialog belongs to a process with no
window, and without it the panel opens **behind the browser**. Rule 90, one process over.

**The typed field stays**, always. The picker is a convenience over a control that still
works (design rule 2), what it returns goes *into the field* rather than straight into a
run, and it goes through the same pre-flight — so the picker cannot produce a path the
typed field would have refused (rule 41).

`POST /api/reveal` opens the root in the Finder, bounded to the root and its programs. It
is the answer to the one cost of Tom's choice of `~/Library/Application Support/DunneFlow`:
that is the correct place for an application's data and is never swept into iCloud Drive —
which matters, because `source.db` holds the private source of whatever was read, and
`~/Documents` on a signed-in Mac would upload it. What it is not is findable, and a page
that names a place the reader cannot reach is rule 89's shape.

### 9. Rule 91, and it cost the thing it is about

**The refusal never arrived.** `_refuse_without_base` was written as `send_error(409, "…
nothing is open, so /api/cover has nothing to answer about — open a program first")`. That
second argument is the HTTP *reason phrase*, and `http.server` encodes that line as
**latin-1**; the em dash raised `UnicodeEncodeError` from inside the error handler, where
there is no error path out, and the connection closed with nothing on it. `curl` reports
exit 52, *empty reply from server* — naming neither the route, the code, nor the sentence.

Worse than the failure the gate was written to prevent: a route answering an empty payload
at least answers. This looks like a server that crashed.

The fix is one argument along — `explain` is the body, encoded UTF-8. The rule is the
general shape, because every one of these looks like an ordinary string until it is not: an
HTTP reason phrase, a filename, a SQL identifier, a shell argument, a header value, an
environment variable — each a channel narrower than the prose being put through it, and
none of them validating on the way in.

**No test that calls a handler directly could see it**, which is the other half. So
`tests/test_cold_start.py` binds a real port, and one of its assertions is simply
`assert "—" in body`.

### 10. Frozen, and the ground truth run through it

`packaging/dunneflow.spec` and `packaging/dunneflow_app.py`. `uv run pyinstaller
packaging/dunneflow.spec --noconfirm` → **`DunneFlow.app`, 31 MB, unsigned**, in 23 s cold
and 7 s warm.

`datas` carries everything something reads *as a file*: the rules loaded as YAML, and the
detectors' loader plus both extractor trees **hashed** rather than imported, because rule 12
puts the reader in the key and a reader that exists only inside the archive hashes to
nothing. Plus `web/static`, `web/vendor`, and `copy_metadata('dunneflow')` — which is how
`tool_version()` keeps working with no frozen branch at all; the binary's maps record
`0.1.0`.

**No arguments means `serve`, and that decision belongs to the application rather than to
the CLI.** A command-line tool run bare should say what it takes; an application that has
just been double-clicked has no way to say anything back, and printing usage into a window
nobody opened is the same as doing nothing.

Found while testing exactly that: on a machine that has never run DunneFlow the default root
does not exist, so the start page named a directory the reader could not open and *Show me*
refused something that was simply not there. `serve` now creates it **only when nobody named
a directory** — one the reader typed is never created, because a mistyped path would
otherwise become a new empty root reporting no programs in a place they have never used
(rule 49). Creating a directory is not repairing a store: rule 20 forbids a read bringing a
*database* into being, and nothing on this path opens one.

**Ground truth through the binary** — `../society-2026-08-29/src` with
`--standards ../dunnecorp-standards`, 628 files and 2,064 documents in **37.7 s**:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| The four declared executables | **1,381 · 423 · 292 · 112**, all resolved |
| `naming.md` against the `CORP` fixture | byte-identical; its three rules in the checked lane |
| The research paper's naming rules | **zero** |
| Conformance verdicts | **4 checked · 1 no population · 10 not checkable** |
| Stated rules | 12, including all seven rows of the `style.md` table |
| The binary's `extractor` vs the checkout's | **equal** — `9:e8c9ac8a851c41b7` |

### 11. Looked at, not only tested

Screenshots and a real pointer, per the standing habit. The start page on an empty root and
on a root of two; the shared dialog opened at the pointer from the start page; a program row
pressed at the pointer landing in the shell with `renderer — 14 files` in the select;

**The first pointer attempt missed, and it was rule 90.** `osascript -e 'tell application

One layout nit fixed from the screenshot rather than from a test: the root row centred its

### What is left, and it is two things

**Signing and notarisation**, which decide the non-technical experience — an unsigned `.app`

**One candidate rule is filed rather than minted, for Tom to take or refuse:** *a module's
