## 2026-09-09 — milestone 3: signed with a Developer ID, and a universal build that refuses to lie

Tom: *"Resume project work with a project build, sign, and install commands for me."* Three
decisions were his, taken before any of this was written: a signed `.app` inside a signed
`.dmg`, an **App Store Connect API key** for notarisation, and **universal** rather than
arm64-only.

**What was found before anything was decided**, because the shape of the work turned on it:

| | |
|---|---|
| `Developer ID Application: Thomas Williams (G3RLJWV327)` | present and valid |
| `Developer ID Installer` for the same team | present, and not needed — no `.pkg` |
| stored notarytool credentials | **none**, and that is one of the two things left |
| PyInstaller's Darwin bootloaders | already universal2 (`x86_64 arm64`) |
| every Python on this machine | **arm64 only** — uv's and Homebrew's alike |
| Mach-O files in the bundle | three: the bootloader, `libpython3.12.dylib`, `yaml/_yaml…so` |
| a universal2 PyYAML wheel on PyPI | **none, for any version** |

Those last two are the same fact from two sides, and they decided the whole universal question.

### The extension that cannot be universal is the one nothing uses

PyYAML's C extension is the single file in the bundle that cannot be built for both
architectures, and it is never called: every one of the eight call sites in this program is
`yaml.safe_load`, which is the pure-Python `SafeLoader` whether or not `yaml._yaml` imports.
`yaml/__init__.py` already takes the extension inside a `try` and records its absence in
`__with_libyaml__`, which nothing here reads. So it is **dropped from the bundle** rather than
worked around, and the arm64 build is one Mach-O file lighter for it.

**Both names, and the first spelling did nothing.** `excludes = ["_yaml"]` built and shipped the
extension exactly as before: the module is `yaml._yaml`, and `yaml.cyaml` is the wrapper that
imports it. Excluding the extension alone would be worse than not excluding it — an
`ImportError` where `__init__.py` has a fallback — so it is
`excludes = ["yaml.cyaml", "yaml._yaml"]`, and the note in the spec says why both.

**The guard is a pair, and it reads syntax rather than text.** One half asserts nothing under
`src/` asks for `CSafeLoader`, `CLoader`, `CDumper` or `__with_libyaml__`; the other asserts the
spec still drops both names. Either alone is worth nothing: a guard saying *nothing uses it* is
empty if the spec has quietly started shipping it, and a spec that drops it is a defect the
moment somebody reaches for the C loader. The first spelling of the first half was a scan, and
it reported **its own docstring** as the violation — rule 34, in a file that has already paid
for it three times, so it walks the AST.

### `DUNNEFLOW_ARCH`, and rule 49 in the place it matters most

`target_arch` on the `EXE` comes from `DUNNEFLOW_ARCH`: unset is the machine doing the building
— today's seven-second gate, untouched — and `universal2` is a release. Asked for `universal2`
under an interpreter that cannot produce one, **the spec raises**, naming the interpreter it
found and the installer that fixes it.

This is the one place a fallback would have been unrecoverable. A "universal" build that quietly
came out arm64 would build, sign, notarise, staple, image and install without a word, and be
found by a colleague on an Intel Mac with nothing on this machine to look at. The check is on
`sys._base_executable` rather than `sys.executable`, because a virtual environment's `python` is
a stub that says nothing about what is behind it.

**And it cannot be uv's interpreter.** uv's managed Pythons and Homebrew's are single-arch by
construction — python-build-standalone ships no universal2 build at all. `python-3.12.10-macos11.pkg`
is the last universal2 3.12 (3.12.11 is source-only; checked, not assumed) and
`release.sh venv` builds `.venv-universal` from it. A build-only interpreter, disturbing neither
uv nor the project environment.

### `packaging/release.sh`, and what it refuses to do

One verb per step — `venv build sign notarize dmg verify install all` — so any of them can be
run alone while something is being worked out. Four things about it are decisions rather than
mechanics:

* **No `codesign --deep`.** Apple deprecates it, and it applies the *outer* bundle's
  entitlements to everything nested, which is the exact opposite of what an empty entitlements
  file is trying to guarantee. Every Mach-O file is **found**, never listed — a dependency added
  tomorrow brings its own dylibs, and a hand-written list would leave them ad-hoc signed inside
  a Developer ID bundle — and signed on its own, deepest first, the bundle last. The bundle's
  own main executable is left out of that loop because signing the bundle signs it.
* **The `.app` is notarised and stapled before the `.dmg` exists**, and the image is notarised
  and stapled in its own right. Two submissions rather than one: a stapled image alone leaves
  the dragged-out app needing a network round trip on first launch, and a reader opening an
  unfamiliar tool offline is the case this has to survive.
* **`ditto`, never `zip(1)`.** A `.app` is a directory of symlinks and extended attributes and
  `zip` flattens both; what Apple receives has to be what was signed.
* **The version is read off the bundle**, never spelled a second time in the script: the spec's
  `CFBundleShortVersionString` is the one answer (rule 51), and `test_frozen.py` holds the
  script and the spec to one spelling of `DunneFlow.app` (rule 41).

### The entitlements file asks for nothing, and that was measured

Every PyInstaller guide carries the same four entitlements, copied from each other. None is
indicated here and each was checked: the picker spawns `/usr/bin/osascript`, whose `activate`
and `choose folder` are Standard Additions running **inside osascript itself**, so no Apple
Event leaves this process; CPython 3.12 has no JIT and nothing builds a ctypes closure; and
every Mach-O file in the bundle is signed by the identity that signs the bundle, so library
validation has nothing to refuse.

**Pressed rather than argued.** `POST /api/pickdir` against the signed app running out of
`/Applications` spawned `osascript` as PID 1488 with the app as its parent, and it held the
`choose folder` dialog open until it was killed — an AMFI refusal exits immediately — with
nothing denied in `log show` for the whole window. That is the evidence for an empty file, and
the file says a key added later needs the failure that earned it recorded beside it.

**It cost a defect of its own.** The first version put the explanatory comment between the XML
declaration and the `DOCTYPE`, and used `--` inside it. AMFI's parser is stricter than most:
`Failed to parse entitlements: AMFIUnserializeXML: syntax error near line 9`, with codesign
refusing to sign at all. Both constraints are now written into the file, where the next person
to explain something in it will read them.

### The gate found something the gate could not previously find

`uv run mypy .` — the command `CLAUDE.md` prescribes — **fails whenever a build exists**, and
had never been run with one because every previous build lived in a session scratchpad. `.`
overrides `files = ["src", "tests"]`, and `dist/` holds a *copy* of this package: the spec
bundles both extractor trees and the detectors' loader as data so `rules_fingerprint()` has
files to hash (rule 12). mypy finds two modules with one name and stops **before checking
anything at all** — `Found 1 error in 1 file (errors prevented further checking)`, over a clean
source tree. `exclude = '^(dist|build|\.venv-universal)/'` in `pyproject.toml`, because the
artifact is not source.

### What was proved, and what was not

**Proved.** The signed bundle reports `flags=0x10000(runtime)`, the full
`Developer ID Application` → `Developer ID Certification Authority` → `Apple Root CA` chain,
`TeamIdentifier=G3RLJWV327` and a secure timestamp; it satisfies its Designated Requirement;
`ditto` into `/Applications` leaves the signature intact; launched through LaunchServices it
serves the start page. **The ground truth was retaken through the signed binary** and every
figure held — 628 files, the four executables at **1,381 · 423 · 292 · 112**, `naming.md`
byte-identical to the `CORP` fixture at 278 bytes, the research paper yielding **zero** naming
rules, conformance at **4 checked · 1 no population · 10 not checkable**, and
`extractor = 9:e8c9ac8a851c41b7`, which is the checkout's, so the two builds still read each
other's maps.

**Not proved, and said rather than glossed.** The build in `/Applications` is **arm64 and
unnotarised**: the universal build waits on the python.org interpreter and notarisation waits on
Tom's App Store Connect key. Gatekeeper's answer today is *"rejected — source=Unnotarized
Developer ID"*, which is what a correctly signed, un-notarised app is supposed to say. And the
analysis through the binary took **56 s wall / 22.9 s user** against a recorded 37.7 s — a
different measurement under the same label, since it ran off the external volume into
`/private/tmp` rather than reproducing the recorded conditions, so it is **not** entered in
`PERFORMANCE.md` and nothing is claimed from it either way (rule 24).

**A double-click would collide with 8787**, which a previous session's server holds and which
was not stopped. `serve` defaults to that port and the application defaults a bare argv to
`serve`, so the Finder launch was checked at `--port 8890`.

### Where it picks up

Two once-only commands, both Tom's, both written into `release.sh`'s header and `CLAUDE.md`:
install python.org's universal2 3.12.10, and store an App Store Connect API key with
`xcrun notarytool store-credentials dunneflow`. Everything downstream of them is written.
Then the icon, then Windows.

## 2026-09-10 — milestone 4: the application says what it is doing, and a build that runs anywhere

The folder was renamed to `DunneFlow` and the company became **Dunne, Corp.** — a C-corp, no
longer an LLC. That was the whole of the asked-for work, and it took twenty minutes. Everything
below came out of running the signed build afterwards, which is the point worth keeping: **the
1,368 tests prove the source tree, and every defect this session lived in the artifact or in the
surface a first-time reader meets.**

| | |
|---|---|
| tests | 1,368 → **1,401**, mypy and ruff clean throughout |
| defects found | **eight**, none reported by a test |
| features | the way back, a movable maps root, a Dock presence, notarisation |
| the binary | universal2, Developer ID, **notarised and stapled**, in `/Applications` |
| `extractor` | still `9:e8c9ac8a851c41b7` in both builds (rule 12 holds) |

### The rename, and what it exposed

`DunneCorp LLC` appeared exactly once, in the topbar. `documenter` appeared in no source file
at all — only in generated state that had gone stale: **both virtualenvs** (editable install and
every console-script shebang pointing at the old path), `output/dunneflow` (schema 5 against a
current 9, with 5,800 absolute paths), a dead scratchpad path in `standards.db`'s WAL, and
`build/`, `dist/` and every cache. All regenerated; `migrate` could not help, because the map
predated the fingerprint that migration is allowed to re-stamp.

Two things fell out of it:

* **`adopt_revision` did not re-stamp its `tree`.** It filled an empty one and left a recorded
  one alone, while `open_working` overwrites. So `source.db` moved to the new leaf and
  `docsource.db` kept the old — one snapshot recorded as read from two different trees, which is
  the disagreement that method's own docstring says must never happen (rule 51).
* **`types-PyYAML` was installed by hand and never declared**, so `uv run mypy .` had only ever
  been green on this machine. Rebuilding the venv found it.

### The stall: three analyses that finished and reported themselves frozen

Tom ran three analyses from the packaged app. Each froze — at *step 7 of 7*, then *2 of 7*, then
*2 of 7* — and the start page stayed at *"No map has been made yet"*. **All three had finished**:
`complete = 'yes'`, full maps on disk.

```
ReferenceError: loadPrograms is not defined
    at tick (http://127.0.0.1:8787/static/analyze.js:416)
```

`analyze.js` called a **`shell.js` global**. The shell defines it; `start.html` loads only
`analyze.js` and `start.js`. It threw on the one tick that ever sees `state === "done"`, *before*
the panel repainted and before the loop returned — so the panel froze on whichever poll last
landed, which is why a 90-second tree stopped at 7 of 7 and a fast one at 2 of 7.

The hook it should have used — `changed()` — was **wired by both hosts and called by nobody**.
One defect with two halves: a documented contract entry that was dead, and an undocumented
global that only one host had. `tests/test_analyze_boundary.py` holds the class: no identifier
called in `analyze.js` may be a top-level declaration of `shell.js`.

### There was no way back, and now there are two

`/` is the shell for as long as a base is open, and nothing closed one — so the maps-directory
control became unreachable the moment a reader opened anything. `POST /api/close` is
`switch_program` with no destination (1 ms); `GET /start` always serves the start page and is
the drastic route, typeable when `shell.js` has thrown (design rule 20). The shell's `<select>`
gained `× Close this map` on `Analyze.OPTION`'s existing pattern.

**`/api/close` is the first thing in this tool's life that makes `opened` go true → false**, and
that is a new state: a request can pass the route gate and reach `current` after the base has
gone. `NothingOpen` would escape to `socketserver.handle_error` and close the socket with
nothing on it — rule 91's symptom by a different door. Both dispatch paths catch it now and
answer as the gate would.

### Maps can be kept somewhere else

`Move…` on the start page: `web/roots.py`, `POST /api/root`, copy-verify-delete so a failure
leaves the originals untouched and takes the partial copies with it. Verified through the signed
binary: **287 MB onto an external APFS volume in 2.3 s**, old root emptied, maps opening from the
new location.

**The pointer has three states and the third is the ordinary one.** An unplugged drive raises
`MapsRootGone` rather than falling back, because `cmd_serve` calls `mkdir(parents=True)` and
`/Volumes` is an ordinary directory *on the boot disk* — a created pointer target would put a new
empty maps root on precisely the drive the reader was clearing, and then report no programs in it
(rule 49). **A pointer's target is never created.** `serve` falls back to the platform root and
*says so*, on the terminal and in a banner.

**And a checkout neither reads nor writes it.** Found the hard way, immediately: a checkout's
`serve` moved two maps into a scratchpad and stamped that path into the *real*
`~/Library/Application Support/DunneFlow/root`, so the packaged application would have opened
next and told its reader their maps were on a disk that was gone. The tell was `test_frozen.py`
failing with a path from another session — the fixture had made the whole file non-hermetic.

### Three more, each found on the way past

* **A false refusal on first use.** Both `analysis.check` call sites passed the output root as
  *the program being read* with nothing open. The frozen default root is called **DunneFlow**, so
  analysing any directory of that name was refused with *"its graph is open here"* over a server
  holding no graph. `check`'s own docstring forbade exactly this and was unenforced (rule 30).
* **A handle leak on every program switch.** `switch_program` captured four things and closed
  two; `standards.db` leaked on both paths, silently, since `--standards` landed (rule 36).
* **Repeat launches.** Measured: three double-clicks, **three servers** on 8787, 50595 and 50596,
  each holding its own stores. `_free_port`'s wander is right for its own case and wrong for this
  one. `already_serving` joins a DunneFlow reading the **same root** — so two roots are still two
  servers, and a developer is not silently sent to the wrong one.

### The Dock had no dot, and the fix had to cost no entitlement

Tom, from a screenshot: *"Most users will not understand how to find a running process and will
just continue launching it over and over."* `lsappinfo` named the cause exactly —
`type="Foreground"` but **`!cgsConnection`**. `LSBackgroundOnly` was already false; the plist was
never it. A command line tool in a bundle never touches AppKit, so the window server has nothing
to indicate.

The one-line version — `[NSApplication sharedApplication]` — buys the dot and a Dock icon that
**cannot be quit**, which is worse than no dot. So `macapp.py` moves the server to a background
thread and gives the main one to `[NSApp run]`; quit is `NSApplication`'s own default handling of
the quit Apple Event. **No delegate**, because that means Python methods on an Objective-C class,
which means `ctypes.CFUNCTYPE` closures, which means `allow-unsigned-executable-memory` — and
`entitlements.plist` is empty because it was measured to be. A test asserts the module contains
no `CFUNCTYPE`. Verified on the signed hardened build: registers, serves, quits, entitlements
still `<dict></dict>`, nothing denied in the AMFI log.

Ctrl-C is handed back to the OS on that path only: Python's SIGINT handler runs between bytecodes
on a main thread that is now inside ObjC, so it would appear dead until an unrelated event woke
the loop. Every store this process holds is read-only, so there is no write to interrupt.

### Notarisation, which was one credential and not a certificate

Tom: *"I thought the presence of the credentials was sufficient."* The keychain had **Developer ID
Application** and **Developer ID Installer**, both valid — and they sign. Notarisation is an
authenticated upload to Apple's notary service, and a certificate cannot authenticate an HTTPS
call because the private key never leaves the Mac. `notarytool history` said so in as many words.
One `store-credentials` later the step ran unattended: **Accepted**, stapled, and Gatekeeper
flipped from *rejected — Unnotarized Developer ID* to **accepted — Notarized Developer ID**.

### Snap-to-fit framed a dot

Reported as *"you can't tell what you're seeing until you zoom out, then you can see giant node
spheres."* `bounds` ends `radius: r || 1`, and one node with no neighbours has `r === 0` — so the
fit framed **two world units**, measured at 3 units against a plate 669 across, at all three
views since they share one `scale`.

The floor is half the hosting plate, measured from the **drawn positions** and clamped on the
**scale** against `Math.min(w, h)`. The first spelling floored the radius, which guarantees the
share across the width and lets a short pane crop the height — 56% wide but 35% tall in a 258×165
pane. After: **50% in the tighter direction, 78% in the wider**, at default, top-down and tilt
alike, node exactly centred, with the whole-stack, busy-node and whole-plate cases byte-identical
to before.

### Universal by default

Unset `DUNNEFLOW_ARCH` meant *this machine*, which made the fast build easy and the shippable one
the thing you had to remember — and forgetting is silent, because an arm64 bundle runs perfectly
on the machine that made it. **12.9 s universal against 11.5 s host**, so the cheap default was
buying nothing. `host` is still one word for the verification gate.

**A default is a habit, so the artifact is checked rather than the command.** `require_universal`
gates `sign`, `notarize`, `dmg` and `install` — deliberately not `build` or `verify`, since one
makes the thing and the other must stay able to say what is wrong with it.

### Two tests that passed over the defect they were written for

Both are rule 34, and both are worth remembering because the file they were added to already
warns about it.

* The `analyze.js` boundary scan reported `loadPrograms` as a leak **after it was fixed** — the
  explanatory comment names it. And its first stripper, which removed string literals too, was a
  JavaScript parser written in regular expressions: a regex literal in `shell.js` carries a
  double quote, which opened a string the scanner closed thousands of lines later, and
  `Analyze.wire` vanished from a 20,000-line file with no error. It strips comments only now.
* The universal-default test asserted `"or 'universal2'" in ast.unparse(func)` and **passed over a
  spec whose default had been deleted**, because the refusal one line below reads *"Leave it unset
  for 'universal2'"* and `for` ends in `or`. It reads the syntax now: the assignment must be a
  `BoolOp(Or)` whose fallback is that constant.

Every fix this session was mutation-checked — the defect reintroduced, the test watched to fail,
the fix restored.

### Open

The **icon**. `packaging/icon/build_icon.py` draws a hare leaping a river as geometry rather than
a picture: `GAP` is 96 canvas units of blue between them (3 px at 32), the river runs the full
width, and the hare is a near-black silhouette because value contrast is all that survives at
32 px — the tan-on-blue candidate dissolved into its own background. Ears are upright, not swept:
laid along the spine they were geometrically clear of the back and still merged into it by eye.
**Not committed and not wired in**; `icon=None` in the spec, and Tom has not passed judgement.

Then **Windows**, and a **`.dmg`** whenever something needs handing over — `release.sh dmg` works
now that the credentials are in the keychain.

## 2026-09-10 — the user guide, and the one control that named a pair it was not showing

The asked-for work was documentation: DunneFlow had none for the person it is built for. Everything
below came out of **driving the product in order to photograph it**, which is the same shape as the
session before it — the tests prove the source tree, and the defect lived in the first surface a
reader meets.

| | |
|---|---|
| written | `docs/` — 17 files, 1,879 lines, **29 screenshots** taken from a live server |
| tests | 1,401 → **1,402**, mypy and ruff clean throughout |
| defects found | **one**, in the version-pair control; not reported by a test |
| corpus | `docs/` is DunneFlow's own documentation now — **9 documents → 26** |
| `README.md` | rewritten; it still ended *"the interactive dashboard is designed but not yet built"* |

### The guide, and who it is addressed to

Sixteen numbered files plus an index, in the register the tool is built for: someone who reads code
and does not write it. Installing · getting the code · the start page · the first map · the shell ·
the six views · chasing rabbits · Settings · comparing two versions · when it refuses · the command
line.

Three rules held throughout, and each is worth keeping for whoever writes the next page.

* **Name every control by the words on it.** `◇ Keep this`, `‹ out`, `show crossings`,
  `+ Analyse a directory…`. All 44 quoted labels were grepped back against `web/static/` at the end;
  one had drifted in my prose and not in the product.
* **State what a thing costs**, because the product does. The force layout is 89 ms with a GPU and
  9.7 s without; the findings overlay is 1.3–4.1 s the first time. Documentation vaguer than the
  screen is documentation that will be believed over it.
* **Never cite a rule number.** `RULES.md` is for whoever builds the tool. A tutorial says *the map
  refuses because the analysis that wrote it never finished*.

`docs/02-getting-the-code.md` is the one a reader will not expect and is the one that had to exist:
**DunneFlow never asks a version control system anything.** git, Perforce, Lore, a zip on a memory
stick — get a directory, point the tool at it. The page teaches the two traps that make a map lie
rather than fail: the default branch that is three months stale, and a sparse checkout or a narrow
Perforce client view, where **what is not on disk is not in the map**.

### What photographing it found

**The version-pair control named a pair it was not showing.** On a fresh session with two versions,
the menu read *DunneFlow · on its own* while the strip beside it read *compared with
dunneflow-2026-09-08*, the routine list marked itself, and the code overlay drew.

`comparedRev` has **three** states — *nothing chosen yet* (`""`), *chosen: on its own* (`ALONE`), and
a revision — and that distinction is load-bearing and already recorded: collapsing the first two is
the defect Tom reported months ago, when choosing *on its own* went on naming a pair.
`comparedRevInForce()` was fixed then, and `versionStrip()` was fixed after it with a comment saying
exactly why: *"Two answers to 'what is this held against', and fixing one fixed nothing a reader
could see."*

**`buildRevControls()` was the third answer, and the only one the reader can click.** It derived its
compared end from `chosenPair().compared`, which is empty for *nothing chosen yet* and *chosen: on
its own* alike. One line:

```js
-  const compared = pair.compared || "";
+  const compared = comparedRevInForce();
```

Verified in the browser across all four states with `localStorage` cleared, each surviving a reload:
`""` → names the pair · `ALONE` → *on its own*, `comparing()` false · an explicit revision → names it
· and the **reversed base**, which matters because the fallback keys on `serving` and not on `base` —
`dunneflow-2026-09-08 ← DunneFlow`, with `captured:` correctly flipped to *base first*.

*What was not changed is the default.* A two-version program opens **comparing**, so the routine
marks and the code overlay draw on a first visit; the fallback exists for that and its comment says
so. The defect was the control misreporting, never the behaviour.

### The guard that watched it happen

`test_the_pair_control_shows_the_pair_that_is_actually_in_force` has that name and does not test it.
It asserts that the keys `buildRevControls` reads off `chosenPair()` are keys `chosenPair()` returns
— which catches the *previous* defect in that function and is blind to this one, because
`pair.compared` is a real key being read for the wrong question. Rule 37 exactly: a guard that checks
a name appears has not checked that anything happens.

`test_the_pair_control_takes_its_compared_end_from_the_one_function` is beside it now, asserting the
compared end comes from `comparedRevInForce()` and that `comparedRevInForce` still tests for `ALONE`.

**And the mutation check first proved nothing, which is worth recording.** Reverting the line with a
first-occurrence string replace edited a *different* function: two other places legitimately hold
`const compared = comparedRevInForce();`, and the first is 1,200 lines above `buildRevControls`. The
test passed, correctly, over a file where the control was still fixed — a green mutation check that
had mutated nothing (rule 59, from the other side). Anchored on the surrounding comment it fails with
the diagnosis.

### The corpus check, which the guide had to pass

`docs/` sits at the repository root, which is DunneFlow's documentation root — so the guide is read
back as DunneFlow's own corpus. That is correct and wanted, and it is also the one way a tutorial can
put a false fact into the map.

Measured before and after. Naming rules from `docs/`: **zero**, which is the one that mattered — a
tutorial about naming is exactly the shape `_table()` fires on. Definitions: **one**, and it was
mine. The heading *"Where a definition came from"* was read as a glossary section and minted the term
`Where a definition came from` at `HEADING_PARA`. The heading is *"Following a citation back"* now,
and the corpus gains 17 documents and **no** definitions and **no** rules.

The fix belongs in the tutorial and not in the detector: the detector read that heading exactly as it
should, and rule 1 says precision beats recall in the other direction too — a section heading that
announces a definition is a section heading that announces a definition.

### Every map in `output/` was stale, and nothing said so until it was opened

`serve output/mensores` refused on `standards.db`; the graph was stale too, and so were both sealed
snapshots and `output/beads` and `output/dunneflow`. Rebuilding the Society pair is the three-command
recipe and costs two analyses; Tom's call was to **analyse DunneFlow itself and clone an older
version into a sister directory**, which is what the screenshots and the comparison chapter are of:
`../dunneflow-2026-09-08`, a worktree at `f795bc3`, sealed as `FOR_COMPARISON`, against the current
tree. 864 routines → 910, and 49 deleted · 63 behaving differently · 14 edited only.

It is a better corpus for a guide than Society, and not only because it was to hand: every routine a
screenshot names is one the reader can go and read.

### One stale sentence in `BRIEFING.md`

*"Local variables, arithmetic and control flow are deliberately absent"* — the control-flow half was
amended on 2026-09-07 and Shape mode is the amendment. Corrected in the file whose whole job is to
orient a fresh context, and in `README.md`, which said it too.

### Open

Nothing from this session. The **icon** and **Windows** are where they were.

The guide has **no page on the anomaly worklist**, deliberately: it is a navigator destination rather
than one of the six views, and it is the one surface whose discipline — severity, confidence and
blind spot as three different questions — deserves a page of its own rather than a paragraph.

## 2026-09-15 — the map the application read as documentation, and rule 92

Found by looking at what five days of real use had left on disk, rather than by a test. The
maps root the packaged application writes to — `~/Library/Application Support/DunneFlow` —
held four maps, and the one of **DunneFlow itself** had a `docs@….db` of **289 MB** beside a
6 MB graph. That ratio is the whole story: 13,449 tables and 161,047 table rows, out of a
program whose own prose is a few megabytes.

### What it was

| | the app's map | the checkout's (`output/dunneflow`) |
|---|---|---|
| documents read | 147 | 8 |
| of those, from `output/` | **122** | 0 |
| stated naming rules | **122 — every one** | 0 |
| definitions | 680, of which **655** from `output/` | — |
| `docs@….db` | **289 MB** | small |

So the map the application built of this program stated 122 naming rules **about Mensores**,
mined out of `output/mensores/map@…/06-governance.md` and its siblings, and 96% of its
glossary's documentation tier came from the same place. It is the failure `walk.py` already
records as fixed — *"every one of the 942 rules it then claimed to have found came from
them"* — arriving again through a door the fix never covered.

### Why the defence was absent

`exclude = frozenset({out_dir}) | revisions.program_dirs(out_dir.parent)`, at both call
sites, and `out_dir.parent` **is** the output root. `program_dirs` asks the right question
and asks it the right way: *does this directory hold a `graph*.db`*, by content and never by
the name `output`, which is a fine name for a directory of hand-written prose (rule 30). It
even stated its own bound honestly — one level down and no deeper, because a recursive search
would *"cost every project a walk to protect against a layout nobody uses."*

**That layout is what an installed application does.** From a checkout the output root is
`./output`, inside the tree being read, so the set enumerates exactly the maps in the way.
Frozen it is a directory in the reader's Library, so the same expression enumerates something
with no bearing on the tree at all — and a checkout's own `output/`, full of maps, went
straight back into the corpus. **The defence was assembled from where the run writes, and
installing the application moved that out of the tree the run reads.** Rule 92.

### What 1,402 green tests were saying

Nothing, and the reason is worth more than the fix. `tests/test_map_index.py:197`,
`test_a_map_is_not_read_as_documentation`, drives the whole of `cmd_analyze` and asserts this
exact property — with `out = tmp_path/"out"` beside `tree = tmp_path/"src"`. Every test in
the suite put the output root inside the analysed tree, because that is what a developer's
arrangement looks like. The suite proved the one shape in which the defect cannot appear.
Rule 24's family at the level of a fixture.

### The fix

Ask the question of the tree, on the walk that is already happening. `discover_docs` prunes a
nested checkout off `os.walk`'s own listing at no `stat` cost (rule 57); a map's spine is in
`filenames` for the same price. Four parts:

* **`revisions.names_a_map(names)` and `holds_a_map(path)`** — one spelling of the marker.
  `any(glob("graph*.db"))` was written out **three times**, twice in `program_dirs` and once
  re-implemented in `serve.where`, whose own docstring called it *"the same question `analyze`
  asks"* while asking it separately. Adding a fourth in `walk.py` would have been rule 51's
  defect committed inside the fix for rule 57's. A test over the AST refuses a fourth, and was
  checked by putting one back: it names `serve.py:3544` and the exact expression.
* **`discover_docs` prunes a map wherever it sits**, by `dirnames`, so a program directory
  takes its `map@<revision>/` with it. **Applied at the root too**, unlike the checkout
  marker, and that asymmetry is the point: the corpus is itself a checkout and that is why
  the root is exempt there, but a corpus is never itself a map.
* **`exclude` stays**, narrowed to `{out_dir}`, for the one thing a marker cannot see — this
  run's own output directory, created before the documents are scanned and holding no graph
  until after. `program_dirs(out_dir.parent)` is gone from both call sites: it is a no-op that
  would read as the live defence and rot. Its eleven other callers in `serve` and `roots` are
  untouched, and its docstring now records what its own bound cost.
* **`WalkStats.maps`, and two sentences** — *a map of a program, not documentation about one*
  for the corpus walk, *not a standard* for the standards walk, because the standards reader
  named the directory and the corpus reader did not. Design rule 1, and the number is larger
  here than the 14% a pruned worktree cost: silently, this is 83% of what the reader can see.

### Measured, through the binary, because that is where it lived

`DUNNEFLOW_ARCH=host`, analysing this checkout:

```
documents 26 (read 26, cached 0, removed 0, failed 0): 25 definitions, 0 stated rules
  skipped output/mensores@2026-08-29T19-43-39Z — a map of a program, not documentation about one
  skipped output/dunneflow — a map of a program, not documentation about one
  skipped output/mensores — a map of a program, not documentation about one
  skipped output/beads — a map of a program, not documentation about one
```

147 → **26** documents, 122 → **0** stated rules, 655 → **0** definitions out of `output/`,
289 MB → **0.68 MB**, 161,047 table rows → **830**. And `output/dashboard-uitest.md` — a
hand-written page sitting loose in `output/` — **is still read**, which is the property the
name blacklist was rejected for, demonstrated on the real tree rather than in a fixture.

The binary still stamps `extractor = 9:e8c9ac8a851c41b7`, the checkout's, so the two builds
go on reading each other's maps (rule 12).

### The poisoned map, replaced — and one thing that came out of doing it

Re-analysed in place: **`removed 121`**, and the store's content became correct immediately.
The *file* stayed at **275.5 MB**, because SQLite does not return freed pages to the
filesystem and `optimize()` is `PRAGMA optimize` — query-planner statistics, not space.
`freelist_count` was **70,350 of 70,539 pages, 99.7%**. One `VACUUM` took it to **0.64 MB**.

Deliberately *not* made a code change. A removal that large is the defect's own footprint and
not a thing analysis does; adding a `VACUUM` to every run would cost every reader time for a
case that should never happen again. Recorded here so the next person who sees a map that
shed documents and did not shrink knows which pragma is which.

**`/Applications/DunneFlow.app` is still the 2026-09-10 notarised build and does not have
this fix.** The map it wrote has been replaced with a correct one, but the application itself
will reproduce the defect until a release is cut. That is the first thing on the list.

Gates: **1,408** tests (six new), mypy clean over 139 source files, ruff clean.

## 2026-09-15 — the three search flags, outside the box they belong to

Reported by Tom with two pictures: the `Aa`, `|ab|` and `.*` flags sitting outside the
topbar's search field, and further outside the wider the window got.

**The mechanism, and it is two correct rules 3,400 lines apart in one file.**
`.srch-flags` is `position: absolute; right: .35rem`, which is an offset from
`.tb-searchwrap`. So the wrapper and the field have to end in the same place. They did not:
`max-width: 26rem` was on `.tb-search` (`tokens.css:780`, from when the field was a bare
flex item in the toolbar row) and the wrapper that was later put around it is `flex: 1 1
auto` with **no cap at all** (`tokens.css:4179`). The field stopped at 26rem; the wrapper
went on absorbing every spare pixel in the toolbar; the flags went with the wrapper.

**Measured in the browser rather than reasoned about**, at `rootFontPx 16`, with the
toolbar's width forced so the flex distribution is the real one:

| toolbar | wrapper | field | flags past the field's right edge |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,222 px | 438 | 416 | **16 px** |
| 1,600 px | 816 | 416 | **394 px** |
| 2,000 px | 1,216 | 416 | **794 px** |
| 2,560 px | 1,776 | 416 | **1,354 px** |

The overhang is exactly `wrapper − field − .35rem` and grows one-for-one with the window.
So it is not a wide-window bug: it is wrong at **every** width except the single one where
the wrapper happens to equal the field, and Tom's first picture is that defect at 16px —
which is why the initial view already showed it "flowing out of the box".

That is rule 53's family read backwards. A layout bounded by arithmetic is right at one
window size; this one was bounded in the wrong *element*, so it was right at one width and
wrong either side. Rule 71's companion supplies the rest: a class name is global and a
stylesheet gives no warning, so the rule that put a wrapper round the field never learned
that the field already capped itself.

**The fix is to move the cap onto the box the flags are measured against** — `max-width:
26rem` on `.tb-searchwrap`, `max-width: none` on `.tb-searchwrap .tb-search` so the field
fills it. Nothing else moves: `.tb-right` is already `margin-left: auto`, so the slack the
wrapper used to eat goes where it was always meant to and the right-hand group stays
pinned. Verified from the served stylesheet with the trial override removed: the flags sit
**6 px inside** the field at 760 · 900 · 1,222 · 1,600 · 2,000 · 2,560 · 3,440 px, and at
all four combinations of `topfit` and `panefit`, which are the settings that touch these
same three elements.

**The guard, and it caught itself first.** `test_the_search_flags_are_capped_on_the_box_
they_are_measured_against` asserts the *relationship* rather than either number: whatever
element the flags are positioned against carries the cap, and nothing inside it re-caps
itself. Its first spelling matched `:root[data-topfit="on"] .tb-searchwrap { min-width:
8.5em }` — a real rule for a different question — and failed against perfectly correct CSS.
**Rule 54 inside the guard written for this defect**: a check that names the wrong container
has not checked anything. The selector is anchored to the start of a line now, and the test
was run against the original CSS to watch it fail before it was kept.

**1,409** tests, mypy clean over 140 source files, ruff clean.

## 2026-09-15 — the icon settled, and a second release

Tom supplied `rabbit_icon.png` at **800×528**, replacing the 266px crop that shipped an hour
earlier, and the numbers say what it bought. The upscale to a 1024 canvas falls from **3.85×
to 1.28×**, so 512 and 1024 stop being soft — which was the one stated cost of the previous
one. Fill contrast is **unchanged at 1.75:1** against the same ground, and that is worth
recording rather than glossing: the ratio `build_icon.py`'s docstring warns about is not what
decides this icon. The **dark outline** carries the silhouette where the fill cannot, and it
is heavier in this drawing; the four-point star reads where the old fan of thin rays turned to
mush below 64px. Compared at 128 · 64 · 32 · 16 against the one it replaced, it is better at
every one.

**The conditioner learned one rule from it, and it is a rule rather than a fix.** `compose()`
centred the art on the canvas, which was right for a drawing that sits inside its own frame on
all four sides — the first candidate did. This one runs off its **left, right and bottom**
(measured: margins 0, 0, 0, with 26px only at the top), because the rabbit is cut level at the
neck to lean out of frame. Centring undid that: it floated the flat cut in mid-canvas with
blue underneath, where it reads as an image that failed to load rather than a head leaning
out. So every edge the art meets in its own frame it now meets in this one, full-bleed
horizontally when it runs off both sides, and only the edges with a margin get ground. **Read
off the source, never set by a flag** (rule 30) — the drawing says which kind it is, and
centring is still what a fully-inset drawing gets.

## 2026-09-15 — the Diagram frames what you picked, and design rule 26's other half

Tom, on a Diagram: *"the view does not change between lines on the ROUTINES… maybe what should
happen is that parts of it are highlighted, so I can use the fit feature, but that just centers
the entire Diagram, not a subset of it. Is this a bug, or just how it works?"*

**Driven before it was answered, and two of the three premises were wrong.** The diagram is not
all the routines — it is one compartment, 111 boxes for `dunneflow` and 2 for `packaging`. And
selecting a routine *does* change it: from the `packaging` compartment, picking `serve` switched
the drawing to `dunneflow`, because `diagramWanted()` reads the plate the selection lit.
`markDiagramSelection()` marked the right boxes on every selection tried.

**What was true is that none of it could be seen.** Fitted to a 537×240 pane, the marked boxes
measured **7×3 px and 9×2 px** — a 3px accent stroke on a box three pixels tall, with the view
never moving to it. So a correct selection was indistinguishable from one that did nothing,
which is exactly what was reported.

So this was never a bug in the plumbing; it is **design rule 26's third paragraph, unbuilt for
this view**: *"the list must not move the camera … so an off-screen selection is stated and
framing it is one click away."* The stack has both halves — `offScreenNote()` and **find it**.
Diagram mode had neither.

### What was built

* **`dgmFit(subset)`** frames a set of drawn boxes, defaulting to the whole drawing. The default
  is load-bearing rather than polite: `renderDiagram()` fits a drawing that has just replaced
  the old one, and `render()` pays a fit that was deferred because nothing had been laid out.
  Graph mode can default the other way (`subset ?? g.members`) because its fit is the only one
  it has; here **`fit` has to stay the way back** (design rule 20), so the selection is the
  argument and never the default.
* **`dgmSelectionFrame()`** is the marked boxes and everything an arrow joins them to — Tom's
  call on what to frame, and the reason the feature is worth having: two boxes alone fill the
  pane and take every arrow out of it. The neighbours come from `diagramNow.edges`, which the
  server already sends keyed by arrow, so it costs no request (rule 45, as that payload's own
  docstring puts it: the answer rode in with the picture).
* **The note**, on the narrow path — `markDiagramSelection()` writes one span and never calls
  `renderDiagram()`, which would rewrite the mount and throw away the reader's pan and zoom.
  **Three sentences, never two** (design rule 21): nothing at all when nothing is selected,
  *N boxes selected* with the button when the selection is here, and *what you picked is not in
  this compartment* when it is not — which is the answer this code has always given by
  returning 0 and saying nothing.
* **`data-dgm="fitsel"`**, the same attribute with a new value, so `WIRED_ATTRS` is untouched.

### Two defects found by measuring, both mine, both silent

**The expansion was a flood fill.** Written as one loop over the arrows testing and adding to
the same `Set`, it is not a one-step expansion: a box added early matches later arrows in the
same pass, so the frame grows transitively in whatever order the payload lists its edges. It
framed **97 of 111 boxes** and the fit zoomed *out* — 11.2×5.3 px became 7.1×3.3. Order-
dependent and invisible: the median box in this compartment has 3 neighbours and looked
perfect. The seed is snapshotted now.

**The handler ignored the attribute it routed on.** `if (fit) { dgmFit(); }` is correct with one
button and silently wrong with two — the second matches the same selector, calls the
whole-drawing fit, and so renders, looks live and does the wrong thing. Design rule 16 with
something actually happening, which is the harder kind to see. Both are guarded, and the guard
was checked by spelling each defect back and watching it fail.

### The numbers, and how the two constants were chosen

Degree over `pkg:dunneflow`'s 111 boxes: **median 3, p75 5, p90 8, max 31**, with 7 isolated.
So framing the neighbourhood is right for almost every box and does nearly nothing for the
busiest — `_Handler` touches 31 of 111, spread over the whole drawing.

**`DGM_MIN_MARK = 12`** is the answer to that, and it is stated about the subject rather than as
a ceiling on the frame, because *I must be able to see what I picked* is the sentence the reader
would say. **Per box, never over their union** — the first spelling measured the marks' combined
bounding box, which contains the gap between them, so two distant marks satisfied a promise
neither kept and the boxes stayed 17×8 and 22×5. 12 was measured rather than picked: the median
box's neighbourhood already lands its marks at 28×11, so a higher floor would override a frame
that was working; the busiest lands at 22×5, where a mark stops carrying its label.

**`DGM_SHARE = 0.18`** is the ceiling underneath it, `visibleFloor`'s mechanism one geometry
over — clamped on the scale and not on the bounds, for its reason — and deliberately **not** its
number: `PLATE_SHARE = 0.5` is recorded as a statement about a *plate*, which is the
neighbourhood a node sits in, and here the neighbourhood is already in the frame. Its remaining
job is the 7 isolated boxes, which have nothing to set a frame from.

Measured through the served page, marks at fit-all against marks after **frame it**:

| selected | neighbours | before | after | in view |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `_Handler.do_GET` | 31 | 7×3 · 9×2 | **37×17 · 48×12** | 26 boxes · 62 arrows |
| `run` | 3 | 7×3 · 6×2 | **35×17 · 30×12** | 27 boxes · 79 arrows |
| `serve` | — | 7×3 · 6×2 | **38×17 · 30×12** | 29 boxes · 77 arrows |

The busiest box and the median one now behave the same, which is the job. `fit` returns to all
111, so the way back is real (design rule 20). All three sentences of the note were read off the
page, the third by pinning the compartment picker to `<small outside>` and selecting elsewhere —
and the **frame it** button is correctly not drawn there.

### What deliberately did not change

**No auto-fit on selection.** Design rule 26 is explicit that the list must not move the camera,
and rule 73 says a picture must not move under a gesture. Tom asked for it on the button.

**1,410** tests, mypy clean over 140 source files, ruff clean.

## Paused 2026-09-15 — and what a Windows session actually faces

Everything from this session is committed and pushed. `/Applications/DunneFlow.app` is the
universal2, Developer ID signed, notarised and stapled build carrying all of it, and
`dist/DunneFlow-0.1.0.dmg` is beside it.

**This is a survey, not a plan.** Nothing below has been tried on Windows, and saying which
parts are untested is most of its value.

### Already written for Windows, and never exercised

`runtime.platform_output_root()` has a `win32` branch — `%LOCALAPPDATA%/DunneFlow`, falling
back to `~/AppData/Local`. Its own docstring says it is **untested** and why it exists anyway:
*"a wrong default is worse than an unexercised one, and a `KeyError` from an absent branch
would be worse than both."* That is the first thing to put a real path through, because every
other frozen behaviour hangs off it — the maps root, the `root` pointer that moves it, and
`MapsRootGone` when the drive it names is absent.

### Refuses in words already, so nothing crashes — but nothing works either

Each of these is guarded by `sys.platform != "darwin"` and answers a sentence rather than
raising. A Windows reader meets a working application with three macOS-shaped holes in it:

| surface | what it says today | what Windows needs |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /api/pickdir` (`serve.py:2992`) | *"the folder picker is macOS only — type the whole path instead"* | a native folder dialog, and the typed field stays either way (design rule 2) |
| `POST /api/reveal` (`serve.py:3034`) | *"revealing is macOS only"* | `explorer.exe /select,` or equivalent |
| `macapp.available()` | `frozen() and sys.platform == "darwin"` | nothing, probably — the Dock problem it solves does not exist on Windows, and a taskbar entry comes free. **Check before building anything**: `macapp.py` was bought to fix a real reported symptom, and a Windows equivalent needs its own symptom first. |

### Not written at all

**Packaging is entirely macOS.** `release.sh`'s seven verbs are `codesign`, `notarytool`,
`iconutil`, `lipo`, `hdiutil` and a `BUNDLE` — none of which exists there. A Windows build is
its own script, and the questions it has to answer are different ones: one-file or one-dir,
whether to sign at all (an unsigned binary gets SmartScreen, which is not Gatekeeper), and
what the installer is. **`DUNNEFLOW_ARCH`'s two answers are `host` and `universal2`, both of
which are macOS ideas** — the spec refuses rather than falling back (rule 49), so it will
refuse honestly on Windows rather than produce something odd.

**The icon is `.icns`.** Windows wants `.ico`, which `build_supplied_icon.py` is most of the
way to already: it composes a 1024 master and a size ladder, and Pillow — the tool it already
uses — writes `.ico` directly, so the ladder is there and only the container changes. The
drawing and its canvas rules are platform-free.

### What does not need re-deciding

The analysis path, the stores, the dashboard and every rule in `RULES.md` are platform-free and
were never the macOS part. **Rule 92 in particular is now a Windows fact as much as a macOS
one**: the corpus exclusion is asked of the tree being read rather than computed from where the
run writes, so it holds wherever the maps root lands — which on Windows is somewhere else again.

### One thing this session cost, worth carrying

`pkill -f "dunneflow serve"` matched a server Tom was reading and not just the test servers that
started it. His page reported *"The diagram could not be drawn. Failed to fetch"* — an error
naming the feature that had just shipped, when the drawing was fine and the server was gone.
**Kill by port, never by name.** A process this tool did not start is not its to end.

## Windows, made to run — 2026-09-15

The survey above was written without a Windows machine to hand and said which parts of the
claim were untested. This is the session that put a machine under it. **Every gate is green
on Windows 11 / Python 3.12.4 — 1,417 passed, 1 skipped, mypy clean on `darwin`, `linux` and
`win32`, ruff clean — and the packaged application is built, installed and exercised.**
Nothing about macOS changed: every platform branch keeps the darwin path it had, verbatim.

The survey's own list was short and it was right as far as it went — the picker, reveal, the
Dock, and packaging. **What it could not see is that the three biggest defects were not on
it**, because each was a line that is correct on the machine it was written on and wrong on
the machine it was run on. That is the shape worth carrying, and it is rule 92's family:
a defence, a key or a guard derived from the process rather than from the subject.

### 1. Stored paths were spelled in the writer's alphabet — rule 93

The one with consequences. `str(p.relative_to(root))` stores `web\serve.py` on Windows where
the same commit stores `web/serve.py` on macOS: one file, two keys. Six writers, all correct
where written — both extractors, `entrypoints`, `version`, `walk`'s two cache keys, and
`fingerprint_files`.

Found by running the suite, but **not reported as a path problem by any of it**. The
conformance lane said `files / kebab-case` was **NO_POPULATION** over 78 files it had failed
to find, because a `paths:` glob is POSIX and `fnmatch` does not know `web\serve.py` is under
`web/`. `PurePosixPath(p).stem` returned `web\serve`. The corpus listed paths back differently
from the set it had just scanned. In the shell, the *leaf* every pane draws with
`split("/").slice(-2)` came out as the whole path.

The sharpest is `fingerprint_files`, which inverts rule 12: the label goes into the hash, so
the two builds compute **different fingerprints from identical bytes** and each discards the
other's map as *written by a different tool* — the exact refusal `resource_root()`'s layout
exists to prevent, arriving through the one thing that layout does not control.

Remedied as rule 51 always prescribes: `schema.stored_path`, beside `make_id`, because a
stored path *is* an identity. Measured after: **0 backslash paths** in any column, the
`../../pyproject.toml` case spelled right, and the binary and the checkout both stamping
`9:d6179cee25581502`.

**What makes the family hard to see is that the reading side was already right.**
`conformance` reaches for `PurePosixPath`, `migrate` matches `LIKE '/%'`, the shell splits on
`/` — every consumer had decided a stored path is POSIX and said so in code. Only the writers
had never been asked, because for as long as there was one platform the question had one
answer.

### 2. Stopping an analysis did not reach the pool — the jam, reproduced whole

`start_new_session=True` is **accepted and silently ignored** on Windows, so every analysis
ran in the server's own group and `stop` reached the parent alone. Measured: **17
descendants**, `terminate()`, and `run`'s read loop **still running 60 seconds later** with
the panel saying `working` over a child that had gone. That is the jam `_signal_group`'s
docstring describes, arriving on the other platform through the same fix.

`own_group()` now decides the spelling once — a new session, or `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` —
and the ladder has two rungs on both: `SIGTERM`/`SIGKILL` to the group, or a **console break**
then `taskkill /F /T`. Measured on a pool of eight: the break takes 8 descendants to 0 and
leaves exit `0xC000013A`; `terminate()` took 9 to 9.

*Three smaller things fell out of it.* `signal.SIGKILL` does not exist on Windows and was
referenced unconditionally — three mypy errors, and an `AttributeError` waiting on the second
rung. `text=True` on the child's pipes decodes with the **locale**, which is `cp1252` here
while the child writes UTF-8. And `was_stopped` now knows both spellings of the evidence,
because a negative exit code is POSIX's and not a fact about stopping.

**One residue, bounded and paid for.** A packaged Windows build is windowed and has no
console to raise a break in, so it must use the forceful rung, which leaves exit 1 —
indistinguishable from a broken analysis. `note_forced` records that this process did the
killing; *before* the kill, because `taskkill` returns after the child is already gone and a
note taken afterwards **loses the race** (built that way first, and every stop on the
packaged build went on reporting a failure); and **withdrawn if the kill could not be
delivered**, which is what keeps it a record of what happened rather than of what was asked.

### 3. A guard named the plausible exception class, not the real one

`os.kill(pid, CTRL_BREAK_EVENT)` with no console does not raise `OSError`.
`GenerateConsoleCtrlEvent` fails with `WinError 6` and CPython returns a value with the error
still set, so what arrives is `SystemError: <built-in function kill> returned a result with an
exception set`. Uncaught, it killed the handler thread: **`POST /api/analyze/stop` closed the
connection without a response**, the Stop button reported a network failure, and the analysis
was left running by nothing at all.

Found only by pressing the signed build (rule 48) — the checkout has a console, takes the
polite rung, and never reaches the line. Rule 42's family, and the wrong class was the
plausible one.

### Everything else, in one breath

* **The CLI could not be piped.** `print` went to the locale encoding; 535 box-drawing
  characters, six arrows and four emoji in this program's own sentences are outside cp1252,
  so a redirected or piped run ended in `UnicodeEncodeError` from inside `print`. Everything
  else about this tool had already settled on UTF-8 — every file it writes names the
  encoding — and only the two streams were left to chance. `cli.speak_utf8()`, at the one
  function every way in passes through, and only where the encoding is not already right.
* **The folder picker and reveal** are built rather than refused: `pick_folder` and
  `reveal_dir` decide the platform once, and most of what either costs is making the dialog
  open *in front* of the browser — rule 90, twice. Both pressed through the real routes:
  `{"picked":"C:\\Users\\…"}` and `{"revealed":true}`.
* **`.gitattributes`.** Git's default on Windows is `autocrlf=true`, which would check the
  hashed extractor files out with CRLF — same commit, different bytes, different fingerprint.
  Worth noting that **this session introduced that defect itself**, in nine files, by patching
  them with `Path.write_text` and no `newline=`; caught by the file it was writing.
* **`macapp.available()` needed nothing**, as the survey guessed. It was bought for a
  reported symptom — a Dock icon with no running indicator — and Windows gives a taskbar
  entry for free. A Windows equivalent still needs its own symptom first.

### Packaging

`packaging/release.ps1`, four verbs: `build · verify · zip · install`. Three of
`release.sh`'s seven are absent for stated reasons rather than for want of time — no `venv`
(one architecture), no `sign`/`notarize` (SmartScreen is a warning where Gatekeeper is a
refusal, and `verify` **says the build is unsigned** rather than letting a dialog say it), no
`dmg`. Nothing in it reaches a network, and `test_frozen.py` asserts that.

**Two executables**, and the second is not a convenience. `console=False` costs nothing at a
macOS shell, which hands a bundle its streams; a Windows GUI-subsystem binary is given **no
standard streams at all**, so `DunneFlow.exe analyze …` would do the work and print none of
it — and the gate that exists to run ground truth *through the binary* would have nothing to
read. One `Analysis`, one `COLLECT`, `DunneFlow.exe` and `dunneflow-cli.exe`. The names differ
by more than case because **NTFS is case-insensitive** and the second `EXE()` would otherwise
overwrite the first in silence.

The icon is `dunneflow.ico`, from the **same composed canvas** as the `.icns` — Pillow writes
it anywhere, `iconutil` is macOS's, so off a Mac the `.icns` is left untouched and the script
says so. Its ladder is its own: Explorer's medium-icons view is **48px**, which nothing in
the macOS ladder is. The rounding is macOS's convention carried over deliberately, so the
mark in the taskbar and the mark in the Dock are one application.

Measured: **33.7 MB** built, a **16.6 MB** zip, 3.1 MB per executable. The installed
application was run as a reader runs it — no arguments — and it **created
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\DunneFlow`**, which is `platform_output_root()`'s win32 branch and the thing
the survey named as untested; served the start page on 8787; reported that root back through
`/api/programs` with no programs and no `root_gone`; and revealed it in Explorer.

### One number this session could not reproduce

`RULES.md` states **3,241** rule citations across `src/` and `tests/`, retaken 2026-09-15 with
the command it carries. That command here gives **2,979 on the unmodified HEAD** and 3,009
after this session's work — with and without the `__pycache__` exclusion alike. Left exactly
as it is rather than overwritten: retaking a measurement means reproducing its conditions, and
a figure taken with one `grep` cannot be corrected with another (rule 24, which is the rule
that paragraph is about). Worth settling on a Mac.

### What looking found, which the gates did not — same day

Tom ran the installed application and reported three things. **Every gate was green when he
did**, which is the part worth keeping: 1,417 tests, mypy on three platforms, a build, a
verify and a ground truth through the binary all said yes, and none of them was pointed at
what a person sees.

**1. "The directory chooser does not open."** It opens. Measured from the packaged server:
on screen in **0.6s warm**, `WS_EX_TOPMOST`, foreground, in front. What it does not do is
*say anything while it is opening* — and the first picker on a machine pays to load the
toolkit it draws with, which is several seconds cold against an `osascript` that is
effectively instant. For all of that time the button was exactly as it looks when nothing is
wired to it, which is design rule 16 read from the other end: **a working control that looks
broken is the same defect as a broken one that looks fine.** Both call sites now say
*Opening…* before the `await` and are disabled while it runs; the start page restores the
label in a `finally`, because a throw must not leave it saying that for ever.

*This entry first said the foreground problem could not be reproduced. It was wrong, and the
correction is worth more than the claim.* Tom pressed it afterwards: **"I had to alt-tab to
get to the chooser, but it was there."** So the dialog does land behind the browser, and every
measurement saying otherwise was taken from an **interactive shell** — which has the
foreground rights a server process does not, because it received the last input. Rule 24 in
its own words: the instrument measured a different thing under the same name, and it did so
three times, confidently, with numbers.

**Accepted at the keyboard**, 2026-09-15: *"The application seems to work fine on Windows, so
that is approved."*

**The chooser is documented rather than fixed, which is Tom's call and the right one.** Windows will
not let a background process raise a window, and that is the rule rather than a bug in it:
the browser owns the foreground, DunneFlow does not, and the workaround —
`AttachThreadInput` onto the foreground thread to borrow its rights — is a trick to be
reached for when something is actually broken, not when a dialog is one Alt-Tab away.
`docs/01-installing.md` and `docs/04-your-first-map.md` say where it goes and how to reach
it. The *Opening…* state stays regardless: it was a real defect on its own, and it is what
tells a reader the chooser is coming rather than absent.

**2. The About dialog asserted something it cannot know.** *"The tree it was read from **has**
moved on since; this map has not."* Every other line in that dialog is a fact the map
recorded; that one was a statement about the world, made by a dialog that has not looked at
the world since the analysis — and read straight after one it is simply false, which is where
Tom met it. It says **may have** now. Rule 13's family: a claim on screen that no query could
answer. The guard asserts the *shape* rather than the wording, so a rewrite cannot reintroduce
it in other words.

**3. `release.ps1` could not be read by the PowerShell Windows ships with.** This session
wrote it, ran it only under `pwsh`, and never noticed. Windows PowerShell 5.1 — which is what
`powershell` means on every Windows machine — reads a BOM-less `.ps1` as **ANSI**: an em dash
inside a double-quoted string decodes as two characters, the closing quote goes with them, and
the failure is reported as *"The string is missing the terminator"* forty lines further down,
where nothing is wrong. Found when a probe script of this session's own writing failed exactly
that way. A UTF-8 BOM fixes it and costs PowerShell 7 nothing; the guard asserts it **only
where the file holds non-ASCII**, because a rule about a file is not a rule about the failure.

**And one more Windows fact, from the same run.** `release.ps1 build` failed with
`UnauthorizedAccessException` on `libcrypto-3.dll` because DunneFlow was running — Windows
will not let an open file be replaced, where macOS will happily rebuild a bundle out from
under a running copy. The raw error names a file the reader has never heard of and no action
they can take (rule 89), so `build` and `install` now ask first and name the process and the
command that ends it.

## 2026-09-15 — Linux Mint, made to run

Third platform, same shape as the second: a branch of its own (`linux`), nothing about macOS
or Windows changed, and every platform branch keeps its existing path verbatim. Every gate
green on Linux Mint (XFCE, X11), Python 3.12.3 — **1,446 passed, 1 skipped**, ruff clean, mypy
clean on `darwin`, `linux` and `win32` alike. One test skips, and it is the macOS maps root
asserting Apple's layout; the Linux one beside it skips on a Mac for the same reason.

**The survey was mostly right and the suite found the defect first**, which is the opposite of
the Windows session and worth noticing. The first `uv run pytest` on this machine came back
**1,418 passed, 1 skipped, 2 failed**, before a line had been read.

### What the suite caught: two of four rungs

`_interrupt_group` and `_kill_group` are two rungs with two branches each — four guards over
one question, *could this ask be delivered?* The Windows pair was widened to `SystemError` and
`ValueError` when the packaged build proved `os.kill` raises the first of those with no console
to break in. **The POSIX pair beside them was not.** It still named
`(OSError, AttributeError, TypeError)`, which was right on the day it was written and had
simply never been asked the newer question.

Nothing about that is Windows-shaped. The test that caught it is parameterised over all three
classes *because the contract is "this function answers"*, and says so in its own docstring. It
passed on Windows because the branch it runs there is the widened one, and on macOS because no
POSIX rung there had ever been made to fail. Linux ran the narrow branch and it raised straight
through into the handler thread — where the cost is already on record: **a Stop button that
reports a network failure over an analysis still running.**

`UNDELIVERABLE` is the one tuple now. The second rung gained the test the first one had (it had
none on any platform), and a third test asserts over the source that no rung spells its own
classes. Rule 51, recovered from rule 42's fix.

### The picker and the reveal, which Linux answers as ladders

The only two places in `web/` that are not portable by construction, and the only two with no
Linux branch at all — each returned the sentence saying so. Both are a convenience over a
control that still works (design rule 2), which is what made refusing affordable and why this
could wait for the platform to be real.

**Linux ships no one dialog, so it has a list.** `_LINUX_PICKERS` is tried in order, promoted
by `XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP` so Plasma is offered kdialog's — *promoted, never excluded*, so a
Plasma session with only zenity still gets a picker. Neither installed refuses naming both
(rule 89). `org.freedesktop.portal.FileChooser` is deliberately absent: its result arrives on a
signal, which means a D-Bus binding this tool will not grow for a convenience.

**Exit 1 means two things, and the display check is what separates them.** Measured on zenity
3.44.2: a cancel exits **1 with an empty stderr**; a failure to open the display exits **1 with
a line on it**. One code, told apart only by text that a healthy desktop also writes for
harmless reasons. So `_desktop_session` rules out the failure that actually happens *before
anything is spawned*, and what is left reads as the cancel. The residue is stated rather than
hidden: a dialog that opened and then broke reads as a cancel too.

**Rule 90 costs nothing here, and that is measured rather than assumed.** macOS needs
`activate` and Windows a topmost owner form; the zenity dialog took focus from the terminal on
its own, with `_NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW` moving to it.

**The reveal is two rungs and `xdg-open` is the second.** `FileManager1.ShowFolders` is the
desktop's own reveal — an activatable D-Bus service, no MIME default consulted. `xdg-open` is
what everybody reaches for first and answers a slightly different question: it hands the
directory to whatever the desktop says opens `inode/directory`, and **on this machine
`xdg-mime query default inode/directory` answers `org.gnome.baobab.desktop`** — a disk usage
analyser. It opened Thunar regardless, because XFCE's `xdg-open` routes through `exo-open` and
never reads that default. One rung is right by construction and the other was right by luck.
`--print-reply` is load-bearing: without it `dbus-send` exits 0 for having *sent* a message
nobody may be listening for (rule 76). An exhausted ladder reports the **last** rung's reason,
because `xdg-open` is the rung every desktop has.

**Pressed rather than reasoned about** (rule 48), against the live session:

| Pressed | Came back |
|---|---|
| a real dialog, accept button via XTEST | `('/home/reader/dunneflow', '')` |
| the same dialog, closed from the window manager | `('', '')` — a clean cancel |
| no `DISPLAY`, no `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` | the refusal, and **nothing spawned** |
| `reveal_dir` on a real directory | Thunar, through rung one |
| the same with `dbus-send` shimmed to exit 1 | Thunar, through `xdg-open` |
| both rungs shimmed to fail | `xdg-open`'s own sentence, not the bus's |

`tests/test_desktop.py` is the first test either function has had **on any platform**.
`sys.platform` is monkeypatched rather than skipped around, so the Linux reader is exercised on
all three machines — a suite that only ran it here is precisely how the stop rungs came to be
guarded three ways.

### The maps root, and the trap that has no counterpart

`platform_output_root` already had a Linux branch, written as the conventional location and
marked untested. It was wrong the way an untested branch usually is: it named `~/.local/share`
as a literal where the XDG specification names **`$XDG_DATA_HOME`**, whose default that merely
is. Three states now, the third being the specification's own — a **relative** path is invalid
and must be ignored, which here is not deference: it resolves against the working directory,
and a desktop entry gives a process none worth the name.

**And `--output --help` was one machine's path printed to every reader.** It read
`~/Library/Application Support/DunneFlow` as a literal, so a Windows reader had already been
told their maps default somewhere no Windows has ever had. It asks the function now.

**The trap is that `~/.local/share/DunneFlow` is the obvious place for both things.** It is
where an application's files go under `$HOME`, and it is already the reader's *maps* root. On
macOS the pair is `/Applications` and `~/Library/Application Support` and cannot collide; here
the natural spelling of both is one directory. Installed there, the program would sit inside
the tree its own `Move…` offers to relocate and inside the corpus its own analyses walk — and
nothing would say so until somebody moved their maps to an external disk and took the
application with them. The binary goes to `~/.local/lib/dunneflow`; a test asserts no install
target lands in `platform_output_root()`, and was mutated to prove it fails when it should.

### Rule 94, minted from the spec before it was built with

`packaging/dunneflow.spec` named only `_WINDOWS` and said everything else by negation. Exactly
true while there were two platforms:

* `BUNDLE` under `if not _WINDOWS` would have built a `.app` on Linux, and **PyInstaller would
  have reported success** — there is no step in a spec that checks what a bundle is for;
* `ICON = "dunneflow.ico" if win32 else "dunneflow.icns"`, over a guard that raises when the
  named file is missing, would have refused the build over a macOS icon container it would then
  never have used — rule 49 pointing the wrong way.

**A negation is a fine way to say *the other one* and no way at all to say *the other two*.**
Caught by neither gate and by no test: `mypy --platform linux` type-checks a `BUNDLE` call
perfectly, and the suite proves the source tree rather than the artifact. Found by reading the
spec before building with it, and pinned afterwards — the guard's *name and its definition*
both, because asserting on a name alone would pass a `_MACOS` redefined to mean anything
(rule 37).

### The build, and the one check that is not a size

**9.5 s, 32 MB, a 13 MB tarball, glibc 2.14 the floor.** The binary stamps
`extractor 9:d6179cee25581502` — which is what this checkout computes and what the **Windows**
build stamped. Both directions pressed: the checkout opened the binary's map and the binary
opened the checkout's, 925 routines either way. Rule 12 holds across all three platforms.

**`verify` printed that fingerprint and compared nothing** — rule 37, in the step written to
defend rule 12. It reads the stamp back out with the binary's own `query` now and refuses on a
mismatch. And `tar` named its first archive `DunneFlow--linux-x86_64.tar.gz`: `app_version`
asked the binary for `--version`, which this CLI has not got; argparse printed usage to a
swallowed stderr and an empty string went into a path. It reads the dist-info the spec bundles,
which is the same file `tool_version()` stamps into every map.

**A third icon container out of the same master** — `hicolor/`, ten PNGs at the freedesktop
sizes, verified through the GTK icon theme at 24, 32, 48 and 256. Never from `dunneflow.svg`
beside it: that is the geometric candidate, which was not the one chosen.

**And the `.ico` regenerated 1,665 bytes smaller.** Under Pillow 12.3.0 it came out 98,590
bytes against the committed 100,255 — same ladder, same master, same visible mark, a different
encoder. The committed file was restored untouched and the docstring's *byte for byte* claim
gained the condition it never had (rule 24): it holds against the Pillow that wrote it, not
across versions of it. A byte comparison reads as *the drawing has not changed* and also fails
when only the library did.

### Pressed as a reader would, end to end

Installed into `~/.local`, launched **from the XFCE application menu**: served the start page,
Chrome opened on it. A second launch joined the first through `already_serving` rather than
starting a second server — which is the Dock running-indicator's whole job, done by the program
instead of by the window server, and better. `/api/reveal` opened Thunar; `/api/pickdir` opened
a dialog and cancelled cleanly. An analysis ran through `self_argv()` re-executing the
*installed* binary, was stopped mid-run (`"stopped on signal 15"`, map left marked unfinished),
then run to completion — 1,644 documents — and opened as the base, with About reporting
`tool_version 0.1.0`. `uninstall` took back all thirteen files and left 102 MB of maps
untouched.

`StartupNotify=false` in the desktop entry is measured, not conventional: this process maps no
window, so the launcher's busy cursor would spin for the twenty seconds a desktop waits before
giving up on an application that did in fact start.

### Two things this session could not do

**The ground truth was not run.** None of the four Society trees is on this machine, and
neither is `../dunnecorp-standards` — so no Mensores figure was retaken here and none is
restated as though it had been. What was pressed instead is DunneFlow's own tree and
`../dunnenote`: real code, enough to exercise the binary end to end, and honest about being a
different measurement.

**And the citation count did not reproduce.** `RULES.md` recorded 3,241 · 2,422 · 819 · 128 as
of 2026-09-15; run against that very commit it comes back **3,297 · 2,463 · 834 · 128**.
Nothing is wrong with the command — it was taken partway through a session and the session kept
writing, so a true measurement of a tree that no longer existed was committed as a live one.
Rule 24, in the sentence about counting rules, one turn after the last time. The figures are
retaken last this time: **3,323 · 2,486 · 837 · 129**.
