# DunneFlow v2 — the record starts here

*Everything above this line is **v1's** record and is not rewritten: it says what was built
and what it was called at the time, which is the one thing a record may not be edited to
change. v1 itself is at `../DunneFlow`, untouched and still runnable. `V2-START-HERE.md` is
the state; `PLAN-v2.md` is the design; this is the chronology.*

## 2026-09-17 — the MCP server, brought to the front

**Tom's call on the ordering, and his reasoning is the part worth keeping.** Asked whether
to clear the ingest wiring first or take the API surface, he said the existing tool is
usable as-is and that defects found in it along the way should be *"rolled into that feature
work at the appropriate time"* rather than scheduled as work of their own. So the MCP server
moved from `PLAN-v2.md`'s chunk 4 to the front — it is the one chunk that delivers a new
capability without touching ingest, so it could be written against a tool that was not
moving underneath it.

**The gate could be read and not run, and that was found before anything was touched.**
`V2-START-HERE.md` pointed at a golden re-take script "recorded in `HANDOFF.md`'s v2
entries"; there were none, because this section did not exist until today. `tools/golden.py`
is that script, recovered *against the recorded values* rather than written from memory —
sha256 over every field, NUL-terminated and not NUL-separated, which is one byte and the
difference between reproducing the record and inventing a second self-consistent
convention. Five of the seven digests, all 25 row counts and all five distributions come
back byte-identical.

**Two digests did not, and are redefined rather than carried.** `routines.body` and
`calls.resolved` record values whose statements were never written down, and a bounded
sweep — permutations up to three columns wide over ten candidates, six orderings, ten
separators, three renderings of NULL — did not recover them. Bounded and abandoned rather
than finished, and the file says so: *we did not find it* is not *it is not there*. A
recorded number whose definition is lost is a label and not an identity, so the remedy is to
state the definition. It costs the gate nothing, because the artifact is the v1 graph itself
and a digest is only ever compared between two graphs computed by one script.

**One distribution was recovered on the way**, and it is what makes the rest credible:
`calls confidence` reads INFERRED 788 in the record and 24,891 unfiltered, because
confidence is stored on all 30,544 call rows including the 24,103 that resolved to nothing.
The predicate is `callee_id IS NOT NULL`.

### What was built

Six commits, each green on all three gates and each leaving the golden where it was.

1. **`writable=False` means read-only.** It was assigned and never read again — it chose
   mkdir-versus-refuse and refuse-versus-discard, and left an ordinary read-write handle
   under all fourteen reading sites. `?mode=ro` on the existing parameter rather than a
   second one beside it, because two parameters answering *can this connection write* would
   have left the lie in place at thirteen sites to close it at one. `read_only_uri` is the
   one place that spelling lives, escaped, because a `?` in a directory name eats `mode=ro`
   and hands back a writable connection to a database that does not exist.
2. **Rule 95**, minted while reading the fingerprint to be sure the change could not move
   the golden: `code_extraction_inputs()` globs where the reader *lives* and not what it
   *reads*, and `sql.py` shapes every `sql_ops` row from outside every key. Recorded, not
   acted on; it belongs in the fingerprint chunk.
3. **Three answers moved to where all their callers pass**, before the caller that would
   have copied them existed: `lookup.py`, `flows.ways_in_affected`/`governance_over`, and
   `serve.glossary_sidecars`. Verified byte-identical over 123 lines of real output against
   `HEAD`'s `src/` side by side.
4. **The wire** — `jsonrpc.py` and `server.py`, alone, with an honest empty `tools/list`.
5. **Nine tools and two resources.**
6. **The three analysis tools.**

### What driving it found that reading it would not

* **`notifications/initialized` was gated behind the flag it sets.** It was refused —
  correctly, on its face — the flag stayed false, and every method after the handshake was
  refused for ever. Every handler was right and only the order was wrong.
* **Every refusal answered under a null id**, because `parse` raised before the id was read.
  JSON-RPC reserves null for the case where the id could not be *detected*; a client that
  gets null for a request it sent with `id: 7` has a reply it cannot account for, which
  reads as a hang rather than a refusal.
* **`self._initialized = False` overwrote the handler named `_initialized`.** An attribute
  and a method share one namespace, and neither gate said so.
* **`NothingOpen` carries no message at all.** The dashboard's sentence lives in
  `_refuse_without_base`, where it is delivered — so `why()` over one yields `NothingOpen: `
  and nothing else, an empty refusal, which is the failure the gate exists to prevent.
* **The first `_as_markdown` invented a `section["title"]` and a `row[key]`** that
  `web/documents.py` does not build. Every document would have rendered as empty headings
  over nothing, and nothing would have raised.

### Open, and stated

* The two redefined digests. If anybody recovers the original statements, add them to
  `REPRODUCES` rather than editing a number.
* **Which protocol version Claude Code actually sends is not yet known here.** The server
  negotiates properly and logs what it was asked for; the first real session records it.
* `DocStore`, `SourceStore` and `DocSourceStore` still carry `writable=False` without
  meaning it.
* `ingest/` still has no tests, and is still absent from the no-egress guard in
  `test_about.py` — it belongs there and goes in when it is wired.

## 2026-09-17 — the walk, wired to the registry

`ingest/` was written as a shape and nothing routed through it. It does now: `walk.py`
names no language, imports no extractor, and asks the registry which reader owns a file.
`PLAN-v2.md`'s chunk 2, finished — the gate was that the golden does not move, and it did
not.

**The gate, run rather than asserted.** Society re-analysed by this build against the
preserved v1 graph: `tools/golden.py <v1> <v2>` reports **7 of 7 digests identical**, and
the whole written report — all 25 row counts, all five distributions — diffs clean against
`output/GOLDEN-v1.txt` apart from the two digests that file's own statement was lost for
and which the script redefines. The four `[project.scripts]` executables still reach
**1,381 · 423 · 292 · 112**, and conformance still reads **4 checked · 1 no population ·
10 not checkable**. 1,540 passed · 1 skipped, mypy clean over 157 files, ruff clean.

### What changed, and the reasons that are not obvious

* **`is_test_path` is deleted, not moved.** Its rule-5 precision is carried across whole —
  a marker matches at an **edge** and never as a substring, because `_test_stage.py` is a
  pipeline stage and was once dropped from a map entire for containing the word — and what
  it could not do is spell a test any way but Python's. Its three tests in
  `test_comments.py` now ask the Python plugin's own `DiscoveryRules`, which is what says
  the move carried the spelling across rather than approximating it.
* **`--jobs` crosses the seam, and that is the one thing the host tells a reader about
  parallelism.** `InProcessPlugin` owns the pool by design, so wiring it left `--jobs`
  assigned and read by nobody — a flag that silently stopped reaching the only extractor
  there is. It is on `extract` now, documented as *the machine's owner speaking, not the
  host's opinion of the reader*: a reader decides what a number of jobs means and one with
  nothing to spend it on ignores it.
* **`IngestPlugin.lost` is on the contract.** A file that will not parse comes back as an
  empty `FileFacts` carrying its error and the host counts it; a file whose worker *died*
  never comes back at all, so only the reader can say it existed. Without it a crashed
  worker is a file that leaves the map with no symptom anywhere.
* **Three new counters, and the fourth is deliberately absent.** `unclaimed` (suffix →
  count), `tests_excluded` (per language) and `pruned` (directory name → count) fire today
  and are printed by `walk_residue`. `declined` is not built: no language can be declined
  in a build whose only reader needs no toolchain, and a counter for a state this build
  cannot reach is rule 35 with a sentence attached. It lands with the first out-of-process
  plugin, which is the first thing that can raise `ToolchainMissing`.
* **The residue is one line per kind and never one per file.** A run that pruned four
  hundred `__pycache__` directories has one fact to report; the paths are not kept.
  Measured on DunneFlow's own tree: *unread: 46 .jpg, 15 .png, 8 .js, …*, *left out as
  tests: 65 python*, *pruned 19 directories: `__pycache__` ×12, …*. On Society: seven
  suffixes, no tests, nothing pruned.
* **Five names added to `SKIP_DIRS`** — `target`, `vendor`, `obj`, `Pods`, `DerivedData`:
  other languages' build output, which `DOC_SKIP_DIRS` has partly had all along. `.gradle`,
  `.build` and `.turbo` are deliberately **not** listed, because everything below a dot is
  already pruned and a second answer is how two rules come to disagree. Checked before
  adding them that Society's `src` holds no directory of any of those names.

### The map prune, and the root asymmetry that runs the other way

The code walk now prunes a directory holding a map, on the free test `discover_docs`
already uses. It was never needed while only Python was read — a program directory holds
no `.py` — and it became needed the moment the walk started *saying what it had passed
over*: analysing DunneFlow's own tree reported twelve unread `.db` files that are this
tool's own writing.

**Applied below the root and never at it**, which is the opposite of the document walk's
asymmetry and for the opposite reason. There, `--docs` pointed into a program directory is
the failure rather than the ordinary case. Here the root is the tree somebody named, and a
graph written *beside* the source it was taken from is ordinary — `--output .` is one, and
so is every test in this suite that keeps its store inside the tree it analyses. The first
version pruned at the root too and **fourteen tests went red at once**, every one of them a
tree reading as a map because its own `graph.db` sat in it. An empty map and a line about a
directory is exactly the shape of failure rule 49 is about.

*Candidate rule, not minted:* **a marker read off the disk says different things about the
root and about what is below it, and which of the two is the failure case depends on what
the reader named.** The next free number is 96; `PLAN-v2.md` already holds the other
candidate, `Entrypoint.declared` as a field rather than a substring test.

### Open, and stated

* **`tests/test_mcp_tools.py::test_a_second_analysis_is_refused_and_told_what_is_running`
  failed once in fifteen runs and passes alone.** It starts a real analysis of a one-file
  tree and immediately asks for a second; when the first finishes first there is nothing to
  refuse. A check that cries wolf has already failed (rule 43), and the fix is the test's
  rather than the slot's — left for whoever owns it, because weakening the assertion would
  lose the property it is there for.
* `ingest/` and `plugins/` are **in** the no-egress guard now, which was the condition
  recorded when it was left out.
* `CLAUDE.md`'s *Adding a language* still says "write one extractor, nothing else changes".
  It is registration now. That rewrite is chunk 14 and is deliberately not taken here.

## 2026-09-17 — `lang` becomes a discriminator

`PLAN-v2.md`'s chunk 3, and the cheapest possible proof that the column works: nothing in
v1 ever branched on `lang` — no `WHERE lang =`, no `GROUP BY lang` anywhere in `src/` — so
it was written, stored, selected, shipped to the browser as a display string, and never
read by a condition. It is read by four now, and the gate held: **7 of 7 digests
identical**, every row count and distribution unchanged, 1,562 passed · 1 skipped, mypy
clean over 159 files, ruff clean.

### The default that was a claim

`Routine.lang` and `DataStructure.lang` defaulted to `"python"`. That was never wrong while
there was one reader, and it is the worst possible default the day there are two: a plugin
that forgot to say would have had every routine it emitted claim to be Python, in the one
column nothing reads twice. They default to `""` now.

**Not deleted outright, which is what the plan said, and the reason is worth recording.**
A required field has to be passed at construction, and the four construction sites are
inside the Python extractor — so making it required is exactly the per-record duplication
the stamping design exists to remove, and it would have left a plugin able to set the field
on record 39 of 40. A blank is the honest third state: a record nobody stamped claims
nothing, and `stamp_lang` refuses it rather than storing it.

* **`ingest.stamp_lang` is the one place a language is written onto a record** (rule 51).
  `FileFacts.lang` is the only place one travels; the in-process reader stamps on the way
  out of `extract`, and the codec will stamp on decode, so both kinds of reader pass
  through one function rather than two that have to be kept in step.
* **A record that arrives carrying its own language is refused**, never overwritten and
  never accepted. Two answers to one question are only ever noticed when they differ, and
  by then the map is written.
* **The host verifies the claim** — `_verify_lang` in `walk.py`, `language_of(path)`
  against `facts.lang`, refusing and naming both. A manifest is a label and the running
  reader is the identity (rule 30), and this is the seam a reader on the far side of a pipe
  arrives through.

### `load_rules` has three answers now, and the middle one is the change

It returned an empty `RuleSet` for any missing YAML. For Python that branch never fired —
which is exactly why it read as harmless — and on a new language it fires on the first run
and every boundary, every way in and every CLI mount silently disappears into a map that
comes back whole and plausible (rule 49). Now: a language whose plugin **declares** a rules
file gets it; one whose plugin declares **none** gets an empty set, because that is a
decision somebody wrote in a manifest and not an absent file inferred into one (rule 30);
and a language nobody ships, or a declared file that is not there, is **refused** by name.
The default argument is gone for `discover`'s reason — a question with a default answer is
a question nobody has to ask.

### Five claims about Python, four of them now derived

`resolve/languages.py` is the one place the fact is read (`SELECT DISTINCT lang FROM
files`, shipped beside the sentence per rule 13) and the one place the sentence is
composed. **It counts what was read and never what this build can read**: a version that
reads TypeScript, pointed at a Python tree, must still say Python or the sentence describes
the tool instead of the map (rule 24). Three answers, never two — no source at all is its
own sentence.

The spelling in prose is the plugin's own (`PluginManifest.display`, `"Python"`), with the
stored key as the fallback, because a map may hold a language whose reader is no longer
installed and inventing a capitalisation is a guess about somebody else's product name.

* the mirror's ABSENT band carries `{languages}` and `Band.spot()` fills it — `replace`
  and not `format`, because every other band is prose full of punctuation and one stray
  brace would turn a page into an exception
* `13-mirror.md`'s *Read this first*, and `dunneflow mirror`'s closing line
* `render/mirror.py`'s own docstring, which asserted it in passing

**The fifth is deliberately not derived, and that is a decision rather than an oversight.**
`render/traceability.py` excludes *Python builtins* from symbol evidence, and the list is
`dir(builtins)` of this interpreter. Deriving that sentence from what the map holds would
make it a claim and not a fix — there is no list of TypeScript's or Go's builtins here, so
*the builtins of every language read are excluded* would be false the first time a second
language arrived. The page names the language instead, and the note beside `_BUILTINS` says
the list moves when it moves into `python.yaml` with its twin in `resolve/calls.py`, which
is the resolver chunk's work.

### What a run says about languages, on all three channels

* the summary: `read: python 628`, beside `unread: 70 .json, …`
* `--progress-json`'s `done`: `"languages": {"python": 628}, "unread": {".json": 70}`
* **the About dialog**: *Read from — Python 628*, from `/api/about`'s new `languages`
  block. Verified in the browser against Society, not just in a test: the row draws, and it
  draws the plugin's word rather than the stored key. A map that records no language for
  any file says so rather than drawing an empty row (design rule 21).

### Open, and stated

* `Routine.lang` and `DataStructure.lang` are blank-by-default rather than required. If a
  future reader wants the stricter shape, the cost is passing the language at every
  construction site inside every extractor — and the refusal in `stamp_lang` is what makes
  the blank safe today.
* `CLAUDE.md`'s *Adding a language* is still v1's sentence. Chunk 14.

## 2026-09-17 — rule 12, split per language

`PLAN-v2.md`'s chunk 5. One key protected every fact in the map, so editing the reader for
one language would discard every other language's facts — which is the thing that makes a
TypeScript plugin unmergeable in a repository that is mostly Python. There are three keys
now, and the gate held: **7 of 7 digests identical**, 1,575 passed · 1 skipped, mypy clean
over 160 files, ruff clean.

| Key | Holds | Moves when |
|---|---|---|
| `meta.extractor` | `annotations.yaml`, `detectors/__init__.py`, `ingest/*.py`, **`schema.py`** | anything every reader passes through changes |
| `files.extractor` | per row: `<plugin version>:<hash of its rules and its reader>` | that one language's reader changes |

**`schema.py` joins the core key and `SCHEMA_VERSION` stops being load-bearing.** The bump
is by hand and a forgotten bump is precisely rule 12's failure mode. The number stays for
the two things a hash cannot do: it is the generation a person reads off `meta`, and it is
what a plugin declares it was written against, so a reader whose facts no longer fit is
refused by name rather than by a hash nobody can interpret. It is **10** now —
`files.extractor` is a stored-shape change.

**`ingest/*.py` is in the core key and `canonical/` still is not**, on the test this list
has always applied: what does extraction actually read. The registry decides which reader
sees a file, the contract decides what a reader may say, and `stamp_lang` writes a field
into every record — all three shape what a fact *is*. A canonicaliser still cannot change
a fact, only whether two facts compare equal, and it cost a sealed snapshot once to learn
that (rules 25 and 62).

### Two places where the plan was not followed, and why

* **The per-language stamp is a column and not `meta.extractor.<lang>`.** The plan had
  both. Two places recording one fact is two numbers about one thing (rule 40), and the
  meta key is derivable from the column while the column can express something the key
  cannot: a map half-updated by an interrupted run. So the rows are the authority and
  `language_stamps()` is the one place they are read. It also keeps `meta` at 16 keys,
  which is what let the golden's row counts stay byte-identical.
* **A language's own rules file is in that language's key, not the core.** The plan's table
  put `detectors/*.yaml` in the core, which would make editing `typescript.yaml` discard
  the Python graph — the exact outcome the chunk exists to prevent, and the opposite of its
  own stated goal. `_SHARED_RULES` is the core's list (`annotations.yaml`, which mines
  governance markers from comments and prose alike) and a plugin declares its own. **The
  glob became a list, so the directory is now the authority**: a test asserts every
  `detectors/*.yaml` is in exactly one key, because a rules file in no key at all is loaded,
  hashed by nothing, and invisible to rule 12 — rule 95's shape one directory over.

### What a changed reader now costs, measured

Pressed end to end rather than asserted, by moving the Python plugin's declared version
and analysing again:

```
the python reader has changed — 1 file dropped and read again; every other language kept its facts
```

The core stamp did not move (`10:ac876498ab54a443` before and after) and the row's stamp
did (`1.0.0:…` → `1.0.1:…`). With the version put back, a **read** of that map is refused
by name: *holds facts from a reader this build is not: python (read by 1.0.1:81094cd…)*,
with the sentence saying that analysing again re-reads only the language that changed. A
read may refuse and may never repair (rule 20), and it did not: the rows were still there
afterwards.

**Three states, never two, twice over.** A language this build has **no reader for** is
left alone rather than refused — its rows cannot be re-read and cannot be checked, and
refusing a map over a plugin somebody uninstalled would refuse it for ever; the walk
already says that language was not read this time, which is the fact somebody can act on
(rule 89). And a map with **no such column at all** — what `dunneflow migrate` leaves —
says nothing rather than reading as stale (rule 63).

### The reader must say where it lives, and the manifest is still only a label

* An **in-process** plugin declares `reader: extractors/python`, package-relative, and is
  refused without one: its bytes would be in no cache key at all, which is rule 12
  unenforced for every fact it produces. An out-of-process plugin is refused *with* one —
  its own bytes are its `fingerprint` files, the **built bundle** and never the source tree.
* A plugin naming no `fingerprint` files at all is refused. A declared version alone is a
  label that does not move when somebody edits the reader (rule 30), which is exactly when
  it must.
* `in_process` in the manifest is now read, and cross-checked against `ingest._IN_PROCESS`:
  a disagreement refuses naming both. What runs in this process is decided by that table
  and never by a data file.

### Packaging, and the guard that caught it

`schema.py`, `ingest/` and `plugins/` are hashed, so frozen they must travel as **data** or
they hash nothing. `tests/test_frozen.py` derives what the spec must bundle from the keys
themselves and failed the moment `ingest/` joined one — which is the defence working rather
than a test needing an update. `plugins/` is bundled **wholesale**, and a second test walks
the registry rather than a list beside it: rule 92 says a defence assembled from an
enumeration does not survive a new member, and `extractors/python` and `extractors/docs`
were exactly such an enumeration.

**Verified through the binary, as `CLAUDE.md` requires when `packaging/` or `detectors/`
moves.** A host build analysing Society reports the same two stamps the checkout computes
— core `10:91525594e021b516` and python `1.0.0:5ad58664e93395f9` — and the two builds open
each other's maps, 4,823 routines either way.

### Measured

`lang_fingerprint` is cached, and that was a measurement rather than a habit:
`write_file_facts` stamps every row, so an uncached answer re-reads and re-hashes the whole
reader once per file — 628 times over ten files on Society. Extraction of Society is 2.2 s
warm with the cache, against 4.7 s without it on the same tree and the same disk state.

### Open, and stated

* `CLAUDE.md` quotes v1's fingerprint (`extractor = 9:e8c9ac8a851c41b7`) as a measured
  packaging figure. It is still true of v1 and is no longer true here; that file is v2's to
  rewrite in chunk 14, and no figure in it has been retaken (rule 24).
* `migrate.py` re-stamps a schema-5 store to the current core value and says nothing about
  per-language stamps. It cannot: such a store has no `extractor` column, and the reader
  that produced its rows is long gone. `language_stamps()` answers *nothing recorded* for
  it, which is why a migrated snapshot still opens.

## 2026-09-17 — the resolver, split per language

`PLAN-v2.md`'s chunk 6. `resolve/calls.py` was one 281-line function that was Python all
the way down: it split `callee_expr` on dots, knew `self` and `cls`, walked `__init__.py`
packages, and asked **this interpreter** what its builtins were. The walk had already been
made to group by language and dispatch; resolution had not, so the first TypeScript file
extracted would have had its calls put through Python's name rules — chunk 9's defect,
arriving three chunks early and silently.

The gate held: **7 of 7 digests identical** against the v1 graph, `calls.resolved`
included — that digest is `(site_id, callee_id, confidence, external, ambiguous)`, which
is precisely the tuple §1g says must not move. **1,588 passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean
over 164 files, ruff clean.

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Who decides a boundary call is external | Python's resolver (rule 2) | the driver, before dispatch |
| Who writes `UPDATE calls SET callee_id` | three places in one function | `resolve/calls.py`, once |
| What a resolver returns | a target, and four counters it maintained itself | `Edge` or `NoEdge`, and no arithmetic |
| Which routines can win a bare name | every routine in the map | that language's |

### The seam, and why `NoEdge` carries two fields

`resolve/contract.py` is `ingest/contract.py`'s shape one subject over. A resolver is
handed its own language's non-boundary call rows and yields one `Decision` per row, in the
order it was given them; it never writes to the store and never counts.

**`Edge | NoEdge` rather than `str | None`**, because a missing target carries two facts the
driver cannot recover: how many definitions competed, and whether the match was *rejected
as implausible* or simply never found. They are separate fields and not one because a single
row can be both — a bare call to a builtin is suppressed **and** has its rivals counted —
and flattening the pair moves `ambiguous` with no symptom anywhere.

A resolver answering the wrong number of rows is **refused rather than zipped**: decisions
pair with rows by position, so a short answer does not lose edges, it misplaces every one
after the discrepancy.

### Three answers where a language has no resolver, never two

A language with one is resolved. A language with none has every call left **external and is
named**, with its count, in `ResolveStats.unresolved_langs`. That is not a placeholder:
TypeScript extraction lands at chunk 9 and its supplied edges at chunk 10, so there is a
whole chunk during which a TypeScript map legitimately has no internal edges — honest and
shippable, as long as it says so. Silence there reads exactly like a program that calls
nothing.

### `_BUILTINS` — measured across five interpreters, not recalled

`frozenset(dir(builtins))` is a fact about the **analysing machine's Python version** in a
value that decides what a call means, and no fingerprint hashed it: two builds at the same
commit on two machines would disagree about the same program and nothing would move to say
so. It is `builtins:` in `detectors/python.yaml` now, hashed by `rules_fingerprint()` like
every other rule, with its twin in `resolve/traceability.py` reading the same list.

The list is the **union of `dir(builtins)` over CPython 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13**,
taken by running all five through `uv` rather than written from memory:

| | 3.9 | 3.10 | 3.11 | 3.12 | 3.13 | union |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| names | 152 | 155 | 157 | 157 | 159 | **159** |

Every earlier version is a subset of 3.13, so the union *is* 3.13's set and no question of
precedence arises. The seven names that differ over that range — `aiter`, `anext` and
`EncodingWarning` (3.10), `ExceptionGroup` and `BaseExceptionGroup` (3.11),
`PythonFinalizationError` and `_IncompleteInputError` (3.13) — are exactly what the
analysing machine used to decide. A union is also the precision-favouring direction (rule
1): a name in the set is *suppressed*, so a name here wrongly costs an edge in a program
that shadows a builtin, and a name missing is the false edge rule 3 was minted from.

**The diff, measured and not assumed.** On Society, **no call site spells any of the seven**
— the resolution digest is unmoved, which the golden confirms. That is a fact about this
corpus and not about the change: what it says is that the machine-dependence happened to
cost nothing *here*, not that it costs nothing (rule 24). What is now true regardless is
that a 3.9 machine and a 3.13 machine produce the same map.

**Quoted throughout in the YAML, and the loader refuses a non-string entry by name.**
Unquoted, `True` and `False` are YAML booleans: the list would hold two `bool`s, read
correctly, hold the right number of entries, and silently stop suppressing two of the
commonest words in the language (rule 49). A comment saying *quote them* is a comment.

### Rule 95's gap, shut — and the rule itself is not

`sql.py` shapes every `sql_ops` row and was in **no cache key at all** — editing SQL parsing
left every cached graph stale and undiscarded. It joins `core_extraction_inputs()` rather
than Python's, because §1e settles the judgement of a string literal as the **host's**: a
plugin reimplementing `looks_like_sql` means the same string in a `.py` and a `.ts` file
can be read two different ways, which is rule 51 in the fact contract.

**What is shut is the instance, not the class**, and rule 95's own body says which: the
remedy it names is a key built from the reader's *resolved imports*, and this is the honest
interim form it also names — the glob plus the named few, with a test that asserts the named
few rather than only that the glob still globs (rule 37). The next module that reaches out
of `extractors/python/` will be in no key either, and nothing will say so.

`tests/test_frozen.py` failed the moment it joined — `sql.py` is hashed and so must travel
as **data**, or frozen it hashes nothing. That is the guard working rather than a test
needing an update, exactly as it did for `ingest/` in chunk 5.

### Two smaller things, in scope because they are this defect

* **`resolve/cli.py` read `load_rules("python").cli_launches`.** The whole truth with one
  reader, and the shape that makes a second language's CLI vanish without a symptom: the
  entrypoints are there, the calls are there, and nothing joins them. It is the union over
  the languages **the map holds** now, off the graph rather than off the plugins this build
  ships (rule 24).
* **`receiver_words` was declared and read by nothing.** `plugins/python/plugin.json` has
  carried `["self", "cls"]` since the day it was written while the resolver spelled the set
  itself — rule 35's exact shape, a declared value with no symptom when it is wrong. The
  resolver reads the manifest, and a test asserts the literal is gone from the source.

### Read as syntax, not as text — rule 34, paid for again

The test that no resolver reads this interpreter's builtins was written as a substring scan
and failed immediately: both modules that stopped doing it explain **why** in a comment, and
every such comment contains every word the scan looks for. It parses the file and asks
whether anything under `resolve/` still *imports* the module, which no amount of prose can
answer wrongly. `test_frozen.py` had already learnt this about PyYAML's C extension.

### Measured

| | |
|---|---|
| Golden gate, v1 graph against this one | **7 of 7 digests identical** |
| Society | 628 files, 4,823 routines, 30,544 call sites, 6,441 internal calls |
| Resolution | 5,653 certain · 788 inferred · 4,063 external, 21% internal |
| The four executables | **1,381 · 423 · 292 · 112** |
| Conformance | **4 checked · 1 no population · 10 not checkable** |
| The research paper | **0** naming rules, from 12 stated corpus-wide |
| Call sites spelling a builtins-delta name | **0** |
| Resolution of Society | 0.9 s |

**Through the binary as well as beside it**, because `detectors/` and `packaging/` both
moved. A host build reading its own 92-file tree stamps core `10:cef6b94462148e63` and
python `1.0.0:bbc593d505e58080` — both what the checkout computes — and the checkout opens
the binary's map, 1,043 routines either way.

**Both stamps moved, and each for its own reason**, which is the split doing exactly what
chunk 5 built it for: core `10:91525594e021b516` → `10:cef6b94462148e63` because `sql.py`
joined it, and python `1.0.0:5ad58664e93395f9` → `1.0.0:bbc593d505e58080` because
`python.yaml` gained the builtins block. A `typescript.yaml` edit would have moved neither.

### Open, and stated

* `resolve/entrypoints.py`, `resolve/flows.py` and `resolve/naming.py` are **not** split.
  They are rules-driven or language-neutral; `flows.py:215`'s substring test for *declared*
  is still scheduled onto chunk 12, where a `package.json` `bin` exists to outrank a
  guessed `main`.
* **Resolution is in no cache key and does not join one.** `resolve_calls` re-runs over the
  whole store on every analyse, so rule 12 has nothing to say about it. Worth writing down,
  because this chunk moved code that looks exactly like extraction and a later session
  reading `resolve/python/` beside `extractors/python/` could reasonably assume otherwise.
* The `builtins` list will go stale: CPython 3.14 will add names and nothing here will
  notice. That is the trade the declaration buys — it is now a decision somebody has to
  make rather than a value that varies by machine — and the retake is one `uv` command per
  version, recorded above.

## 2026-09-17 — the codec and the wire, proved against the extractor we already know

`PLAN-v2.md`'s chunk 7, which the plan itself calls *the chunk that de-risks everything*.
Everything from the TypeScript plugin onward assumes a reader on the far side of a pipe can
send `FileFacts` indistinguishable from the ones this process makes. Nothing had ever tested
that, because there had never been a reader on the far side of a pipe —
`ingest._load()` refused one by name: *"this build has no worker for it yet"*.

So the worker, the codec and the handshake were built, and proved by running **the Python
extractor itself** through a subprocess. A difference between the two answers is then the
protocol and can be nothing else.

**The gate held, three ways.** 628 files of Society, **zero differing** by dataclass
equality; the graph written over the wire gives **7 of 7 golden digests identical** against
both the v1 graph and the in-process v2 one; and the map it wrote reports the four
executables at **1,381 · 423 · 292 · 112** and conformance at **4 · 1 · 10**. **1,647
passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean over 171 files, ruff clean.

### The measurement the chunk exists for, and it overturned the obvious answer

| | Per file | |
|---|---:|---|
| in-process, pool | 1.73 ms | what a run costs today |
| in-process, serial | 4.57 ms | the honest comparison |
| out of process, sequential | 6.75 ms | **1.48×** |
| — the codec | 2.12 ms | 98% of the overhead |
| — the pipe and the round trip | 0.05 ms | 0.3% of the run |

**The transport is free.** A round trip is **0.022 ms**, measured directly over 2,000
requests rather than by subtraction; spawn and handshake are 70 ms, once. The
one-file-at-a-time shape the plan specified costs nothing worth recovering and
**pipelining would buy nothing** — the obvious optimisation is the wrong one, which is
worth writing down before somebody spends a chunk on it.

**And the codec was 8.7× slower than it is**, which was found by measuring rather than by
reading: `typing.get_type_hints()` re-resolves a class's annotations on every call and
caches nothing, so asked once per record it made **serialising a file's facts cost four
times what parsing the file cost** — 18.25 ms against 4.57 — and 99% of the protocol's
whole overhead. This module's own docstring had claimed `typing` cached it. `codec._plan`
is cached per class now; the plan is still derived, and what is cached is the derivation.
Full figures in `PERFORMANCE.md`, including the before.

### The codec — reflective, and four refusals because they are four facts

Driven by `dataclasses.fields()` and `get_type_hints()`, never a table of hand-written
pairs: a hand-kept list drifts the moment somebody adds a field, and here the drift is
silent in the worst direction — a field that stops travelling is a *fact that stops
existing*, in a map that opens perfectly and reports a smaller program.

| What arrived | Answer |
|---|---|
| an unknown key | dropped, and **named in `FileFacts.errors`** — a newer plugin may know more than this build, and that is not an error |
| a missing field with no default, or a wrong type | **refuses the record**, naming the class, the field and what came. `"7"` is not `7` |
| an enum value that is not a member | **refuses and quotes it**, listing the members. Never coerced, never defaulted |
| a line that is not JSON | **refuses the language once, loudly** — not skipped 600 times quietly |

A refused record refuses its whole **file**: keeping the other thirty-nine routines is a
map that is quietly smaller with nothing anywhere saying a file was read badly.

**A shape the codec has never seen is refused on the *declared type*, not on a value**, and
that distinction was found by the test written for it. `encode` omits a field left at its
default, so a `complex` field nobody had set yet sailed straight through and would have
failed on the day somebody set it, in whichever run happened to be first. The check moved
into `_plan`, where it is cached and costs nothing per record.

**`lang` is refused on a nested record**, stricter than `stamp_lang`'s test on purpose.
That refuses a *disagreement*, which is right for a reader that cannot disagree with
itself; over a pipe, a plugin that sends the field **at all** is a second answer to a
question `FileFacts.lang` has already answered. It is not encoded either, so a plugin
author cannot learn to send it by watching what the host does.

### The worker

`ingest/worker.py` knows frames and nothing above them — `mcp/jsonrpc.py`'s split, one
protocol over. NDJSON, the same framing the MCP server speaks.

* **Every request carries an `id` and every reply must echo it**, including `hello`, `open`
  and `close`, which the plan's sketch shows without one. Uniform, because the first plugin
  to answer `open` while a file request is outstanding would otherwise be read as having
  answered the file. Proving that needed a worker that *lies*: rewinding the host's counter
  proves nothing, because a well-behaved worker echoes whatever it is given and the two
  agree again (rule 37).
* **The handshake is checked against the manifest** on lang, version, protocol and schema
  version, and a disagreement refuses quoting both (rule 30).
* **The hash travels and is echoed**; a mismatch is recorded as a failure naming both
  hashes rather than filed under a hash it does not describe (rule 12).
* **stderr is drained on its own thread into a 4 KB ring and never parsed** —
  `runtime._desktop_session`'s lesson: text a healthy process also writes cannot be a
  control channel. A chatty plugin is a working plugin, and a test says so.
* **A dead worker is respawned once and the file it died on is not retried.** Retrying is
  how one poison file refuses a whole language — the fresh worker meets the same file and
  dies again, and the second death is the refusal. So one crash is a fact about a file and
  two is a fact about the reader.

### `test_frozen.py` caught a real bug, and it was the interpreter

`plugin_argv` spelled `sys.executable` for a plugin whose toolchain is `python`. Right in a
checkout, and **frozen `sys.executable` is DunneFlow** — the plugin would have been started
by running the application with a script path as its subcommand. The guard that found it
exists for exactly that shape and has now found it twice.

So `runtime.py` gains its fifth question, `host_interpreter()`, and the distinction it
makes is the whole point: `self_argv` answers *how do I run this program again*, this
answers *what interpreter may I hand somebody else*, and in a checkout they are the same
executable — which is precisely why it had to be written down. A frozen build **refuses**,
naming what a real Python plugin would have to do instead. The only one that exists is a
test double and tests do not run frozen (rule 35).

The same pass caught `dotted.py` finding its fixtures through `Path(__file__)`. Through
`resource_root()` now, and frozen it says where they should be and what to do — rather than
reporting that nothing failed.

### The dotted-name contract, written down at last

`detectors/python.yaml`'s header has claimed since it was written that rules match *"the
dotted form of a call expression"*. That normalisation is **the real interface between any
extractor and the rules** — every `exact`, `prefix`, `method` and `contains` is matched
against it — and it was undocumented, unversioned, and known only to the one extractor that
implemented it. A plugin that spells expressions differently does not fail: it makes every
rule miss, and the map comes back with no boundaries, no ways in and no CLI, looking exactly
like a program that has none.

`ingest/dotted.py`'s docstring **is** the contract, eight clauses, with
`tests/fixtures/dotted/cases.json` beside it. Two things about how it is run:

* **Through the reader's ordinary `extract`, not a conformance frame.** A protocol surface
  that exists only to be tested proves that surface and not the one maps are built from.
  So the same runner serves both kinds of reader with no branch, and
  `dunneflow ingest-conform python` passes in this process and over the wire alike.
* **Rules 5, 6 and 7 are named as *unexercised*, never counted as passing** (design rule 1).
  A report saying *8 of 8* about a language with no syntax for three of them means nothing.
  Clause 7 — `new Foo()` plus `CallSite.is_construction` — is the contract's one
  unimplemented clause, and it stays unimplemented: a field nothing sets is a field nothing
  can be trusted to set. Chunk 9 adds it with the reader that fills it.

Two clauses were **discovered by writing the cases** rather than transcribed from the plan:
a subscript kills the chain *anywhere* in it and not only at its root
(`reg.handlers['x'].run()` is `""`, because naming it means deciding what `handlers['x']`
is, and deciding that is resolution), and the fold in clause 2 applies repeatedly
(`a.b(1).c(2).d()` → `a.b.c.d`).

### `dunneflow ingest-schema`

`schema.py` as data — 29 record types, 230 fields, 14 enumerations — out of the same
reflection the wire uses, so the descriptor a plugin generates its types from and the wire
it then talks cannot describe two different shapes (rule 13). Its purpose is that a
`SCHEMA_VERSION` bump breaks a plugin's **build** rather than its output, which is the one
failure mode a fact contract across a process boundary has and one inside a process does
not. It names the host-owned fields, because that is the thing a plugin author will
otherwise get wrong.

### Where the double lives, and why it is not where the plan put it

`PLAN-v2.md` says `plugins/python-oop/`. It is `tests/plugins/python-oop/`, and the reason
is the registry's own rule: `_load()` reads every `plugins/*/plugin.json` at import and
`suffix_owners` refuses two readers claiming one suffix, naming both. Shipped beside the
real Python plugin it would refuse the build at import; claiming another suffix it would
not read the files the comparison is about. So it is built through `read_manifest` and
`OutOfProcessPlugin` — the public path, minus the registry — and a test asserts it is not
in the shipped directory.

Its misbehaviour is driven by seven environment variables, because the failure paths that
matter most run least: a worker that cannot be made to die, lie, throw, echo a wrong hash,
answer with somebody else's id, or write prose on stdout leaves every one of the host's
refusals proved by reading it rather than by running it.

### Measured

| | |
|---|---|
| Society over the wire vs in process | **0 of 628 files differ**, by dataclass equality |
| Golden, wire graph against v1 | **7 of 7 digests identical** |
| Golden, wire graph against in-process v2 | **7 of 7 digests identical** |
| The four executables, over the wire | 1,381 · 423 · 292 · 112 |
| Conformance, over the wire | 4 checked · 1 no population · 10 not checkable |
| Payload | 21.5 MB of JSON for 628 files |
| Dotted conformance | 10 of 10 exercised, 3 named unexercised, in process and over the wire |

**Both fingerprints moved, each for its own reason**, which is chunk 5's split still doing
its job: core `10:cef6b94462148e63` → `10:95a28959eb3fa92e` because `ingest/*.py` gained
four modules, and the python row stamp is **different in the map the double wrote**
(`1.0.0:9718762d…` against `1.0.0:bbc593d5…`) because the double is a different reader with
different bytes. Opening that map with the normal build is refused **by name** — *holds
facts from a reader this build is not* — which is the split working across a process
boundary, and was worth pressing rather than assuming.

**Through the binary**, because `ingest/` is in the core key and `cli.py` grew two commands:
a host build stamps core `10:95a28959eb3fa92e` and python `1.0.0:bbc593d505e58080`, both
what the checkout computes. Frozen, `ingest-conform` says the fixtures are not in an
application and where they live — rather than reporting that nothing failed.

### Open, and stated

* **`lost` is always nought for an out-of-process reader**, and that is not an oversight.
  It means *a file that never arrived at all*, which is the only thing an in-process pool
  can say when a worker dies — the parent cannot attribute the death to a file. Here the
  host holds the pipe and knows exactly which request was outstanding, so a death produces
  a record naming the file and the reason. The better answer is kept rather than degraded
  to match the worse one, and `WalkStats` counts it off `ff.errors` like any other failure.
* **A file the reader threw on is not cached** — no `content_hash` — so it is read again
  next run. A file that will not *parse* still is, with its hash, which is v1's behaviour
  preserved deliberately. The difference is that one is a fact about the file and the other
  is a fact about the reader.
* **One worker, not `manifest.workers` of them.** Python declares 1 and the TypeScript
  growth axis is per-`tsconfig.json`, which is chunk 9's shape. A pool built now would be a
  pool nothing exercises (rule 35).
* `ingest/manifest.py` and `ingest/discovery.py` stay unsplit, as chunk 5's deviations
  already recorded: they work, and they are in the fingerprint key, so moving them is churn
  that discards graphs for no behaviour.
* **`CLAUDE.md` was not touched, and that is a deliberate departure from this chunk's own
  plan**, which listed it among the files to update. `V2-START-HERE.md` states that where
  that file describes *commands* it describes v1 — so adding `ingest-schema` and
  `ingest-conform` to its command block would put v2 state in the one file that declares
  itself v1's, which is the split it exists to keep. Chunk 14 owns the rewrite, and the two
  commands are in `--help`, in this entry, and in `V2-START-HERE.md` until then.

## 2026-09-17 — the string-literal split, and the 65 routines it invented

`PLAN-v2.md`'s chunk 8, done **before** TypeScript exists so that TypeScript never sees the
old shape. `FileFacts` gains `literals`; the Python reader stops deciding what a string
*means* and reports the strings; `ingest/literals.py` runs today's SQL and artefact
scanning for every language at once.

**The gate held.** Society: **7 of 7 golden digests identical**, 4,823 routines, and the
four tables the split actually moves — `artefacts` 364, `sql_ops` 1,055, `db_tables` 43,
`db_indexes` 73 — **byte-identical to v1 row for row**. Over the wire through
`tests/plugins/python-oop/`, **0 of 628 files differ**. Through the frozen binary, 7 of 7
again, and the binary and the checkout stamp the same two fingerprints
(`11:59503f09d349e32b` core, `1.0.0:5ed1444ffe4c8c48` for the reader) and open each
other's maps, 4,823 routines both ways. **1,670 passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean over 173
files, ruff clean.

### Why the judgement is the host's

There is nothing about `looks_like_sql` or `_scan_artefact` that is Python's: both take a
string and an extension table and neither has ever looked at a syntax tree. A plugin
carrying its own copy means the same `"INSERT INTO queue (id) VALUES (?)"` reads one way in
a `.py` and another in a `.ts` — not because the languages differ, because two people wrote
two scanners. Rule 51 in the fact contract, which is the most expensive place to have it.

It also keeps `detectors/<lang>.yaml` the extension point: teaching the tool that
`.parquet` names a file is a YAML edit that moves the fingerprint and re-reads every
language, rather than a YAML edit **plus** a plugin rebuild — and the rebuild is the half
somebody forgets. And it shrinks the plugin contract to one rules-facing thing,
`ingest/dotted.py`'s normalisation: one contract with one fixture instead of four.

**Three things stay with the reader, each because only the reader can do them.** The
interpolation — `f"{root}/g.json"` still names `g.json`, and assembling that text needs the
module's own constant table and the tree that holds it. The routine a string sits in — by
the time facts reach the host, a line number is all that is left of where anything was. And
**not being a docstring**, which is rule 9: a docstring opening *"Insert candidate into
capture_queue"* is a sentence about a statement, and admitted host-side it would be a
statement.

### The defect the split created, and it is the interesting half

The first run of the gate reported **2 of 7 digests moved** — `routines.id` and
`routines.body` — from a change that touches no routine at all. 65 of Society's 628 files
had gained a `<module>` routine, and every one of them owned **nothing**: zero SQL
operations, zero artefacts.

`_owner()` mints the synthetic module-scope routine on demand and appends it, so *the
module scope was a routine only where something belonged to it* — true by accident, because
whichever fact asked first did the minting and a file with nothing at module level had
nothing asking. A **string** has to name an owner before anybody knows whether it is a fact,
so asking there minted the scope for every file with a module-level string. A 1.3%
inflation of every routine count in the map, decided by whether a string cleared a bound
that exists to save wire. **Rule 96**, and rule 49's shape exactly: the filter that hides
is the one whose effect looks like an ordinary number.

So **preparing the module scope is now separate from claiming it**. `module_scope()` builds
the row and appends nothing; `_owner()` claims it, as every fact-recording caller always
did; `_owner_id()` names it without claiming, because `make_id` is derived from names and
needs no row to exist. `ingest.literals` claims it if and only if one of those strings
turned out to be a fact. `FileFacts.module_scope` carries the prepared row across the wire,
and `stamp_lang` stamps it whether or not it is ever claimed — it is a record inside these
facts like any other, and it is the one the host may still append *after* stamping.

*This is the second time in v2 that a change with no business touching routine counts
touched them, and both were caught by the same gate. The counts holding is not the claim —
`routines.id` is a digest of the sorted ids, and a total can hold while its contents swap.*

### `LiteralKind`, and the glob that has been losing

`?` in an interpolated string is the placeholder the reader left where a value goes; `?` in
a string somebody typed is a glob. The old scan could not tell them apart and treated every
one as a placeholder, so `"chaos_?.py"` — a real pattern, and `Artefact.is_pattern` exists
to say so — was refused. `StringLiteral.kind` is `PLAIN` or `INTERPOLATED`, and the
placeholder test now applies only to the second. **Measured before it was taken: Society's
`artefacts` rows are byte-identical either way**, so the reading costs the golden nothing
and gains the case it was written for.

### The bound, and the reason for it that turned out to be false

The plan says the reader applies `_scan_sql`'s `6 ≤ len ≤ 200_000` before sending and
reports what it dropped. Two corrections, both measured.

**Six is SQL's own bound and cannot be the shared one.** The shortest string that can name
a file is three — `x.y`, a one-character stem and a one-character extension, both of which
a `detectors/<lang>.yaml` may legitimately declare. Applying SQL's floor to the artefact
question is a bound written for one question quietly deciding another. On Society it
happens to cost nothing (the shortest artefact literal there is **seven** characters) —
which is not the same claim as *it cannot cost anything*. So `LITERAL_MIN` is 3 and six
stays inside `_sql`.

**And the floor is not what saves the wire.** Of 46,524 strings the floor at three drops
4,022; taking six would drop a further 6,861 and save **0.43 MB of a 26.5 MB payload,
1.6%**. The ceiling is the half that earns its place — a vendored blob has no business
being lexically scanned for SQL. The comment that first justified the floor by the wire was
written before the measurement and has been corrected; it was wrong in the direction this
project keeps paying for, a plausible reason for a real decision.

**What it dropped is said out loud.** `FileFacts.literals_dropped` travels with the facts,
`WalkStats.literals_dropped` sums it per language, and the run says
*strings not judged: 4,022 python — outside the 3–200,000 character bound a reader applies
before sending*. A filter that runs in a process the host cannot look inside is exactly the
silent one design rule 1 forbids.

### `reports_literals` stops being a field nobody reads

It was declared in every manifest and on the wire and compared nowhere. It decides whether
the host judges a language's strings at all now, so a manifest saying yes over a process
saying no is a map with no SQL and no named files in it and nothing anywhere saying why —
so the **capabilities are checked in the handshake**, beside lang, protocol, schema and
version, and a disagreement refuses the language quoting both. `judge` refuses both
directions too: a reader that declared none and sent some, and a reader that sent `sql` or
`artefacts` it judged itself. A language that genuinely reports none is a **real answer**
and the run says so — *no strings reported by: kotlin — that language contributes no SQL
and no named files to this map*.

### Figures

| | |
|---|---|
| strings Society spells out | 46,524 |
| reported | 42,502 |
| dropped by the bound | 4,022 |
| the host's judgement | 0.12 ms a file, **75 ms** for the corpus |
| literals on the wire | 3.8 MB of 26.5 MB — 14% |
| protocol overhead over serial | 1.58×, from 1.48× before the split |

`SCHEMA_VERSION` is **11**: the stored shape did not move, but what a plugin must emit did,
and a reader built against 10 that sends no literals would now produce a map with no SQL in
it. That is precisely the refusal the number is still kept for.

### Found by this chunk's gate and **not fixed**: the rendered map is not run-to-run stable

Comparing chunk 6's map against chunk 8's turned up row-order differences in documents this
change has no business touching, so the obvious suspicion was the `<module>` fix shifting
rowids. It is not. **Two analyses of Society by the same build, minutes apart, differ**:

| Document | run 1 vs run 2 | run 1 vs run 3 |
|---|---:|---:|
| `01-entrypoints.md` | 4 | 4 |
| `06-governance.md` | 2,215 | 2,076 |
| `07-database.md` | 4 | 0 |
| `09-anomalies.md` | 4 | 8 |
| `10-glossary.md` | 104 | 104 |
| `11-naming.md` | 0 | 4 |
| `12-traceability.md` | 988 | 910 |

**Every difference examined is order and not content** — the same rows, and the same items
inside a `<br>`- or `;`-joined cell, in another sequence. Nothing is lost and no number
moves; `07-database.md` and `11-naming.md` each came out stable in one pair and unstable in
the other, which is what a coin looks like.

**The cause is one shape in several places.** `analyze_tree` collects facts through
`as_completed`, so which file is written first varies per run and so does every rowid. A
query with no `ORDER BY`, or one ordering on a column with ties — `render/database.py:99`
is `ORDER BY name` over index names that repeat across migrations;
`resolve/naming.py:276` is `sorted(exceptions, key=lambda e: e.name)`, a stable sort whose
input order is rowid order, and `_console` occurs in three files — then returns rows in
whatever order the pool happened to finish in. Rule 66 exactly: *an order the tool cannot
defend is not an order*, and these are undefended ties rather than wrong answers.

**It is v1's, not v2's.** The pool and its `as_completed` predate the `ingest/` seam;
chunk 2 moved them from `analyze_tree` into `InProcessPlugin` unchanged. And it is not
`SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`-shaped either — the timestamps are already stated on every page.

**Left alone deliberately**, and this is the one place in the chunk where that is a choice
rather than a finding. It is seven documents across both stores and several renderers, it
touches no stored fact (the golden proves that: 7 of 7 digests identical, and a digest is
over the *sorted* ids), and rolling it into chunk 8 would make the chunk's own gate
unreadable — a report that has to be diffed against a baseline cannot also be the thing
being changed. It is a chunk of its own, and the fix is a total order on every rendered
list rather than a stable pool, because a stable pool would buy determinism by giving up
the parallelism.

*It is worth saying plainly that the map has been like this for a year and nobody noticed,
including every session that diffed two maps by hand. The gate that found it was looking at
something else.*

## 2026-09-17 — TypeScript, extraction only: a second language, read by another program

`PLAN-v2.md`'s chunk 9. A pnpm package at `src/dunneflow/plugins/typescript/`, bundled by
esbuild into one committed `main.bundle.cjs` with the TypeScript compiler inlined, speaking
the NDJSON protocol chunk 7 proved. **No supplied edges**: every TypeScript call is left
external, and the run says so.

**The gate.** `../DunneNote` at 0.9.0: **443 program files read, 0 failed**, 315 left out
as tests, 1,518 routines, 708 structures, 139 boundary touches. Python unmoved — Society
still **7 of 7 golden digests identical**, 4,823 routines, 5,653 certain · 788 inferred ·
4,063 external. **1,699 passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean over 175 files, ruff clean. The
frozen binary reads a TypeScript tree and stamps the same two fingerprints the checkout
does (`12:7bd00b06f965e1a2` core, `1.0.0:4507b02b56cfefe4` for the reader).

### Ground truth, and three of the plan's numbers do not reproduce

Every figure was retaken rather than carried (rule 24), and the plan's were checked by hand
against a tree that has moved since.

| Claim | Plan | Measured now |
|---|---|---|
| `.ts`/`.tsx` on disk | 767 | **758** |
| files importing `@tauri-apps/api/core` | 30, 29 of them tests | **31, 29 tests** |
| program files importing it | **one** | **two** |
| `.svelte` | 70 | **81** |
| `fetch` in non-test `.ts` | once | **never** |

**The 767 counts nine directories.** `apps/desktop/tests/visual/__screenshots__/` holds
directories named `cal-month.spec.ts`, `canvas.spec.ts` and seven more, each full of PNGs,
and `find -name "*.ts"` matches a directory as happily as a file. 758 is the file count, and
the walk's own arithmetic closes exactly: **443 read + 315 left out as tests = 758**, with
nothing claimed-but-unread.

**The second Tauri file is `legacy/v0.1/src/lib/ipc.ts`.** The seam is still a seam — one
per copy of the program, and `legacy/v0.1/` is a second copy kept in the tree with its own
`tsconfig.json`. The property the plan wanted from it holds and is what the map reports: 29
test files import that module and **not one of them is in the map**, which is the test
exclusion working. The claim *exactly one program file* was true of a tree without the
legacy copy.

**And `fetch` is never called in a non-test `.ts` at all** — see the network defect below,
which is what that zero found.

The three the plan named that do reproduce: **`packages/api-types` reports 0 boundaries**
over 206 files and 205 `TYPE_ALIAS` structures — the failure it says to look for, and it
does not happen; the 283 `.rs` and 81 `.svelte` files are **reported unclaimed by name and
count**; and `apps/host-http` is Rust and is absent rather than quietly missing.

### Four defects found, every one by something that was written to find it

**`crypto.createHash("blake2b512", { outputLength: 8 })` is wrong twice**, and it is the
line the plan specified. Node's OpenSSL refuses it outright — `not XOF or invalid length` —
and had it worked it would still be the wrong hash, because BLAKE2b puts the digest length
in its **parameter block**: `blake2b(b"ab")[:8]` is `b32c0573d242b3a9` and
`blake2b(b"ab", digest_size=8)` is `0e52b5f187de1088`. A reader that shipped the truncation
would mint ids that look exactly like ids and match nothing in the map. So BLAKE2b is
implemented in `src/ids.ts` from RFC 7693, and parity is asserted against **the reader's
real output** rather than a vectors file it never reads: a fixture nobody runs proves a
function nobody calls (rule 35), and a conformance frame added to be tested would prove that
frame rather than the one the map is built from.

**One act became two rows.** `localStorage.setItem("seen", "1")` matched the call rule with
`seen` as its target *and* the `subscript: [localStorage]` rule with `setItem` as its
target — rule 40, two detectors recording one act. A property access that is being *called*
belongs to the call rule; `process.env.PORT`, which is not called, is still the other's.

**A loop stopped being a loop when its receiver had no name.** `["a","b"].map(fn)` has no
dotted form by clause 3, so no call is recorded — correctly — and the comprehension was
inside that same test, so the span disappeared too. Rule 3 governs what may be matched
against a rule, never whether a span exists; Python records `[f(x) for x in ["a","b"]]`
without hesitating. **+18 comprehensions on DunneNote**, 222 → 240.

**`fetch` matched `fetchImpl`.** `RuleSet.network_profile` is `dotted.startswith(prefix)`,
which is exactly right for `requests.` and `httpx.AsyncClient` and exactly wrong for a bare
name. Python's own rules hid it for a year because **every one of them contains a dot**;
TypeScript's `fetch`, `WebSocket` and `EventSource` do not. DunneNote reported exactly one
network call and it was `fetchImpl` — a parameter holding an implementation — in the corpus
whose ground truth is that no program file calls `fetch` at all. A key with no dot now
matches exactly (rule 5), in the host and in the reader. *The residue is stated*: a call
through a name that holds `fetch` is a network call and is no longer reported as one.
Knowing that needs the far end of the name, which is resolution, and chunk 10 is where it
comes back.

### And two the corpora found that no test would have

**An overload set is one name declared three times.** uigen died with
`UNIQUE constraint failed: routines.id` on its generated Prisma client, where
`PrismaClient.$transaction` is declared twice. Not broken code — it is how TypeScript
spells an overload. `extractors/python/extract.py:_identity` has had the ordinal since it
was written; this reader had not.

**Python reads text with universal newlines and Node does not.** The host hashes what
`Path.read_text` gave it, and Python turns `\r\n` and a lone `\r` into `\n`; `readFileSync`
keeps them. So every CRLF file hashed differently on the two sides, and the echo check
refused it — **correctly, and with the wrong reason**: *changed while it was being read*,
about a file that had not changed. Measured on uigen: **2 of 54 files**, both generated with
CRLF, both reported unreadable in a map that was otherwise perfect, and neither would have
been read on any later run either. It was a property of one implementation's default and is
now a term of the protocol, `ingest.contract.SOURCE_TEXT`, stated in the file a plugin
author reads — and the echo's sentence names both things that look like this, because a
race and a reader that decodes differently are one symptom and two facts.

*Both of these were found by running the tool on a real tree rather than by a test, which is
`CLAUDE.md`'s own reason for keeping the ground truth: unit tests on a toy program cannot
catch a defect that only appears at scale.* uigen went from 161 routines to **566** once the
two files were readable.

### What the reader does, and what it deliberately does not

`ts.createSourceFile` per file, **no program and no checker**. Chunk 9 is extraction only,
so the compilation is not needed yet; `open` already takes the whole file set, which is the
shape chunk 10 builds the program in without touching the protocol. Saying so is the point —
a `ts.createProgram` over `node_modules` paid for nothing would be the easy thing to leave in.

**An anonymous function is not a routine.** Declarations, methods, and functions or arrows
*bound to a name* are; a callback passed inline is not, and its calls and boundaries belong
to the nearest named routine. Naming one means inventing a word for a reader to look for in
a file that does not contain it (rule 30), and thousands of `<anonymous>` rows is rule 1's
own subject. React's components are named; `useEffect`'s callbacks are chunk 11's.

**There is no `BROWSER` kind**, which `PLAN-v2.md` settled by counting. `fetch` and
WebSocket are the network under another name; `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB
are persistent named storage shared across an origin, which is what DATABASE means, with the
store's own key as the target. The DOM is the program's own rendered output rather than its
environment and is **not reported at all** — 81 `.svelte` files' worth of `querySelector`
would be thousands of rows drowning the panel they were added to. A test asserts the residue
rather than leaving it in prose.

### Four words for `ArmKind`, and the plan named three of them

*catch, do, switch*, said the plan; two of those are right. A `switch` is a **point**, and
its arms are `case` — already there — and `default`, which was not. And TypeScript has no
`elif`: it writes `else if`, two words, which is what its rung is called. The enum's own
docstring is what chose them — *the word in the source, and nothing invented* — and reading
the rule rather than the summary is the whole of the difference. `EXCEPT` stays Python's and
`CATCH` is TypeScript's; spelling one language's arm with the other's word is the same
defect as renaming it.

### The three things that keep a second reader honest

**The rules travel; they are never baked in.** `detectors.rules_document` sends
`typescript.yaml` **as written** in the `open` frame, so a YAML edit moves the core key and
re-reads every language with no plugin rebuild (rule 51). What the plugin transcribes is the
four match tests and nothing else, and a test puts the same dotted names through both.

**The types are generated, not transcribed.** `tools/gen_facts_ts.py` writes `src/facts.ts`
from `schema.py`, and a test regenerates and compares. It exists because the hand-written
version was wrong inside an hour: a `NetworkCall.library` field that does not exist, which
the codec drops and names in `FileFacts.errors` — and `WalkStats` counts a file with an
error as **failed**, so every TypeScript file holding a network call would have been
reported unreadable in a map that otherwise looked perfect.

**The dotted contract is kept, and clauses 5, 6 and 7 stopped being hypothetical.**
`dunneflow ingest-conform typescript` is 12 of 12 with rules 5, 6 and 7 exercised for the
first time; Python is 10 of 10 with those three correctly named unexercised. Clause 7 is
asserted **both halves** — `new Foo()` must spell `Foo` *and* carry `is_construction`, or a
reader that flattened the two would pass on the name alone (rule 37). And the report no
longer lists rule 8 as unexercised when one of its cases ran: rule 8 is a case per receiver
word, `self`, `cls` and `this`, so a language that skips two and passes one has exercised it.

### Two packaging defects this chunk created, and both are closed

**`detectors/typescript.yaml` would not have shipped.** The spec named `python.yaml` and
`annotations.yaml` by hand, which was the whole truth while there was one language;
`load_rules` would have raised `RulesMissing` on the first `.ts` file in the signed
application and nowhere else. It globs `detectors/*.yaml` now — which is what
`core_extraction_inputs()` has always done, so the hand-kept list was already a second
answer waiting to disagree with the key (rule 92).

**And `node_modules` would have shipped with it.** `_tree(PKG / "plugins")` was right while
a plugin was one `plugin.json`; the TypeScript reader brings several thousand files of
workshop. The bundled list is derived from the **manifests** now — `plugin.json` plus each
one's `fingerprint` — which buys the stronger property rather than merely excluding a
directory: *what ships and what is stamped are the same bytes by construction*. 41 MB
built, and the plugin directory in the bundle is three files.

### Also fixed on the way past

**`unresolved_langs` was filled by chunk 6 and read by nothing.** `resolve/calls.py`'s own
docstring promised a language with no resolver would be *named* with its count; the counter
existed and nothing printed it — rule 35's shape, in the sentence that is the whole
difference between *nothing resolved* and *nothing to resolve*. Chunk 9 is the first run
where it fires, and a run now says *left external for want of a resolver: typescript 4,990*.

**And `load_rules` silently lost its cache** for about an hour: an edit inserted
`rules_document` between `load_rules` and its `@lru_cache`, so the decorator landed on the
new function and the YAML would have been re-parsed once per file. Caught by
`test_languages.py` calling `load_rules.cache_clear()`.
