| | |
|---|---|
| DunneNote, cold | **1.5 s** for 443 files — 3.4 ms each |
| warm, nothing changed | 0.1 s |
| spawn and handshake | 0.18 s, once |
| the bundle | 9.5 MB, TypeScript 5.9.3 inlined |
| control points | 1,236 guards · 459 decisions · 275 loops · 240 comprehensions · 210 handlers |
| constructions | 299 |
| the application | 41 MB |

`SCHEMA_VERSION` is **12**: `CallSite.is_construction`, and the four `ArmKind` words.

*`typescript@7` cannot be used, and it is what `npm install typescript` gets you today.* The
Go port's JavaScript entry exposes no `createProgram` and no `SyntaxKind` — measured,
`undefined` at 7.0.2 and `function` at 5.9.3. The plugin pins 5.9.3.

## 2026-09-17 — supplied edges: the checker names the far end

`PLAN-v2.md`'s chunk 10. The TypeScript reader builds a `ts.Program` per `tsconfig.json` in
`open` and answers a new `edges` frame out of the checker; `resolve/typescript/calls.py`
turns each location into an id. **Nothing guesses**: a call the checker did not resolve is
left external, and a bare name is never matched against a routine that happens to share it.

**The gate.** `../DunneNote`, against chunk 9's honest floor of *0 internal, 4,990
external*:

| | chunk 9 | chunk 10 |
|---|---|---|
| internal edges | **0** | **1,935** |
| rate | 0% | **38% internal** |
| of which supplied by a toolchain | — | **1,935**, all of them |
| ambiguous (several declarations) | — | **0** |
| resolved outside the map | — | 2,868 |
| the checker could not resolve | — | 187 |

Python unmoved: **7 of 7 golden digests identical**, 4,823 routines, 6,441 internal calls.
**1,727 passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean over 178 files, ruff clean. `SCHEMA_VERSION` is
**13**. The frozen binary and the checkout stamp the same two fingerprints
(`13:4601e63bc473ecfe` core, `1.0.0:066b557e0b6ae705` for the reader) and open each other's
maps, 1,935 supplied edges either way.

**Extraction did not move, and that was the risk worth measuring.** Both passes now walk the
program's source files rather than each parsing its own, so an argument had to become a
measurement (rule 24). Every chunk 9 figure reproduces exactly: 1,518 routines, 708
structures, 139 boundary touches, 299 constructions, and 1,236 guards · 459 decisions · 275
loops · 240 comprehensions · 210 handlers.

### Twelve edges read against the source, because a rate is a number

Two are worth writing down, and both are cases a name could not have got right.

**`resyncState(state, current.value)`** in `numeric-field-action.ts:109` resolves to
`resync` in `numeric-field.ts:140`. Line 50 of the caller is
`import { resync as resyncState, … }` — and **line 105 of the same file declares its own
`function resync()`**. A resolver matching the expression finds nothing called
`resyncState`; one matching the target's name finds two. The checker had already chosen,
because choosing is what it did to type the call.

**`hierarchy.selectNode(pageId)`** in `search-jump.ts:82` resolves to
`HierarchyStore.selectNode` in `hierarchy-store.svelte.ts:116`. The receiver's type is the
whole answer and it is the one thing a reader without a checker cannot have.

### Rule 97, and it is the defect of the chunk

**The bundled compiler was shipping without its own standard library.** esbuild moved every
line of TypeScript's *code* into `main.bundle.cjs` and none of the ninety-nine `lib*.d.ts`
files the compiler opens **by path** at run time, off `__dirname` — which after bundling is
the plugin's directory, where no such file exists and none ever will.

It does not refuse. It builds a program with no `Array`, no `Promise`, no `Map` and no DOM,
types every value through one of them as `any`, and **answers every question it is asked**.
Measured both ways on 5,119 call sites:

| | edges | outside the map | could not resolve |
|---|---|---|---|
| **with the libraries** | **1,935** | 2,868 | **187** |
| without | 1,931 | 472 | **2,587** |

**Four edges.** The map is the same map, and a check on the number this chunk exists to
produce would have passed. What moved was the *account*: the run went from saying it could
not name the far end of half the program's calls to saying those calls go to `Math`, `JSON`,
`Set` and the DOM — external, and right.

**It was found by splitting a residue rather than by a test.** Chunk 10 first reported one
number for *could not name the far end*, and 2,587 of 5,119 was too large to leave alone.
Separating *the checker said, and the answer is not here* from *the checker could not say* is
what made a missing library visible at all — design rule 21 paying for itself one process
away from where it was written. The remedy is `src/libs.ts` and `build.mjs`' `tsLibs`
plugin: 99 files, 3.0 MB, read at bundle time and served from memory under a sentinel path
that is on no disk. A build with no `node_modules` **refuses**, and `Session.open` says so in
its diagnostics if an empty one ever arrives — because what this defect proves is that
nothing else would.

### And a regression from chunk 6 that had been in the record for a day

**`ResolveStats.external` had stopped counting external calls.** v1 counted one in the tail
every no-target path fell through; the chunk 6 split gave each `NoEdge` its own branch and
kept the count only on the boundary one. So Society read **4,063 external** over 30,544 calls
of which 24,103 leave the program — 4,063 being the `at_boundary` count wearing another word
— and `5,653 + 788 + 4,063` reaches nowhere near the total it is printed beside.

It is in chunk 9's entry above as a recorded figure and it was wrong. The true number is
**24,103**, the store's own, and `certain + inferred + external` is now the total (rule 13).
Found by chunk 10's gate rather than by a test, because a resolution rate is the first figure
anybody checks the arithmetic of; `test_supplied_edges.py` is that test now.

### Three more, each found by reading rather than by a failure

**`NdjsonWorker.respawn` re-opened a worker without its rules.** `open` was spelled out a
second time there and the `rules` key was left off, so a worker that died once read the rest
of the run with **no boundary rules at all** — no boundaries, no SQL, no network, and nothing
anywhere saying why. The plugin's own warning for that case exists and goes to stderr, which
the host never parses (rule 35). The frame is built in one place now (rule 51), and it
matters more after this chunk than before: a respawned worker has to rebuild its programs
too, and the two are the same omission.

**The `opened` frame's `diagnostics` and `program_ms` had been discarded for three chunks.**
Both fields were declared in chunk 7 and filled with nothing; this chunk gave them something
to say and then threw it away. They reach the run now:

```
  read: typescript 443
    typescript (no tsconfig): 206 files
    typescript apps/desktop/tsconfig.json: 226 files
    typescript legacy/v0.1/tsconfig.json: 11 files
    typescript opened in 0.7s
```

**Nothing checked that the committed bundle was the committed source** — rule 37 in the one
place it could cost a whole feature. Everything that tested the bundle tested that it
*exists*, that the fingerprint names it, and that `node main.bundle.cjs` answers `hello`, and
all three pass over a bundle built from last month's source. This is the first chunk to edit
`src/` after the bundle was committed, so it is the first time an entire `edges`
implementation could have sat in a file nothing runs. `build.mjs` takes
`DUNNEFLOW_BUNDLE_OUT` now and a test rebuilds to a scratch file and compares bytes.

### The design, and the three decisions inside it

**A supplied edge is a whole-program fact, so it is stored whole.** `SuppliedEdge` is in
`schema.py` beside `CallSite` and deliberately **not** a field on `FileFacts`: a checker's
answer for `a.ts` is built out of `b.ts`, so an edge filed under its caller goes stale the
moment `b.ts` moves a function and `a.ts` does not change — the line it names would point at
whatever drifted into that position and nothing would be re-read to notice. So
`supplied_edges` is keyed by language, replaced whole whenever that language's reader is
opened, and **`forget_file` does not touch it**. A run that reads no file of a language
changes none of its edges, and they are still true because nothing of that language changed.
Pressed: a warm DunneNote is 443 cached, 0 parsed, and the same 1,935 edges.

**A target is named by location and resolved by node identity, not by re-deriving a line.**
`line_start` is taken from a different node for each of the five shapes a routine is written
in — the declaration for a `function`, the *member* for a class field holding an arrow, the
whole `VariableStatement` for `const f = () => {}`. `Extractor.anchors` records which node
each routine was made at, the edge pass walks a checker's declaration up to the first anchor,
and a second function that worked the line out again would disagree on exactly the shapes
nobody tests (rule 51). The host still keeps a containing-span fallback and a name check, and
**both fired nought times out of 1,935** — which is what says the two sides agree.

**One program per `tsconfig.json`, inside the plugin.** `PLAN-v2.md` puts the growth axis at
one worker per project; realising it in the plugin costs the host nothing — no protocol
change, `workers` still 1, the same file set. It is not tidiness: `legacy/v0.1` declares
`paths: { "$lib/*": ["src/lib/*"] }` relative to itself and one options object holds one
`paths` map, so a single program would silently fail to resolve every `$lib` import in one of
the two copies of that program. Root names are the **host's** file set and never the
tsconfig's `include`, or the 315 test files the walk excluded would come back.

**`INFERRED` is never produced for TypeScript**, and `resolve/contract.py` now carries the
per-language table. Where the checker gives several declarations the answer is external with
the count in `ambiguous`, exactly as Python answers a name collision; `INFERRED` is a claim
that a name-uniqueness argument was made, and for a checker none was made or needed (rule 6).
On DunneNote it happens **0 times**.

### What is deliberately not closed

**The `fetch`-through-a-name residue stays open**, and chunk 9's entry above says this chunk
is where it comes back. It is not, and the reason is the corpus rather than the mechanism:
DunneNote calls `fetch` in **no program file at all**, and the only `fetchImpl` in the tree is
in `client-http.test.ts`, which the map excludes. Reporting a boundary out of a whole-program
pass is a real feature and building it here would mean building it with no population to
measure it against. The mechanism is now in place — the checker can say what a name holds —
and it wants a corpus that contains one.

## 2026-09-17 — TSX and React: the component tree is the flow

`PLAN-v2.md`'s chunk 11, against `../DunneCorp` (`dunne-web` 0.1.0) with `../uigen` as the
second opinion. Five things, and the two that were not on the list are the ones worth
reading.

**A JSX element is a call.** In a React program the component tree *is* the flow, and chunk
9 left it unread: `app/(marketing)/services/[slug]/page.tsx` rendered eleven components and
the map said it called one function. A tag that names a value is a call site — the tag is
the callee through the same dotted contract, the props are its keyword arguments, and the
checker names the far end exactly as it does for `f(x)`. An intrinsic element is not: a bare
lowercase tag is React's own signal for a *string*, which is the page rather than something
the program calls, and it is the same judgement `detectors/typescript.yaml` already makes
about the DOM.

The arithmetic closes exactly. **215** capitalised tags by grep over the 123 files read,
minus **42** that are type names in generic positions, is **173** — the number of call sites
recorded, with no tag missed and nothing recorded that is not one. Every one of the 173 was
resolved by the checker: 116 to routines in this map, 57 to libraries, and `unknown` did not
move from 8.

**The 36 ways in nothing in the files declares.** A Next.js page carries no decorator, no
registration call and no telling export name: the *path* is the declaration. So
`detectors/typescript.yaml` gains a `routes:` section — which directories start a route
tree, which filenames are a page and which a handler, and which segments are not URL — and
`plugins/typescript/src/routes.ts` is the one place it is read. All 33 route names were
printed and read by eye against the tree: no `(marketing)` group survives into any name,
`[slug]` and `[...nextauth]` are kept as the program wrote them, `app/(marketing)/page.tsx`
is `/`, and each lands on the component its file default-exports. Three handler verbs, named
verb-first.

`export const { GET, POST } = handlers;` is next-auth's own spelling and no scan for exported
functions finds anything in it. Both verbs are ways in whose routine is `None`, and the
anomaly detector read that correctly with no help: `ENTRYPOINT_NO_TARGET`, SUSPECT, blind
spot *"may be supplied by a dependency"*. It is.

**The boundary a name cannot reach.** Three of DunneCorp's four most interesting boundaries
are written in ways no spelling rule can find — a local `const` holding a client, a factory
call, a typed receiver — and the checker resolved every one of them to type the call. A
`packages:` table matches the package a call lands in, and a package rule outranks a name
rule, because a name rule is a guess about what somebody called a variable and a package
rule is what the compiler worked out. One call is still one boundary (rule 40).

Two things the measurement said that a guess would not: `.prisma` is where 130 of DunneCorp's
calls resolve, because a generated client's types live in `node_modules/.prisma/client`; and
`doc.send(…)` — the one call that actually reaches DynamoDB — is declared by `@smithy/core`
rather than by `@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb`, which declares only the command. The entries that are
**absent** matter as much: `zod` is 169 calls and is validation, `prosemirror-*` is 143 and is
a document model in memory, and `@types/node` is 159, which would collapse every file,
process and console boundary into one target called `node`.

`target:` is a named strategy now. DunneCorp's 130 DATABASE rows named `{ where: { email } }`;
`receiver_tail` names the model, and the 13 targets are the Prisma schema — user 34, ticket
15, service 15, booking 12. A promise tail is dropped first, because
`db.user.update({…}).catch(…)` folds to `db.user.update.catch` and named `update` where every
other row named a table.

**A hook's callback is a routine** nested in the component (rule 10), so what an effect
touches is filed under the effect. The name is stated and never invented: `const save =
useCallback(…)` is **save** — and that is the only way that arrow becomes a routine at all —
and a bare `useEffect(…)` is `useEffect`, the word written at that line. The population is
stated rather than implied: **20** over every TypeScript tree here, 4 in DunneCorp, 16 in
uigen, 0 in DunneNote.

**And the map says two things it does not claim.** A directive prologue is a word written
above the thing it marks, which is what a decorator is, so `"use client"` and `"use server"`
go in `routines.decorators`. The Ways in chapter prints *27 routines in 8 files are marked
`use server`*, the sentence saying why they are not claimed, and the query that returns
exactly 27 — design rule 13, and the printed query was run. The words are the language's:
which marks exist, whether each is claimed and what is printed about it all come from
`detectors/<lang>.yaml`, because a sentence about React written into `render/markdown.py`
would be a claim no language could edit.

### Three defects, and only one of them was on anybody's list

**A `.d.ts` is not program source, and uigen is what says so.** It vendors a generated Prisma
client as `src/generated/prisma/*.d.ts`; read as program code it contributed **422 routines
with no bodies, 632 structures and 83 BROKEN anomalies** — every one an overload set in a
library's declarations reported as a name collision in somebody's program, out of a command
that exits non-zero on BROKEN. A declaration file declares and never implements.
`DiscoveryRules.skip_names` is the third kind of *not mine*, beside `skip_dirs` and the test
rules, and only the reader that claims `.ts` can say a `.d.ts` is a header. uigen is 566 → 144
routines, 655 → 23 structures, 83 → 0 broken. What it costs is stated: DunneCorp's
`types/next-auth.d.ts` is 3 real interfaces and they go with it.

**112 of DunneCorp's 403 internal edges were a routine calling itself**, and the package rule
would have masked the first two rather than fixing them. `new DynamoDBClient({})` after
`const { DynamoDBClient } = await import(…)` resolved to the *binding element*, which sits
inside `getDocClient`, so the climb walked up out of it and found the enclosing routine.
Pulling that thread found four shapes, each measured: a destructured binding, a parameter, a
`const` bound to something that is not a function, and a **type** — `run(action: () => R)`
calling `action()` resolves to the `FunctionType` in its own annotation. Plus one stopping
condition in the climb, which the four cannot express: it must not walk out of a function
this reader did not record, or `const f = useCallback(() => {…})` reports the enclosing
component calling itself.

`const [x, setX] = useState()` is the commonest line in React, so a React map was **27%
self-calls** — a number that reads as a busy program rather than a broken reader (rule 49).
DunneCorp 403 → 291 internal edges and 58 self-calls → 0; DunneNote 1,935 → 1,867; uigen 302
→ 241. Twelve self-calls remain across the three corpora and **every one is genuine
recursion** — three read against the source, including a React tree component that renders
itself, found through JSX.

**Chunk 11d shipped a false BROKEN anomaly before it was right.** Two effects in one uigen
component are two routines with one qualname, and `NAME_COLLISION` said exactly what it is
written to say: *defined 2 times, only the last one exists at run time*. The program is fine;
the name was this reader's. So the two cases are kept apart rather than the detector taught
an exception — a name the **program** chose twice is a collision and is the finding; a name
this reader applies by convention carries the ordinal that says which one it is. `useEffect`
and `useEffect#2`, in the qualname and not only in the id.

### Two claims corrected, both of them prose

**`namedFunction`'s docstring named two shapes the reader does not record** — `{ f() {} }` and
`x.f = function () {}` — and had said so since the day it was written, with nothing ever
asking it for one (rule 37, in prose). Measured before it was written down: **20
object-literal methods and 84 property functions** across the three corpora, so it is a real
gap of about a hundred rather than a rounding error. Stated and not closed: closing it would
move the routine count this chunk holds fixed to prove it changed nothing but JSX.

**Four files said `detectors/*.yaml` is in the core extraction key so an edit re-reads every
language.** True when written and made false by chunk 5's own split: `_SHARED_RULES` is
`annotations.yaml` alone and a language's YAML is in *its* stamp. Right about why the file
travels and wrong about what editing it discards, which is the half a reader acts on.

### Figures

| files read | 121 | 442 | 46 |
| routines | 209 | 1,518 | 160 |
| internal calls | 291 of 1,175 (25%) | 1,867 of 5,119 (36%) | 251 of 782 (32%) |
| boundary touches | 252 | 139 | 52 |

**Python is untouched: 7 of 7 golden digests identical**, 4,823 routines, 6,441 internal

*Cost: DunneNote cold 2.9 s against chunk 10's 2.7 s, 0.7 s of it building programs either

### What is deliberately not done

**The zod hole is stated here rather than counted in the map**, and that is a departure from

count beside it reads more true than silence, not less.

**Conditional rendering is still not a decision.** `{cond && <X/>}` is out, because

element. **`useEffect` as a rate** is still deferred: judging it needs the dependency array,

**Open question 6 — naming and conformance per language — is still open**, and it now has a

the next measurement is whether the lanes need splitting or only their denominators do.


## 2026-09-17 — manifest providers: what a program declares about itself

`PLAN-v2.md` build-order row 12, and the last of the four confirmed v1 defects.

Before this, one manifest existed as far as the tool was concerned. `cli.py:283` walked up
for `pyproject.toml`; `resolve/entrypoints.py` read `[project.scripts]` out of it;
`resolve/version.py:_from_pyproject` read `[project] version` out of the same file. A
`package.json` `bin` and a Cargo `[[bin]]` were invisible, so **DunneNote, DunneCorp and
uigen each recorded no version at all** and DunneNote recorded no way in.

`resolve/manifests/` is six providers, one per filename, plus a registry. `resolve/` is in
no fingerprint, so the package invalidates nothing by existing; `Entrypoint` gaining two
fields is what discards every stored map, and `SCHEMA_VERSION` is **14**.

### Tom's criterion, and it changed the design mid-plan

The plan scoped discovery to a walk **up** from the analysed tree. Asked about it, Tom:
*"I need to be sure that any module that has inputs and/or outputs is included, because
that is 'flow'. It doesn't matter how the tree is traversed, it must include the entire
application."*

That settles it, and not the way the plan had it. A `bin` is a way in and a way in is
where flow starts, so a manifest is read **wherever the code walk reaches one** — which
turned three predicted ways in for DunneNote into four, and admitted its Cargo workspace
members, its `packages/api-types`, and its in-tree `legacy/v0.1/`. Walk-up-only would have
seen none of them.

`walk.discover` collects them off the listing it had already taken, rather than walking
again: `SKIP_DIRS`, every dotted directory and every directory holding a map are gone
before a filename is looked at (rule 92, rule 51). Measured — `node_modules`, `.next`,
`dist`, `build`, `target` and `vendor` are all pruned, so no build output and no vendored
package is reached, and **Society's `src/` holds no nested manifest at all**, which is what
makes the golden safe by construction rather than by luck.

### The rest of the decisions, taken in the session

* **`go.mod` declares no version of the program.** Its `go` directive is a toolchain floor
  — `go 1.25.6` in beads-main — and reporting it would be `_from_dunder`'s refusal in
  reverse: a number certainly in the file and certainly not the answer. What it does
  declare is a `/vN` module-path suffix, Go's only way to say *this is major version 2*,
  recorded as a major and **saying it is a major only**. Tom's call, against the plan's
  table, which said go.mod "answers version".
* **All six providers**, with the record stating that `build.gradle.kts` is proved by
  fixtures and nothing else — there is no such file anywhere on this machine (rule 24).
* **`legacy/v0.1/` is read and named.** Its code is already in the map; pruning a
  directory by its name would be a guess this tool refuses.
* **`"scripts"` is never a way in.** 31 of them across the four JavaScript corpora —
  DunneNote 4, DunneCorp 16, uigen 8, Society 3 — every one declined by name.

### `declared` becomes a field, and two sites were parsing prose

`flows.py:259` decided *was this declared* with `"[project.scripts]" in e.evidence`, a
substring test against a sentence `web/waysin.py:120` renders verbatim and
`tests/test_waysin.py:127` pins byte for byte. It is the **primary sort key** of the
way-in list, so every declared TypeScript executable would have ranked below a guessed
name for ever. Seven sites tested that string; two went further and **parsed** it —
`resolve/cli.py:153` and `render/markdown.py:218` both recovered the target with
`evidence.rsplit("= ", 1)[-1]`, a value `Entrypoint.target_expr` had been carrying since
the family was written.

`declared` and `target_kind` are both **host-owned** (`ingest.codec._HOST_OWNED`): a
manifest is read in this process after extraction, so a reader that sends either is
refused rather than believed — `Routine.lang`'s defence, two records over. Neither appears
in the generated `facts.ts`, and a test asserts it.

The marker was also **already lying**: `[project.gui-scripts]` entries were merged into the
same dictionary and labelled `[project.scripts]`, in the one string a reader is shown
unparsed. Each table names itself now.

### Rule 98, and it is the defect of the chunk

`anomalies._entrypoint_problems` had been right for a year and began reporting DunneNote's
`dunnenote-host` — the front door of that application — as *leads nowhere*. Nothing about
the detector changed; what changed is that a manifest can now declare a way into a
language this build has no reader for. The finding was about DunneFlow and was filed
against somebody else's program, which is `anomalies.py`'s founding discipline arriving
through a feature instead of a detector. **Chunk 11 paid the same bill**: admitting `.d.ts`
turned uigen's vendored Prisma client into 83 BROKEN.

And the first fix did not finish it. Suppressing the unreadable languages left
`@dunnenote/api-types` still SUSPECT, over 289 lines of `export type { X } from './X'` — a
file that is in the map, was read, and declares no routine because there is nothing to
declare. `binding_note` gives **five answers and only one is a fault**: names no file ·
no reader claims the suffix · the language is one this map holds none of · read and
declares nothing · **not a file this map holds**. One function, so the panel, the Markdown
renderer, the run's own output and the anomaly worklist cannot disagree (rules 51 and 13).

*Both were found by running it and reading the anomaly, not by a test.* The tests came
after.

### Rule 99, found on a corpus no chunk had read before

beads-main declares `beads-mcp = "beads_mcp.server:main"` in
`integrations/beads-mcp/pyproject.toml`. The module is real and is stored as
`integrations.beads-mcp.src.beads_mcp.server`, because a module name here is derived from
the tree somebody pointed `analyze` at — so the exact match answers *no* and the map says
a real front door leads nowhere. Rule 64's family, one level down: there one root was the
wrong root, here there are several and the analysed tree is none of them. The exact name
first, then a **dotted-suffix** match taken only when exactly one routine has it.

### Three more, each found by running it

**`ways_in` dropped every unbound declaration**, so the four DunneNote gained would have
been in the `entrypoints` table and on no screen. A declared one is kept now; a
conventional `main` that resolved to nothing still goes, because nothing declared it.
**`_flows` then crashed on `d["roots"][0]`** — uigen, `IndexError` — and the Flows page
states them in a section of their own instead, because a page mentioning none of
DunneNote's four would read as a program with nothing to trace. **`render/network.py`**
excludes them from the zone map: a zone answers *which process is this routine in* and an
unbound way in holds no routines.

### Identity, and why the golden holds

`make_id("script", name)` at the package root, `make_id("script", <manifest path>, name)`
below it. The root's declarations are the program's own and their names are its contract —
which is also v1's mint, so Society's four script ids are byte-identical. A member's `bin`
is identified by the member **and** the name, because two members may each declare `serve`
and `INSERT OR REPLACE` would keep whichever was walked last: a way in disappearing with no
error anywhere (rule 35's shape). A collision is refused and named rather than overwritten.

| manifests read | 2 | **20** | 1 | 2 | 7 |
| declared version | none (`dynamic`) | **0.9.0**, two witnesses | **0.1.0** | **0.1.0** | 0.49.2 |
| ways in | 178 | **0 → 4** | 36 | 3 → 4 | 33 |
| `scripts` refused | 3 | 20 | 16 | 8 | 14 |
| anomalies | 0 broken · 94 suspect | 0 · 0 | 0 · 2 | 0 · 0 | 0 · 1 |

**Society is unmoved: 7 of 7 golden digests identical**, 4,823 routines, 6,441 internal

`main`, no version — and its three `scripts` are declined by name; its `pyproject.toml`
says `dynamic = ["version"]`, which is now a *stated* absence rather than a silent
fall-through to the directory-name guess, and the map still records `2026-08-29` INFERRED.

DunneNote's four: `@dunnenote/api-types` (LIBRARY, from `main`), and `dunnenote`,
`dunnenote-host` and `calnote` — three Rust binaries, two of them found by the

Extraction is untouched: 1,518 routines, 1,867 internal calls, 708 structures, 139

beads-main is the one corpus with a real `bin`, and it was not on the plan's list: `bd` and

Go and Swift have populations and neither declares much, which is the point: beads-main and

**1,798 passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean over 188 files, ruff clean. The frozen binary reads
DunneNote to the figure and both builds stamp `14:c6cd0c4e1d15e9e3` core and
`1.1.0:92eb0d173e9807a7` for the TypeScript reader, and open each other's maps.

### What is deliberately not done

**A workspace is not modelled.** Cargo members are read because the walk reaches them, not
because `members = [...]` was followed; `version.workspace = true` is **named and not
resolved**, 14 times on DunneNote and collapsed to one line. `pnpm-workspace.yaml` is not
read at all.

**`package.json` `exports` is read only where it names a single target.** uigen's Prisma
client has nineteen subpaths across six runtime conditions; that is one package declaring
one entry point in many dialects, and picking a condition would be this tool choosing a
module system on the reader's behalf.

**`build.gradle.kts` has no population on this machine** and its tests are fixtures. Said
here rather than left to read as measured.


## 2026-09-17 — open question 6: the naming lanes across a mixed corpus

`PLAN-v2.md` §6.6, deferred by chunk 11 for want of a mixed corpus. There is one now:
DunneFlow's own `src/` reads as **107 Python files and 11 TypeScript**, and the lanes were
measured against it, against both pure-TypeScript corpora, and against Mensores.

**The plan guessed the answer and the guess was too narrow.** It expected a denominator
problem confined to mixed maps. Two of the four defects below are already wrong on a
**single-language** TypeScript map and have been since chunk 9, and one of them would have
turned the split into a *new* false result: split naively, TypeScript's routines report
**72.4%** camelCase, under `MIN_PREVALENCE`, so the tool would have replaced a false `D`
with a false *"this program has no convention"* about a population that is 116 of 116
consistent.

### What was wrong

| | Defect | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `case_style` returns one answer where several are true | DunneNote routines **1,151 → 1,297** of 1,348; DunneNote parameters **gap → camelCase 515/519**; DunneFlow commands **snake 14/16 → kebab 16/16** |
| 2 | a dotted name judged by substituting `.` → `_` | **387 of DunneNote's 389** unreadable module names contain a dash; per segment, kebab 221 and 210 honestly `other` |
| 3 | the derived lane mines across languages at once | DunneFlow's own tree: `[D] 1,014/1,114` with 100 exceptions, every one a TypeScript name |
| 4 | conformance measures an unscoped stated rule across every language | *"Functions: snake_case"* → 1,014/1,114, 100 exceptions, all TypeScript names obeying TypeScript |

**Defect 1 is rule 100 and it is the one worth carrying.** `widget` is snake_case,
camelCase *and* kebab-case; `DDL` is SCREAMING_SNAKE and PascalCase. The function's own
docstring said a one-word name is *"counted with the majority"* — it was counted with
whichever of five `if`s came first, and that order was written when Python was the only
language. Nothing recorded that a choice was being made.

**Defect 2 had a predicate to match, and nobody could ever have run it.**
`STYLE_PREDICATE["kebab-case"]` required a dash, and the three `str.replace` calls that
widened the dotted predicates touched none of its substrings. So a dotted kebab claim
carried a query answering a different question — and only DunneNote having no module
convention at all kept it off a screen. `DOTTED_STYLE_PREDICATE` is written out beside
`STYLE_PREDICATE` now rather than produced by patching it.

**Defect 4 is rule 49's failure mode inside the module written to prevent it.** The
distinction, which is now in the source: a path-shaped scope is *refused* because nothing
supplies which paths; an entity scope in a mixed map is the opposite case, because **the
map supplies which languages it holds**. Splitting reads a fact where widening guessed a
population. So `check_rule` returns a **list**, each result names its language and carries
a `blind_spot`, and a standard declaring `paths: ['**/*.py']` has closed the axis itself
and is never labelled — only the languages that actually hold some of the population are
split, so one is one.

### The decisions taken in the session

* **Only the spelling lanes split**, Tom's call on the measurement. CASE, the gaps and
  HOUSE_PREFIX carry a language; AFFIX and LEAKAGE do not. An affix is a word a team chose
  rather than a way of spelling one, and the privacy population is `visibility = 'private'`,
  which no other reader here records at all — 0 of DunneFlow's 122 TypeScript routines. A
  test asserts it, so the decision cannot drift into place unnoticed.
* **Conformance splits rather than refuses**, also Tom's call. Refusing would have been
  consistent with the path-scope rule and would cost a Python shop its whole conformance
  lane the day it added one TypeScript file.
* **One language means no language.** `languages.read` decides, and a single-language map
  is measured exactly as it was: no language in a claim, none in a query. That is what
  keeps every recorded figure reproducible, and it is also the honest answer — a map
  holding one language has no language axis to state.

### Three defects found by running it

* **Two population queries had no `WHERE` at all**, so appending the language clause
  produced a syntax error rather than a narrower answer. The whole suite passed, because no
  fixture had ever held two languages. `tests/test_naming_languages.py` now runs every
  population's language clause as SQL.
* **The split lost a row, and rule 32 is the name for it.** `dunneflow` is declared in
  `pyproject.toml`, which no reader claims and which therefore has no row in `files`;
  scoped by its own file it belonged to no language and simply vanished — *15 commands*
  over a map holding 16, with every number on screen still looking right. A command's
  language is the language of the code it starts, asked first, and the declaring file only
  then. The guard is arithmetic: every population's split totals must sum to its unsplit
  total.
* **`dotted` was read off the label**, which now carries a language in front of it, so
  `"Python modules" in DOTTED` is false and every module would have become an exception
  again — the defect that line's own comment records, reintroduced by a cosmetic change.
  It is read off the *scope* instead.

### What it costs, and what it does not

`resolve/` is in no fingerprint, so nothing here invalidates a stored map and no
`SCHEMA_VERSION` moved. Nothing under `runtime.py`, `packaging/`, `detectors/` or
`extractors/` was touched, so the frozen-binary gate does not arise.

**Mensores is byte-identical in all eight populations** — routines 3,906/3,907, parameters
1,796/1,798, classes 1,127/1,179, structures 641/671, modules 628/628, tables 171/183,
commands 118/123, environment variables 110/120 — and the golden is **7 of 7 digests
identical**. Verified in the dashboard as well as on the command line: the derived page
draws sixteen conventions each naming its language, and the checked page draws the
per-language heading, the population and the *false alarm if* line.

## 2026-09-17 — chunk 13: packaging, and the gate that had been broken for eight chunks

`PLAN-v2.md`'s chunk 13 is one line: *the spec bundles `plugins/` wholesale; the
fingerprint-equality gate extended to compare per-language stamps between binary and
checkout.* The first half was already done — chunk 5 wrote `_plugin_files()`, derived from
the manifests so that what ships and what is stamped are the same bytes by construction,
and `tests/test_frozen.py` has asserted it since. The second half turned out to be a
repair before it was an extension.

### What was actually there

| Script | State before this chunk |
|---|---|
| `release-linux.sh` | called `dunneflow.detectors.rules_fingerprint` — **raises `ImportError`** |
| `release.ps1` | same function, same `ImportError` |
| `release.sh` (macOS) | **no fingerprint check at all** |

Chunk 5 split `rules_fingerprint()` into `core_fingerprint()` and `lang_fingerprint()`.
Both scripts that asked the question asked it by writing `from dunneflow.detectors import
rules_fingerprint` into a here-doc and a `-c` argument, so the rename did not touch them and
nothing failed until somebody ran a release — in the step written to defend rule 12, on no
test path, saying nothing for eight chunks. **Rule 51 in a shell script**: a Python question
kept at a shell call site rots as the Python moves, and there were three call sites with
three spellings, one of which had never asked at all. macOS is the platform the tool is
developed on and the only one whose builds are signed, notarised and handed to anybody.

And both probe trees were the wrong tree. Linux read `src/dunneflow/web` and Windows
`src/dunneflow/canonical`; both are Python to the last file, so **no script has ever
compared a TypeScript stamp** — they would have passed on a build whose TypeScript maps the
checkout refuses. Rule 37, in the step whose own comment quotes rule 37.

### `tools/fingerprints.py`

One place the question is asked, and the three scripts run it. Beside `tools/golden.py`,
which is the same shape of thing: a gate a person runs, not a module the application
imports.

* **It proves the property rather than a proxy for it.** Printing two hex strings and
  diffing them tests this file's arithmetic. What a colleague meets is
  `Store(writable=False)` raising, so the gate **opens each build's map with the other
  build** and lets `_refuse_if_stale` and `_refuse_if_a_language_is_stale` speak — their
  sentences already name the language and say that re-analysing costs only that language.
  Both directions, because *both builds open each other's maps* is the claim the record has
  been making by hand since chunk 5.
* **The stamps are printed beside the result**, agreeing or not, because a check whose
  evidence is not shown is a tick (rules 13 and 37).
* **No language is named here** (rule 92). The list is `ingest.PLUGINS`, so a third reader
  joins this gate by existing.
* **A language that contributed no rows is a refusal**, which is the whole of what the two
  old probe trees got wrong. A stamp that was never compared is not a stamp that agrees.
* **Three answers when a language contributes nothing, never two** (design rule 21): the
  tree holds no file that reader claims — a fact about the tree, answered by pointing
  `--tree` somewhere else; it holds them and none was read — a fact about the machine,
  answered by installing the toolchain, and the sentence is quoted from the plugin's own
  manifest rather than copied here (rules 89 and 51); or it was read and disagrees.
* **`candidates()` asks the plugin's `DiscoveryRules`**, so *this tree holds none* means
  what the walk means by it — tests and `.d.ts` excluded, per language, because `test_a.py`
  and `a.test.ts` are two different spellings and a shared rule gets both wrong.

### Pressed, in all three of the ways it can fail

Not asserted — done, against a copy of the real build with one bundled file perturbed:

| Perturbed | What the gate said |
|---|---|
| nothing | `they agree on all 3 stamps, and each build opened the other's map` |
| `--tree src/dunneflow/canonical` | `typescript: … holds no file it claims (.cts, .mts, .ts, .tsx), so its stamp was never compared` |
| bundled `plugins/typescript/plugin.json` | binary `1.1.0:af854a44b61588eb` against checkout `1.1.0:92eb0d173e9807a7`, core and python unmoved — **and** `holds facts from a reader this build is not: typescript` |
| bundled `schema.py` | binary `14:ebb285976b712cbc` against checkout `14:c6cd0c4e1d15e9e3`, **and** `was written by a different version of DunneFlow` |

The third is chunk 5's partial discard, visible: core agrees, python agrees, one reader
moved, and only that reader's rows are refused.

### And a second defect in the same file, hidden by a filesystem

`require_universal` — which gates `sign`, `notarize`, `dmg` and `install`, the four steps
whose output reaches somebody else — looked for the executable at
`$APP/Contents/MacOS/${APP_NAME%.app}`, which is **`DunneFlow`**. The spec builds
**`dunneflow`**: on macOS the bundle supplies the name a reader sees, so the binary does not
have to, and `EXE(name=…)` is lowercase everywhere but Windows. It has worked for a year
because **APFS is case-insensitive by default**. Formatted case-sensitive — an option at the
volume, and the default on some CI images — every step after `build` would have refused a
perfectly good bundle with *"there is no executable — run '$0 build' first"*: rule 49 with a
plausible sentence on it, and the spec's own NTFS note (`DunneFlow.exe` and `dunneflow.exe`
are one file there) is exactly this hazard one platform over.

`BIN` is the one spelling now, used by `build`, `require_universal`, `verify` and the gate,
and `tests/test_frozen.py` pins it against `EXE(name=…)` — reading the **`orelse`** of the
conditional, because the `if` branch is Windows' answer. The assertion is on the lines that
reach *into* `Contents/MacOS/` and not on the expression: `${APP_NAME%.app}` is a fine way
to name the notarisation zip, and banning it outright reported that line as the defect it is
not (rule 34, arriving in the guard rather than in the prose — caught by writing it the
broad way first).

**1,830 passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean over 191 files, ruff clean.

* **`node` is required to verify the TypeScript half**, and that is stated rather than

  distinction `release-linux.sh`'s own comment was written about. A machine without node
  gets the refusal that names it.
* **`--one-way` exists** for a machine that has the binary and cannot analyse with the
  checkout. It says so in the summary line rather than quietly checking half of what the
  other form checks.

The last chunk in `PLAN-v2.md`. Its line is two clauses — *rewrite "Adding a language";

### `CLAUDE.md`

**"Adding a language" said the same four lines for a year**, and they were a claim about a
tool that had never been asked: *write one extractor that emits `FileFacts`; nothing else
changes*. Asked twice, it turned out to be nearly true and to leave out everything about
how a reader gets there. It is now the six things to do, what you get free and must not
reimplement, and three things that will bite — each of the three being a rule this tree
paid for (`SOURCE_TEXT`'s newlines, rule 97's `lib*.d.ts`, rule 98's re-run detectors).

**The promise at the top of it is asserted rather than claimed.** *Nothing above the graph
names a language* was measured before it was written: two renderers and forty-odd dashboard
modules hold **not one string constant** spelling `python` or `typescript`, and `walk.py`
holds none either, where it used to open with `from .extractors.python.extract import
extract_file` — which is the whole of what *only Python is extracted* ever meant.
`tests/test_languages.py` holds it, derived from `PLUGINS` rather than a list of names
(rule 92) and reading **constants** rather than the text, because a docstring giving
*python 628 · typescript 412* as an example is not a violation of the rule it describes
(rules 34 and 43).

Under `resolve/` two places name one legitimately — `RESOLVERS`, the dispatch table, and a
language's own package — and **one does not**: `traceability.py` asks Python's builtins of
every corpus, including one with no Python in it. That is open question 6's shape one
module over, it is unmeasured, and the test pins the count at **one** so it cannot grow
quietly.

Three entries added or corrected beside them: `ingest/` (six modules, `stamp_lang`,
`SOURCE_TEXT`, and why it is in the core key while `canonical/` is not), `plugins/<lang>/`
(the manifest, and why `fingerprint` names files for one kind of reader and globs for the
other), and `extractors/python/` as the in-process plugin's reader rather than an import.
`detectors/*.yaml` and `resolve/` gained the per-language halves they had grown.

**And `canonical/`'s paragraph was factually wrong.** It said a canonicaliser living in
`extractors/python/` would be hashed by `code_extraction_inputs()` and *"discard every
graph on the machine"* — the whole truth while there was one key. Chunk 5 put a plugin's
own files in **that language's** stamp, so the cost is now every Python row in every graph,
sealed snapshots included. Smaller, and not acceptable: that is still the one store that is
not derived losing facts nothing can rebuild (rules 25 and 62).

### The flag two refusals had been promising

Writing the chapter about refusals found it. `ingest/outofprocess.py` tells a reader whose
machine has no Node to *"run again with `--without typescript` and the map will say those
files were declined"* — and **`--without` did not exist**. `declined` was a parameter on
`ingest.enabled`, `suffixes` and `discovery`, and **no caller had ever passed it**: rule
35's shape in an argument, and rule 89 broken by the sentence written to keep it.

Tom's call was to wire it rather than reword the sentence, and it is now:

* **`ingest.decline()` is the one place a name is judged** (rule 51), with two refusals.
  `--without pythn` that is simply not in the set reads as a run that declined nothing, and
  *I turned Python off* against *I typed it wrong* is the entire map (rule 49). Declining
  **every** language is refused too: that is a map with no code in it rather than a smaller
  one, and a reader who meant `--no-docs` is told so.
* **`declined` filters last in `discover`, and that placement is the whole of what it
  reports.** Taken off `rules` instead, a declined language's suffixes would leave
  `suffix_owners` and its files would land in `unclaimed` — *no reader here claims `.ts`*,
  said by a build that has one. Two facts that look identical in a map with **opposite**
  remedies (design rule 21). Asked after the skip and test rules, the count is exactly the
  files that would have been read, so the number answers the only question anybody has
  about it: *what did I lose*. A test asserts the three sets are disjoint and the
  arithmetic closes.
* **The walk says it and the map records it.** `declined by you: 11 typescript — this build
  has a reader for that language; drop --without to read them`, and `analysis_args` gains
  *typescript not read* — which is `_args_said`'s own docstring arriving at its purest
  case: a map read `--without typescript` and a map of a program actually written in one
  language hold exactly the same rows.

Measured on DunneFlow's own tree: **107 read, 11 declined**, 118 accounted for, and 0.8 s
against 3.7 s because Node is never started.

### The user guide

Three chapters gained the subject they were missing entirely — **the tool reads two
languages**, which appeared nowhere in 4,009 lines of documentation. `01-installing.md`
gains *which languages it reads and the one thing you may have to install*;
`15-when-it-refuses.md` gains the two refusals a v2 reader can actually meet (the missing
toolchain, and the per-language stale map, which names the language because *this map is
stale* over a Python map whose forty TypeScript files are the problem sends somebody to the
wrong place); `04-your-first-map.md` gains *what it read, and what it left out*, which is
design rule 1's own subject and had no chapter.

**And writing it found a second gap, stated rather than fixed.** `_emit` writes to stderr
and `dunneflow serve` runs the analysis `--quiet`, so **the residue never reaches the

Every cross-reference and anchor in `docs/` and `docs/tutorial/` was checked mechanically

## 2026-09-17 — the map is the same map twice, at last

The fifth v1 defect, found by chunk 8's gate and left alone deliberately because a report
that has to be diffed against a baseline cannot also be the thing being changed. It is a
chunk of its own and this is it.

### Reproduced before it was touched

Two analyses of Society by the same build, minutes apart: **7 of 15 documents differ**,
1,488 lines in `06-governance.md` and 656 in `12-traceability.md`. The other eight differ
only in the snapshot instant, which is correct and is what the cover states three of.

### The probe is a reversal, not a second analysis

`tools/ordering.py`. It copies a program, **reverses the physical row order of every
table**, re-renders, and diffs the documents with the *written at* line normalised — the
one line that is meant to differ between two renders of one snapshot.

Two real runs shuffle *some* of the order and catch *some* of the ties, differently each
time; that is why the record has `07-database.md` stable in one pair and unstable in the
next, which is what a coin looks like. **Reversal is the worst case and is the same every
time**, so a map that survives it survives any order, and a run that reports nothing has
actually checked something (rule 37). Against the same graph the two real runs differed on,
reversal found **12 of 15 documents and 26,000 differing lines**.

Reversing is safe and that was established rather than assumed: nothing in either store
declares an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`, so no rowid is anybody's key — every identity here is a
`make_id` string, deliberately — and the one place a rowid is held at all reads and updates
it inside a single pass. `meta` is left alone, because it is the map's identity and
rewriting it is the one edit that could change what the store *means*.

### What was fixed, and the shape it always had

Nineteen sites across nine modules, all of one kind: **an order that was two-thirds of an
order**. Either SQL with no `ORDER BY` or one whose tail is not unique, or a Python
`sorted()` whose key ties. Rule 66 exactly — undefended ties, never wrong answers.

| Where | What it was |
|---|---|
| `resolve/flows.py` | the breadth-first walk had **no order at all** — and `max_nodes` truncates it, so row order decided *which routines a flow diagram draws* |
| `resolve/cli.py` | `cli_mounts` had none either, so an undefended order decided which six commands `command_tree_diagram` puts in the picture |
| `store.py` | `entrypoints` `ORDER BY kind, name` — `main` is the commonest name in any tree |
| `render/database.py` | `db_indexes ORDER BY name` — an index name repeats across migrations |
| `render/page.biggest_first` | `key=lambda k: -len(groups[k])` written **eight times**, every one of them tied on count and settled by `dict` insertion order |
| `resolve/glossary.py`, `mirror.py`, `traceability.py`, `naming.py`, `conformance.py`, `anomalies.py` | sightings, definitions, exception lists and detector populations, all in row order |

**`biggest_first` is `render/page.py`'s** for rule 51's reason, which is that module's whole
argument: eight call sites is eight places to forget. `resolve/flows.py` spells its own
rather than importing it, because `render/` reads `resolve/` and never the other way round.

### Measured

**Zero.** Every document byte-identical under a full row reversal, and **two real analyses
of Society now differ in nothing at all** — all fifteen documents, timestamps normalised,
0 differing lines. **7 of 7 golden digests identical**: no stored fact moved, which is what
says this was ordering and not content. `resolve/`, `render/`, `store.py` and
`anomalies.py` are in no fingerprint, so **no stored map anywhere is invalidated** and all
three stamps are unmoved. **1,843 passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean over 193 files, ruff
clean.

### The test, and proving its baseline

`tests/test_ordering.py` renders a fixture twice — once straight, once with every row
reversed — and asserts byte-identical. **Every file in the fixture is a tie somebody
actually shipped**, reduced to the smallest program that still has it: two `main` ways in
in different modules, one index name on one table created in two files, one routine name in
two modules, one annotation value in two places.

**The first fixture was wrong and the mutation test is what said so** (rule 59). It created
`idx_shared` on `widget` in one file and on `gadget` in the other — two rows with one name,
which *looks* like the Society case and is not: the renderer groups indexes by table, so
each landed in a bucket of its own and the tie never arose. Reintroducing the
`render/database.py` defect left the test green. With both indexes on one table it goes red,
and three of four mutations are caught.

**The fourth is not, and that is worth stating rather than glossing.** Undoing `ways_in`'s
reach tiebreak leaves the test green, because `store.entrypoints()`'s total order already
settles it — so that tiebreak is defence in depth against `entrypoints()` changing, not the
load-bearing fix, and the suite does not cover it.

### Two things this changes on purpose

`02-flows.md` and `01-entrypoints.md` draw **different routines and different commands**
than they did, because the order that decides truncation moved. The old selection was not a
better one; it was whichever the pool finished first. What a *good* truncation would be is a
product question and is in `BACKLOG.md`.

### And an instrument that could not see, reporting anyway

The probe's first run said *every document is byte-identical under a full row reversal*
over a store it had not changed. It globbed `*.db`, then `graph@*.db`, then `docs@*.db`,
and the first already matches the other two — so every graph was reversed and then reversed
back. Rule 37 in the instrument, which is the one place it costs most (rule 38), and it is
a test now.

*It is worth saying plainly that the map had been like this for a year, that every session
which diffed two maps by hand had seen it, and that the gate which found it was looking at
something else.*

### What the three modes are, and why the probe is the authority

`tools/ordering.py` gains two modes beside the map. It is one file because the reversal is
the instrument and there may only be one of it (rule 51), and because `tools/` is
deliberately not a package, so a sibling could only reach `reverse_rows` by path.

`--survey` reads `web/` with `ast` and counts what no `ORDER BY` defends. The previous
survey said **six** and was wrong in both directions: `ast.literal_eval` raises on an
f-string and it skipped what it raised on, so every `IN ({marks})` query — most of the
interesting ones — was invisible; and it **exempted `LIMIT 1`**, which is backwards,
because a `LIMIT` with no order does not shuffle a list, it picks a different answer. This
one joins an f-string's literal parts, counts a `LIMIT` as the sharpest finding there is,
and exempts on two grounds only: an aggregate with no `GROUP BY`, and a lookup whose
`WHERE` equates **a whole declared key** — read out of the three `SCHEMA_SQL` constants
rather than guessed from the shape of a column name, so `id = ?` is exempt because
`routines.id` is a primary key and would not be if it were not. **50 findings of 186
statements** before the work, **36 after**.

`--api` is the probe, and **it found things the survey cannot see and cleared things the
survey names**. Two of the three biggest defects were queries that *had* an `ORDER BY` —
on a column with ties — and two were not in `web/` at all. Of the nine sites the backlog
named, one was real, and the evidence against the other eight is that the probe could not
make any of them move.

**Three passes and not two**, because an instrument has to know its own noise floor: the
straight copy is asked twice, so what differs between two readings of *one* copy is named
as noise instead of being forgiven by a hand-kept list of keys. Exactly one key is
normalised by name, `ms`, because three routes report how long they took and a noisy route
is held *out* of the findings — leaving it would take four routes out of the gate for ever
and report the run green.

### Rule 101, and the miss that earned it

The probe reported `/api/wayin` identical over a `_mount_name` that answers `ledger` in one
row order and `books` in the other — the site the backlog had already called **certain**.
Both statements were true: the route has two shapes, and only the one carrying `inside`
asks what a sub-application is mounted under. **A route is not a branch.** Three remedies
were all needed — a route with more than one shape is asked more than once; a parameter
that came back **empty** is a gap in the plan and is named, because `/api/table?name=` is a
refusal identical on both copies; and a route that **raised** is named too, because it
raises the same way twice. The empty-parameter check found two more the moment it existed.

## 2026-09-18 — the residue reaches the application, and two slots that were not slots

Three items out of `BACKLOG.md`, taken in that order because the two small ones clear the
ground the feature lands on. Tom's call on the slate and on where the residue goes.

### `/api/programs` listed a program twice — backlog 3, and rule 103

`_r_programs` unions the directory being served with `revisions.program_dirs(out_root)`.
`here` has been `out_dir.resolve()` since the day it was written; the listing resolved
nothing. Under a maps root reached through a symlink those are two unequal `Path` objects
naming one directory, so the open program appeared twice in the `<select>` and the copy
that was **not** marked as the one being read was the listing's. Reproduced exactly:
`['alpha', 'alpha', 'beta']`.

**The reach is narrower than the backlog said, and saying so is the point.** `cmd_serve`
and the MCP session both go through `serve.where`, which resolves both halves, so the
application a reader runs was never wrong here. What is exposed is `_Live`'s two-argument
form, where `out_root` is derived as `out_dir.parent` and keeps whatever spelling the
caller had — and `tools/ordering.py:777` is exactly such a caller, which is how the probe
met it. The first end-to-end test written for this **passed at the previous commit**,
because it went through `where()`; it was rewritten against the shape that actually
reaches the defect rather than kept as a test that cannot fail (rule 37).

The fix is one place (rule 51): `program_dirs` resolves its root before it lists. The
**root** is canonicalised and the children are not, deliberately — `resolve()` on a child
that is itself a symlink would name a program outside the root that is listing it, and a
map kept on another disk and linked in is still this root's program. `programs_under` is
new and is the same question without the root: five callers spelled that exclusion as
`if d != out_root`, which against an unresolved root is false for exactly the directory it
excludes, so the two halves had to move together.

**The workaround came out with the defect.** `tools/ordering.py` resolved its own
temporary directory to get past this; a probe that canonicalises its own root can never see
this class of defect return (rule 43), so it now runs on the symlinked root it is handed —
and `--api` is green on all 43 routes that way.

### One slot, two analyses — backlog 9, and rule 104

The flaky test was `test_a_second_analysis_is_refused_and_told_what_is_running`, and the
backlog's hypothesis was that the first analysis simply finished before the second was
asked for. That is possible and was never established. **There is a second mechanism, and
it was there all along**: `analysis_running` asked `analysis_proc.poll()` and nothing else,
so between `claim_analysis` returning `True` and `on_start` handing the child over the slot
read as free. Measured in three lines and no timing at all — two `claim_analysis` calls in
a row both return `True`.

What follows is worse than a duplicated report. The loser overwrites the report; then its
`on_start` overwrites `analysis_proc`, so the **first** child is unreachable —
`analysis_stop` cannot signal it, nothing will ever poll it — and it goes on writing into
the same output root as the run that displaced it.

Asking the child was the right answer to the right question (rule 30: a label outlives the
thing it names, and a watcher that dies leaves `working` true for ever). It is simply not
the *whole* question, because the child does not exist yet. `analysis_running` is
`claimed and (no child yet or the child is alive)` now, which is not a superset of either
half (rule 36) — and what makes *claimed* safe to trust is that the watching thread's own
`finally` gives it back, rather than a caller saying it is finished.

`_Live.start_analysis` is the one place a claim is taken, started and released. It was
eleven duplicated lines in `_p_analyze` and in `mcp/session.py`, so whatever either did
about a claim that never became a child it had to do twice (rule 51). `stop_analysis`
gained a third answer for the instant between a claim and its child: signalling a `None`
would be an exception where a sentence belongs, and *nothing is running* over a claimed
slot is a refusal the reader can see is false, because the panel on their screen says it
started (design rule 21).

The test itself no longer races. There is no way to hold a child open from the far side of
a pipe, so the refusal is asked of the object that makes it — `Session.analyze`, with
`start_analysis`'s `run` seam holding the slot until the test lets go. The wire stays
`test_mcp.py`'s subject.

### The walk's residue reaches the application — backlog 2

`walk_residue` has worded these sentences since the walk became multi-language, and
`analyze` has always printed them — through `_emit`, which is stderr, which `serve` empties
with `--quiet`. So *unread: 8 `.js`, 5 `.go`…*, *left out as tests*, *pruned 16
directories* reached a terminal and never the dialog that made the map. Design rule 1 held
for the command line and not for the surface this tool is actually for.

Three surfaces now, and they are three readers rather than three copies. The terminal is
unchanged. The `--progress-json` stream carries a `residue` record **once**, the moment the
walk knows: the fact is fixed and the steps after it are many, so putting it on every line
would multiply four sentences by however long resolution takes. And `meta.walk_residue`
holds it on the map, because a panel is dismissed and a map is kept.

**The stickiness is a term of the contract rather than a convenience.** `note_analysis`
replaces the report whole — deliberately, so a field from a previous step cannot survive
into this one — so without carrying `residue` across as it carries `began`, the panel would
show it for the fraction of a second before the next line arrived. Its *arrival* counts as
movement and being carried does not, or a watched run would never look silent, which is the
one thing `moved` exists to prevent. A fresh claim replaces the report outright, so a new
run never inherits the last one's.

**Three answers in *About this map*, and the panel deliberately has two.** Not recorded is a
map written before `analyze` could say; an empty list is *nothing was left out*, which is a
real answer and needed a key that is always written; lines say which (design rule 21). The
panel flattens the first two on purpose — a running commentary announcing *nothing was left
out* on every healthy analysis is noise on the common case, and until the record arrives
the true answer is *not yet*. Text that will not parse reads as *not recorded* rather than
as *none*, because a plausible value standing in for a failure is how the failure hides
(rule 49).

**Design rule 31 came out of looking at it.** The panel is `position: fixed; bottom: 1rem`,
so it grows *upward*, and what is at the top of it is the head and the **Stop it** button.
Measured with fourteen wrapping lines of residue: 558px of content in a 562px window and
the panel's top edge at **-71px** — the reader told something and losing the control that
acts on it in the same paint. Capped and scrolling now, on `.an-why`'s precedent.

Verified in the browser rather than only in tests: `/api/about` returns the three states,
the row renders in the dialog, and a real analysis of a 118-file mixed tree carried five
residue lines through to `done` and drew them in the panel as a closed disclosure with its
count.

one it was told.

## 2026-09-18 — what a dropped async call costs, per language; and a finding of mine retracted

Backlog 6 done. **Backlog 7 was wrong and is withdrawn**, and the error was mine.

### `ASYNC_NOT_AWAITED` — backlog 6, and it was two defects

`gstack` produced **2 BROKEN**, and `dunneflow check` exits non-zero only on BROKEN, so
this was the CI gate failing over correct code. Both findings were wrong and for different
reasons.

**One was a data defect.** `detectors/typescript.yaml` declared
`WebSocket: {protocol: WS, async: true}` and the same of `EventSource`. Both are
**constructors**. Read off the bundled `lib.dom.d.ts`, which is the authority this reader
already carries: `new(url: string | URL, protocols?: string | string[]): WebSocket`. Nothing
there returns a promise — you attach handlers to what comes back — so *"never awaited"* was
trivially true and meaningless. Both are `async: false` now, and the NETWORK boundary row is
untouched: the defect was the flag beside the call, not the call.

`socket.emit` is left alone and that is **stated rather than quiet**. It is probably wrong
in the same way — `emit` is fire-and-forget and `emitWithAck` is the awaitable one — but no
map this tool has read holds a single `socket.emit` and socket.io's types are in no corpus
here, so there is nothing to check a change against (rule 24).

**The other was the finding's own words.** *"The coroutine is created and never run"* is
exactly true of Python, where `f()` on an `async def` builds a coroutine that never executes
until something awaits it, and **false of JavaScript**, where the promise runs whether or
not anybody holds it. The instance it fired on sits three lines under the comment *"No
await; this is fire-and-forget"* and ends in `.catch(() => {})` — the rejection handled
explicitly. Correct code, called broken, in a vocabulary belonging to a language with no
coroutines in it. Rule 98, and the second time this session that a judgement written for
Python has been put to TypeScript.

**The language declares what it costs**, `unawaited_async` in each reader's own rules file:
`inert` for Python, `runs` for TypeScript. `anomalies.py` reads it off `files.lang` — per
row, not per map, because a mixed map holds both answers at once — and **names no language
at all**, so a third reader answers for itself on the day it is registered. `_ASYNC_COST` is
the one place the two answers are spelled, with three fields because the severity, the
sentence and the blind spot are three claims and the old finding got all three wrong
together. TypeScript's is **SUSPECT**, and its blind spot names the `.catch()` and the
fire-and-forget idiom that make it a false alarm — which is the anomaly discipline's only
rule.

**Empty means the detector does not fire**, and a word the table does not know is **refused
by name** rather than defaulted. A severity is a claim about what dropping a call costs, and
a misspelling would otherwise arrive as a severity nobody chose in the one command a CI job
trusts (rule 49).

**There was no test for this detector at all**, which is how it stayed wrong for a year and
why the change would otherwise have passed in silence. Ten now, in
`tests/test_async_not_awaited.py`; six of them fail against the previous commit, split
between the data fix and the wording. And `anomalies.py` **joined the above-the-graph
guard** — it is a judgement over the graph like the renderers are and had simply never been
covered, which is the gap that let it tell every language about coroutines.

gstack goes from **2 broken · 1 suspect** to **0 broken · 2 suspect**.

### Backlog 7 is withdrawn, and it was my measurement

I reported that a `fetch` whose URL is a concatenation headed by a name is not recorded as a
boundary, on three sites in gstack. **All three are inside template literals** — lines
13–695 of `cookie-picker-ui.ts` and 52–616 of `compare.ts`, which are HTML pages returned as
strings: `export function getCookiePickerHTML(serverPort: number): string` returns
`` `<!DOCTYPE html>…` ``. The `fetch` calls in them are browser JavaScript in a string, not
calls this program makes. **DunneFlow is right to exclude them**, and my grep was counting
string contents as code.

The accounting is exact. Of **35** `fetch(` occurrences in gstack's 157 program files:
**29 recorded** as NETWORK boundaries, **4 inside template literals**, **2 method
definitions** (`fetch(req, server) {`, a Bun/Deno handler), **0 unaccounted** — and no
recorded row without a matching source line. That is **29 of 29, no false positives**: the
result I reported as a defect is a clean sweep.

What is left is a residue rather than an item, and it is worth stating because the number
on the page invites the wrong reading: a program that serves browser JavaScript as a string
really does cause those requests, and this map cannot see them. NETWORK counts *what this
program calls*, never *what this program causes*.
