## 2026-09-18 — the diagram says what a box does, and it costs no colour anyone was using

Tom, looking at Diagram mode: *"some nodes only ever have links inbound and some only ever
outbound. Is it possible to render sinks and emitters as different shapes or with different
colors? Each has a different role, as do the nodes that can do both."*

### What the measurement changed about the ask

**It is four roles, not three**, and the one nobody names is the largest. Across four maps
— Mensores 930 boxes, DunneNote 244, DunneFlow 169, gstack 163 — the split runs 9–23% emits
only, 25–40% receives only, 15–26% both, and **30–44% nothing either way**. Folding that
fourth state into any of the other three would say something false about a third of the
drawing (design rule 21). It is also what makes the colour affordable: `none` is the
untinted ground, so only three tints have to be found.

**Shape was not available, which the ask offered first.** Design rule 4 already spends shape
on *kind* — a bold box for a class, a plain one for a file, a cylinder for a boundary, a note
for a way in, a dashed ellipse for a port — and stroke means *selected* and *hovered*. Fill
was the free channel, and design rule 4 says how to spend it: an explicit **colour by**
selector, one dimension at a time. The stack has had one for a year (*what it is* / *which
plate* / *what changed*); the diagram had none. So this is that control, with *what it does*
as its first dimension and **nothing** as its default, which leaves the diagram opening
exactly as it did.

### The decision Tom made, and its cost

A box's flow can leave the compartment entirely, and crossings are not drawn unless asked
for (rule 19). So *role as drawn* and *role including crossings* are different answers —
on DunneFlow, *both* is 26% one way and **57%** the other. Rule 87's trap, and not one to
resolve silently.

Tom's call was **all of it, drawn or not**: the role is a fact about the program rather than
about the toggle, and it is the same reading `unlinked` has always taken — `role_none`
equals it by construction, and a test says so, because the panel prints one and the legend
prints the other and a reader seeing them disagree would be right to worry.

**The cost is stated on the legend rather than discovered**: with crossings undrawn, a box
can be coloured with no arrow leaving it. The sentence is dropped the moment the crossings
are drawn, because then it is not true of what the reader is looking at. Pressed: turning
crossings on changes **0 of 40** roles, which is the property that makes the reading worth
having.

### A fourth hue does not exist, and that is measured

Blue for *receives* against violet for *both* came out **ΔE 1.4** apart under deuteranopia
in the light theme — the same colour. That is `tokens.css`'s own note about the difference
channel being at capacity, one channel over. So direction is carried on **blue against
amber**, the axis dichromacy leaves alone, and *both* is separated from both by lightness
and chroma instead — rule 69's own remedy, the one `--diff-moved` already uses.

Worst separation over the four states, taking the worst of normal vision, deuteranopia and
protanopia and never an average: **26.1 light, 19.3 dark**, against the shipped red/green
difference pair's 12.7 and 9.5. Every tint carries `--text` at **7.4:1 or better**, because
these are fills with a label written across them rather than dots on a ground — a different
question from what `--graph-*` is measured against, and a tint that swallows its own label
is a filter (design rule 1).

### The mechanism, which is why the control is free

The role rides into the SVG as a **`class`**, never a Graphviz `fillcolor`. Graphviz writes
`class=` straight into the `<g>`, so the browser recolours every box by setting one
attribute on the pan container: no refetch, no second `gv.layout()` on a picture that takes
93–179 ms to lay out, and the reader's pan and zoom survive. A `fillcolor` would bake one
answer into the drawing and cost a relayout per toggle. It also keeps the colours in
`tokens.css` with every other colour, so both themes and every palette reach them.

`applyDiagramColour()` runs from `renderDiagram()` rather than only from the handler — the
renderer rewrites the mount, so an attribute set in the handler alone would survive until
the next paint and then vanish (rule 78).

`mermaid()` is the one place a fill is written twice, and the reason it is allowed to be:
its whole job is source a reader copies somewhere our stylesheet and our themes do not
exist, so the `classDef`s carry light-theme values with them — and only for the roles a
compartment actually uses, so a plain compartment emits none.

**A port and a way in get no role**, deliberately. A port stands for a whole other
compartment and a way in is the world outside reaching in; each already has its own list and
its own lane, and giving either a part in this compartment's flow would answer about the
wrong subject — and put colour on something the legend's counts do not cover (rule 32).

### Gates

**1,895 passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean over 196 files, ruff clean. Twelve new tests; all
twelve fail against the previous commit. Verified in the browser rather than only in tests:
the classes survive the WASM Graphviz, the fills change on the four states in both themes,
the selection stroke still wins over a tinted box, the legend's four counts add to the box
count beside them, and switching the control neither refetches nor relays out.

## 2026-09-18 — the comparison lane, asked a question it could get wrong

`BACKLOG.md` item 2, closed — and it turned out to be a defect rather than the thin
evidence it was filed as. The item said `tools/ordering.py --api` probes `/api/changes`,
`/api/anomalychanges` and `/api/filechanges` of a Society pair differing in **three source
files**, which is a real result from a small population. Both of its suggested remedies
were taken, and they answered different questions.

### The wide pair, which settled the population and found nothing

Society's `origin/main` at `09b9ef11` against the branch head at `03ebbd93` — **384 Python
files against 628**, 523 changed under `src`, three months apart. Cloned read-only into a
scratchpad, analysed, sealed, and the branch head analysed beside it as
`output/mensores-wide`; the old tree is gone and the snapshot does not need it, which is
what a sealed snapshot is for (rules 25 and 62).

The comparison lane goes from three files to a real corpus:

| | |
|---|---|
| `only_in_base` · `only_in_compared` | **2,733** · 58 |
| `behaves` · `edited_only` | 395 · 369 |
| structures, either side | 364 · 2, with 29 declaring differently |
| `/api/filechanges` · `/api/anomalychanges` | 632 rows · 63 |

**Every route answers the same thing under a full row reversal.** So the backlog's
suspicion about the population was right and its conclusion would have been wrong: the lane
is clean at 2,733 rows exactly as it was at three.

### And then the measurement that mattered

A clean run over rows that cannot tie proves nothing (rule 37), so the next question was
whether the wide pair holds a **tie** — two rows equal on the key each list is ordered by,
`(module, qualname)` for a routine and `(module, name)` for a structure.

**It holds none. Neither does any map to hand**: zero tied keys over **9,972 routines**
across Mensores at both ends, DunneNote, DunneCorp and DunneFlow's own tree. And the
fixture in `tests/test_ordering.py`, built out of ties for exactly this reason, answered
`/api/changes` with **three lists of one row each**.

So the lane had never been asked a question it could get wrong, which is a different claim
from *the lane is right* and is the one the evidence supported.

**The tie is constructible, and both shapes are ordinary.** `_identity` mints a second
declaration of one name an id of its own — `make_id(qualname, "#2")`, deliberately, so that
colliding definitions keep separate identities — and leaves `(module, qualname)` identical.
A nested class is keyed on `module.Outer.Config` while its `name` column says only
`Config`, so two classes of one module each holding a `Config` are two ids with one
`(module, name)`: `class Meta` in Django, `class Config` in Pydantic.

Planted in the fixture — both `twin`s edited, a `spare` declared twice and only on one side,
both `Config`s gaining a field — `/api/changes` **differs under reversal**. Nine sites, and
they were four `ORDER BY`s, four Python `sorted()`s and one more found on the way out.

### Rule 105, and why half of this was invisible to the instrument

Reverting the four Python sorts and leaving the SQL fixed, the probe reports the route
**clean**. Their input is a set — `both = here_d.keys() & there_d.keys()` and the two
subtractions beside it — and `sorted` is stable, so rows equal on the key keep the order the
*set* iterated in. That order is `PYTHONHASHSEED`'s, not the rows'. Reversing every table in
the store moves it not at all.

Measured over 20 seeds against the unfixed structure sort: the two `Config` rows came back
one way **12 times and the other way 8**, with the reversal probe reporting the route clean
on every one of them. A route can be reversal-clean and still hand two readers different
pages, and a third reader a third page after a restart.

**The fix is not a better probe.** `_settle` is the one place the closer is spelled (rule
51) and it closes on the row's `id`, so there is no equal pair left for stability to decide
— whatever the input's order was. Source order first, because the position is what a reader
wants when two rows are otherwise the same row; the id makes it total. A position orders and
never keys, which is `changes.py`'s own rule.

The gate is stated as the property rather than through the instrument, because a seed-varying
test would pass 1.7% of the time with the defect present, and a check that cries wolf has
already failed the other way round (rule 43). Two tests: one asserts the fixture still holds
a tie in each of the three lanes (rule 37, aimed at the fixture), the other that every lane
is served in `_settle`'s order and that `_settle` separates rows `(module, name)` cannot.
Both fail against the previous commit, as does the reversal probe.

### The ninth site, and the survey that found it

`--survey` gains rule 105's population beside the `ORDER BY` one, and like it decides
nothing: **5 of 26** `sorted()` calls over a set take a `key=`, which is where a key that
does not separate every member can hide. Two were the defect. Two in `resolve/flows.py` are
total — `BoundaryKind` has ten members and ten distinct values, no aliases — and were
checked rather than assumed.

The fifth was `serve.py`'s program list: `key=lambda p: p.name.lower()`, under a comment
saying *"sorted by name so the order is total"*. It is not — `Mensores` and `mensores` are
two directories on a case-sensitive volume, which is the same filesystem trap chunk 13 paid
for in `require_universal`, and one hash seed's opinion apart in this list. Now
`(p.name.lower(), p.name)`, which makes the sentence beside it true.

**The survey is a floor rather than the population**, and that is in `BACKLOG.md` as a
residue: unorderedness propagates, so a dict built by iterating a set and then sorted over
its `.items()` is the same defect and is invisible to a reader of the source.
`web/changes.py` held two of each, and only the two written as set algebra are in the count.

### Gates

**1,897 passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean over 196 files, ruff clean. The wide pair and the
fixture both come back clean under a full row reversal, and nothing stored moved — `web/`
is in no fingerprint and no analysis code was touched.

## 2026-09-18 — two enumerations found on the road to a third language

Chunk B1 of the C++/Kotlin work, and both of these were found by planning the route rather
than by walking it. Neither is a new feature and both are repairs to the seam a third
reader has to come through.

### `canonical/` was reading a table that had already moved out of it

`canonical/__init__.py` declared `LANG_SUFFIX = {".py": "python", ".pyi": "python"}` under
a comment reading *"it is here now because here is the one place that consults it"* — and
`ingest/__init__.py`'s docstring has said since chunk 5 that **the table moved there and
became derived from the manifests**, quoting that exact sentence as the thing that stopped
being true. The move was recorded, the copy was left behind, and the copy was the one being
read: `canonical()` asked the hand-written table and nothing else asked anything. Two
modules each documenting that they owned one question, and the one that said it had taken
it over was not consulted.

**It had drifted in both directions**, which is what a second answer always does.

* It did not know `.ts`. So from the day TypeScript landed, a canonicaliser for it could
  have been written, registered in `CANONICAL`, and **never once reached** — the lookup
  that decides whether to call one could not name the language, and the comparison would
  have fallen through to *as written*, which is indistinguishable from this module's own
  honest fallback (rule 49). Nothing would have failed.
* It claimed `.pyi`, which **no reader claims at all**. Harmless only because no `.pyi`
  fact exists to compare.

`canonical()` asks `ingest.language_of` now. The two directions of the fallback are stated
where they were flattened: *no reader claims this suffix* and *one does and has no canonical
form* are different facts and neither is inferred from the other.

**And the test that guarded it could not fail.**
`test_only_the_python_canonicaliser_knows_how_to_canonicalise` asserts
`set(CANONICAL) <= set(LANG_SUFFIX.values())` — no canonicaliser filed under a language no
suffix produces, rule 35 in a table. Asked of a table holding only Python, the right-hand
side was `{"python"}` and the left could only ever be a subset of it: a true assertion about
a question that could not come out wrong. Asked of the registry it is a real question again.
Its unclaimed-suffix probe was the literal `.kt`, which chunk C would have quietly turned
into a claimed one; it picks the first genuinely unclaimed suffix now.

### The spec named the one reader it could find

`packaging/dunneflow.spec`'s `datas` read `_tree(PKG / "extractors" / "python", …)` — two
lines under a comment arguing that the rules directory is *"globbed, never named, and that
is rule 92 rather than economy"*, and four above one saying of the plugins that *"nothing
here enumerates"* them. **Both of those were rewritten when TypeScript found them.** This
one had not been, because Python is still the only reader that runs in this interpreter, so
the enumeration was still accidentally complete.

What it would cost lands later and quieter than either of the other two. A new in-process
reader's manifest ships (`_plugin_files` finds it), its rules ship (the glob finds them),
the registry loads it, every existing assertion in `test_frozen.py` passes — and the
reader's own bytes are not in the bundle, so `lang_fingerprint` has nothing to hash and the
application meets its first file of that language in somebody else's hands.

`_reader_files()` derives it from each manifest's `reader` field, on `_plugin_files()`'s own
precedent, and refuses by name when a declared reader is not there. **Measured: the derived
list is byte-identical to the named one today** — 2 files, same destinations — so this ships
exactly what it shipped before and will go on being right when it should not be.

`extractors/docs` stays spelled out beside it, deliberately: it is not a language reader, no
manifest declares it, nothing routes a suffix to it, and it is hashed by
`doc_extraction_inputs()` rather than by any language's key. Two questions, and only one has
a registry to ask.

**A second test was pinning the enumeration rather than the property it was named for.**
`test_the_bundle_layout_matches_what_resource_root_expects` asserted the literal string
`dunneflow/extractors/python` — it passed *because* the spec named Python's reader, and
would have gone on passing while a second one went unbundled. It asks the derived
destination now, which is the claim the test's own name makes.

### Gates

## 2026-09-18 — C++, read without a compiler

The third language, and the first one this tool is not itself written in. `dunneflow analyze`
reads Unreal Engine now: **1,957 files of `Runtime/Core` in 8.1 s**, 31,516 routines, 6,016
structures, 83,068 calls, 750 boundary touches, 0 errors.

### A semantic read was refused on evidence, not on principle

The plan asked clang first. Two measurements closed it. `../UnrealEngine-release` holds
**zero `*.generated.h`** — the tree has never been built, so UnrealHeaderTool has never run —
and `clang++ -fsyntax-only` on `Runtime/Core/Private/Misc/Guid.cpp` dies **fatally** on its
first `#include "Misc/Guid.h"`: one error, no AST, nothing to read. A reader needing a
compilation database would refuse the one tree it exists for.

So it is hand-written and in-process, stdlib only, in `extractors/docs/`'s idiom — and the
same measurement that put the TypeScript reader behind a pipe applies here in reverse:
`libclang` and `tree-sitter` ship no macOS universal2 wheel, and this tool's whole runtime
dependency list is `pyyaml`.

**Eight modules, five phases, one forward pass each.** `lexer` (splice and mask) ·
`preprocessor` · `tokens` · `scopes` (the brace tree) · `names` (the dotted contract) ·
`routines` · `control` · `calls` · `literals` · `extract`. Measured on 300 real Unreal files:
**median 2.2 ms a file, mean 6.9 ms**, against a stated budget of 15.

### The refusal the whole reader is built on

**A declaration with no body is not a routine.** Unreal is 51,282 headers against 23,322
`.cpp`; read as declarations they would roughly double the map with rows holding nothing —
`.d.ts`'s argument in a language where the header is the majority of the corpus rather than
the exception. It also *dissolves* the header-and-`.cpp` double rather than solving it: a
routine is a body, a body is in one place, and there is never a pair to reconcile.

### Rule 98, and it cost the command that gates CI

The first full run reported **3,875 BROKEN**. Every one was `NAME_COLLISION`, whose sentence
is *"Only the last one exists at run time; every call resolves to it and the others are
unreachable"* — which is true of Python, true of TypeScript, and **false of C++**, where
overloading is the language's ordinary mechanism. `operator<<` is defined 180 times in
`Runtime/Core` alone, `operator=` 61 times, `FName::FName` 36.

A judgement unchanged for a year, handed a population it had never been shown — the third
time this tree has paid for it, after `.d.ts` giving uigen 83 false BROKEN and
`ASYNC_NOT_AWAITED` giving gstack two.

The remedy is `unawaited_async`'s, exactly: **a severity is a claim about a language, so the
language declares it.** `redefinition:` is `shadows` for Python and TypeScript, `overloads`
for C++, and **empty means the detector does not fire** — refused by name rather than
defaulted, because a severity nobody chose is worst in the one command a CI job trusts.
`anomalies.py` reads it off `files.lang` per row and names no language. **0 broken, 0
suspect, 7 informational** afterwards.

The residue is stated: a genuine one-definition-rule violation is now **not** reported.
Telling one from an overload needs parameter types, and both arms of an `#ifdef` are read as
live, so even an identical signature twice in one file is usually the two arms.

### Six defects the corpus found, each a plausible map rather than an error

* **`GENERATED_BODY()` stole the first method's body.** It carries no `;`, so its `()` read
  as a parameter list — every UObject's first method was called `GENERATED_BODY` and owned
  `Tick`'s body. And `public:` after it read as a **member-initialiser list**, because `:` is
  how one begins. An access label is a statement boundary now.
* **`UCLASS(Blueprintable) class FOO_API AThing : public AActor`** is a name, a parameter
  list and a base clause — the exact shape of a constructor. A record keyword can never sit
  between a parameter list and a body, so one there means the candidate was a macro.
* **Chained calls took their arguments from the wrong parentheses.**
  `IFileManager::Get().FileExists(*InPath)` recorded a target of `').FileExists(*InPath'` —
  a string that is in the file, starts mid-expression, and is an argument to nothing.
* **String-literal arguments were invisible.** Literals are blanked so a `{` inside one is
  not a brace — which also meant `getenv("HOME")` had an empty target, in a reader whose
  whole job at a boundary is to say *what* it touches. They are single tokens now, at the
  same offsets.
* **`check`, `ensure` and `verify` were STDIO and are not.** They are assertions: they write
  on failure and otherwise do nothing, so the rule claimed text leaves the program at a line
  where in every healthy run none does. Three of `Paths.cpp`'s five boundaries were `check`.
  Nothing is lost — an assertion is a guard, and `resolve/shape.py` already models guards.
* **Line numbers compounded across continuations.** A continued line was folded into the one
  above and got no entry, on the argument that it is the logical line a compiler sees. It is
  also one lost line number per continuation, growing down the file — every routine below the
  second continuation reported two lines high, in a map that still opens and still looks
  right.

### The file is part of a routine's identity, and that corrected a design assumption

The design said: fold the file in for internal linkage, leave it out otherwise so a header's
declaration and a `.cpp`'s definition land on one routine. The second half was already wrong
— **a declaration is not a routine**, so there is no pair to merge. Left out it is not merely
unnecessary but wrong: `Internal/IO/IoDispatcherFilesystemStats.h` gives its methods empty
inline bodies under one arm of an `#if` and the `.cpp` defines them for real, and with both
arms read as live **221 qualnames in 400 files had a body in two places**. The store refused
the second with `UNIQUE constraint failed: routines.id`, then refused `structures.id` on the
next run for the same reason one table over. `Scope.is_internal` and a `static` check were
written for the abandoned half and went with it (rule 35).

### The probe tree could no longer do its job, and a test said so

`tools/fingerprints.py` read `src/dunneflow` — right for exactly as long as the languages
this build reads were the languages it is *written in*. The package will never hold a `.cpp`,
so `test_the_default_probe_tree_holds_every_language_this_build_reads` failed by name, which
is what it was written to do (rule 92). `tests/fixtures/polyglot/` is the probe now: one real
file per registered language, each with a way in, a boundary, a loop and a branch, because a
stamp compared over an empty map is the nothing the gate exists to refuse (rule 37).

**And building it found a defect older than the language that found it.** The three files
were `probe.py`, `probe.ts` and `probe.cpp`, and that tree cannot be analysed at all: Python
and TypeScript both derive a module name from the path with the suffix removed, so both are
module `probe`, both declare `main`, and `probe.main` is one id in two languages. C++ is
immune by accident of the fix above. It is **`BACKLOG.md` item 6** with the reproduction, not
fixed in passing — the fix changes how an id is derived and discards every stored map.

### Gates

**1,928 passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean over 211 files, ruff clean. The golden is 5 of 7
against the report with its two documented holdbacks. Frozen build in 9.3 s; the bundle
carries `extractors/cpp` and `plugins/cpp` because `_reader_files()` finds them rather than
naming them, and the gate reads all three languages: **4 of 4 stamps agree and each build
opened the other's map**, `cpp 1, python 1, typescript 1`.

**Every stamp moved and that is deliberate.** `detectors/__init__.py` gained `redefinition`
and is in the core key; `python.yaml` and `typescript.yaml` declare it and are in theirs.
Core `14:5576a86c2b32bca0`, python `1.0.0:48a09233720a2c80`, typescript
`1.1.0:dfbeacab493e025a`, cpp `1.0.0:4ecbedb2fa590671`. Every stored map is invalidated and
costs one re-analysis, which is rule 12's safe direction: the alternative is a map whose
rows were judged by a rule this build no longer holds.

## 2026-09-18 — the first tree that is not small, and the defect only it could find

Chunk B3, the measurement chunk, and the plan said it was the one that could come back
negative. It came back with one real defect and one honest limit.

### `Engine/Source/Runtime`: 18,681 files, and the store is the cost

**14 m 54 s wall against 425 s of user CPU** — 49% of one core, the rest spent writing to the
external volume the corpus lives on. `graph.db` reached **766 MB**, 12× `Core`'s for 9.5× the
files. Extraction is not the bottleneck and was never going to be: the reader is 2.2 ms a
file at the median.

Scaled to the whole engine less `ThirdParty` — about 89,000 files — that is of the order of
3 GB of graph and over an hour. **Not measured, and not claimed as a measurement**: what is
claimed is where the time goes, which is a different and smaller statement (rule 24).

### `OverflowError`, fourteen minutes in, in the last pass before the map is written

```
  resolve/naming.py:613 in _beats_coincidence
  math.comb(total, i) * base_rate**i * (1.0 - base_rate) ** (total - i)
  OverflowError: int too large to convert to float
```

Every fact had been extracted, resolved and written. The affix-convention test has computed
an **exact** binomial tail since it was written, and `math.comb(total, i)` past a few
thousand is an integer with more digits than a float has range. It had never fired because no
corpus was big enough — Society's largest population is in the low thousands, and this one is
in the hundreds of thousands.

Three paths now, and the first two exist so that nothing already measured moves. Below the
mean the answer needs no arithmetic — the tail is at least a half and cannot beat a threshold
orders of magnitude smaller, which is also what bounds the loop. The exact tail is summed in
**log space** through `lgamma` while the term count is under 4,000, so every figure already
recorded reproduces unchanged and Society stays on that path. Beyond that, a normal
approximation with a continuity correction, with its conditions written down beside it rather
than left to be discovered.

**It is nothing to do with C++** except that C++ is the first reader to hand this tool a tree
two orders of magnitude larger than the ones it grew up on. That is what the chunk was for.

### And one defect of my own, found the same way

`_redefinition_shadows` — written an hour earlier, in the fix for rule 98 above — asked
`SELECT lang FROM files WHERE path = ?` **once per collision group**, against `MIN(file)`.
Wrong twice: a query per group is tens of thousands of them on a tree this size, and
`MIN(file)` names *one* of the colliding definitions arbitrarily, so in a mixed map one
file's language decided the verdict for a group holding several. The population is filtered
in SQL now, per language, which makes the grouping right as well as the speed — a collision
is between definitions **in one language**, because that is the only scope in which *the
later one shadows the earlier* means anything. An empty list of shadowing languages compiles
to a `WHERE 0` rather than to no filter, because *no rows* and *no filter* are opposite
answers and the second is the silent default rule 49 forbids.

## 2026-09-18 — Kotlin, and a seam that has stopped costing anything

The fourth language, the second hand-written reader, and the first one where the seam was
not the work. `dunneflow analyze` reads Anki-Android: **894 files in 16.1 s**, 6,199
routines, 2,405 structures, 21,474 calls, 2,298 boundary touches, 12 ways in, **0 Kotlin
anomalies of any severity**.

### The corpus was cloned, because there was none

Measured before the plan was written: **one `.kt` file in the whole Developer directory**, a
fixture in `graphify-5`, and no `kotlinc`. Building a reader against that is what rule 24
forbids, so Tom's call was to clone one. `ankidroid/Anki-Android` at `c964d52b` —
**1,416 Kotlin files, no Java at all**, a real application with real ways in.

It turned out to be a **mixed** corpus, which was luck rather than design and is worth
having: the map reads `kotlin 887 · python 2 · typescript 5`, and the two Python files are
genuinely unparseable — `print 'x'` is Python 2 — so the only two BROKEN in the map are true.

### Why it is read without a compiler, and it is not C++'s reason

C++ refused a semantic read on evidence: the demo corpus cannot tell a compiler how it is
built without being built first. Kotlin's compiler **could** be asked, and asking it would
mean a JVM on every machine that reads a `.kt` file and a `kotlin-compiler-embeddable` jar
inside a bundle whose entire runtime dependency list is `pyyaml`. The trade is stated rather
than assumed: what it would buy is resolved calls, and what it would cost is the frozen
application.

### Three things that are Kotlin's and not C++'s

* **Expression bodies.** `fun f() = expr` has no braces, is a routine, and is the *first
  function in the first file of the corpus*. A brace-tree reader finds none of them. Its
  extent is the one heuristic in this reader and is named as one — what it can get wrong is
  where a body ends, never whether the routine exists, its name or its parameters.
* **Most braces open nothing.** `apply { }`, `let { }`, `forEach { }` and trailing-lambda
  call syntax mean a declaration has to be found by its **keyword**, not by its brace. Keyed
  the other way a class with three methods has forty scopes.
* **Block comments nest**, which is the exact opposite of C++'s rule for the same three
  characters — and the concrete reason the two lexers are two modules rather than one.
  A shared module would live in **neither** language's stamp: `lang_extraction_inputs` globs
  `extractors/<lang>/*`, so editing it would change what both readers read and invalidate
  nothing (rule 12). A reader is self-contained or it is not fingerprinted.

### Rule 98 cost nothing this time, and that is the result

Kotlin overloads, like C++ and unlike Python — and `@JvmOverloads` generates more of them. A
year ago that would have been several thousand false `NAME_COLLISION` out of the command
that gates CI. It was one line in `kotlin.yaml`: `redefinition: overloads`. **The first
language to meet a wrong judgement pays for the key; the second one fills it in.**
`unawaited_async: runs` went in beside it for the same reason — `async { }` in a coroutine
scope starts immediately, so a dropped `Deferred` is JavaScript's SUSPECT and not Python's
BROKEN.

### Four defects, all found by the corpus

* **Return types were missing from every routine.** The header was cut at the parameter
  list's `)`, and Kotlin writes the return type *after* it — so there was nothing left to
  read. Six of six functions in the first real file came back with none.
* **`abstract fun go()` stole the next function's body.** The guard that spots *the next
  declaration begins here* compared against where the scan started rather than against the
  token before it, so it never fired on the first token after the parameter list — which is
  exactly where the next declaration sits when this one has no body. The abstract
  declaration became a routine and the real one disappeared, two wrong facts in two lines.
  The set it checks had to grow the modifiers too: `private` sits between them.
* **A `companion object` was `<anonymous>`.** Kotlin names it `Companion`, which is how it is
  addressed from Java and how it appears in a stack trace; inventing a word for something the
  language has already named is not a reader's job.
* **A chained call took its arguments from the first parentheses.** `Room.databaseBuilder(c)
  .build()` would have handed `build` the argument `c`. The same defect the C++ reader had,
  caught here by having seen it there.

### Gates

**1,993 passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean over 223 files, ruff clean. Frozen build carries
`extractors/kotlin` and `plugins/kotlin` because `_reader_files()` finds them; the gate reads
all four languages and **5 of 5 stamps agree with each build opening the other's map**
(`cpp 1, kotlin 1, python 1, typescript 1`). The golden is 5 of 7 against the report with its
two documented holdbacks — Python has not moved.

The core stamp moved again, to `14:e9094721e5b17f6b`, because `ingest/__init__.py` gained an
entry. Deliberate, and rule 12's safe direction.

### What the seam cost, which is the finding

A manifest, a rules file, one entry in `_IN_PROCESS`, one file in the probe tree, one name in
the plugin-set assertion. **Nothing in `packaging/`** — because the spec was taught to find
in-process readers earlier the same day — nothing in `walk.py`, nothing above the graph, and
no new key in the detector grammar. `LANGUAGES.md` says so with the list now complete rather
than hopeful.

**Python is unmoved, and that was the thing to check.** Society's four executables reach

The same analysis, same tree, same build: **8 m 54 s at 88% CPU** and **45 m 42 s at 22%**.

## 2026-09-19 — a definition carries its file, and every map on disk was discarded for it

`BACKLOG.md` item 6, taken deliberately. A tree holding `probe.py` and `probe.ts` side by
side could not be analysed at all:

```
sqlite3.IntegrityError: UNIQUE constraint failed: routines.id
```

Both readers derive a module name from the path with the suffix dropped, so both files were
module `probe`, both declared `main`, and `make_id("probe.main")` was one id in two
languages. **Rule 106**: an identity assembled from names alone is only unique inside one
language's naming. `schema.definition_id` is `(file, qualname[, ordinal])` and
`schema.entrypoint_id` carries the file too; all four readers pass through them, and
`plugins/typescript/src/ids.ts` mirrors both on the far side of the pipe.

### Why the file and not the language

The language is the answer the symptom suggests and it closes only the case that was
reported. `probe.ts` and `probe.tsx` are one module in **one** reader and would collide
exactly as before, so a `lang` part would have bought a fix that survives until the next
corpus. A file is the smaller claim and the true one — a definition is written down
somewhere, once — and it was **already what C++ and Kotlin did**, for a different reason
each. Three of the four readers were right by accident before this was a rule.

A file is not a position (`make_id`): where a definition lives survives everything moving
inside it. What goes in the id is the path *inside the analysed tree*, never this machine's,
or two checkouts of one program would pair with nothing (rule 60) — `test_identity.py` now
asserts both halves of that, because the test that says identity survives a checkout move
reads as denying rule 106 unless the other one is beside it.

### The proof is the fixture's own file names

`tests/fixtures/polyglot/` exists because its files could not share a stem; the README
recorded the reproduction and forced them apart. They are `probe.py`, `probe.ts`,
`probe.cpp` and `probe.kt` again — four files, one module name, three `probe.main`s and a
C++ `main`, three `Setting`s, all distinct. `tools/fingerprints.py` reads that tree, so the
frozen build and the checkout now both prove themselves on the smallest program that could
not be read.

### What a digest cannot tell you, and what was built because of it

Every digest in `tools/golden.py` is taken **over** the thing that moved, so all five that
reproduced v1 moved by construction and said nothing whatever about whether extraction still
reads the same program. `--rekeyed` is the comparison that can: six projections, each table
onto its facts and none of its ids. Against `output/mensores-v1/` — v1's own graph, read by
v1 — **all six are byte-identical**, while all five identity digests moved. Every row count
and all five distributions diff clean against `GOLDEN-v1.txt` as well, the only differences
being two tables and one meta key that did not exist in v1.

`output/GOLDEN-v2.txt` is the live baseline and is **7 of 7**, because this script wrote both
sides of that comparison — so the two holdbacks whose v1 statement was lost do not arise.
`GOLDEN-v1.txt` is kept unedited as the dated record; a report says in its own header whether
its digests are this script's, and `--against` asks that rather than being told by a flag.

## 2026-09-19 — the residue filed that morning, hit by lunchtime

`dunneflow analyze` on `UnrealEngine-release`, from the application, died on:

```
sqlite3.IntegrityError: UNIQUE constraint failed: structures.id
```

This is the residue the rule 106 entry above filed rather than fixed — *two definitions of
one name in one Python file still collide, if they are structures* — and the argument for
leaving it out was that rule 106 is about two **files** and folding a second defect into a
change that was already discarding every map would be two things at once. That argument was
sound and the estimate of how long it would keep was wrong: it cost Tom the next analysis he
ran.

### It is not a broken program, and that is the finding

The blind spot on `REDEFINITION` has named this shape since it was written — *conditional
definitions (`if TYPE_CHECKING:`, platform branches, try/except ImportError) legitimately
define a name more than once and only one is ever live* — and CPython's own standard library
is full of it. Measured over the tree rather than guessed at: **213 of Unreal's 11,565 Python
files** declare one structure name twice.

* `multiprocessing/context.py` — `SpawnProcess` and `SpawnContext`, once under
  `if sys.platform != 'win32'` and once under `else`.
* `ctypes/__init__.py` — `CFunctionType`, inside `CFUNCTYPE` and again inside `WINFUNCTYPE`.
* `pip/_vendor/typing_extensions.py` and setuptools' copy — `Protocol`, on a version branch.

Most of the 213 are test files and `DiscoveryRules.is_test` keeps those out of program
source; the four above are not, and Unreal vendors Python four times over — Win64, WinArm64,
Mac and Linux — so each is in the map four times.

### The fix is the one the routines already had

`_identity` has given a routine an ordinal among real duplicates since the reader was
written. `_structure_identity` is the same three lines with **its own count**, which is the
part worth stating: a routine and a structure of one name are rows in two tables and their
ids never meet, so a shared counter would give the *first* structure of a name a `#2` on
account of a routine — an ordinal that counts something the reader cannot see.

**Only Python was wrong.** C++ keeps `seen` and `seen_records`, Kotlin keeps `seen` and
`seen_types`, and TypeScript shares one map but keys structures under a `struct\0` prefix so
the two never meet. Three readers had it right and the oldest one did not, which is the same
shape as rule 106 itself.

**And it was unreachable until this morning.** While an id was the name alone, a structure
declared twice in one file collided with itself in any tree at all — and no corpus this tool
had read carried one, because none of them vendors a standard library. Putting the file into
the identity did not cause it; analysing a tree eleven thousand Python files wide did.

### Gates

**1,996 passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean over 224 files, ruff clean. The golden is **7 of 7**
against `GOLDEN-v2.txt` and 6 of 6 rekeyed against v1 — Society declares no structure name
twice, so nothing there moves. The whole-tree scan that found the 213 reports **0 files with
a colliding id** over the same 11,565.

### Residue

`ctypes/__init__.py` declares `CFunctionType` inside two different *functions*, and both come
out as `ctypes.CFunctionType` — rule 10 is about a nested **function** carrying its enclosing
scope in its qualname, and a class nested in a function does not. The ordinal makes them two
identities, so nothing collides and nothing is lost; what is missing is that their qualnames
do not say which factory each belongs to. Noticed here, not acted on, and not filed as a task
until there is a reader who wants the answer.

The full-tree analysis started to prove the fix above did that and then ran into something
else. **Both halves are worth having.**

**The fix is proven on the real tree.** Python's phase closed normally: 4,197 files, 82,102
routines, 3,767 structures, 347,005 calls. All four vendored Pythons are in the map, and the

**And then C++ did not close.** `UnrealEngine-release` entire is **165,828** candidate files

## 2026-09-19 — a guard on what may be ingested, and the bound that makes it finishable

Tom, after the Unreal run was stopped: *"Seems like we need an ingest guard to prevent users
from attempting to ingest too much at once, and breaking it down for them."* Two things, and
the second is the one that had to come first.

### Rule 107 — a burst must end, and a transaction is not a bound

`BACKLOG.md` item 7, now closed. `analyze_tree` held **one transaction per language** and the
store is in WAL mode; SQLite cannot checkpoint a log inside an open write transaction, so the
log grew for as long as the language did and then every index insert began reading pages back
out of it. `Store.settle_if_large` ends a burst when the log outgrows half the page cache,
and `WAL_CAP_BYTES` sits beside the `cache_size` it is derived from so the two cannot drift.

**Measured on one part rather than argued** — `Engine/Source/Runtime`, 18,191 files:

| | bounded | unbounded |
|---|---|---|
| wall | **700 s** | stopped at **29 m**, still going |
| log | held at **136 MB**, 62 drains | **533 MB** and growing |
| committed at 10 minutes | **17,664 of 18,191** | **0** |

**The third row is worth more than the first**, and it is the half that is not about speed.
One transaction means a run killed at 28 minutes has nothing to show for it, and
`known_hashes` cannot resume what was never written. The bound made the run *interruptible*,
which is rule 80's property and which no amount of speed substitutes for.

It costs nothing where it is not needed — 3,169 files in 12.9 s bounded against 13.0 s — so
`analyze_tree`'s original sentence stays true and is now true of a bounded thing.

### The guard, and what it cannot cover

`walk.parts_under` cuts a tree into parts no larger than `TOO_BIG`, descending **only into
what is oversized**. Choosing a depth instead would give 109 parts of wildly uneven size; the
adaptive cut gives 86 whose largest is `Engine/Source/Runtime` at exactly 18,191 — the corpus
the recorded run used. That is the tree's own structure answering, not a coincidence.

`TOO_BIG` is **20,000 files**, and the refusal says where that came from: it is the edge of
what this tool is known to read end to end, not a setting. `--parts` prints the whole list,
`--any-size` goes through, and both are named in the refusal (rule 89).

**`serve` was not touched and that is the design.** It runs `analyze` as a child and
`web/analysis.py:_reason` promotes the child's last stderr line — so the refusal reaches the
analysis pane in its own words, where Tom got a traceback.

**And the guard's own defect, caught by its own test.** The first cut made a split directory's
own files a part named for that directory — but `analyze` descends, so the command for
`Engine/Plugins` would have read all 51,069 files under it: the very analysis the guard
exists to refuse, inside the guard's advice. `Breakdown.uncovered` states those files instead.
It is **0 on Unreal** across all 86 parts, which is why the case is stated rather than solved;
solving it needs an `analyze` that can read one directory without descending.

### Gates

**2,004 passed · 1 skipped**, mypy clean over 225 files, ruff clean. Golden **7 of 7** against
`GOLDEN-v2.txt` and 6 of 6 rekeyed against v1 — a commit bound must not move a fact, and does
not.

### Residue

The bound counts **files** because that is the shape of the evidence, and what actually hurts
is rows written. A tree of 19,000 enormous files passes it. In `BACKLOG.md`, with what a
better key would cost.
